#5623. Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5622. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5621. Trump’s Latest Housing Move Promises Major Relief, but Which Buyers Will Actually Save Thousands?

Last month, President Trump signed an executive order aimed at housing affordability.

The multipart order runs the gamut, touching on everything from manufactured housing to permitting to direct the Departments of Agriculture and Veterans Affairs to reduce interest rates on their direct single-family loan programs to adjusting closing cost fees paid by certain homeowners.

The latter has lenders and buyers buzzing, as a cut to closing costs could mean the difference of thousands of dollars when it comes to down payments.

But while the math works out for some, it’s important to recognize some of the serious caveats as well.

Trump’s order includes several different regulations: one targeting mortgage insurance and another lender's title insurance for low-risk refinancing loans.

The latest down payment report from Realtor.com® shows that the national median down payment in the second quarter of 2026 climbed to $27,100, or 13.7% of the typical purchase price, up from 12.9% at the start of the year.  On an annual basis, however, the typical down payment fell from 14.3% year over year, recording the lowest second-quarter level since 2021

Homebuyers who pay less than a 20% down payment are required to buy mortgage insurance for their home loans.

There are two types of mortgage insurance: private and government. If you have a government-backed loan, such as an FHA loan, which allows buyers to put down as little as 3.5%, you pay mortgage insurance to the government. If your loan is not government-backed, you pay private mortgage insurance to your lender.

Trump’s order establishes a pilot program under which the Federal Housing Finance Agency would identify and automatically cancel mortgage insurance for loans that meet cancellation criteria, like necessary equity requirements.

However, the program applies only to new home loans held by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac—aka the government-sponsored loans.

The reason for this insurance is to protect the lender if you fall behind on payments, typically costing between 0.46% and 1.5% of the loan each year based on your credit score. That easily tacks on hundreds of dollars to your monthly bill.

For example, a 1% rate on a $450,000 loan adds $375 straight to your monthly payment. That’s a savings of $4,500 a year, if eliminated.

The executive order also aims to reduce mortgage refinancing costs by making permanent the FHFA’s pilot program that waives the lender’s title insurance policy and allows “cost-friendly alternatives,” according to the White House.

“This is a massive win for American homeowners. We’re talking about reforms that could cut refinancing costs by nearly $2,400 on an illustrative $500,000 loan, as well as a new pilot that would proactively cancel mortgage insurance once appropriate equity thresholds have been met. That’s real money,” says Brendan McKay, Broker Action Coalition’s chief advocacy officer.

The biggest drawback of this initiative is that the pilot program applies only to new mortgages originated after the program launches.

This means current homeowners paying mortgage insurance won’t benefit from this change under the current draft.

On the flip side, the title insurance waiver pilot applies only to low-risk refinances, not new purchases. First-time homebuyers cannot use this waiver to lower their closing costs or free up down payment cash.

Additionally, the program is currently limited to certain refinance loans with loan-to-value ratios of less than 80% in specific geographic areas.

The order also expands a pilot program from 2024 that allows homeowners to skip lender’s title insurance on certain low-risk refinances, potentially saving $500 to $1,500 in closing costs. The move echoes previous efforts to rein in closing fees—which hit a median of $6,000 in 2022—though the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has gone silent after the Trump administration scaled back its operations.

This element of the executive order has industry leaders urging caution.

Seller impersonation fraud attempts doubled from 2024 to 2025, hitting 59% of surveyed title firms, according to the American Land Title Association. Fraud and forgery now account for over 40% of title insurance losses on refinances. When you remove title insurance, you shift this growing fraud risk directly onto the homeowner and the lender.

ALTA’s CEO Chris Morton says that efforts to improve housing affordability are "critical," but warned that any effort to bring title insurance costs down "must also preserve the essential consumer safeguards” that protect Americans' most valuable assets.

"Fraud is unaffordable, and the threats facing homeowners are growing," says Morton. "Now more than ever, we need to ensure that efforts to lower housing costs do not shift significant financial risks onto American families or the broader housing finance system."

Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. She previously served as the managing editor at HollywoodLife.com, the executive editor at PerezHilton.com, and as a managing editor at Mediavine. Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.

#5620. What Each Party Promises on Housing Affordability as Congress Hangs in the Balance

As they jockey for control of Congress in a tight midterm race, Democrats and Republicans have each made promises that their party will focus on housing affordability.

Both parties have spent the year pushing messages about affordability, especially in housing. Homeowners are being hammered with higher insurance and property tax rates. Higher interest rates have frozen the housing market. And young people are overwhelmingly concerned about whether they'll ever own a home at all. With many close races, control of Congress could hinge on these concerns.

Then there's the issue of how to implement laws Congress has already passed. The bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act promises reforms in dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape and encouraging the construction of more homes. Congress will oversee the rollout of those new programs while also working with the final two years of the Trump administration—and the market will be looking to Washington for clarity.

Jeff Holzmann, COO of Dallas-based real estate firm RREAF, tells Realtor.com® the industry needs clear rules to make long-term investment decisions. Broad rules such as the new ban on institutional investors in the housing market require clarity or else they might not achieve the affordability Congress intended with the bill.

"From my operator's perspective, the bigger question is whether these regulations will continue to encourage private capital to invest in building new homes and improving existing ones, as that's what drives our business," Holzmann says. "If that pans out, I believe it can make a real difference in affordability over time."

Over the course of the year, many Republicans have said they want to see reforms to the housing finance system. These rules, they've said, have discouraged banks and financial institutions from infusing money into the housing market.

House Financial Services Committee Chair Rep. French Hill (R-AR) told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in September that he wanted to see reforms to the BASEL III framework, aimed to encourage more banks to finance mortgages and construction loans.

"That should take steps to encourage the large banks to participate in the secondary market for housing," Hill said. "I think Dodd-Frank went too far on this point. Essentially, by the capital standards for a construction loan, pushed a lot of the biggest banks out of that business. It also limited mortgage servicing rights by the large financial institutions. Both of those things, at the margin, raise the cost of liquidity for housing."

Rep. Mike Flood (R-NE), who chairs the Housing and Insurance Subcommittee, said in July he wants to see single-family homebuilding exempted from the prevailing wage requirements in the Davis-Bacon and Related Acts.

Flood and Hill have both said they want to exempt homebuilding materials from the Build America Buy America Act. That adds sourcing requirements to many building materials that drive up their costs.

At the same time, Republicans have also backed the Trump administration's shift of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development away from "housing first" homelessness programs. HUD has repeatedly criticized what Secretary Scott Turner calls a "homeless industrial complex." In alternate, HUD has pursued programs that emphasize treatment and recovery. But it's clashed with states and service providers and pursued "diversity equity and inclusion" programs as well.

Democrats have called for additional spending to help bolster a variety of housing programs, especially those regarding tenant and homeowner protections.

Earlier this year, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Democrats would pursue laws cracking down on junk fees and on predatory companies abusing tenants and using price-fixing algorithms.

A number of Democrat-led bills this year have also proposed expanding funding for Section 8 vouchers, rent relief, programs to help curtail evictions, and expansion of the Low-Income Tax Credit, which produces about 40,000 to 50,000 units a year of affordable housing.

Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), ranking member of the Banking subcommittee, told the Chamber of Commerce in September that both parties must be focused on effective compromise.

"We're woefully lacking in legislation that can move through both the House and the Senate and get to the president's desk," he said.

Democrats are also likely to resume efforts for stricter data center regulation. They sank a Republican-led bill that encouraged utilities to shield ratepayers from data center costs in favor of a proposal with more stringent enforcement powers for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

The party will also have to contend with a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates elected at the local and state level. Those candidates have shown different levels of support for policies like rent control and "housing for all."

The 43-member bipartisan Build America Caucus put out a 95-page primer for issues it would pursue regardless of who is in control of either chamber next year.

Its housing agenda includes fast-tracking residential construction in areas where cities have "outdated" zoning constraints in place. It also wants to see programs that encourage housing near transit and under-used federal land, as well as modernization of building code standards.

“The problem isn't a lack of good ideas; it's the bureaucratic red tape slowing projects down for years," Rep. Sharice Davids (D-KS) said in a statement with the primer.

Democrats and Republicans in Congress have found common ground in some parts of the housing debate. For instance, the More Homes on the Market Act, which would double the capital gains tax exclusion, has attracted over 170 co-sponsors in the House and Senate.

Both parties have pitched changes to the capital gains tax scheme using different methods, but none advanced this year.

Democrats and Republicans have also routinely put forth a few bills aimed at promoting housing innovations and designs. For instance, last week, Reps. Maggie Goodlander (D-NH) and Jefferson Shreve (R-IN) put forth a bill that would encourage pre-reviewed, permit-ready home designs. They said in a joint statement they hope it would mean faster approvals.

"I’m working with Republicans and Democrats to clear away every rule that makes it slower and more expensive to build a home in New Hampshire," Goodlander said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5619. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5618. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5615. Behind Charleston’s Most Famous Gates: The Sword Gate House Asks a Record $35 Million

Some of the most iconic ironwork in Charleston, SC, guards the entrance to a home that’s undergone a complete renovation in the six years since it last changed hands.

The Sword Gate House, at 32 Legare Street is on the market for $35 million, a record-setting ask for Charleston. The estate last sold in 2020 for $10 million.

The house dates to the early 1800s and takes its name from the sword-and-spear gates forged by local ironworker Christopher Werner. British consul George Hopley installed them around 1850, and they’ve drawn crowds of sightseers ever since.

Over two centuries, the property has served as a private residence, a private school, an inn and a vacation retreat. Among its past owners was Jessie Lincoln Randolph, Abraham Lincoln’s granddaughter, who bought it in the 1930s.

The schoolhouse chapter still shapes the property with its towering perimeter walls dating to the 19th century, when the home housed a girls’ academy.

The compound totals 17,142 square feet on roughly 0.87 acre, one of the largest residential lots downtown. The main house holds eight bedrooms, each with its own bathroom, plus two powder rooms.

“The current owners spared no expense and touched every surface of the property, both inside and out,” says Turner. The interiors, which are a true feast for the eyes, were created by designer Cortney Bishop.

When the owners bought the home, its only kitchen was a catering setup on the ground floor. They combined two main-level rooms into a new kitchen and informal dining space with a wood-burning fireplace and a piazza for dining outdoors. The original kitchen stayed in place for caterers and staff, “so the main living level can be party-perfect,” says Turner.

The ballroom remains the estate’s centerpiece, with gilded crown molding and a carved mantel. A custom magnolia chandelier hangs in the curved grand staircase, a nod to the centuries-old magnolia that shades the home’s triple piazzas.

The primary suite stretches across the south side of the second floor, with a soaking tub set before a fireplace, two water closets and a dressing room that Turner says “rivals a stylish boutique.”

Outside, the owners added a heated and cooled pool, a fireside dining area and a linear fountain anchored by a glass conservatory. “This fountain has even been topped with a dining table for an unforgettable celebration under the stars,” Turner says.

As if the main house renovation wasn't enough, a stunning two-story carriage house adds three guest suites, including one with a full kitchen. Two gated driveways and a two-car garage round out the property.

The estate is also a short walk from King Street’s shops and galleries.

“For today’s luxury buyer, time is the ultimate luxury,” she says. “All the hard work of design, restoration, renovation, and investment have already been completed.”

#5612. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5611. This 138-Year-Old Los Angeles ‘Unicorn’ House Is Completely Drenched in Purple—and Listed for $2 Million

A house drenched in purple and set on a hill in Los Angeles, CA offers a window into the past.

“I kind of call it a unicorn. Los Angeles doesn't have a lot of 138-year-old houses anymore,” says listing agent Laurie Turner with Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage – Pasadena. “Los Angeles was a big agricultural zone, and people were coming out west for opportunity and land and things that they didn't have on the East Coast and in the Midwest.”

The Queen Anne Victorian on about half an acre was built in 1888 and is listed for $2 million.

“I just love it. It’s such a happy place to be and it's warm and inviting… and although a little dilapidated right now, you can see what it was when Leonora was living there.”

Leonora Pierotti Thomas bought the place in 1979, and her estate is selling it.

“She was an eccentric artist, never married, [who] had the wherewithal to have a home like this, travel the world, entertain,” Turner says. “I've heard stories. I unfortunately never had the opportunity to meet her, but she just sounds like a kick.”

“It was yellow when Leonora bought it and from what I hear from her cousin, everything about [Leonora] was purple,” Turner explains. “She drove a purple Hummer. The garden hoses were purple. I have a picture that was sent out in memory [of her], and she is with her poodle and she had dyed her poodle’s fur purple.”

The color is prevalent both inside and outside the house and even extends to the newish roof with its purple accents.

The 2,700-square-foot house has four bedrooms and three bathrooms and both the kitchen and primary suite are part of an addition in the past decade. It’s no surprise the kitchen island, some lighting, and several walls are purple.

Everything needs a bit of work. Some of the plaster is coming off the walls, but everything in the house, including the pool, is in working condition.

“I'm calling it a historic restoration project versus a fixer because fixer sounds like a fix and flip,” Turner explains, adding a contractor she consulted said it would cost at least a million dollars to restore it.

“I'm really looking [for a buyer] who has the vision and the wherewithal to update the home, bring it back to its glory, live in it, and do right by the neighbors and the neighborhood.”

Known as Esperanza House, the home stood on the hill before the streetcar even reached the area.

“[My favorite thing about the house] is the approach as you come up Mount Royal and you see the facade and then the driveway comes up. You wrap around the house, and you see the turret there on the front and the colors in the roof and the filigree across the top of the roof line,” Turner says. “It's a nod to the past and it's my job to find the next steward to keep the chapter going.”

Tiffani Sherman is an experienced freelance writer based in the Tampa, Florida area who covers real estate, personal finance, travel, and more for a variety of print and online publications. She works to support her travel habit and has been to all seven continents and about 100 countries. Tiffani is a proud Duke Blue Devil.

#5609. Wabi reels in $55M for its consumer-focused AI assistant

Wabi Inc., the developer of an artificial intelligence assistant for consumers, today announced that it has raised $55 million in funding.

IVP led the seed round with contributions from Amazon Alexa Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. They were joined by a group of angel investors that included Salesforce Inc. CEO Marc Benioff and Shopify Inc. CEO Tobi Lütke. Wabi is now valued at $1.25 billion.

San Francisco-based Wabi was launched last year by serial AI entrepreneur Eugenia Kuyda. She previously founded Replika Inc., another consumer AI startup that had more than 35 million users as of last November. Wabi disclosed today that it’s seeing “strong early demand” but didn’t share specific user base numbers.

The company’s service is accessible via Mac, iOS and Android clients. Its interface is built around a group chat tool with an embedded AI assistant. If a group of friends uses a chat session to organize a meet-up, the AI assistant can find nearby restaurants that could serve as a suitable venue. It customizes its suggestions based on conversation details such as the time at which the participants agreed to meet.

The assistant can also make use of information stored in other apps. An integration with Plaid, a financial data sharing platform, enables Wabi to generate personal budgets and flag unused subscriptions that the user should cancel. A Gmail connector powers an alerting feature that notifies consumers about important messages.

Wabi’s AI assistant doubles as a vibe coding tool. Users can create simple apps to automate tasks such as managing to-do lists and planning events. The AI is also capable of generating simple, two-dimensional games that run directly in the chat window.

The chat interface is flanked by a sidebar that contains widgets relevant to the conversation. If a user is planning a trip, Wabi might display flight departure and arrival dates. Restaurant recommendations appear in vertically organized cards that each contain a photo of a venue’s exterior and a brief description.

“We believe Wabi has the power to become an operating system for life, a place where your people, your tools, and your AI come together to help you do more of what matters,” Kuyda said.

If Wabi proves popular among consumers, large market players could decide to launch similar services. Such competition may require the startup to find additional ways of differentiating its software. Some vibe coding startups have trained custom AI models to set their tools apart from more popular alternatives such as OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex.

Wabi will invest the proceeds from its funding round in growth and product development initiatives. The company’s near-term priorities include the launch of a Windows app.

#5608. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. Know a home with a story worth telling? Nominate it for inclusion in the creative franchise using this form. Tour the first properties and get an alert when each new home debuts using redfin.com/iconic-homes.

#5607. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5606. Cloudera builds its AI strategy around deployment flexibility

Deployment flexibility is changing the enterprise technology equation as businesses weigh new model options against existing data and development investments.

Open-weight models and open-source clouds are renewing interest in on-premises deployment. Cloudera Inc.’s data analytics heritage gives it a foundation for addressing that demand, according to Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor at SiliconANGLE Media and theCUBE.

“Companies want to have control that they don’t think that they’re getting in the public cloud,” he said. “I think Cloudera sees that, and they’re not ashamed to say that this is what they’re all about.”

Gillin spoke with co-host Rebecca Knight (left) at EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed deployment flexibility, platform modernization and Cloudera’s approach to partnerships. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s Anywhere Cloud spans on-premises, private cloud, public cloud and hybrid environments. Beyond that deployment flexibility, its architecture addresses the practical challenge of updating enterprise systems as development requirements change, according to Gillin.

“They realize that forklift upgrades are a terrifying prospect for many [chief information officers], and so they’re modularizing the product so that you can selectively patch and upgrade components that are important to you,” he said. “I think they’re trying to make it easy for customers to migrate to AI a step at a time by modernizing their data and their development platforms, by supporting the various AI development tools that are out there.”

Cloudera’s expanding partner ecosystem was another recurring theme across the day’s interviews and keynote. Those relationships reflect a recognition of where outside expertise can complement its platform, according to Knight.

“It seems as though Cloudera is taking a very wise and selective approach to who they partner with because they can’t be all things to all people, and they know that,” Knight said. “So they are partnering wisely.”

#5605. EXCLUSIVE: Meg Ryan’s Former Montecito Flip Fetches $18 Million—Just 4 Months After Hitting the Market

Actress Meg Ryan's former Montecito mansion has sold for $18 million—just four months after the new owners listed it for $19.9 million.

The 64-year-old "When Harry Met Sally" star purchased the picturesque Picacho Lane abode for $9.5 million in August 2021, then spent several years carrying out a meticulous renovation, adding another 3,000 square feet of space to the home, before relisting it for $22.5 million in February 2025.

It took several months and a fair few price cuts for Ryan to find a buyer—with the actress ultimately settling for the much lower sale price of $16.8 million in a deal that closed in June 2025.

Just two months later, that same buyer relaunched the Santa Barbara spread back onto the market for the much higher price of $21.9 million, but after struggling to secure an offer, it was removed in January of this year.

Then, in June, the home hit the market again, showing off the work that Ryan carried out during her ownership.

Now, the property has found a new buyer for $18 million, Realtor.com® can exclusively reveal.

"Nestled along prestigious Picacho Lane, this newly renovated estate offers sweeping ocean views and timeless elegance," the description noted.

Ryan purchased the California property for $9.5 million in 2021 via an LLC that she has used for a number of her real estate deals over the years. At the time, the property was situated on 6,500 square feet and featured five bedrooms, five bathrooms, and a guesthouse.

However, after she took on ownership of the home, the Hollywood heavyweight gave it a complete transformation, adding 3,000 square feet of living space, including two bedrooms and a half bathroom, while also installing three fireplaces throughout the dwelling, in the living room, primary bedroom, and on the patio.

In addition to the many upgrades that the actress carried out, potential buyers will also have the added bonus of becoming neighbors with a slew of famous faces, including Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, and Gwyneth Paltrow.

The property is surrounded by lush greenery and boasts sweeping views of the sea and mountains.

"Set behind a graceful lone private driveway, the home invites you in with a welcoming entry porch, perfect for morning coffee or evening fireside moments," the listing read.

Upon entering the home, guests are greeted with an expansive living area that boasts cozy couches, an eccentric overhead lighting fixture, and an elegant fireplace.

Adjacent to the living area, there is a formal dining room with a matching marble table, and a black glass divider.

Moving into the chef's kitchen, there are state-of-the-art appliances, a marble backsplash, and built-in black cabinets.

The large island boasts the same marble as the backsplash and seats three people.

The kitchen also has another eating table, which also follows the same marble countertop and fits more than 5 people.

Meanwhile, the primary bedroom comes complete with chic wallpaper, a balcony, and a cozy fireplace.

This space follows the same marble theme and boasts his-and-hers vanities.

"Inside, a thoughtfully curated design balances modern sophistication with serene comfort, flowing effortlessly through richly appointed living areas," the listing added.

Outside, there is a charming patio with a swinging bench, making it the perfect place to take in the gorgeous views.

There is also a water fountain and humble guesthouse.

"Ideal for every stage of life, the flexible layout includes an elevator for added convenience and features a main residence thoughtfully paired with a charming guest house and creative cabin. Whether hosting or retreating, the estate offers boundless possibilities for luxury, inspiration, and ease," read the listing.

Ryan previously gushed about her love for renovation projects while speaking with Architectural Digest.

“I know it sounds crazy to most people, the idea of renovating that many houses, but I love renovating. I think it’s tied to living the actor’s life," she said.

Her son, Jack, 33, who she shares with ex-husband Dennis Quaid, often teases his mom about her home renovation process and has even branded her work "Meg-anized."

She added, "As an actor, you are so rarely in control. You’re always saying words that someone else has given you, standing in a room that someone else has designed, to create a reality that someone else wants to see. But with decorating I am in control; it’s a chance for me to bring my vision into the world."

#5604. Report: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy

Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang was reportedly targeted by a Chinese espionage operation.

The New York Times today cited people familiar with the matter as saying that the ploy involved Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center operator. A Megaspeed executive named Alice Huang or Huang Le, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, reportedly “developed a close relationship with Jensen.” U.S. authorities believe that she is a Chinese asset.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesperson told the Times. “Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

A U.S. Commerce Department official reportedly visited a Megaspeed data center in Malaysia about two years ago. The graphics processing units on the premises weren’t installed in server racks but were instead found in boxes. According to the Times, that raised suspicions Megaspeed was planning to ship the GPUs elsewhere. The Commerce Department subsequently launched a probe into the company.

The Times carried out an investigation of its own by visiting Megaspeed’s headquarters in Singapore and reviewing its corporate documents. The paper discovered that the company’s Singapore director, who appears to be its owner, lives in China. Alice Huang, in turn, was at one point listed as managing director of Megaspeed. The company reportedly removed her name from its corporate documents after the Commerce Department began its probe.

In June 2024, Alice Huang was photographed sitting next to Jensen Huang and other AI industry executives at a party in Taipei. A year later, she reportedly arranged for Megaspeed to purchase about $2 billion worth of GPUs from Nvidia. The Times’ sources stated that the chips were bound to data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia that appear to be used by customers in China.

The U.S. Justice Department took over the Commerce Department’s probe earlier this year. The U.S. intelligence community, in turn, reportedly conducted electronic surveillance of Alice Huang.

Intelligence officials briefed U.S. President Donald Trump about the matter last year. According to the Times, the officials believed that Jensen Huang didn’t know Alice Huang had been trying to gather information for China. Trump reportedly took no action in response to the briefing.

“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security,” the Nvidia spokesperson said.

The chipmaker independently investigated whether any of the GPUs it had sold to Megaspeed may have ended up in China. “The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year,” Nvidia stated today.
