#5603. EXCLUSIVE: NBA Star Dwight Howard Slashes $1.6 Million From Price of His Georgia Megamansion

Former NBA superstar Dwight Howard has cut the asking price of his sprawling Georgia estate by $1.6 million—just two months after relisting the palatial pad.

In September, the 40-year-old basketball legend relisted his longtime Suwanee, GA, mansion for $14.5 million, marking a staggering $3.25 million increase from the $11.25 million price tag he attached to the home when he first put it up for sale in January 2025.

Now, the basketball icon has trimmed that asking price back by a sizable $1.6 million, bringing the new asking price to $12.9 million.

Howard purchased the enormous estate for $8.8 million in 2016, the same year he signed with his hometown team, the Atlanta Hawks.

A decade later, the eight-time NBA All-Star is hoping to score a sizable profit on the property, with his latest asking price coming in $5.7 million above what he originally paid for the spread.

The home, which is represented by Maninga Capehart of HomeSmart, sits on approximately 14 acres and offers 12 bedrooms, 12 full bathrooms, and nine half-bathrooms.

Built in 2010, the European-inspired residence boasts approximately 26,233 square feet of living space, providing no shortage of room for both overnight guests and lavish entertaining.

Indeed, the listing touts the property as one of Georgia's "most distinguished private estates," pointing to its impressive scale, elaborate architecture, and lengthy list of resort-worthy amenities.

Guests enter the mansion through custom double doors that open into a soaring two-story foyer, where a dual staircase, crystal chandelier, hardwood floors, and intricate millwork set an opulent tone.

From there, the home offers an array of formal and informal living areas, including a grand salon and formal dining room, as well as a glass atrium that floods the interiors with natural light.

Entertaining appears to have been a major consideration throughout the home's design, particularly when it comes to food preparation.

In addition to the main chef's kitchen, which is fitted with Viking appliances, there is a separate catering kitchen, a hidden pantry, a walk-in butler's pantry, multiple bars, and several service areas.

The main-level primary suite is equally extravagant, with a private executive office and enormous dressing areas lined with custom cabinetry. Its spa-worthy bathroom adds a sunken soaking tub, steam shower, and dedicated makeup vanity.

The home's additional bedroom suites are spread across the upper level and feature en-suite bathrooms and custom closets, with some offering steam showers and access to private balconies.

A separate multiroom residential suite also comes with its own kitchen and two bathrooms, providing a self-contained living space for family members or overnight visitors.

However, the property isn't solely focused on its sleeping quarters.

One entire level has been transformed into what the listing calls an "entertainment and wellness destination," complete with a private movie theater and kitchenette, billiards and recreation lounge, game and podcast space, and another full kitchen.

There's even a salon and barber area, sauna, and additional bedroom suite on the same level.

Howard won't need to leave the grounds to squeeze in a workout either. A separate two-story fitness and recreation pavilion has its own kitchen and bathroom, allowing the building to double as another space for gatherings.

The sprawling outdoor areas are equally geared toward leisure, with a saltwater swimming pool overlooked by a fully equipped outdoor kitchen.

The 14-acre grounds also include landscaped gardens and an orchard growing blueberries, blackberries, peaches, apples, and figs, while a private drive winds toward the property's lake.

Car enthusiasts, meanwhile, have an enormous amount of space to house their collections.

Although the property's main details advertise a six-car garage, the full listing reveals additional vehicle storage, including a six-car motor court and another six-car lower-level garage.

The garage areas also conceal much more than parking.

Above them sit two separate guest accommodations: a two-bedroom residence with its own kitchen and living and dining areas, and a studio residence equipped with a kitchenette and bathroom.

Perhaps one of the estate's more unexpected features is an underground passage connecting different portions of the property, while an elevator inside the main house provides access to every level.

The listing describes the sprawling compound as a "private legacy estate"—one outfitted to accommodate far more than the day-to-day needs of a single owner.

Howard's ties to Georgia stretch back long before his purchase of the mansion. The Atlanta native attended Southwest Atlanta Christian Academy before jumping directly from high school to the NBA.

He was selected by the Orlando Magic with the first overall pick in the 2004 NBA Draft and spent eight seasons with the franchise before embarking on stints with multiple teams, including the Los Angeles Lakers, Houston Rockets, Atlanta Hawks, Charlotte Hornets, Washington Wizards, and Philadelphia 76ers.

Howard ultimately captured an NBA championship with the Lakers in 2020.

Now, a decade after purchasing his supersized Georgia spread, Howard is once again looking for someone to take it off his hands—albeit at a considerably higher price than when he first tried to sell.

#5602. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5601. Despite cloud boom, Amazon’s stock falls on disappointing earnings and revenue miss

Shares of Amazon.com Inc. fell more than 7% in late trading today after the company missed expectations on earnings and revenue and reported rising negative free cash flow as it continues to throw billions of dollars at its cloud infrastructure build out.

However, investors Friday thought better of the quarter, and the stock fell only about 2% Friday.

The company reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of just $1.89 per share, trailing Wall Street’s target of $1.96 per share by a fair distance. Revenue for the period came to $201.94 billion, up 12% from a year earlier but below the analyst consensus estimate of $202.31 billion.

Amazon’s results looked even worse as its net income dropped to $20.69 billion, down from $21.19 billion in the same period one year earlier. However, that decrease was primarily due to last year’s $9.5 billion pretax gain from its investment in the artificial intelligence startup Anthropic PBC, which was recorded in last year’s quarter.

The company did better in terms of operating income, which is a more direct indicator of its financial health because it excludes profits and losses from investments unrelated to business performance. Operating income for the quarter came to $28.1 billion, above the Street’s forecast of $26.2 billion.

In a conference call with analysts, Amazon Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky reiterated the company’s capital expenditure forecast, saying the company expects spending to reach $220 billion this year.

Technology giants have been spending money at a blistering pace as they strive to build out their data center networks to meet the surging demand for AI infrastructure, but in recent weeks signs have begun to emerge that the capital expenditure splurge may be peaking. This week, Microsoft Corp. said it’s reducing its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion, down from an earlier target of $175 billion, while Alphabet Inc. maintained its forecast of between $195 billion and $205 billion.

However, Amazon’s decision to reiterate its annual capex target obscured the fact that it spent far more during the previous quarter than anyone had expected — or anyone else. Its third-quarter capex bill reached $77.3 billion, well ahead of the Street’s $58.7 billion estimate, and up from $35.1 billion in the same period last year. On the conference call, Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy (pictured) told analysts that the company plans to “spend more meaningfully in 2027,” adding that it has a “clear line of sight to attractive financial returns.”

But investors appeared to be more concerned with how the spending has been eating into the company’s cash flow than any future opportunities it might lead to. The company reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion in the quarter, which came after it posted a deficit in the previous quarter too. Olsavsky said the company spent more in the last quarter because it had to purchase more property and equipment for its AI investments.

Amazon had further disappointment for investors when it offered its guidance for the current quarter. It said it’s targeting between $240 billion and $247 billion in fourth quarter revenue, with the midpoint of that range trailing the Street’s forecast of $244.5 billion. The fourth quarter is traditionally Amazon’s biggest because its retail business benefits from holiday shopping season sales revenue.

The more important business is Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud computing infrastructure unit. It was a bright spot during the quarter, with sales growing 39% from a year earlier to $45..98 billion, just ahead of the Street’s target of $45.9 billion. Jassy told analysts that he’s expecting sales growth to accelerate to “over 40%” in the next year and in fiscal 2028 as a result of the company’s ongoing investments in its AI buildout. “Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working,” he insisted.

According to Jassy, AWS is on track to generate more than $1 trillion in annual revenue within the next five to 10 years.

Despite that boast, the company remains under pressure to start showing more substantial returns from its ballooning capex spending. Jassy responded, pointing to the growing traction in Amazon Bedrock, which is the company’s AI model marketplace, and increased revenue from its Graviton and Trainium AI chips. Indeed, the chips business “continues to grow triple-digit percentages year-over-year,” Jassy said. He added that the company has plans to make the Trainium chips available to external customers toward the end of next year.

Forrester analyst Tracy Woo told SiliconANGLE that AWS’ results stood out, with the unit continuing to drive strong profitability even as it funds one of the largest of all the AI infrastructure buildouts, with Amazon spending significantly more capital than either Google or Microsoft.

“That investment profile suggests Amazon sees future capacity constraints rather than demand constraints,” she said. “For enterprise customers, this demonstrates that cloud competition is increasingly shifting from price to access, with GPUs, foundation models and AI capacity becoming strategic differentiators. AWS’ margin performance suggests customers are currently prioritizing access to these scarce resources over cost optimization.”

The strong showing from AWS was sorely needed because Amazon’s other main business segments struggled to generate much enthusiasm, as both the retail and the advertising units fell short of Wall Street’s expectations. Online sales rose 2% from a year earlier, to $68.47 billion, shy of the $69.68 billion analyst target. That marked a dramatic slowdown from the year-ago quarter, when retail sales grew by almost 10%.

In the advertising segment, revenue rose 11%, to $19.64 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $20.82 billion. Jassy said the disappointing performance in both segments was partly the result of the company’s decision to bring its annual Prime Day sale forward in several countries this year. It typically takes place during the third quarter, but it was held during the second quarter instead to avoid conflicting with the FIFA World Cup in July.

#5600. Pennymac posts $29M profit amid expense cuts, upcoming leadership changes

PennyMac Financial Services posted $29 million in net income for the third quarter of 2026 on $469 million in revenue. Profitability was driven by its $496 billion servicing portfolio while production swung to a pretax loss amid a smaller, more competitive originations market. The company outlined plans to cut annualized operating expenses by $160 million by early 2027, sell $29 billion in low-coupon conventional MSRs for about $490 million in proceeds to pay down debt and repurchase shares, and close its acquisition of Cenlar’s subservicing business in early 2027.  AI Summary

PennyMac Financial Services Inc. (PFSI) on Thursday reported its financial results for the third quarter of 2026, with the California-based mortgage lender and servicer posting net income of $29 million from June to September — down 84% from a year ago but up 32% from the second quarter.

The company enters the final quarter of the year balancing two diverging stories — an originations business that’s being squeezed by the highest mortgage rates in years alongside a servicing business that’s producing healthy results and is set to grow further through a coming acquisition.

Pennymac is also attempting to right the ship through cost-cutting measures, including layoffs, while chairman and CEO David Spector announced coming leadership changes for 2027 during an earnings call with investors and analysts on Thursday.

Spector said that effective Jan. 1, 2027, chief strategy officer Kevin Ryan will take over as the company’s chief financial officer. Current CFO Dan Perotti, who’s been with the company since 2008 and in the CFO’s seat since 2021, will remain in the role through the end of this year and serve in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027.

Additionally, Pennymac announced that president and chief mortgage banking officer Doug Jones will be retiring effective June 30, 2027. Jones has been with Pennymac in multiple capacities since 2011, serving in his current role since March 2021.

“I have absolute confidence in this management team’s ability to carry our strategy forward seamlessly while driving long-term value for our stockholders, and we have a deep bench of talent that is fully prepared to lead PennyMac,” Spector said during Thursday’s call.

The company detailed roughly $160 million in annualized expense reductions from Q2 2026 to Q1 2027. It also announced an agreement to sell $29 billion in unpaid principal balance (UPB) of low-coupon mortgage servicing rights (MSRs). That transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter and generate estimated net proceeds of $490 million, which will largely be used to pay down debt.

The MSR sale also feeds into a broader deleveraging effort. Perotti said that Pennymac’s nonfunding leverage, which ticked up to 1.9x amid the recent rate spike, should trend back toward the company’s roughly 1.5x target over time, aided by the debt paydown and an eventual rate rally.

A company spokesperson confirmed to HousingWire this week that the cost-cutting measures included layoffs.

“Sustained market volatility has continued to reshape loan volumes across the industry, and we have aligned our operations accordingly. As part of that work, Pennymac has made the difficult decision to eliminate select positions within its mortgage fulfillment operations,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

“We are deeply grateful to these team members for their contributions, and we are committed to supporting them through this transition, including severance support. Pennymac remains focused on serving our customers well and on building an organization positioned to grow as conditions improve.”

Spector said that a sharp and fast increase to 30-year fixed mortgage rates — roughly 90 basis points for an average rate of 7.4% at the end of Q3 2026 — has contributed to “one of the most constrained origination environments our industry has seen since 2023.”

Pennymac’s production segment swung to a loss as origination volumes declined and margins softened. Total loan acquisitions and originations during the quarter totaled $24.4 billion in UPB, down 30% from $34.9 billion in the second quarter and 33% below the $36.5 billion figure from the same period last year.

Total fallout-adjusted loan locks were $23.1 billion, down 27% quarter over quarter and 37% year over year. In the consumer direct channel, fallout-adjusted locks fell to $2.8 billion from $4.5 billion in the prior quarter and $3.9 billion a year ago, driven by weaker refinance demand.

In the company’s broker channel, fallout-adjusted locks declined to $4.7 billion from $6.5 billion in the second quarter and $5.9 billion in Q3 2025. For its correspondent channel, locks dropped to $15.6 billion, down from $20.5 billion in the prior quarter and $27.2 billion a year earlier.

Production revenue margins were 76 basis points of total fallout-adjusted lock volume, down slightly from 77 bps in the second quarter and 79 bps points a year earlier.

Pennymac’s production segment also posted revenues of $175 million, down 28% from $243 million in Q2 2026 and 40% from $292 million in Q3 2025. Expenses totaled $182 million, down 11% sequentially but up 7% year over year. The production channel’s pretax loss was $7 million, compared with pretax income of $38 million in the prior quarter and $123 million a year ago.

“By automating labor-intensive fulfillment workflows, we are permanently lowering our cost to produce and uncoupling platform capacity from staffing requirements. This will allow us to maintain lean operation in today’s constrained environment while ensuring substantial operating leverage,” Spector told analysts and investors.

While the company’s originations segment is feeling the impacts of rising rates and lower volumes, Pennymac’s servicing business continues to thrive. Its portfolio ended the third quarter at $737 billion in UPB, a figure that’s expected to surpass $1 trillion after its proposed acquisition of Cenlar Capital Corp. closes.

The $257.5 million deal, announced in February, was initially expected to close by the end of this year, but Pennymac executives have extended the timeline to the first quarter of 2027. It will bring the nation’s second-largest subservicer on board through the first merger-and-acquisition deal in Pennymac’s history.

Pennymac’s pretax income from servicing totaled $99 million in Q3, up from $22 million in Q2. Excluding MSR fair value changes net of hedge results, servicing pretax income was $132 million, up sequentially from $99 million.

Its owned servicing portfolio reached $496 billion in UPB as of Sept. 30, up 6% from a year earlier. Lower prepayment speeds — down to 8.1% compared to 11.6% in the prior quarter — reduced amortization and lifted servicing profitability, reinforcing what Spector described as the natural hedge in the company’s balanced business model.

That dynamic underpins management’s optimism that servicing will contribute to improvement for return on equity heading into 2027. Pennymac’s annualized ROE was 3% in the third quarter, up from 2% in the second quarter but well below the 15% figure from a year ago.

Executives offered further details on the MSR sale and its expected impacts, with Perotti noting that Pennymac will not retain subservicing on this particular transaction.

Spector said Pennymac plans to use the cash primarily to reduce higher-cost debt and repurchase common shares while company stock trades “at a sizable discount to book value.” The move is intended to reallocate capital from low-recapture MSRs to shareholder returns and liability management, while maintaining scale in servicing.

“We continue to evaluate potential MSR sales but … there’s nothing necessarily in the pipeline in terms of sales currently, and it’s something that we continue to evaluate in terms of our capital options,” Perotti added. “When interest rates rise sharply, as they did throughout the third quarter, the fair value of our MSR increases, which expands our available borrowing capacity with our banking partners.”

Editor’s note: Flávia Furlan Nunes contributed reporting to this story.

#5599. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5598. Op-Ed: MLSs can build what brokers want or brokers will do it

Open Real Estate is a broker-backed effort to centralize listing input and control distribution alongside MLSs. The announcement reflects frustration with fragmented IDX and licensing terms and with MLS monetization of broker data without parallel expansion of broker rights.  AI Summary

On Monday, four of the largest brokerage companies in the country — Keller Williams, HomeServices of America, eXp’s parent AGNT and Real REMAX Group, roughly 300,000 agents between them — announced Open Real Estate, a shared listing database that would sit alongside the MLS. The first questions have been about execution, and they are fair. But the more useful question for anyone who runs an MLS is why these brokers felt they needed to build it.

Here is what ORE proposes. An agent enters a listing once, within one business day of signing the listing agreement. The seller chooses who sees it: a participant view for agents at member brokerages, or a market view that goes to MLSs, portals, appraisers and everyone else. We believe those marketing options are too limited, but we support the central idea that brokers keep ownership of their listings and share in whatever value the data generates.

ORE faces challenges. No MLS has committed to take its listings, though MARIS in St. Louis told its members this week that it supports the idea and “recognizes there is room for improvement.” The vendor won’t be chosen until early 2027, and broker-led single points of entry have stalled before. But whether ORE will work isn’t the point. The point is brokers want something better.

One MLS executive, in an article on RIS Media, said as much this week: “I don’t think that these companies would be doing what they’re doing if they were happy MLS customers. They want a better way than what they are presented with right now.”

Strip away the technology and ORE’s open letter reads less like a product plan than a list of things brokers believe their MLSs should already allow.

Not for lack of ambition. MLSs have spent two years building new businesses on broker data. Stellar launched a consumer search site in September. NorthstarMLS and MARIS invested in REcore, an MLS-owned data company. More than 40 MLSs license data through REdistribute, and more than 20 have joined SourceRE’s new connector, built to put MLS data inside AI tools.

Brokers’ rights to the same data have not kept pace. How brokers can use and display MLS listing data is governed by IDX policies and licensing agreements, negotiated one MLS at a time, roughly 400 times over. So when your MLS strikes deals to put your listings in front of AI companies while your own rights to use them haven’t changed, you eventually look for somewhere else to put them. Somewhere like ORE.

The same problem extends to how sellers market their homes. ORE offers sellers two distribution choices, but the industry needs more than two. MLS rules should recognize that a home can be publicly marketed without being distributed everywhere, and that sellers should have meaningful control over when and where their listings appear.

The bigger point is that brokers shouldn’t have to build an alternative network to get these changes. MLS executives can write, and their boards approve, better rules. Rules that create a single point of entry, which some MLSs already offer through technology partners. Rules that give sellers real options while protecting buyers. Rules that let the people who supply the industry’s data use it to serve their customers, wherever those customers now search.

Those rules still need to protect cooperation, accuracy, and fair access. But protecting the MLS’s value shouldn’t come at the expense of innovation.

Brokers aren’t asking MLSs to abandon what makes them valuable. They’re asking MLSs to evolve with the businesses that supply their listings.

ORE is a warning that some brokers are no longer willing to wait.

Joe Rath is head of industry relations at Rocket, which owns Redfin. His family has run a brokerage on Cleveland’s west side since 1972.

#5597. Intel shares plummet 30+% following weak guidance blamed on PC market slowdown

Intel Corp. somehow managed to beat expectations despite facing softness in the personal computer market, but its weak forecast for the current quarter sparked panic among investors, and its stock plunged more than 30% Friday.

The computer chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 52 cents per share, easily beating Wall Street’s guidance of 40 cents per share. Revenue for the quarter rose 21% from a year earlier, to $16.51 billion, edging past the Street’s target of $16.5 billion. All told, the company posted net income of $3.3 billion, down from the $4.1 billion it earned in the same period last year.

However, the results couldn’t mask the poor performance of Intel’s client computing and physical AI business, where revenue dropped 5% from a year earlier, to $8.1 billion, missing the Street’s target. The company was held up by its data center and AI unit, where revenue soared 78%, to $7.3 billion.

The client computing business is struggling because the PC market is currently in decline. Global PC shipments fell 4% in the second quarter according to data from Counterpoint Research, partly due to the soaring costs of memory and other components.

Things are likely to get even worse in the PC market, which is why Intel could only offer a tepid forecast going forward. The company said it’s looking for fourth-quarter earnings of about 25 cents per share at the midpoint of its guidance range, with revenue at between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts are targeting earnings of 43 cents per share and sales of $17.1 billion.

Intel’s finance chief David Zinsner said the company sees the PC slowdown continuing until at least the first half of next year. “We will continue making disciplined investments capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth,” he told investors.

During the quarter, the company suffered a tragic setback when an explosion occurred at one of its chip fabrication plants in Israel, resulting in the deaths of two workers and serious injuries to a third person. That incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over the next two quarters, Zinsner told analysts on a conference call. Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan (pictured) said the “unfortunate and tragic accident” resulted in an “extended shutdown” at the plant, delaying shipments of new 10-nanometer chips.

Today’s stock drop slams the brakes on what had been one of the fastest-growing technology stocks this year. Intel’s stock had been on an upward tear all year, rising more than 150% since January. However, the stock’s growth had already stalled since the beginning of the month amid growing concerns about the tech industry’s runaway spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. “We will remain disciplined as we invest and we will not spend $1 of capital unless we have confidence in the health of our products and process technologies and clear evidence of customer demand,” Zinsner said in an effort to reassure investors.

Intel is best known for the central processing units that power much of the world’s PCs, but its recent revival has primarily been driven by the emergence of agentic AI workloads. Chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini primarily use the graphics processing units sold by rival chipmakers like Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., but AI agents such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse and OpenAI Group PBC’s Dots run more efficiently on CPUs. As agentic AI has grown in popularity this year, so too have Intel’s chips.

“Despite near term headwinds affecting the broader PC industry, we continue to see robust demand for CPUs and more broadly, for all our computing platforms in the long term,” Tan insisted.

However, the demand for Intel’s CPUs has been offset by the struggles of its nascent foundry business, which was spun out as a separate business unit a couple of years ago but has struggled to gain traction with customers. So far, its only major customer is Intel itself.

The company’s fab in Arizona is the only U.S.-based facility that’s able to mass produce advanced logic chips. “We are going to have a couple of customers ready to announce in the next two quarters,” Tan promised analysts on the call. He added that the company is also making “tremendous progress” with its forthcoming 14A chips.

Intel, which had previously fallen behind on its roadmap for seven- and 10-nanometer chips, has been struggling to get back on track but has benefited from a vote of confidence by President Donald Trump, whose administration took a 10% stake in the company last year. Since then, Nvidia and SoftBank Group Corp. have also invested billions of dollars into the chipmaker.

Tan is generally viewed as being more cautious than his predecessor, Pat Gelsinger, who made the decision to spin out the foundry business and try to attract external customers. But at the same time, he has also given the green light to some significant investments such as a new chip fab in Ohio that was first expected to come online last year. So far it hasn’t, but Intel said last week that construction crews have installed the first structural truss at the facility.

Last month, reports emerged that Intel was talking to the high-bandwidth memory chip manufacturer SK hynix Inc. about the prospect of it leasing a part of the Ohio fab’s capacity. The South Korean firm reportedly wants to manufacture some of its memory chips at the new site, but so far nothing concrete has been announced. Tan refused to acknowledge those talks, telling analysts that the company “continues to evaluate unique and highly differentiated opportunities to accelerate our Ohio buildout, and I hope to share more on this in the near future.”

#5595. Marts&Lundy Study Offers New Insight into Incentive Compensation in Higher Education Advancement

Ten-year follow-up explores adoption, program design, and institutional approaches to rewarding performance

LYNDHURST, N.J., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As advancement leaders look for new ways to attract and keep top fundraising talent, Marts&Lundy today released Incentive Compensation in Higher Education Advancement, a new benchmarking study that offers one of the few current views of how institutions use performance incentives to support their advancement teams. Revisiting research first published in 2016, the study provides current insight into program eligibility, structure, performance measures, and perceived outcomes to help leaders make informed compensation decisions. Marts&Lundy is a strategic fundraising consulting firm serving mission-driven organizations around the world.

Employee retention emerged as a central priority: every institution reporting its incentive program's goals identified retention as an objective. Improved employee performance and higher overall fundraising revenue were also prominent goals, reflecting the role incentives can play within a broader talent and advancement strategy.

The research draws on responses from 38 higher education institutions that answered whether they offer incentive compensation to advancement staff. Approximately 16% reported having a program. Among institutions without one, more than 40% said they were currently considering incentive compensation for fundraising roles.

"Advancement leaders tells us they want real data on this topic, and there has been very little to point to," said Penelepe Hunt, Senior Consultant & Principal at Marts&Lundy, who led the study. "This research gives leaders a clearer view of how peers are approaching incentive compensation and practical insight into designing programs in a way that strengthens their institution's goals, culture, and collaborative approach to fundraising."

The report also explores award structures, funding sources, administration, and approaches to recognizing contributions across advancement teams. It offers practical guidance for leaders: engage governance and HR early, start where measurement is strongest, decide deliberately between campaign-specific and permanent program design, and build shared-credit approaches that recognize colleagues across the team.

The study was conducted through an online questionnaire in summer 2026 and included public and private institutions with and without programs. The findings are directional benchmarks from participating institutions rather than estimates for the sector, and reported outcomes reflect respondents' perceptions.

The full report is available at https://martsandlundy.com/special-report-2026-incentive-compensation-in-higher-education-advancement/.

Founded in 1926, Marts&Lundy helps mission-driven organizations unlock the full potential of philanthropy. The firm combines strategic advisory, analytics, campaign planning, communications, donor engagement, and technology and AI enablement tailored to each client's unique circumstances and helps shape ambitious visions, strengthen fundraising performance, and build the capacity organizations need to enable impactful giving and sustainable growth. For more information, visit https://martsandlundy.com.

#5594. AI architecture startup Dream launches with $17M in funding

Dream Technologies Inc., a startup using artificial intelligence to generate building designs, launched today with $17 million in funding.

Andreessen Horowitz led the seed round. It was joined by SV Angel, XYZ, Zigg Capital and several others.

San Francisco-based Dream was founded last year by former Palantir Technologies Inc. executives Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur. Elder headed the software maker’s product design team, while Mathur was the senior vice president of its private sector business. Dream’s leadership team also includes former engineers from Okta Inc. and Siemens AG.

Crafting a building plan manually can take a team of architects several months. Dream has developed a series of AI models designed to speed up the task. According to the company, its algorithms can generate hundreds of design variations in a few minutes. Dream says its software thereby not only accelerates construction projects but also lowers costs.

The company trained its models on data about 100 million square feet of U.S. real estate. The properties in the dataset include commercial buildings, apartments and single-family homes. Dream stores the blueprints its models process using a custom schema, a file that defines how a set of records should be organized. The schema is designed to ease the task of verifying architectural calculations.

Architecture teams craft building designs through an iterative process that involves numerous revisions. Those revisions are time-consuming because implementing even a small change often requires engineers to modify several blueprint elements. For example, adding an extra cooling system to a server hall might necessitate upgrades to the room’s electrical wiring and ventilation system.

Dream says its models speed up such changes. Additionally, they reduce the amount of work involved in adapting an existing building design to a new location. A retailer looking to open a store in a new city could reuse one of its existing venues’ designs and have Dream adapt it to local building codes.

The company’s models generate blueprints through a multistep process. First, they analyze the site where a building is set to be constructed and review the associated operational constraints. Dream uses those data points to generate a layout that defines which building elements should be placed where. Its models then define more granular details such as the dimensions of individual structural components.

“A hallucination in an LLM is a typo. A hallucination in a building is a structural fault, with potentially catastrophic consequences,” said Elder. “We built Dream to be exact — down to how a duct routes through a wall — because precision at that level is what actually shortens timelines and takes cost out of a project.”

The company is also working on a tool that can speed up internal design projects. According to Dream, the tool combines the U.S. real-estate dataset that underpins its models with information about 73 popular design and architectural styles.

Dream doesn’t sell its software but rather provides ready-to-use blueprints to construction and architecture firms. The company acts as an architect of record, which means that it takes legal responsibility for its plans. Dream disclosed today that it’s already supporting 10 construction projects in California and Texas with a combined value of $20 million.

#5593. Silvio Tavares steps down as VantageScore CEO, Anthony Hutchinson named interim leader

VantageScore said president and CEO Silvio Tavares is stepping down after five years. The board appointed Anthony Hutchinson as interim CEO and launched a formal search for a permanent successor.  AI Summary

VantageScore announced on Friday that president and CEO Silvio Tavares is stepping down after five years leading the credit scoring company, with Anthony Hutchinson appointed as interim CEO.

VantageScore‘s board has begun a formal search for a permanent successor, according to a company release. Hutchinson, who previously led VantageScore’s public affairs and government relations efforts, will work with the board and management team during the transition.

The company did not specify Tavares’ reason for stepping down, but the board credited Tavares with leading the company’s growth and strengthening its position in the credit scoring industry.

“We thank Silvio Tavares for his five years of strong leadership of VantageScore,” the board said in a statement. “During his tenure, VantageScore more than tripled its market presence and achieved numerous breakthroughs including widespread adoption in the U.S. mortgage credit-scoring market.”

Tavares said he was proud of the company’s growth and its efforts to expand access to credit.

“Together, we consistently delivered industry leading innovation and growth at a very high scale,” Tavares said. “Along the way VantageScore responsibly expanded access to credit so that millions more creditworthy Americans can achieve their American dream.”

Hutchinson brings more than 30 years of experience in housing finance, public policy and industry leadership. Before joining VantageScore four years ago, he held senior positions at Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae and the National Association of Realtors.

As interim CEO, Hutchinson said he plans to build on the company’s momentum and continue expanding adoption of its credit scoring models. VantageScore 4.0 in particular has gained traction across the mortgage industry since the Federal Housing Finance Agency approved its use by lenders originating loans through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

In September, FHFA Director Bill Pulte also announced that the government-sponsored enterprises would use a single loan-level price adjustment (LLPA) matrix regardless of which approved credit scoring model lenders use.

“VantageScore is helping lenders make more predictive, inclusive and informed decisions across the credit lifecycle,” Hutchinson said. “We are delivering strong business momentum and growing market adoption of the most predictive, innovative and inclusive tri-bureau models and attributes in the U.S. market.”

#5592. Monday.com bets on deployment experts to turn AI agents into real returns

Enterprises have embraced AI for everyday tasks, but turning autonomous agents into measurable business returns is proving far harder. The bottleneck is no longer the technology but the organizational change needed to rewire processes around it.

Software providers are responding by pairing their platforms with hands-on guidance. Since monday.com Ltd. relaunched as an AI work platform, its customers have asked less about what the technology can do and more about how to make it pay off, according to Eran Zinman (pictured), co-founder and co-chief executive officer of monday.com.

“I think what’s hard is the actual business change you have to go through,” Zinman said. “Eventually companies want to see return on investment. Tokens cost a lot of money. You want to see a real impact on your business.”

Zinman spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the challenge of turning autonomous agents into measurable business returns. (* Disclosure below.)

Before asking customers to change, the company tested the change on itself. Under an initiative called Customer Zero, employees set aside their regular jobs for a week and competed to build agents, Zinman explained.

“We said we’re going to stop the company for one week. We literally have done that. Nobody was doing their regular job for a week,” Zinman said. “Everybody was building agents.”

The exercise produced more than 3,600 agents, and about 2,000 are still running, according to Zinman. That playbook now underpins monday Frontier, a new organization that combines managed services and deployment engineers to help customers find bottlenecks and launch AI projects within weeks.

“Adopting AI really requires expertise. I know how hard it is because we experienced ourselves that you have this amazing technology, but how do you actually use it?” Zinman said.

The company is also rebranding as simply monday, reflecting a product built around people and agents sharing one workspace. Zinman rejects predictions that AI will push humans out of the workforce, insisting accountability stays with people.

“AI will never take responsibility for what you’re doing in your business,” Zinman said. “And you need people in the loop. I feel the best combination to adopt AI is people and agents working together where AI is not replacing people; it’s empowering people.”

#5591. INOX SOLAR AMERICAS' U.S. PV CELL FACILITY ON TRACK FOR Q2 2027 PRODUCTION

Construction is progressing well at the 3.0-GW North Carolina facility as it moves into the equipment installation phase

GREENVILLE, N.C., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Inox Solar Americas LLC, a U.S.-based solar technology and manufacturing company specializing in advanced PV cells and high-performance PV modules, today announced that its planned PV cell manufacturing facility in Greenville, North Carolina, with an annual production capacity of 3.0 GW, remains on schedule to begin production in the second quarter of 2027.

"Our continued progress on U.S. PV cell manufacturing represents an important step."

The 515,460-square-foot facility is a key part of Inox Solar Americas' strategy to build a more vertically integrated U.S. solar manufacturing platform. Once operational, domestic advanced PV cell production will complement the company's existing U.S. PV module manufacturing capabilities, providing customers with greater access to U.S.-manufactured solar technology and a more transparent, resilient, and reliable domestic supply chain.

Domestic Manufacturing & Regulatory Compliance

Inox Solar Americas' vertically integrated U.S. manufacturing strategy is designed to provide customers with greater access to domestically manufactured PV cells and PV modules while increasing domestic content across the company's product portfolio. The addition of U.S. PV cell manufacturing will further support customers addressing evolving U.S. domestic-content requirements, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) and Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) considerations, applicable trade requirements, and federal energy-policy provisions. The company's approach emphasizes qualified sourcing, documented manufacturing processes, and compliance readiness to help customers manage increasingly complex procurement and project requirements.

Supply-Chain Security, Transparency & Traceability

Integrating U.S. PV cell and PV module manufacturing will provide greater visibility and control across critical stages of the solar supply chain. Inox Solar Americas is strengthening supplier qualification, component-origin documentation, material traceability, production records, and supply-chain due diligence to support customers seeking greater transparency regarding where and how their products are manufactured. Increased domestic production is also designed to reduce dependence on imported PV cells, mitigate exposure to global supply disruptions and trade-related risks, and provide more reliable product availability for U.S. project pipelines.

Advanced Technology, Quality & Performance

The Greenville manufacturing platform will integrate advanced Galaxionâ¢ monocrystalline PV cell technologies with Inox Solar Americas' U.S.-manufactured Gamma Seriesâ¢ monofacial and Vega Seriesâ¢ bifacial PV modules. Advanced automation, precision cell processing, integrated inspection and testing, process controls, documented quality procedures, and production traceability are designed to provide greater manufacturing control from PV cell production through finished-module assembly. This integrated approach will support consistent product quality, high efficiency and energy yield, durability, and dependable performance across demanding U.S. solar applications.

Bankability, Supply Reliability & Customer Confidence

Expanding from U.S. PV module manufacturing into domestic PV cell production further strengthens Inox Solar Americas' manufacturing capabilities and ability to support large-scale, multiyear customer requirements. The company is building greater manufacturing scale, supply continuity, domestic-content capability, traceability, compliance readiness, and product support. Together with product performance, quality systems, warranty support, and a commitment to the U.S. market, these capabilities are designed to strengthen customer, developer, investor, and lender confidence in Inox Solar Americas and the projects its products support.

"Our continued progress on U.S. PV cell manufacturing represents an important step in building a more integrated and resilient domestic solar supply chain," said Ashok Nair, President & CEO of Inox Solar Americas. "By bringing advanced cell technology, high-performance module manufacturing, and rigorous quality control together within our U.S. manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with reliable supply and the bankability required for their project pipelines."

Inox Solar Americas, founded in 2026 in the United States, is a leading solar technology and manufacturing company specializing in advanced monocrystalline PV cells and high-performance Gamma Seriesâ¢ monofacial and Vega Seriesâ¢ bifacial PV modules. Inox Solar Americas' photovoltaic solutions are engineered to meet the needs of residential, commercial, industrial, community solar, and utility-scale applications, delivering exceptional efficiency, reliability, and long-term value.

Inox Solar Americas acquired Boviet Solar's U.S. PV manufacturing assets in Greenville, North Carolina, USA, including 3.0 GW of annual PV module manufacturing capacity and 3.0 GW of planned annual PV cell manufacturing capacity, expected to come online in 2027. Through localized manufacturing, resilient supply chains, operational excellence, and efficient logistics, Inox Solar Americas is helping strengthen the U.S. solar supply chain and meet growing domestic demand.

Inox Solar Americas is part of the broader renewable energy platform of Inox Clean Energy and the INOXGFL Group, headquartered in India. Backed by the group's financial strength, business stability, manufacturing capabilities, technological innovation, and industry expertise, Inox Solar Americas is committed to delivering high-quality, reliable, and sustainable solar solutions to customers across the U.S. solar energy market.

For more information, visit: inoxsolar.us, inoxclean.com and inoxgfl.com.

#5589. Exclusive: CrossCountry Mortgage demands payment from former LOs, invokes 2-year non-solicitation

Cease-and-desist letters from CrossCountry Mortgage accuse at least 25 loan officers of refinancing CCM-connected borrowers after leaving. The company seeks repayment calculated at 75 bps per loan and warns litigation is reasonably likely.  AI Summary

Top-five mortgage lender CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM) has sent cease-and-desist letters to at least 25 former loan officers, according to documents viewed by HousingWire and interviews with one of their new employers. In the letters, CCM invokes a two-year, non-solicitation window and demands thousands of dollars in combined penalties under their employment agreements.

The company cites a contractual provision creating a “legal presumption” that any mortgage product or service provided to a past, present or future CCM customer violates the agreement. Under that framework, CCM declares that “each loan is presumed to violate your non-solicitation covenant.”

The letters, dated Oct. 29, were sent by Ashley C. Wakefield, senior corporate counsel for Cleveland-based CrossCountry Mortgage. Each document contains the same three-part demand: a cease-and-desist order, a demand for payment based on 75 bps for each refinanced loan, and a litigation preservation notice. CCM gives the recipients 10 business days to respond.

According to the letters seen by HousingWire, the repayment amounts range from several thousand dollars to nearly $20,000 dollars in the case of one letter.

Representatives at CrossCountry Mortgage did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s request for comment.

CCM’s letters lean heavily on restrictive covenants in the employment agreements allegedly signed by the LOs. CCM argues that the agreements contain provisions around confidentiality, nonsolicitation and return of property provisions that survive an employee’s departure.

The company asserts that confidential material covered by the agreements includes all non-public personal information of borrowers that is protected under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. It goes on to say that every loan handled by the LOs during their time there “remains CCM’s sole and exclusive property.”

While the letters obtained by HousingWire address a small number of LOs, many others have left CCM in recent years for other companies. They could be part of a larger pattern of cease-and-desist orders, along with potential litigation, if they’ve closed loans since then with any CCM customers.

RETR data shows that 843 loan officers have left CrossCountry Mortgage in the past 14 months. Sixty-one of them did at least $20 million in volume during that period, although it’s unknown how much of that volume was tied to former CCM clients. Many others are now inactive LOs or have produced no loans.

Beyond the cash demands — which were labeled as payable by check mailed to CCM’s headquarters in Cleveland within 10 business days — the letters call for the recipients to stop originating loans for any CCM customer, prospect or referral source, to stop using any CCM confidential material, and to certify in writing that they’ve returned all company materials.

The letters also include a warning that “litigation over these matters is reasonably likely.” The recipients are instructed to preserve a sweeping range of records, including offer letters and compensation details from their current employer, along with loan files, lead-source data, CRM and loan origination system records, and communications with any current or former CCM borrower.

This preservation demand also mentions personal devices and digital tools, specifically naming email, text and instant messages, voicemails, call logs, calendar entries, shared drives, cloud accounts and “AI chat history.” The recipients are instructed to immediately suspend any auto-delete or device replacement practices, warning that failure to preserve evidence “may expose you to sanctions for spoliation.”

If the recipients don’t comply within 10 business days, “CCM may file suit without further notice,” the letters state.

Editor’s note: Sarah Wolak contributed to this report.

#5588. Brakes built for speed: Why least privilege lets monday.com’s AI teams move faster

As AI agents spread across enterprise workflows, permission management is becoming one of the most practical levers for keeping them safe. Agents act with the access people give them, so the old problem of sprawling privileges now plays out at machine speed.

Governance is often cast as a brake on that momentum, especially as work platforms build agents into everyday tools. The view at monday.com Ltd., which relaunched as an AI work platform with native agents, is that well-designed guardrails let teams move faster, according to Ryan Nigro (pictured), security trust and enablement team lead at monday.com.

“The brakes on a car are not for you to be slowing down constantly,” Nigro said. “It’s so that you could feel confident in going faster.”

Nigro spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how permission management is key to AI agent safety. (* Disclosure below.)

Nigro’s approach rests on least privilege, a concept cybersecurity teams first applied to human users. AI largely does what employees already do, so haywire permissions for people become a problem for agents too, he explained. The fix is to roll out AI piece by piece, granting each tool the minimum access it needs and expanding as results prove out.

“You don’t want to enable all the features and give everybody all the access all at once. That’s just bad permissions,” Nigro said.

Everyday personnel moves create some of the biggest gaps. An employee who shifts from finance to legal can end up holding both departments’ access at companies without strict permission management, Nigro noted. He cited an IBM Corp. study estimating that 80% to 90% of breaches stem from human error tied to over-permissioning.

“It just comes to making sure that your users are properly being given just enough to do their roles but not too much to cause harm,” Nigro said. “There’s no reason why a sales rep should have the ability to change your production environment.”

#5586. Marriott beat earnings expectations and raised its outlook on strong U.S. hotel demand

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Worldwide revenue per available room rose 6.5%, with U.S. and Canada up 7.4%, as Marriott lifted its full-year forecast to 4.5% to 5%

Marriott $MAR International raised its full-year outlook on Monday after reporting third-quarter adjusted earnings of $3.02 a share, up from $2.47 a year earlier, as demand grew at hotels in the U.S. and Canada.

That topped the $2.85 a share that analysts had forecast on average, according to Bloomberg. Marriott stock rose 2.7% in premarket trading.

Revenue per available room, known as RevPAR, rose 6.5% worldwide in the quarter. It increased 7.4% in the U.S. and Canada and 4.4% in international markets, the company said. Worldwide RevPAR rose on higher average daily rates and higher occupancy.

"In the U.S. & Canada, RevPAR rose over 7 percent, with broad-based growth across customer segments and chain scales," CEO Anthony Capuano said in a statement.

Marriott now expects full-year worldwide RevPAR growth of 4.5% to 5%, and the same range for the fourth quarter. It forecast full-year adjusted earnings of $12.07 to $12.14 a share and fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $3.14 to $3.21 a share. The earlier full-year range was $11.64 to $11.81 a share, according to Bloomberg.

The company expects net rooms growth at the low end of 4.5% to 5% for the year. Bloomberg reported that this outlook was unchanged.

Reported net income rose 9% to $794 million, or $3.04 a share, from $728 million, or $2.67 a share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 8% to $7.005 billion. Adjusted EBITDA rose 12% to $1.512 billion.

Capuano said RevPAR in Asia Pacific excluding China rose over 9%, and Europe, Middle East and Africa RevPAR rose over 4%, helped by solid growth in Europe. He said the conflict in the Middle East continued to affect results there, though trends improved meaningfully from the second quarter.

Marriott lifted its full-year RevPAR growth forecast from a prior range of 3% to 3.5%.

The company added 20,100 net rooms in the quarter, and net rooms grew 4.6% from a year earlier. Its development pipeline reached a record 4,209 properties and more than 634,000 rooms, with 44% of pipeline rooms under construction, including hotels pending conversion.

Marriott repurchased 3.5 million shares of its stock for $1.3 billion in the quarter. Through Oct. 28, it has returned about $4.0 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. It expects to return at least $4.8 billion for the full year.
