#5585. A path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table

Housing demand stabilized over the last 2 weeks as mortgage rates eased and the 10-year yield moved below 5%. Mortgage spreads are at 2.23% and, like inventory and price cuts, have remained higher year over year. This week will feature jobs data and the midterms, which can create bond volatility.  AI Summary

Housing demand has stabilized over the last two weeks as rates have fallen a tad, and we can finally see a clear path back to sub-7% mortgage rates. We survived the crazy month of October, when the 10-year had the potential to close above 5.35%, which would have created a backdrop of bond-escalation selling, sending mortgage rates above 8%. That didn’t happen, of course, as the 10-year yield held that key line!

Not only has the 10-year yield now gone below 5% — with mortgage rates closer to 7% than 8% today — but what this month has shown us is that there’s a clear path for sub-7% mortgage rates. Just the move in the last two weeks has stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, so let’s take a look on this Halloween on what needs to happen to get rates lower.

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:

Last week was Fed week, and even Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said tighter policy has created financial pain for some AI companies. The Federal Reserve has been talking more and more about AI being very inflationary for many weeks now, so naturally, when AI companies are having debt-financing issues, and some are missing on their numbers, the 10-year yield has gone lower even with elevated oil prices and economic data staying firm.

However, imagine for a minute that the Iran conflict was over: oil would be trading between $67 and $82. Imagine that the trade war 2.0 doesn’t get worse and you have an AI slowdown; there’s your trinity for lower mortgage rates. Nothing too drastic, but definitely sub-7%, and we’ve all seen what mortgage demand can do when rates drop below 6.64%.

So there’s a pathway to 7%, but there’s also a pathway for rates to stay above 7% if the AI story rebounds, the conflict doesn’t end, and the trade war continues. This, of course, would need the economic data to stay very positive, as it has recently. Since Sept. 10, a clear head-and-shoulders pattern has formed in the 10-year yield so what I said above can break that lower and get us sub-7% rates.

Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multi-year lows. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%, since mortgage rates would already be over 8% now if this were not the case. Not only that, it would have been impossible to get mortgage rates near 7% again without a much bigger move lower with the 10-year yield.That said, when the 10-year yield moves lower at times, spreads can widen after a big move up because their job is to compress volatility. Now, this does wear off over time, and we can head lower again. What you don’t want to see is the Fed suddenly changing course and starting a massive rate-hike cycle, or a credit event like the Silicon Valley Bank crisis.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads were flat at 2.23% from week to week.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level:

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

The key for the last two weeks: lower rates even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending home sales are still higher than two weeks ago. That is all we should take from this move, and we will see how rates affect the data going forward. Rule of thumb for the last three years and 10 months: housing demand typically grows when rates are under 6.64% and heading toward 6%, and doesn’t show growth when rates are over 6.64% and heading above 7%.

Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%.  I expected some week-to-week growth last week, as our tracker showed growth too; we did have a 4% week-to-week gain, but it’s still down significantly year over year. When rates were closer to 6%, every week except one showed year-over-year growth.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:

Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks down year-over-year. In fact, this is the lowest inventory growth in some time. Mostly because rates were lower at the start of the year and we are closer to normal. However, higher mortgage rates and weaker mortgage demand create more inventory, and the year-over-year comps are much easier now than early in the year. These lower comps will be here until July of 2027.

Inventory growth is running at 6.78% even with easier comps.

New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 at a few points this year. One concern I have with rates at current levels is that some sellers might not list because most sellers are also homebuyers. That hasn’t happened yet in the data, so still a very heatlhy year for new listings data.

In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This was true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%, demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1% year over year. In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indexes show growth between 1% and 2%. The latest Case Shiller home price report showed 2.1% growth year over year, but it lags our current data by a few months.

We have a lot of variables this week that can move rates, more than I can count, and they’re big!

We survived the worst-case situation in October, but if this conflict continues, the trade war worsens, and economic data stays firm with an AI rebound, rates could stay elevated. However, today I laid the case for sub-7% rates, and Monday’s episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast will discuss this battle between AI and housing. It will be interesting to see whether the head-and-shoulders pattern we’re seeing with the 10-year yield holds or breaks lower.

This week will be a good test of the bond market’s appetite for bonds now that the AI god has shown some weakness. And now, picture this environment with no more conflict and the trade war not getting worse, we would have already been under 7% today.

#5584. AI agents cut critical research time for humanitarian teams in conflict zones

Humanitarian groups working in conflict zones are finding that agentic AI can shorten the research cycle between a crisis and an informed response.

Cloudera Inc. has built its AI strategy around deployment flexibility, and one nonprofit partner is testing that approach on the front lines. But the aim is to give analysts a faster starting point, not to automate research, according to Aaron Eubank (pictured), director of data science at Prosper Global, formerly Mercy Corps.

“It’s not the final report that’s going to be pushed out to the humanitarian community and teams, but rather a starting point that analysts can use to continue to iterate on their own research,” Eubank said. “We want to keep the agency in the hands of the researchers themselves.”

Eubank spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how multi-agent AI is accelerating humanitarian research, VERA’s early results in conflict zones and the importance of keeping researchers in control. (* Disclosure below.)

Prosper Global works in about 30 countries with communities facing conflict, climate change and economic hardship. Its crisis analysts’ research could take days to weeks, so the organization built VERA with Cloudera, a multi-agent research engine that uses Cloudera AI Studios, runs on Amazon Web Services Inc. and taps models from Anthropic PBC. Agents pull from sources such as ReliefWeb, conflict tracker ACLED and local news, and a final agent assembles the findings, Eubank explained.

“Agents allow us to really kind of tailor the process for how this research is done,” Eubank said. “Then it will allow us to then add further resources in the future and really have a curated research process that we wouldn’t have had with some of the earlier iterations of generative AI.”

In Sudan, VERA cut desk research for an agricultural report from five or six days to two, saving about $1,500, Eubank noted. In Colombia, an employee with no security background produced an election security report in a few hours. VERA, launched in June, also runs in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ukraine.

“The risks and the contexts are different in each place that we work,” Eubank said. “It’s important to really take a measured and slow approach as we go through that.”

#5583. MetaGuard AI Launches Vanguard to Harden Cyber Defenses Through Agentic AI-Driven Attack-and-Defense Simulations

Quantum Ventura spin-off brings affordable, automated cybersecurity to small and mid-sized businesses in the U.S. and Japan, from US$4,999 a year; LK Partners named distributor for Japan and the Asia-Pacific region.

SAN JOSE, Calif., and TOKYO, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MetaGuard AI, Inc., a spin-off of defense technology developer Quantum Ventura Inc., today launched two AI security products: CNRT Vanguard, which stages simulated cyberattacks in isolated test environments to assess defensive responses, and CNRT CodeLens, which checks software code for security flaws and offers fixes. Available immediately, both products expand CyberNeuro-RT (CNRT) into a comprehensive cybersecurity platform.

CyberNeuro-RT redefines cybersecurity with autonomous, AI-powered defense for Petabyte-Scale Enterprise Intelligence.

Michigan State University, IIT Palakkad, OpenPOWER Foundation (a Linux Foundation member), SRM University-India, and Objection Automation Inc. are running proof-of-concept trials. In a controlled test reported by Quantum Ventura, Vanguard's AI defender agents shut down a password-guessing and network-scanning attempt in under a minute â closing the targeted port before the attacker agents could strike again.

Vanguard: rehearse attacks and identify defensive gaps

Vanguard (from US$4,999 a year) runs automated exercises in which AI agents act as attackers and defenders. Using a prebuilt lab or a replica of the customer's environment rather than live systems, the agents attack, detect, and respond in a continuous cycle. Exercises run in isolated, disposable virtual machines with safeguards. Vanguard scores each exercise and identifies gaps in detection.

Vanguard records attack and defense actions as labeled training data generated by the simulations. Customers can export it in CNRT-compatible or custom formats and use it to retrain CyberNeuro-RT's machine-learning models or other detection models.

CodeLens: catch security flaws before software release

CodeLens (from US$3,999 a year) uses AI agents to analyze software source code in an isolated virtual machine where AI reviewer agents challenge each finding to reduce false alarms. CodeLens then prioritizes the vulnerabilities based on how easily attackers could exploit them. Fixes are offered for manual review or automatic application.  Both products support Claude, GPT, or fully local AI models.

"Vanguard's closed-loop red-team/blue-team architecture strengthens customers' defenses with data from realistic attacks, so their defenses can be hardened with every exercise," said Srini Vasan, President and CEO of Quantum Ventura.  "Vanguard and CodeLens add more firepower to the unified CNRT ecosystem at affordable price points."

LK Partners, Tokyo, has been appointed master distributor for Japan and Asia-Pacific.

"As cyberattacks increase, CNRT gives Japan's small and medium-sized businesses affordable access to enterprise-grade AI protection," said Yasuyuki Morikawa, CEO of LK Partners.

#5582. SpaceX is reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile for wireless market push

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Any deal for EchoStar's wireless unit may require consent from AT&T and T-Mobile, whose networks Boost Mobile leases

SpaceX is negotiating to acquire EchoStar’s Boost Mobile wireless service, or to secure use of its network, Reuters reported, citing The Washington Post.

SpaceX has been in discussions with EchoStar over the past several months about rolling out a wireless service of its own, according to The Washington Post, which cited unnamed sources. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk met with EchoStar Chairman Charlie Ergen last month.

Boost Mobile leases its network from AT&T $T and T-Mobile $TMUS. Its leasing agreements may not carry over to a buyer unless the carriers sign off, so a SpaceX service may need their consent, according to The Washington Post.

According to Reuters, SpaceX intends to construct a mobile network, called Starlink Mobile, that blends satellite and terrestrial technology. The network would link its orbiting satellites to land-based equipment in order to take on AT&T, Verizon $VZ and T-Mobile. A Boost Mobile deal would give SpaceX a customer base already in place and a way to distribute its service, according to Reuters.

EchoStar's wireless customer count stood at 7.38 million as of the second quarter's close, with Boost Mobile and Gen Mobile accounting for most of them.

SpaceX has set a long-term goal of $1 trillion in revenue and is working to launch a fourth nationwide mobile operator, according to MarketWatch. MarketWatch put the market opportunity at about $235 billion.

Separately, a published report described exploratory talks between Musk and tower operator Crown Castle, according to MarketWatch.

SpaceX and EchoStar had not responded to requests for comment, according to Reuters.

EchoStar stock climbed roughly 3.4% before the opening bell Monday, while T-Mobile stock dropped 2%. Shares of AT&T and Verizon also edged lower.

#5581. AI’s production push puts data platforms on the hook for results

Enterprise data platforms must turn AI pilots into measurable business returns while overcoming the data access, sovereignty and cost barriers that stand between experimentation and production.

The conversation is shifting from what AI can do to how companies make it pay off. One data platform provider has responded by folding its post-sales teams under a single leader, giving customers one voice from onboarding through renewal, according to Patricia Bogoevici (pictured), chief customer officer of Cloudera Inc. The mandate now is to align those teams with customers’ business objectives and help them make better use of the technology they have already paid for.

“When I look at things in terms of customers, for me, technology makes sense only when customers are using it,” Bogoevici said. “I am measured on how customers realize value with Cloudera.”

Bogoevici spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed moving AI into production, improving customer adoption and measuring business value. (* Disclosure below.)

The barriers customers face fall into three categories, starting with data access, according to Bogoevici. A study of more than 1,300 information technology specialists found that roughly 80% named data access as the biggest obstacle. Governance and sovereignty come next, because data sits scattered across silos with differing rules on where it can live.

“Not [all] data can be moved to cloud. Not [all] data needs to be in every place,” she said. “It’s about protection, it’s about sovereignty, it’s about on-prem and it’s about air-gap environment.”

The final hurdle is scale. A pilot running on a subset of data rarely shows what a full deployment will cost or return, which leaves total cost of ownership and return on investment unclear, she explained. Cloudera’s answer is Anywhere Cloud, which it plans to release in November, alongside a partnership with Mistral AI SAS that brings open-weight models into the platform.

“It’s one thing to run the pilot in a subset of data,” Bogoevici said. “It’s a completely different thing to run it [at] full scale and understand the results you get from the AI models and understand the value and how you calculate it.”

#5580. How metro-level trends create compelling multifamily opportunities

Arbor and Chandan Economics flag select Carolinas, coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros where supply pressure is easing

As multifamily fundamentals strengthen, new data show why smart market selection is becoming one of the industry’s biggest competitive advantages. The factors driving national multifamily growth — including population, job gains and rental demand — are causing metro-level performance to increasingly vary. Arbor Realty Trust and Chandan Economics’ latest Top Markets for Multifamily Investment Report Fall 2026 highlights this shift and identifies the areas benefiting most from the trend.

In various parts of the country, and for different reasons, select markets with strong upside stand out.

The research report explains that well-positioned investors are more likely to realize returns in these targeted markets where supply pressures are easing, renter demand remains durable, affordability supports resident retention and financing remains accessible.

As national multifamily fundamentals remain stable, metro-level market performance is less predictable. Some metros are experiencing stronger occupancy, broader rent growth and declining development activity, while others continue to work through elevated supply pipelines.

This divergence reflects differences in the timing and scale of new deliveries, as well as local economic and population growth trends. Markets with less supply pressure have generally returned to stronger operating fundamentals more quickly than those still absorbing a large wave of new construction.

For example, markets that consistently attract new residents often benefit from stronger housing demand and greater long-term stability. In recent years, metros such as Raleigh, Nashville and Charlotte have recorded significant domestic migration alongside positive natural population growth, helping strengthen rental demand even amid broader economic uncertainty, according to the report.

Arbor’s research suggests that the strongest-performing markets are those where economic growth intersects with housing constraints. Intense renter demand is being driven by a combination of population growth, labor market strength, limited housing supply and overall market tightness.

Raleigh serves as a compelling example. The market ranks among the leaders in both population and employment growth while maintaining a low unemployment rate and favorable business environment. The combination of improving vacancies and the presence of major universities that help create a consistent pipeline of highly educated workers is supporting both economic expansion and apartment demand.

As financing decisions are becoming more closely tied to market-specific fundamentals, dependable agency financing can provide greater certainty in competitive markets. Arbor’s comprehensive platform is uniquely positioned to help investors connect opportunity, financing, and execution across the country.

Partnering with an experienced lender that understands local supply-demand dynamics and can help borrowers access disciplined capital is key to staying ahead in markets with strong fundamentals.

#5579. XTEINK Launches AI InkApp Store, Bringing AI Creation to E-Readers

AI creation, an open API, on-device runtime, and app distribution let users turn ideas into apps for magnetic e-paper devices.

NEW YORK, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XTEINK, a pioneer in ultra-portable magnetic e-paper devices, today launched its AI InkApp Store to international markets. The platform connects AI-assisted creation, an open API, on-device runtime and app distribution, turning plain-language prompts into shareable apps.

Through InkApp AI Studio, users describe a feature in words and AI generates the code. They can preview and refine it in a browser-based simulator, then send apps directly to a compatible device or submit them to the store for review and distribution.

The platform currently supports the XTEINK X4 Pro, with support for the X4 Classic expected by the end of 2026. XTEINK's magnetic e-readers have earned prestigious recognition from TIME, Lifehacker, and WIRED for their innovative design and portable reading experience.

XTEINK's product philosophy began with a simple idea: add a lightweight reading screen to the back of a smartphone. AI InkApp Store extends that idea from reading to creating, letting users build tools for their daily routines, from reading companions and to-do lists to custom clocks and interactive games.

"From my first day at XTEINK, I wanted to expand what the device could do," said Eric Xu, head of AI at XTEINK. "I want anyone interested in using natural language to interact with an e-paper device to be able to create apps that meet their own needs."

XTEINK began prototyping AI-generated e-paper apps in January 2026, made it a formal project in March and launched InkApp AI Studio in July. By Oct. 29, more than 100 developers worldwide had created over 700 projects and engaged in over 18,000 AI conversations. Across its global app store, more than 360 apps were available, about half of them user-created, and the store had received over 1,100 submissions, including updates.

The platform handles image conversion, interface components, fonts, app storage and device compatibility. Made public on Oct. 10, the InkApp API reached version 2.17 by Oct. 29, following 34 iterations and 20 proposals co-created with the users and developers. Capabilities include live internet access, auto-save, reading status, Bluetooth keyboards and customizable interfaces.

The open API provides a foundation for development, the on-device runtime executes apps, AI Studio supports creation and preview, and the app store connects creators with users. Apps are tested in simulators and on devices, while store submissions undergo human review. Together, these four components enable users to create, test, deploy, and share their own applications. They also extend XTEINK's brand idea, The Other Side: the other side of your phone can hold the content you chooseâand run the apps you create.

XTEINK InkApp AI Studio is now available. The XTEINK X4 Pro has an MSRP of $99, comes in Space Black and Mist Gray, and is available through Amazon and XTEINK's website. The XTEINK X4 Classic has an MSRP of $79, comes in Space Black and Mist Gray, and is available through Amazon and XTEINK's website.

About XTEINKXTEINK is creating a new category of e-readers that redefines where and how people read. With a focus on exceptional portability and simplicity, XTEINK's innovations have helped millions of readers discover new ways to enjoy their favorite books. Building on its magnetic-native hardware design, XTEINK is developing an ecosystem that brings together licensed reading content, open apps, and third-party developers. In just one year since the company's founding in 2025, XTEINK has become one of the most popular e-reader brands on Amazon U.S., with its devices now available in 71 markets. #5577. The race to deploy AI agents finds a familiar hurdle in data access

That shift favors companies that have spent years governing sensitive data at scale. Cloudera Inc. is betting on Cloudera Anywhere Cloud, a hybrid data and AI platform that spans public clouds and on-premises environments. The company has long been strong on governance, security and scalability but weaker on usability, a gap the new platform was built to close, according to Leo Brunnick (pictured), chief product officer of Cloudera.

“It turns out that the model is ultimately not going to be what separates your success from your competitor’s success,” Brunnick said. “The things that are going to separate you are, number one, your unique data. Your unique data and your unique processes, your alpha — what makes you a business.”

Brunnick spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI agents must follow users’ data permissions, the forces pushing AI workloads back into corporate data centers and how packaged blueprints and partnerships can simplify private AI adoption. (* Disclosure below.)

Customers rarely want a new platform for its own sake, so Cloudera is selling solutions to specific problems instead. Its packaged blueprints and expanded partnerships with Mistral AI SAS, Nvidia Corp. and Vast Data Inc. target private AI use cases such as fraud detection. Mistral, which specializes in open-weight models for on-prem inferencing, also lends Cloudera something it has lacked in the AI market.

“Cloudera already had the capabilities. What we don’t have is a lot of credibility around AI. People don’t think of us as an AI company,” Brunnick said. “What Mistral is allowing us to do is increase our capabilities slightly and increase our credibility astronomically.”

The harder work lies in governance. Agents need to see data across the entire company to be useful, so each one must know who the user is and what that user is permitted to see, Brunnick explained.

“Since the agent needs to be able to see everything in the company, the agent needs to know who you are and what your permissions are,” Brunnick said. “That’s what they need to get right so they can actually put stuff into production that doesn’t blow up on them.”

#5576. Stop competing on commission splits: Make agent production a recruiting advantage

A split-first recruiting strategy invites a race to the bottom. Brokerages can compete by proving how their operating system, workflows and automation help agents respond faster, nurture more contacts and convert more transactions.   AI Summary

Commission splits have long been one of the most visible and powerful tools brokerages have to attract agents. And while compensation will always matter, competing primarily on splits can put brokerages in a difficult position. The reality is that there is always another brokerage willing to offer agents just a little bit more.Brokerage leaders have an opportunity to rethink how they approach recruiting by shifting the conversation from what agents keep to what they can produce. After all, a better split of $0 is still $0!

A more sustainable recruiting strategy is to compete on something that matters just as much to agents – their ability to build a productive book of business. For brokerage leaders, that means shifting the recruiting conversation from percentage splits to how they are going to help them produce.

Agents don’t join a brokerage simply to receive a commission split. They join to build a business. They need opportunities, marketing support, tools to manage their pipeline and systems that help them stay connected with prospects and past clients alike.

Yet, many agents struggle to consistently turn those resources into transactions. Leads go unanswered. Prospects fall through the cracks. Databases become outdated. Agents push follow-up aside when they’re busy with active clients. For brokerages, this creates an opportunity to differentiate.

Instead of positioning technology and support as a collection of features and offerings, brokerages can make them part of a broader production strategy that helps agents spend more time on revenue-generating activities. By demonstrating how technology functions as its own operating system, keeping agents on task and productive, brokerages can articulate how workflows impact transactions. That is a much more compelling recruiting conversation than competing on just another percentage point.

Today’s technology lets brokerages truly rethink how they support agents. Automation and agentic AI platforms can not only take on repetitive activities such as initial lead engagement, follow-up, database nurturing and marketing outreach, but proactively manage workflows to prioritize and determine the best next step to help agents achieve their goals and deliver outcomes. These innovations provide agents with what they need most – time and space to focus on building client and prospect relationships.Before sending agents out into the wild with new technology advancements in hand, brokerages need to review the existing agent workflow and identify where productivity breaks down.

That insight can inform where and how current technology innovations can provide support, and addressing those gaps can create leverage across the firm.

An agent who has an agentic AI system consistently working leads and nurturing relationships has more opportunities to convert. An agent who spends less time on repetitive administrative tasks has more time for prospecting, appointments and clients. And a brokerage that can demonstrate that productivity advantage has a stronger story to tell prospective recruits.

A production-focused recruiting strategy also gives brokerage leaders a better way to demonstrate their value. That doesn’t mean promising every agent a specific number of transactions, however. Markets, experience level and individual business practices vary and play a role in compensation. But it does mean showing agents that the brokerage has built an infrastructure designed to help them create and convert opportunities.

That distinction matters for retention as well. When agents can see the connection between the resources their brokerage provides and the growth of their business, the brokerage becomes more than the company holding their license and becomes a true partner in their production.

Commission splits are easy to compare. Production support is harder to replicate. For brokerages competing for talent, that can be an advantage. The strongest recruiting proposition may not be the brokerage that promises agents they can keep the most from every transaction; it may be the one that can credibly demonstrate how it helps agents create more transactions in the first place.

To do so, that requires a shift in mindset. Don’t just recruit agents with an offer, recruit them with a business-building strategy. When brokerages make agent production a core part of their value proposition, recruiting, technology and retention stop being separate initiatives. They become components of the same goal: helping agents build more productive, sustainable businesses and creating a brokerage that grows alongside them.

Dave Carter is the VP of Marketing at Lofty.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5575. Sedin Technologies Honored with 'Excellence in Maintenance Management' Award at MaximoWorld 2026

SUNNYVALE, Calif., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sedin Technologies, the company behind the EAM360 mobile platform for IBM Maximo, received the 'Excellence in Maintenance Management' award at MaximoWorld 2026, the premier global conference for IBM Maximo and enterprise asset management (EAM) professionals.

Organized annually by Reliabilityweb to recognize achievements in asset performance and operational reliability, the MaximoWorld Awards select winners from a highly competitive pool of global nominations submitted by top-tier enterprises and technology integrators worldwide. Out of this global field, Sedin Technologies emerged as the winner in the 'Excellence in Maintenance Management' category for its outstanding contributions to asset digitalization, operational resilience, and field workforce enablement.

The award recognizes Sedin's continued commitment to helping organizations strengthen maintenance management with smarter, more connected solutions built for IBM Maximo.

The recognition follows Sedin's expertise in IBM Maximo Application Suite (MAS) migration paired with a full EAM360 mobile application rollout for a billion-dollar hospitality brand headquartered in Las Vegas, with sites across the Asia-Pacific region. Delivered across five integrated resorts operating 24/7, the program unified five siloed sites onto a single global IBM MAS SaaS instance and rolled out EAM360 to a 3,000+ multilingual frontline workforce completed in phased go-live waves with a six-hour cutover and zero downtime to live operations.

Backed by 11 certified professionals, the Maximo practice brings deep expertise across MAS modernization, integrations, and managed services. Built on this foundation, EAM360 extends Maximo into the field through native, offline-first mobile apps for technicians, inspectors, storekeepers, and managers on iOS and Android. With seamless Maximo integration and AI-driven assistance, Sedin helps asset-intensive organizations improve data accuracy, reduce downtime, and make smarter maintenance decisions.

The complex upgrade delivered displayed strong partnership and collaborative spirit. Sedin Technologies, the client, and IBM together achieved flawless migration despite numerous challenges and aligned closely on planning, execution, and risk mitigation. From database conversion and tight downtime windows to large-scale data movement and integration reconfiguration, the teams addressed each hurdle through shared ownership and technical synergy. The successful, first-time-right go-live stands as a testament to the power of partnership, trust, and coordinated execution. The transformation enabled measurable business outcomes through improved system reliability, scalability, and operational efficiency.

"Most migrations end at go-live. We treat it as the starting line. The real test is whether the technician on the floor finds the work easier the next morning, and on this program, the answer was a clear yes. We cleaned up years of inconsistent data, redesigned maintenance workflows across sites, and gave every field user an app they actually want to use: simple, intuitive, and built for frontline work. That blend of strong Maximo delivery and a field-first mobile product is what sets us apart. This MaximoWorld recognition tells us our approach is working, and we look forward to bringing it to more asset-intensive organizations worldwide."â Arul Varadarajan, Managing Partner & EAM Practice Head, Sedin Technologies

Sedin Technologies is a technology services company serving clients across North America, the Middle East, and Asia Pacific. #5574. Beyond the books: Real-time data is driving a small-business lending surge

Small businesses have long treated cash flow management as an afterthought, tallying expenses after the money is gone. Now, financial platforms are folding payments, payroll, credit and lending into one system that can see money moving both ways — and predict where it is headed.

That shift puts software providers in direct competition with banks for small-business credit. Intuit Inc. says its view of both sides of the ledger, paired with AI pushing finance toward automation, gives it an edge traditional lenders cannot match, according to Todd Denbo (pictured), senior vice president of lending and commercial leader of Money at Intuit.

“We can see the expenses you’ve got queued up,” Denbo said. “For us, we can effectively predict that you’re going to have a cash flow shortage. That’s why we’ve got our lending businesses as well, so we can proactively offer lines of credit or a term loan to bridge that gap.”

Denbo spoke with theCUBE’s Alison Kosik and Christophe Bertrand at Intuit Connect, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Intuit uses real-time financial data and AI to help small businesses manage cash flow and automate financial tasks. (* Disclosure below.)

Intuit lent about $400 million a year four years ago and almost $7 billion in its most recent fiscal year, according to Denbo. That growth reflects data averaging 625,000 data points per small business across the 10 million companies already on the platform. Because those businesses manage their finances on Intuit’s platform, the company can see money coming in and going out as it happens.

“Most lenders in this space rely on outdated trends that are from the commercial credit bureaus or the personal credit bureaus, or they’re trying to infer data that is just very challenging to infer,” Denbo said. “All of that is real-time.”

Intuit has also added spending data through its QuickBooks-integrated business credit card, which lets owners control employee spending before money leaves. The company has extended QuickBooks into Claude and ChatGPT as well, though automation still stops short of moving money on its own, Denbo explained. AI can handle the financial groundwork while business owners retain the final say over actions involving their money.

“We are gathering the data, we’re analyzing the data, we are packaging a response or a draft,” Denbo said. “But when it comes to anything that is moving money or sending a draft out, that’s where we’re waiting for, effectively, a human intervention.”

#5573. Marriott posted earnings that beat expectations as U.S. hotel demand rose

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Marriott raised its 2026 RevPAR growth outlook to 4.5% to 5% as RevPAR in the U.S. and Canada rose 7.4% in the quarter

Marriott $MAR International reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $3.02 a share on Monday, up from $2.47 a year earlier, as hotel demand in the U.S. and Canada grew.

That topped the $2.84 a share analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal. The average estimate in a separate analyst survey was $2.86 a share, according to The Associated Press.

Reported net income rose 9% to $794 million, or $3.04 a share, from $728 million, or $2.67 a share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 8% to $7.005 billion. That topped the $6.93 billion analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal, though it fell short of the $7.04 billion estimate cited by The Associated Press.

Revenue per available room, known as RevPAR, climbed 6.5% worldwide as hotels charged more per night and filled more of their rooms. RevPAR rose 7.4% in the U.S. and Canada and 4.4% in international markets, led by Asia Pacific excluding China, where it rose over 9%.

"In the U.S. & Canada, RevPAR rose over 7 percent, with broad-based growth across customer segments and chain scales," Anthony Capuano, Marriott's president and chief executive, said in a statement.

Capuano said results in the Middle East were still being hurt by the conflict there, though conditions had gotten better since the second quarter.

Marriott raised its full-year 2026 worldwide RevPAR growth outlook to 4.5% to 5%. The prior forecast was 3% to 3.5%, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The company expects full-year adjusted earnings of $12.07 to $12.14 a share. The prior range was $11.64 to $11.81, according to The Wall Street Journal. Marriott expects per-share adjusted profit for the fourth quarter to land between $3.14 and $3.21.

Adjusted EBITDA rose 12% to $1.51 billion. Marriott added about 20,100 net rooms during the quarter, and net rooms grew 4.6% from a year earlier.

Its development pipeline reached a record 4,209 properties and more than 634,000 rooms. The company bought back $1.3 billion of its stock in the quarter.

#5572. Longbridge’s Larissa Morrell on the evolution of reverse mortgage products and partnerships

Longbridge Financial is scaling HELOC for Seniors after its first year, with a focus on expanding distribution beyond retail. Newly promoted VP Larissa Morrell said monthly volume is about $5 million and the company built a dedicated sales team to support borrowers.  AI Summary

Last month, Longbridge Financial announced a key leadership move with its promotion of Larissa Morrell to serve as the company’s vice president of product development.

Morrell, a former director of sales logistics and development at Reverse Mortgage Funding, is tasked with leading product development efforts across Longbridge’s technology, operations, compliance and sales teams. She has more than 25 years of industry experience and her promotion follows the company’s recent moves to expand its offerings beyond traditional reverse mortgages.

She played a key role in last year’s launch of HELOC for Seniors, which provides additional borrower flexibility through interest-only payments and a funding timeline of as little as five business days.

“In speaking with [CEO] Chris Mayer quite some time ago, it was very evident that we had this huge number of borrowers who needed some sort of product to best fit where they were in their retirement planning,” Morrell told HousingWire’s Reverse Mortgage Daily.

“Maybe they weren’t ready for a reverse mortgage yet, but they did need to be able to get some equity out of their house. They also didn’t want to go into payment shock after 10 years or so, when they would probably be at the point where they’re retiring, so a traditional HELOC wasn’t right for them.”

In the latest installment of the Monday Morning Q&A, Morrell offered her thoughts on the first-year success of HELOC for Seniors, the company’s strategy to serve a multitude of borrower types, and potential paths for the industry to grow awareness and business as seniors contemplate how to utilize trillions of dollars in home equity.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Neil Pierson: Take us through the work that went into releasing HELOC for Seniors, how it’s been received and who it’s been able to help.

Larissa Morrell: Launching HELOC for Seniors has absolutely been one of the greatest accomplishments of my career.

We needed to come up with a product that really suited that particular borrower need. And the best way we were able to do that is through Chris’s partnerships. He had a relationship with the Figure Technology Solutions team, and so we were able to fast track what we were trying to do through the Figure platform.

Quite honestly, that was able to give us a launching pad that went a lot faster than if we were to build it ourselves. We were able to launch in about a year or so, which is pretty incredible when you think about it. In the year since we launched it, it’s really been about taking a look in the mirror and saying, “Where do we have to do things differently?”

I’ll give you a good example of where we might have missed the mark with our particular borrower demographic. The way we launched our platform, it was very online. And people in the younger borrower demographic, they’re absolutely comfortable with being online. They’re OK with applying online. They’re OK with uploading their documentation online.

But we also found that people still like actually talking to a loan officer to help them. Initially, we did not have a sales team specific to HELOC for Seniors, but we found that we had to build one. We wanted to make sure we had salespeople who could further support this concept, answer borrower questions and help them through the process.

In building that team to support HELOC for Seniors, that’s when we really saw the rubber meet the road. That combination of building a specific sales team along with the technology, that’s where we saw things really improve.

Pierson: How successful has the product been from a loan count or volume perspective? It won’t show up in HECM or proprietary reverse mortgage data, but where does it stand in relation?

Morrell: We’re consistently hitting $5 million a month with it, so it’s definitely not a bread-and-butter, core type of business for us, but it is a way for us to have an additional outlet for customers who need a HELOC and don’t want a reverse mortgage.

I think you’ll see, over the course of the next year, is how we’re going to be changing different parts of that product to further expand our distribution. And distribution is the key. Right now, we have a very small population of salespeople who are selling the product, but now we’re going to be focusing on a larger distribution network through our wholesale partners, where we can really get volume numbers increasing, as opposed to just our retail business.

Pierson: About this time last year, Longbridge announced it was lowering the rate to 7.99% on its Platinum proprietary products. Is that still intact today or have you raised the rate?

Morrell: Our current rates have increased slightly, but we have made significant amounts of changes to our Platinum product suite. A really significant change was lowering the loan amount. With home values, we go as low as $300,000. We rolled out in additional states last week. We’re rolling out in Wisconsin this week.

Initially, when we launched our Platinum product, it was really considered to be more of a jumbo product. It was the coasts that we focused on, because those tend to have the higher-value homes. But now we have so much more opportunity with the entire country, with the loan limits having a $300,000 minimum.

In this particular economic market, we have something called the Platinum Promise. In a market that seems to bounce all over the place, what a borrower qualifies for at the time of their application could change. Instead of changing our PLF tables throughout the application process, we give them 30 days from the time they apply to opt out, so they don’t have the uncertainty that if rates happen to change, will the amount of money I qualified for drop by $30,000 or $40,000? We’ve seen that happen.

Pierson: Let’s talk about the two distinct groups of reverse mortgage borrowers today. There’s the needs-based borrower, who wants cash right away. You’ve also got the affluent borrower with a higher home value and more income who uses the loan as a retirement planning tool. As a company, how are you thinking about these groups to serve them differently?

Morrell: We absolutely run the gamut of who we’re talking to every single day. You have needs-based borrowers who, at the end of the day, just need as much money as humanly possible. We also have the other spectrum that you mentioned — clients who are affluent and want to use this particular product to make sure they’re setting themselves up for the future.

We have something called Platinum Preserve, which actually allows the borrower to protect a certain amount of their home value. If they’re worried about whoever is inheriting their house, this allows them that sense of security that they’re not taking all the equity out.

Another thing I’ve experienced over my years in the reverse mortgage industry is that, historically, a reverse mortgage was really something for people of the older retiree demographic — late 70s, 80s, 90s. Now we do not have that same demographic. Now we’re looking at people of a younger generation. They’re still working. They might be using a reverse mortgage to pay off credit card debt or cover increasing expenses.

You can say we’re looking at completely different borrowers. Madonna is old enough to get a reverse mortgage. Kris Jenner could be our spokesperson. These are the people you don’t think of getting a reverse mortgage, but they are old enough.

Pierson: Before coming to Longbridge, you spent some time with MetLife, a large and well-known insurance company. How do insurance companies as a group relate to reverse mortgages? Are there some missed opportunities there for product partnerships or capital investments?

Morrell: A challenging part of our industry is that insurance agents and financial advisors cannot be paid for the referrals of reverse mortgages. As much as we would love for them to offer our products, there’s just a split that we cannot be accepting leads from referral sources like a MetLife and they could actually receive something in return. That’s how agents work; they want to get compensated for those referrals.

It doesn’t mean that we aren’t talking to people like that all the time, but unlike our partners and friends in the UK, where insurance agents and financial advisers can get paid for reverse mortgage referrals, we don’t have the same regulations here in the United States. If we could compensate those agents, that would be a windfall, because I think they completely understand where it fits in the puzzle.

Pierson: Big banks used to be involved in the reverse mortgage space, and there are reasons why they’ve pulled back, but there’s been talk recently about credit unions expanding their presence. Should traditional reverse mortgage lenders be paying more attention to those companies? Would you welcome more competition in the space?

Morrell: Absolutely — we always want more competition, to have so many more opportunities to allow people to understand the product. As I mentioned earlier, distribution is really our biggest challenge, and we do have partners in our broker channel that are credit unions.

Brokers are sometimes threatened — if I’m a credit union and I’m offering a reverse mortgage, does that mean the lender is going to end up offering their products, which will take away from the core credit union business? But at the end of the day, to put a reverse mortgage or a HELOC for Seniors in the product suite for credit unions and banks, that’s absolutely what we would want to do, so we can continue to make these products mainstream.

It doesn’t make sense to just have the small market of originators available when these products could help the entire country with their current challenges, in terms of what the cost of living looks like compared to their retirement income.

Pierson: Home equity investments have been something of a controversial topic in the reverse mortgage space. Do you see HEIs as a direct competitor? Do you think they’ll be offered by more brokers and lenders once the regulatory aspects are worked out?

Morrell: You bring up a good point about the regulatory aspect, and that’s where we need to make sure there’s a level playing field. At the end of the day, we need to protect our borrowers’ interests. Do they truly understand what they’re signing up for and are there the same guardrails in place so that a borrower understands what that means for their house and their future? Are they being counseled on what that particular product is doing for them?

I do view them as a competitor, I would say, but it’s not an apples-to-apples comparison in terms of what we’re offering to our borrowers and what the HEI market is looking to do. I do think there probably needs to be more regulation so that the lines are not as blurry.

But obviously, right now, there’s so much home equity that people are trying to leverage and use to a borrower’s advantage. I don’t condemn people using those products because we’re all trying to figure out the products that best meets the customers’ needs.

#5570. Intuit targets the mid-market ERP gap with AI

Growing companies that outgrow entry-level accounting software face a hard choice: Stay put or gamble on a mid-market ERP that promises automation but often brings cost and disruption. Artificial intelligence is now giving financial software providers a way to close that gap without forcing businesses through a risky migration.

Intuit Inc. is pushing finance toward automation, and its mid-market strategy targets companies caught between small-business tools and legacy systems. Those businesses face the problems of success, such as more customers, more entities and more currencies, and need technology to help them scale, according to Ashley Still (pictured), executive vice president and general manager of mid-market at Intuit.

“Actually, 50% of mid-market ERP implementations fail,” Still said. “So, 50% of businesses that leave their existing financial platform to go to what they think will be a better platform for them actually fail in that implementation. It typically costs $60,000 and six months.”

Still spoke with Alison Kosik and Christophe Bertrand at Intuit Connect, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why mid-market ERP migrations fail, how Intuit Enterprise Suite fills the gap and how AI agents are taking on routine finance work. (* Disclosure below.)

Intuit’s answer is Intuit Enterprise Suite, which lets growing companies scale on the platform where their data already lives instead of starting over. Intuit has added industry-specific editions for construction, manufacturing and nonprofits. Still described the product as the CFO’s command center.

“First, they actually can see a complete view of the business for the first time ever, all of their entities in one place, consolidated financials,” she said. “That really is game-changing because it gives them the ability to make real-time decisions.”

Accounting firms are central to the plan, since 70% of mid-market businesses work with an accountant or advisor, according to Still. Intuit is automating routine work such as categorizations and reconciliations, while its new Agent Studio lets a business or firm build a customizable agent just by describing what it needs. Accounting firms Citrin Cooperman and Sorren have already put agents into production through the tool, she noted.

“The point is the expectation is that more and more of the tedious work is done for a finance team or done for a firm rather than them having to do everything themselves,” Still said.

#5568. Oil prices fall more than 4% as Iran peace talks ease supply fears

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Brent crude for January delivery fell 4.2% to $108.68 a barrel, reversing some of last week's gains ahead of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections

Oil prices tumbled by upwards of 4% Monday, with negotiations to bring the U.S.-Iran conflict to a close soothing worries about Middle East supply.

Brent crude futures expiring in January slid 4.2% to $108.68 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate contracts due in December declined 4.3% to $99.61, while the January contracts shed 4.2% to reach $97.90.

The declines wiped out part of the previous week's rally. Brent had closed out October at a six-month peak.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that negotiations with mediators from Qatar about reopening the Strait of Hormuz were still under way, though no deal had been reached. He added that Iran had sent a delegation headed by a deputy foreign minister to Qatar, while no face-to-face meeting with U.S. officials was on the schedule.

Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, described the move as a technical pullback after last week’s strong gains, according to CNBC. He cited continued optimism about a diplomatic breakthrough, along with a weekend that passed without significant fighting escalating.

The risk of renewed fighting remains. According to The Wall Street Journal, the U.S. has instructed a number of Gulf Arab states to get ready for a possible brief but intense military operation against Iran once Tuesday's midterm elections are over. President Donald Trump has yet to reach a conclusive decision about resuming strikes.

Seven OPEC+ producers decided Sunday to leave their targets for December output as they were. The group, whose members include Saudi Arabia and Russia, will next convene on Nov. 29 to assess output for January.

Regional attacks also continued over the weekend. The Saudi-led coalition announced Sunday an operation against assets that the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen depend on for their drone and missile efforts.

Vice President JD Vance wrote last week to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, to try to revive peace talks. Trump said he had approved the outreach, which was meant to outline a possible structure for talks rather than present a full peace plan.

Qatari mediators also offered a new plan to end the fighting among Iran, the U.S. and Israel. A high-ranking Iranian official dismissed the offer as unacceptable. The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, but the agreement collapsed.

#5567. Strata Land launches as builders face land-capital squeeze

Strata Land Partners launched with backing from Wafra and Hunt and about 1,300 lots. The platform, led by former Landsea Homes president Michael Forsum, targets builders facing tighter land-capital conditions.  AI Summary

A new institutional land-capital player is entering the U.S. homebuilding market as deteriorating industry economics force builders, land sellers, and financial partners to reconsider who bears the risks of residential development.

Wafra, a global alternative investment manager with approximately $30 billion in assets under management, and Hunt Companies, the nearly 80-year-old real estate investment enterprise, announced Monday the launch of Strata Land Partners. The new platform, led by former Landsea Homes president and COO Michael Forsum, will begin with projects totaling approximately 1,300 single-family lots and a mandate to provide flexible land financing to public and private homebuilders and developers nationwide.

New-home demand remains under pressure, builder incentives and mortgage-rate buydowns continue to erode margins, and land prices have been slow to reflect the changed economics of homebuilding. With little evidence that demand-side challenges have bottomed out, builders face the prospect of difficult operating conditions persisting through 2027 and 2028, and potentially beyond.

For builders, the stakes extend beyond securing capital to acquire and develop land. They include preserving financial nimbleness and agility during periods of slower sales, protecting operating margins, and opportunistically securing competitive positions without carrying land obligations that become increasingly burdensome when absorptions come at such a high cost.

For investors entering with fresh capital, however, those conditions create opportunities. Land valuations are beginning to adjust to gravity, established capital providers face pressure from legacy commitments structured in a bygone era of lower rates, easier terms and higher valuations, and capable builders increasingly need financing relationships that can accommodate an uncertain outlook.

Forsum believes these conditions create an opening for Strata.

In an exclusive interview with HousingWire TBD, Forsum described an opportunity to establish a different relationship between builders and their capital providers, informed by four decades of operating homebuilding businesses and investing in residential land.

“I’ve been on the other side of this. I’ve worked with banks, land bankers, and others, and I always felt like I was more of a means to an end to them than a business partner,” Forsum said.

Strata’s formation reflects a broader shift in global investment strategies toward U.S. residential construction and development. As The Builder’s Daily reported after the Zelman Housing Summit, international investment groups are becoming increasingly influential in homebuilder acquisitions, land financing and residential real estate investment, even as near-term housing fundamentals deteriorate.

Wafra brings institutional investment expertise and approximately $30 billion in assets under management, though Strata’s specific capital commitment has not been disclosed. Hunt brings a substantial real estate operating and investment platform, including its recent acquisition of View Homes, which CEO Natasha Gandhi is positioning for future expansion.

The investors’ ambitions are grounded in a long-term view of U.S. housing demand, notwithstanding the industry’s immediate difficulties.

“The U.S. faces a structural shortage of housing, and Strata will enable builders to deliver homes while navigating uncertain environments alongside a creative thought partner able to deliver bespoke, tailored solutions,” said Ryan Brenner, Wafra’s managing director and head of alternative real estate.

For Forsum, the opportunity is more immediate. Builders continue absorbing mortgage-rate buydowns, incentives and elevated construction costs, leaving land as one of the remaining places where development economics must adjust.

“We’re finally starting to see proof out there that things are changing,” he said, describing emerging pressure on land valuations.

Strata intends to enter that adjustment with fresh capital, without the burden of previously acquired assets or financing arrangements negotiated under more optimistic market assumptions.

Forsum’s selection gives Strata something institutional capital alone cannot provide: decades of experience identifying where land investments create competitive advantage and where they can undermine a homebuilding business.

His career includes operating leadership at KB Home, Ryland and Taylor Woodrow/Morrison, followed by residential private equity investment work at Starwood Land Ventures.

At Landsea Homes, Forsum helped build a startup into a multiregional public homebuilder through organic expansion, acquisitions and integration. The strategy depended on identifying capable local operating teams, valuable land positions and opportunities to achieve meaningful market scale.

The underlying principle was that local market knowledge, land access, operating discipline and sufficient scale needed to reinforce one another.

That experience informs Forsum’s conviction that land remains the decisive variable in an industry increasingly able to standardize other parts of its business.

“The one thing that remains unique and always will is land,” Forsum said.

He believes that a builder’s long-term success depends substantially on managing its future land pipeline cost-effectively, without assuming financial risks that could overwhelm the operating business when market conditions change.

Among Strata’s potential customers, Forsum sees a particularly compelling opportunity in privately held homebuilding companies whose operating capabilities and local market expertise may outstrip their access to institutional capital.

Many have spent decades building relationships with landowners, brokers, municipalities, trade contractors, and homebuyers. They understand local development risks and have a time- and cycle-tested ability to deliver homes profitably.

What they often lack is the financial capacity and flexibility of larger publicly traded competitors. That disadvantage becomes more pronounced during a prolonged U-shaped housing downturn.

Public builders generally have greater access to corporate liquidity and financing arrangements that enable them to control future lots without owning all the underlying land. Private builders often rely more heavily on banks, project-level financing, and their own balance sheets to fund acquisition and development.

As sales slow and financing conditions tighten, those differences can determine which builders preserve their pipelines and which must curtail investment, surrender opportunities or accept increasingly expensive capital.

Forsum believes traditional capital providers sometimes underestimate privately held builders because they do not fully understand the operating businesses behind those builders’ financing requests.

“There’s a really big group of private, really well-run, thoughtful, hardworking builders out there that I have run across in my career, some of them I bought, that are just outstanding at what they do,” he said.

Yet, he added, those operators “just don’t get the respect and the nod from the capital markets.”

That take draws on Forsum’s Landsea experience, in which acquiring established regional builders required evaluating not only land assets but also the management teams, local relationships, and operating practices that made those businesses successful.

In Forsum’s view, the economic value of a builder’s land position cannot be separated from its ability to entitle, develop, construct and sell homes in a particular market.

“This isn’t a riskier group. In some cases, it could be even less risky,” Forsum said.

The proposition is not that private builders deserve preferential financing or relaxed underwriting standards. Rather, demonstrated operating competence, local knowledge, and disciplined land investment should play a more prominent role in how capital providers assess risk and structure transactions.

Strata’s announced focus includes helping builders secure land, finance lot development, and manage capital efficiently. Forsum indicated that its ambitions extend beyond traditional land banking.

“We have a broader mandate, but it could be a lot of different things,” he said.

Strata’s opportunity is not simply to provide more capital to homebuilders but to recognize and finance operating capabilities that conventional capital providers may undervalue.

Its success will depend on how it structures investments, prices capital, allocates risk, and responds when projects encounter the inevitable difficulties of a cyclical business.

For land sellers and brokers, a well-capitalized new participant could broaden transaction opportunities as builders become more selective. For homebuilders, the potential value lies in securing financing relationships that remain viable when market conditions deteriorate.

“Strata was built by builders, for builders,” Forsum said in the announcement. “Having spent my career in homebuilding, I see significant demand for a strategic capital partner that understands the industry’s operational nuances and thoughtfully supports builders in achieving their goals.”

The proposition will be tested in a market where builders must protect their businesses from near-term demand weakness while securing the land needed for eventual recovery.

For Forsum, Strata extends the land strategy that helped build Landsea Homes: identifying where value resides, understanding the operating capabilities needed to realize it, and structuring capital commitments around that knowledge.

For the builders Strata hopes to serve, the question is whether that experience translates into better land economics, greater financial flexibility, and stronger businesses over a cycle that may still have years to run.

#5566. The hidden threat in Anthropic’s prospectus: diseconomies of scale

GUEST COLUMN by Jason Bloomberg

As potentially the largest IPO in history, Anthropic PBC is breaking new ground. Its prospectus lists 88 risk factors covering 93 pages alone. From artificial intelligence posing an existential threat to humanity to the possibility AI will blackmail people, the company lists a litany of risks that should make any potential Anthropic investor wary.

One potentially company-sinking risk factor, however, does not explicitly appear in the prospectus: diseconomies of scale.

Diseconomies of scale occur when a company’s average cost of producing each unit of output increases as the company grows.

You would think that given the time and effort that Anthropic devoted to ensuring its list of risk factors was complete that they would have included this one. There is a reason, however, that they missed it, despite the fact that diseconomies of scale is the elephant in the room.

We’ve been down this road before with cloud computing. The fundamental economic driver of the hyperscaler clouds was economies of scale: the larger they became, the lower their cost of each unit of output, leading to massive growth and profitability over time.

Since the AI boom requires massive data center buildouts just as cloud computing does, it might be reasonable to assume that AI will experience the same economic benefits of massive growth that cloud computing enjoyed.

This assumption, however, is likely to be false. To understand why, we must take a look at how the software and cloud businesses scale – and why AI is so different.

Throughout the history of enterprise computing, software has benefited from its negligible marginal cost.

With physical goods, from automobiles to chicken nuggets, every unit has a raw materials and production cost. The more widgets you make, the more those costs add up.

Software is fundamentally different. Once a vendor has spent the money to build an application, it can sell that application to as many customers as it can find, where the cost of delivering additional copies of that application is negligible compared to the original cost of developing it.

This negligible marginal cost enables software vendors to become immensely profitable as their business scales.

Computer hardware, in contrast, is nothing more than more widgets – the more you deploy, the greater your materials and production costs.

Cloud computing combines both software and hardware in its offerings. The software may have negligible marginal cost, but each cloud provider must shell out money for each physical server.

To address this cost challenge, cloud providers take advantage of economies of scale.

The hyperscalers built their clouds by deploying massive numbers of commodity servers. As each firm expanded its business, the cost of each unit of output – say, the cost of providing a server instance or a unit of cloud storage – decreased.

As a result, the cost of servers went down as they scaled, and the cloud computing firms became increasingly profitable as they grew, despite the fact that their business models depended on hardware as well as software.

Back to Anthropic and the rest of the frontier large language model providers: Ostensibly, AI is just a type of software, and Anthropic is running its software in hyperscaled data centers that are essentially clouds. This underlying assumption is implicit in the company’s prospectus.

This assumption, however, is flawed. Frontier model vendors require graphics processing units and other premium, expensive hardware from day one – and their specialized processor requirements continue to accelerate as they rapidly innovate their software.

This advancing specialized processor requirement didn’t impact the rise of the cloud. True, each cloud provider eventually added various specialized hardware instance types as they grew, but those instances didn’t change the fundamental economics of the cloud business.

Anthropic, in contrast, doesn’t have the luxury of deploying commodity hardware to achieve economies of scale. Instead, it must build out expensive servers that only get more expensive as LLMs’ processor requirements continue to advance.

There are also diseconomies of scaling the human side of the AI boom that contrast with the growth of the cloud.

The hyperscalers certainly require an experienced workforce with deep expertise to deploy their clouds and keep them running. But as they grew, they were able to leverage such personnel more efficiently. An admin who managed a thousand physical servers could easily manage 10,000 or a million as the underlying cloud platforms matured.

Unlike the cloud providers, however, Anthropic and the other frontier model vendors must continually scale up the expertise of their teams. New LLMs aren’t simply scaled-out versions of older ones. Each one requires new expertise from expert humans.

Anthropic is battling its competitors to innovate quickly and roll out increasingly powerful models on unprecedented timeframes. As a result, frontier LLM vendor teams experience diseconomies of scale that the hyperscalers never had to face.

Anthropic and the rest of the frontier LLM vendors suffer from a fundamentally novel economic reality, because they must continue to increase their hardware capabilities while upskilling their workforce so they can competitively innovate their software.

They can’t simply run increasingly powerful models on commodity hardware – or even the same hardware they ran the previous generation model on. They must increase their investments in hardware at a pace that keeps up with the pace of software innovation.

The end result is a diseconomy of scale the technology industry has never seen before. We are so used to the negligible marginal cost of software and the massive economies of scale of the cloud, that we are simply unprepared for the diseconomies of scale that frontier LLM vendors like Anthropic must negotiate.

Even though the frontier model marketplace is still quite new, we’re already seeing the impact of its inherent diseconomies of scale as token costs become an increasingly significant expense for consumers of AI.

As LLMs become more powerful and the hardware they require becomes an increasingly expensive bottleneck, it’s just a matter of time until token costs become prohibitively high for a range of AI-based applications.

Anthropic and the other LLM model vendors can try to respond by increasing the efficiency of their more powerful LLMs or rolling out less powerful, and thus less expensive models – assuming their customers buy into these moves.

We may also eventually reach a plateau where the models are sufficiently powerful and the hardware is sufficiently performant, thus enabling more familiar economies of scale to take over. However, no such plateau is in sight.

The question potential Anthropic investors must ask, therefore, is whether the company’s leadership position in the LLM market is a strength or a weakness? Just how far can it innovate and grow before its offerings are too expensive? And what does it do then?

Jason Bloomberg is founder and managing director of Intellyx, which advises business leaders and technology vendors on their digital transformation strategies. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. All of Intellyx’s content is 100% human generated, including this article. Anthropic is not an Intellyx customer.
