#5565. Manufacturing PMI® at 55.5%; October 2026 ISM® Manufacturing PMI® Report

New Orders Growing; Production Growing; Employment Growing; Supplier Deliveries Slowing; Raw Materials Inventories Growing; Customers' Inventories Too Low; Prices Increasing; Imports Growing; Exports Growing

TEMPE, Ariz., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Economic activity in the manufacturing sector expanded in October for the 10th consecutive month, say the nation's supply executives in the latest ISMÂ® Manufacturing PMIÂ® Report.

The report was issued today by Susan Spence, MBA, Chair of the Institute for Supply ManagementÂ® (ISMÂ®) Manufacturing Business Survey Committee.

"The Manufacturing PMIÂ® registered 55.5 percent in October, 1 percentage point above the September figure of 54.5 percent. The overall economy expanded for the 24th month in a row. (A Manufacturing PMIÂ® above 47.5 percent, over a period of time, generally indicates an expansion of the overall economy.) The New Orders Index expanded for the 10th consecutive month after four straight readings in contraction, registering 55.5 percent, up 0.2 percentage point compared to September's figure of 55.3 percent. The October reading of the Production Index (59 percent) is 2.3 percentage points higher than the 56.7 percent recorded in September and the highest since November 2021 (60.5 percent). The Prices Index remained in expansion (or 'increasing' territory), registering 75.2 percent, a 2.7-percentage point decrease compared to September's reading of 77.9 percent. The Backlog of Orders Index registered 54.6 percent, down 1.8 percentage points compared to the 56.4 percent recorded in September. The Employment Index reading of 52.4 percent is down 0.3 percentage point from September's figure of 52.7 percent," says Spence.

"The Supplier Deliveries Index indicated slowing performance for the 11th month in a row after one month in 'faster' territory. The reading of 59.1 percent is up 0.1 percentage point from its September reading of 59 percent. (Supplier Deliveries is the only ISMÂ® PMIÂ® Reports index that is inversed; a reading of above 50 percent indicates slower deliveries, which is typical as the economy improves and customer demand increases.)

"The Inventories Index registered 51.4 percent, returning to expansion and up 2.8 percentage points compared to September's reading of 48.6 percent. The Customers' Inventories Index reading of 41.6 percent is the same as in September.

"The New Export Orders Index gained 0.3 percentage points in October for a reading of 51.2 percent versus 50.9 percent in September. The Imports Index registered 52.9 percent, an increase of 1.9 percentage points compared to September's reading of 51 percent."

Spence continues, "In October, U.S. manufacturing activity remained in expansion territory. Of the five subindexes that make up the PMIÂ®, four (New Orders, Production, Supplier Deliveries and Inventories) grew faster than the previous month, while Employment growth slowed down by 0.3 percentage point. In October, general sentiment got worse for a third month in a row, with 34 percent of the comments positive and 66 percent negative (a 1-to-2 ratio of positive to negative sentiment). Among negative comments, pricing volatility was mentioned in 62 percent, longer lead times 41 percent, tariffs 25 percent and the Iran war 21 percent; most comments mentioned multiple factors.

"In October, three of four demand indicators (the New Orders, Backlog of Orders and New Export Orders indexes) remained in expansion, and the Customers' Inventories Index remained in 'too low' territory, contracting at the same rate as last month. A 'too low' status for the Customers' Inventories Index is usually considered positive for future production.

"Regarding output, the Production Index expanded for the 12th month in a row, with the positive-to-negative comment ratio improving to 2 positive comments for every negative one (compared to the 1.6-to-1 ratio in September). The Employment Index remained in expansion but lost 0.3 percentage point. The positive-to-negative comments ratio on Employment was 1.8-to-1 in October.

"Finally, inputs (defined as supplier deliveries, inventories, prices and imports) were mixed, with the Supplier Deliveries Index increasing 0.1 percentage point, the Inventories Index gaining 2.8 percentage points and returning to expansion, and the Prices Index decreasing 2.7 percentage points. The Imports Index gained 1.9 percentage points, to 52.9 percent versus 51 percent in September.

"Looking at the manufacturing economy, 6 percent of the sector's gross domestic product (GDP) contracted in October, compared to 2 percent in September, and 6 percent of manufacturing GDP was in strong contraction (defined as a composite PMIÂ® of 45 percent or lower), compared to 2 percent in September. The share of sector GDP with a PMIÂ® at or below 45 percent is a good metric to gauge overall manufacturing weakness. Of the six largest manufacturing industries, five (Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Transportation Equipment; Chemical Products; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products) expanded in October."

The 12 manufacturing industries reporting growth in October â listed in order â are: Plastics & Rubber Products; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Textile Mills; Primary Metals; Transportation Equipment; Fabricated Metal Products; Furniture & Related Products; Chemical Products; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products. The three industries reporting a contraction in October are: Printing & Related Support Activities; Paper Products; and Nonmetallic Mineral Products.

ISMÂ® Manufacturing PMIÂ® Report data is seasonally adjusted for the New Orders, Production, Employment and Inventories indexes.*Number of months moving in current direction.

COMMODITIES REPORTED UP/DOWN IN PRICE AND IN SHORT SUPPLY

Commodities Up in PriceAluminum* (35); Copper (16); Corrugated Products (7); Diesel Fuel (3); Electronic Components (10); Energy; Freight (8); Fuel (8); Memory Components (8); Methanol; Oil Based Products (7); Paper Products; Printed Circuit Boards (4); Resins (9); Semiconductors (5); Steel (12); Steel â Hot Rolled (10); Steel â Stainless (9); Steel Products (11); and Tungsten.

Commodities Down in PriceAluminum*; and Polypropylene Resin.

Note: The number of consecutive months the commodity is listed is indicated after each item.

OCTOBER 2026 MANUFACTURING INDEX SUMMARIES

Manufacturing PMIÂ®The U.S. manufacturing sector expanded in October for the 10th straight month following a 10-month period of contraction, registering 55.5 percent, an increase of 1 percentage point compared to September. All five subindexes that directly factor into the Manufacturing PMIÂ® â New Orders, Production, Employment, Supplier Deliveries and Inventories â were in expansion territory, one more than in September. Of the six largest manufacturing industries, five (Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Transportation Equipment; Chemical Products; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products) expanded in October. A reading above 50 percent indicates that the manufacturing sector is generally expanding; below 50 percent indicates that it is generally contracting.

A Manufacturing PMIÂ® above 47.5 percent, over a period of time, generally indicates an expansion of the overall economy. Therefore, the October Manufacturing PMIÂ® indicates the overall economy grew for the 24th straight month. "The past relationship between the Manufacturing PMIÂ® and the overall economy indicates that October reading (55.5 percent) corresponds to a 2.7-percent increase in real gross domestic product (GDP) on an annualized basis," says Spence.

New OrdersISMÂ®'s New Orders Index expanded in October with a reading of 55.5 percent, an increase of 0.2 percentage point compared to September's reading of 55.3 percent. "Of the six largest manufacturing industries, four (Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Transportation Equipment; and Chemical Products) reported increased new orders. Demand sentiment in October was 1.8 positive comments for every negative comment, a very slight improvement from last month's 1.7-to-1 ratio," says Spence. A New Orders Index above 51.9 percent, over time, is generally consistent with an increase in the Census Bureau's series on manufacturing orders (in constant 2000 dollars).

The 11 manufacturing industries that reported growth in new orders in October, in order, are: Textile Mills; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Machinery; Primary Metals; Computer & Electronic Products; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; Plastics & Rubber Products; Transportation Equipment; Chemical Products; Fabricated Metal Products; and Paper Products. The four industries reporting a decline in new orders in October are: Printing & Related Support Activities; Nonmetallic Mineral Products; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; and Wood Products.

ProductionThe Production Index expanded in October for the 12th month in a row, registering 59 percent, a 2.3-percentage point increase compared to September's reading of 56.7 percent. This is the index's highest reading since it registered 60.5 percent in November 2021. "Of the six largest manufacturing industries, four (Computer & Electronic Products; Transportation Equipment; Machinery; and Chemical Products) reported increased production. Panelists had a 2-to-1 ratio of positive to negative comments regarding output, up from September's 1.6-to-1 ratio," says Spence. An index above 52 percent, over time, is generally consistent with an increase in the Federal Reserve Board's Industrial Production figures.

The 11 industries reporting growth in production during the month of October â listed in order â are: Primary Metals; Computer & Electronic Products; Plastics & Rubber Products; Textile Mills; Transportation Equipment; Machinery; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; Chemical Products; Paper Products; Fabricated Metal Products; and Nonmetallic Mineral Products. The three industries that reported a decrease in production in October are: Printing & Related Support Activities; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; and Wood Products.

EmploymentISMÂ®'s Employment Index registered 52.4 percent in October, 0.3 percentage point lower than September's reading of 52.7 percent. "Of the six big manufacturing industries, four (Machinery; Transportation Equipment; Computer & Electronic Products; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products) reported higher levels of employment in October. The panelist comment ratio of hiring to managing/reducing head counts was 1.8-to-1," says Spence. An Employment Index above 50.3 percent, over time, is generally consistent with an increase in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data on manufacturing employment.

Of the 18 manufacturing industries, eight reported employment growth in October, in the following order: Plastics & Rubber Products; Wood Products; Machinery; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Primary Metals; Transportation Equipment; Computer & Electronic Products; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products. The five industries reporting a decrease in employment in October are: Printing & Related Support Activities; Nonmetallic Mineral Products; Paper Products; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; and Chemical Products.

Supplier Deliveriesâ Delivery performance of suppliers to manufacturing organizations was slower in October for the 11th consecutive month. "The Supplier Deliveries Index registered 59.1 percent, 0.1 percentage point higher than September's reading of 59 percent. Of the six big industries, five (Computer & Electronic Products; Machinery; Transportation Equipment; Chemical Products; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products) reported slower supplier deliveries," says Spence. A reading below 50 percent indicates faster deliveries, while a reading above 50 percent indicates slower deliveries.

The 12 manufacturing industries reporting slower supplier deliveries in October, in order, are: Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Fabricated Metal Products; Computer & Electronic Products; Machinery; Nonmetallic Mineral Products; Furniture & Related Products; Primary Metals; Plastics & Rubber Products; Transportation Equipment; Chemical Products; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; and Miscellaneous Manufacturing. Two industries (Textile Mills; and Paper Products) reported that supplier deliveries were faster in October.

InventoriesThe Inventories Index registered 51.4 percent in October, up 2.8 percentage points compared to the reading of 48.6 percent in September. "Of the six big industries, three (Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; Transportation Equipment; and Machinery) expanded inventories in October," says Spence. An Inventories Index greater than 44.5 percent, over time, is generally consistent with expansion in the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) figures on overall manufacturing inventories (in chained 2000 dollars).

Of 18 manufacturing industries, the seven reporting higher inventories in October â in the following order â are: Printing & Related Support Activities; Plastics & Rubber Products; Textile Mills; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; Transportation Equipment; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; and Machinery. The six industries reporting lower inventories in October â listed in order â are: Wood Products; Paper Products; Primary Metals; Fabricated Metal Products; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; and Chemical Products.

Customers' Inventoriesâ ISMÂ®'s Customers' Inventories Index remained in "too low" territory in October, with a reading of 41.6 percent, the same as September. (For more information about the Customers' Inventories Index, see the "Data and Method of Presentation" section below.)

No industry reported that customers' inventories were too high in October. The 11 industries reporting customers' inventories as too low in October, in order, are: Nonmetallic Mineral Products; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Primary Metals; Paper Products; Fabricated Metal Products; Chemical Products; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; Transportation Equipment; Machinery; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; and Computer & Electronic Products. Seven industries reported no change in customers' inventories in October compared to September.

Pricesâ The ISMÂ® Prices Index registered 75.2 percent in October, 2.7 percentage points lower than the 77.9 percent reported in September; this reading also indicates that raw materials prices increased for the 25th straight month. Five of the six largest manufacturing industries â Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Chemical Products; Transportation Equipment; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products â reported price increases in October. "The Prices Index reading is still being driven by (1) increases in steel and aluminum prices that impact the entire value chain, (2) tariffs applied to many imported goods and (3) increases in petroleum-based products as a result of the Middle East conflict. Higher prices were reported by 53.1 percent of respondents in October, down 5.5 percentage points from September's 58.6 percent," says Spence. A Prices Index above 52.8 percent, over time, is generally consistent with an increase in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Producer Price Index for Intermediate Materials.

In October, the 16 industries that reported paying increased prices for raw materials, in order, are: Furniture & Related Products; Printing & Related Support Activities; Fabricated Metal Products; Nonmetallic Mineral Products; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Machinery; Paper Products; Textile Mills; Wood Products; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; Computer & Electronic Products; Primary Metals; Chemical Products; Plastics & Rubber Products; Transportation Equipment; and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products. No industries reported paying decreased prices for raw materials in October.

Backlog of Ordersâ ISMÂ®'s Backlog of Orders Index registered 54.6 percent in October, a decrease of 1.8 percentage points compared to the September reading of 56.4 percent. Of the six largest manufacturing industries, four (Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; and Transportation Equipment) reported expansion in order backlogs in October.

The 11 industries reporting higher backlogs in October â listed in order â are: Textile Mills; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Plastics & Rubber Products; Fabricated Metal Products; Paper Products; Primary Metals; Machinery; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; Computer & Electronic Products; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; and Transportation Equipment. The three industries reporting lower backlogs in October are: Wood Products; Nonmetallic Mineral Products; and Chemical Products.

New Export Ordersâ ISMÂ®'s New Export Orders Index remained in expansion territory in October, registering 51.2 percent, up 0.3 percentage point from September's reading of 50.9 percent. "Among panelists' comments, the positive-to-negative sentiment ratio was 1-to-1.3," says Spence.

Of the 18 manufacturing industries, the two that reported growth in new export orders in October are: Chemical Products; and Transportation Equipment. The nine industries that reported a decrease in new export orders in October â in the following order â are: Wood Products; Printing & Related Support Activities; Petroleum & Coal Products; Paper Products; Fabricated Metal Products; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Machinery; and Computer & Electronic Products. Seven industries reported no change in exports.

Importsâ ISMÂ®'s Imports Index registered 52.9 percent in October, a 1.9-percentage point increase compared to September's reading of 51 percent.

The seven industries reporting higher imports in October â listed in order â are: Plastics & Rubber Products; Miscellaneous Manufacturing; Primary Metals; Computer & Electronic Products; Transportation Equipment; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; and Machinery. The three industries that reported lower volumes in October are: Wood Products; Paper Products; and Fabricated Metal Products. Eight industries reported no change in imports in October compared to September.

â The Supplier Deliveries, Customers' Inventories, Prices, Backlog of Orders, New Export Orders, and Imports indexes do not meet the accepted criteria for seasonal adjustments.

Buying PolicyThe average commitment lead time for Capital Expenditures in October was 175 days, one day less than in September. The average lead time in October for Production Materials was 87 days, three days more than in September. The average lead time for Maintenance, Repair and Operating (MRO) Supplies was 46 days, three days less than in September.

About This ReportDO NOT CONFUSE THIS NATIONAL REPORT with the various regional purchasing reports released across the country. The national report's information reflects the entire U.S., while the regional reports contain primarily regional data from their local vicinities. Also, the information in the regional reports is not used in calculating the results of the national report. The information compiled in this report is for the month of October 2026.

The data presented herein is obtained from a survey of manufacturing supply executives based on information they have collected within their respective organizations. ISMÂ® makes no representation, other than that stated within this release, regarding the individual company data collection procedures. The data should be compared to all other economic data sources when used in decision-making.

Data and Method of PresentationThe ISMÂ® Manufacturing PMIÂ® Report is based on data compiled from purchasing and supply executives nationwide. The composition of the Manufacturing Business Survey Panel is stratified according to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) and each of the following NAICS-based industries' contribution to gross domestic product (GDP): Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; Textile Mills; Apparel, Leather & Allied Products; Wood Products; Paper Products; Printing & Related Support Activities; Petroleum & Coal Products; Chemical Products; Plastics & Rubber Products; Nonmetallic Mineral Products; Primary Metals; Fabricated Metal Products; Machinery; Computer & Electronic Products; Electrical Equipment, Appliances & Components; Transportation Equipment; Furniture & Related Products; and Miscellaneous Manufacturing (products such as medical equipment and supplies, jewelry, sporting goods, toys and office supplies). The data are weighted based on each industry's contribution to GDP. According to U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) estimates (the average of the fourth quarter 2024 GDP estimate and the GDP estimates for first, second, and third quarter 2025, as released on January 22, 2026), the six largest manufacturing industries are: Chemical Products; Transportation Equipment; Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products; Computer & Electronic Products; Machinery; and Petroleum & Coal Products.

Survey responses reflect the change, if any, in the current month compared to the previous month. For nine indicators (New Orders, Backlog of Orders, New Export Orders, Imports, Production, Supplier Deliveries, Inventories, Employment, and Prices), this report shows the percentage reporting each response, the net difference between the number of responses in the positive economic direction (higher, better and slower for Supplier Deliveries) and the negative economic direction (lower, worse and faster for Supplier Deliveries), and the diffusion index. For Customers' Inventories, respondents report their assessment of their customers' stock levels of respondent companies' products this month (rather than last month): too high, about right, and too low. Responses are raw data and are never changed. The diffusion index includes the percent of positive responses plus one-half of those responding the same (considered positive).

The resulting single index number for those meeting the criteria for seasonal adjustments (Manufacturing PMIÂ®, New Orders, Production, Employment and Inventories) is then seasonally adjusted to allow for the effects of repetitive intra-year variations resulting primarily from normal differences in weather conditions, various institutional arrangements, and differences attributable to non-moveable holidays. All seasonal adjustment factors are subject annually to relatively minor changes when conditions warrant them. The Manufacturing PMIÂ® is a composite index based on the diffusion indexes of five of the indexes with equal weights: New Orders (seasonally adjusted), Production (seasonally adjusted), Employment (seasonally adjusted), Supplier Deliveries, and Inventories (seasonally adjusted).

Diffusion indexes have the properties of leading indicators and are convenient summary measures showing the prevailing direction of change and the scope of change. A Manufacturing PMIÂ® reading above 50 percent indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally expanding; below 50 percent indicates that it is generally declining. A Manufacturing PMIÂ® above 47.5 percent, over a period of time, indicates that the overall economy, or gross domestic product (GDP), is generally expanding; below 47.5 percent, it is generally declining. The distance from 50 percent or 47.5 percent is indicative of the extent of the expansion or decline. With some of the indicators within this report, ISMÂ® has indicated the departure point between expansion and decline of comparable government series, as determined by regression analysis. For the Customers' Inventories Index, numerically, a reading: above 50 percent is "too high," equal to 50 percent is "about right," and below 50 percent is "too low." However, in practice and in the context of other data, customers' inventories may be considered to be "about right" if the diffusion index is between 52 percent (the high side of about right) and 48 percent (the low side of about right).

The ISMÂ® Manufacturing PMIÂ® Report survey is sent out to Manufacturing Business Survey Panel respondents the first part of each month. Respondents are asked to report on information for the current month for U.S. operations only. ISMÂ® receives survey responses throughout most of any given month, with the majority of respondents generally waiting until late in the month to submit responses to give the most accurate picture of current business activity. ISMÂ® then compiles the report for release on the first business day of the following month.

The industries reporting growth, as indicated in the ISMÂ® Manufacturing PMIÂ® Report, are listed in the order of most growth to least growth. For the industries reporting contraction or decreases, those are listed in the order of the highest level of contraction/decrease to the least level of contraction/decrease.

Responses to Buying Policy reflect the percent reporting the current month's lead time, the approximate weighted number of days ahead for which commitments are made for Capital Expenditures; Production Materials; and Maintenance, Repair and Operating (MRO) Supplies, expressed as hand-to-mouth (five days), 30 days, 60 days, 90 days, six months (180 days), a year or more (360 days), and the weighted average number of days. These responses are raw data, never revised, and not seasonally adjusted.

#5564. Apple stock's big rally leaves little room for error as it reports earnings

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Apple stock trades at 36 times expected earnings, nearly double the S&P 500, as investors await its fiscal fourth-quarter results

David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Apple $AAPL is scheduled to discuss fiscal fourth-quarter results on a conference call at 5 p.m. ET on Monday, with its shares having rallied 25% since bottoming out in late June.

The rally has lifted Apple's market capitalization by about $1 trillion. Apple stock trades at 36 times expected earnings for the next 12 months, nearly double the S&P 500's multiple and its highest valuation since 2008, according to Bloomberg.

"Apple is in the 99% percentile of its historical valuation, and when something is priced so fully, there's risk if something unexpected comes along," Ben Carew, co-chief investment officer at Tandem Investment Advisors, said, according to Bloomberg. Tandem holds the stock.

Wall Street expects an 11% jump in fiscal fourth-quarter sales to $113.5 billion, along with a 6% gain in net income to $29.2 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would bring full-year sales growth to 15%, the best since 2021, with growth projected to slow over the next two years.

The results will give investors an initial read on demand for the iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable iPhone, which starts at $1,999 and launched last month. Delivery times have been pushed to next year, according to Bloomberg. Analysts say the wait may simply point to constrained inventory, while accounts of screens cracking could dull the product's draw outside the early-adopter crowd.

Component costs are another concern. Apple stock had its steepest single-session drop in 16 months after the company’s last report in late July, when shortages of parts dented its revenue outlook, according to Bloomberg. As memory prices climb, profit growth is forecast to decelerate to its slowest rate in six quarters, according to FXStreet.

Investors have favored Apple as other large technology companies face scrutiny over AI spending. Apple's free cash flow is projected to climb by over 40% to $141.5 billion in fiscal 2026, whereas Alphabet $GOOGL, Meta $META and Amazon $AMZN are forecast to continue running negative free cash flow, according to Bloomberg. Apple overtook Nvidia $NVDA as the most valuable company on Friday, with a market value of $5.03 trillion.

Wall Street has grown more cautious. Six or more analysts have cut their ratings on the stock since July, according to Bloomberg. Loop Capital lowered its rating to hold in October, and Bank of America $BAC dropped the stock from its U.S. 1 list on Friday. Under 60% of the analysts that Bloomberg follows rate the stock a buy, according to Bloomberg, and its share price sits higher than the mean analyst target.

Apple closed above $5 trillion in market value for the first time on Oct. 14. Apple raised prices across its product range, including older iPhone models, as memory and storage chip prices climbed. The stock has gained 25% since the first round of increases.

The call will mark CEO John Ternus’s debut at the helm of an earnings discussion, according to FXStreet. Ternus became CEO on Sept. 1, and Tim Cook became executive chairman.

#5563. As Anthropic finally files for its IPO, rising risks aren’t slowing the AI buildout – yet

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

The other artificial intelligence shoe dropped this week, as Anthropic filed for what surely will be the second blockbuster AI initial public offering of stock this year.

Nearly 70,000 words in the filing list a ton of risks, but in short, it’s making unimaginably huge bets on buying computing power, it’s uncertain on how long customers will keep spending on AI in the face of dubious returns — and of course there’s the really-not-unusual “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” And as Jason Bloomberg writes, the unmentioned risk is that AI as of today doesn’t have the economies of scale that made software so lucrative.

But it’s hard to imagine it won’t be crazily successful if and when it happens before Thanksgiving. They’ll join the 70% of Nvidia employees who are millionaires. Shed another tear for anyone looking for affordable housing in the Bay Area — we’re not building our way out of this, no matter what YIMBY folks hope.

One interesting wrinkle: SpaceXAI, the other AI IPO earlier this year, will be hoping Anthropic’s offering is successful, since it’s supplying a large chunk of that compute. Same with other AI partner/rivals such as Google and Microsoft.

And Anthropic isn’t alone in amassing cash to continue buying and building more AI infrastructure. Meta this week said it will issue $95 billion in nonvoting stock to build even more. Few, least of all universal backstop Nvidia, seem to think the AI and data center backlash will dent this investment. But that doesn’t mean everyone will win. As SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said this week, self-servingly but perhaps not wrongly (Gartner agrees), a lot of AI neoclouds are going to go belly-up.

Investor worry extends to the big cloud providers too. Despite a continued boom in its cloud business, Google parent Alphabet saw its stock swoon more than 12% Thursday, vaporizing more than $500 billion in market value as it reported a slow quarter for search and ads — perhaps because AI chatbots are siphoning off people’s attention. Microsoft fared better thanks to its resilient application layer on which it can apply AI. But despite strong cloud revenue growth, Amazon stock fell on concerns it could be spending too much on infrastructure. All that came to a head Friday, when the Nasdaq tanked, down almost 3%.

Seems like investors are just generally skittish. On a tear this year until now, Intel stock plunged almost 30% after its Thursday earnings report, on concerns the PC business is slowing. Fortinet also fell more than 20% following its report that included a slightly lower outlook.

For some wider perspective on the AI buildout and what’s needed to make it pay off, check out Dave Vellante’s Breaking Analysis, a late addition here Saturday, a conversation with analyst Crawford Del Prete.

Don’t relax yet. Next week there’s another earningspalooza, including Apple, AMD, Supermicro, Qualcomm, Arm and Palantir.

So an apparent Chinese spy for some time has been hanging around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who evidently didn’t know she was more than a customer executive. Lordy. The New York Times laid out the bones of the U.S. government’s concern, but read it carefully and it sure seems like there are some missing dots throughout. Perhaps this kind of espionage is more common than we know where there’s a nexus of big money and geopolitics, but this may not be the last we hear of it, even if the Trump administration is shrugging.

Oh, and there’s an election next week that might change things… in unpredictable, not necessarily great ways for the economy. Fasten those seatbelts. And vote (but not for the wrong people, thanks).

UK's biggest commercial news app to put video and personalisation at its heart  as part of Sky News 2030

WASHINGTON, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sky News has expanded its strategic partnership with Arc XP, the media platform built inside The Washington Post and run by publishers worldwide, to provide the technology underpinning its new app and website, targeted for launch by the end of 2027.

The agreement marks a significant step forward in Sky News 2030, the organisation's five-year transformation to become a premium, video-first news organisation built for the digital future, with a focus on innovation and better experiences for audiences.

As the UK's biggest commercial news publisher app*, Sky News is investing from a position of strength, with video views on its app more than doubling year on year. The new app and website will take that experience further, putting video at the heart of the offering, showcasing more original reporting and giving audiences more personalised ways to discover and follow the stories that matter to them.

The investment aims to make Sky News an even more compelling destination for its journalism, deepening engagement with existing users, strengthening direct audience relationships and creating new commercial opportunities, including premium and paid-for products.

David Rhodes, Sky News Executive Chairman, said: "Today's partnership will give audiences even more reasons to come directly to Sky News for a best-in-class, video-first experience.  It's a step change that will deliver more personalisation and better commercial outcomesâand deliver them by the end of next year.  We're so pleased to be on this journey together with the people at Arc XP and their partners across the news industry."

Matt Monahan, Arc XP President, said: "More people now find news through AI summaries and search results instead of going to the newsroom that did the reporting. Arc XP helps newsrooms win those audiences back, keep them, and grow revenue. With Sky News, we're building a video-led, personalised app and website that brings audiences straight to Sky's journalism, with Ask Sky News answering their questions from Sky's own reporting. At Arc XP and The Washington Post, we're proud to help newsrooms like Sky's get their critical journalism to more people."

Working closely with Sky's product and technology teams, Arc XP will provide its media platform, backed by AWS, to underpin the new platforms, including tools for mobile apps, video and personalisation. The technology will give Sky News greater flexibility to innovate, develop new products and support the next phase of its digital transformation.

The expanded agreement builds on the organisations' existing work on Ask Sky News, an AI-powered conversational search experience that demonstrates how new technology can make trusted journalism more accessible and intuitive for audiences.

Sky News has generated nearly 4.5 billion social video views in 2026 to date, demonstrating its position as a major global news brand and the growing appetite for its journalism across digital platforms. This reach reflects the scale of Sky News' ambition as it continues to invest in the future of news.

#5561. Binance absorbed $4.7 billion in withdrawals after record North Korea hack

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Net outflows are under 3% of the $166 billion in assets Binance holds, and deposits are rising, a spokesperson said

Binance has seen net withdrawals totaling $4.7 billion as of London's Monday morning, in the wake of the biggest crypto heist ever recorded, a company spokesperson told Bloomberg.

The outflows amount to under 3% of the exchange's $166 billion asset base, the spokesperson said. Withdrawals have been in line with what the exchange anticipated, while deposits have been "steadily increasing," the spokesperson said.

Hackers took about $6.3 billion in tokens from Binance's hot wallets, according to CNBC. Bloomberg put the figure at $6.4 billion. Binance detected the hack last Thursday evening, according to Bloomberg. The FBI has attributed the theft to North Korean hackers.

Binance reopened withdrawals to customers on Sunday following a freeze, according to Bloomberg. The Bitcoin network was the first to reopen, followed by the Ethereum network and BNB Smart Chain, according to CNBC.

Binance teamed up with industry partners such as stablecoin issuers to lock down nearly half of the stolen funds, according to Bloomberg. The company pledged to absorb the entire loss and had restored roughly 95% of it by Sunday.

Binance said it is paying for the replacements with its Secure Asset Fund for Users, a slice of its Futures insurance fund and corporate treasury reserves, according to CNBC. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said, according to CNBC.

Co-Chief Executive Officer Yi He wrote on X $TWTR on Sunday that part of the withdrawals reflect internal moves among Binance's own wallets, not customers leaving, according to Bloomberg.

How the attack happened remains unclear, according to CNBC. Binance first said the attack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. Co-CEO Richard Teng subsequently described a more intricate chain of events than one engineer's misused permissions.

Bitcoin held roughly steady on Monday, changing hands near $77,700.

#5560. Krafton-backed Ludo Robotics releases robot intelligence model designed around human intent

Ludo Robotics Inc., a subsidiary of major South Korean video game publisher Krafton Inc., today debuted Ludi 0.2, a robotics artificial intelligence system built to understand people and interact with them in the physical world.

Headquartered in Palo Alto, Ludo spun out of Krafton, a company that primarily publishes video games and is best known for the ultra-popular “PUBG: Battlegrounds.” Ludo also has a research and development lab in Seoul where it combines the efforts of researchers and engineers across robotics, machine learning and AI.

Krafton Chief Executive CH Kim also helms Ludo as CEO, with Krafton’s Chief AI Officer Kangwook Lee serving as its chief technology officer.

Why did a video game company form and back an AI robotics company? Krafton said it believes AI makes games more responsive and replayable. It also has strong roots in simulation, interaction and real-time systems, which have immediate applications in the bridge between the digital and physical, where the interaction between humans and robots lives.

“Robots are becoming increasingly capable of performing physical tasks, but understanding and responding to people remains a major challenge,” said Lee. “Ludi 0.2 represents another step toward our goal of bringing conversation, reasoning and physical action together so robots can better understand human intent, respond to feedback and adapt as situations change.”

The company introduced the first version of Ludi 0.1 in August 2026. It combines a vision-language model for reasoning and dialogue with specialized navigation and manipulation capabilities. Today’s next-generation model has advanced its capabilities, forming more natural human-robot interaction, including social intelligence, memory and reasoning, tool coordination, gesture interpretation, and physical movement.

The company said it’s working toward a final version of Ludi that will integrate perception, dialogue and physical action.

The objective is to integrate communication, reasoning and physical action into one “brain.” The model would watch what’s happening, listen to commands and speech, interpret those commands alongside human gestures and physical movements and reason about the environment. This would happen in real time, coordinating similarly to how another human decides on actions based on another person’s actions in their workspace.

This is the “Holy Grail” of physical AI, where intelligent robots can perform actions not just in industrial environments and warehouses, but also retail and domestic spaces such as restaurants, living rooms and kitchens.

Krafton said much of its work includes proprietary foundation models and co-playable characters developed in collaboration with Nvidia Corp., AI teammates designed to understand players in real time. Ludo builds on this foundation to develop the same kind of intelligence into real-world robots.

Startups are bringing the physical world to robots so they can see objects and grab and move them with increasing capability. Interpreting human intent and responding to social cues from people around the robot, however, remains elusive. Simulation makes it easy for physical AI to prepare robots to work with objects and around humans, but it doesn’t always prepare them to model human behavior.

#5558. Netflix's ad ambitions are stalling as viewing hours stop growing

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Netflix's third-quarter revenue rose 12% to $12.9 billion, while its 2026 ad revenue forecast fell to about $2.7 billion

Netflix $NFLX cut its 2026 advertising revenue forecast to about $2.7 billion from about $3 billion, the company said in its Oct. 20 shareholder letter.

Netflix attributed the cut to a slower-than-expected rollout of some ad product capabilities. The company also acknowledged investor concern about its view hours growth and said it seeks to accelerate that growth.

Netflix said third-quarter revenue grew 12% from a year earlier to $12.9 billion. Growth came mainly from subscription revenue, with advertising revenue also rising. Operating margin was 34.6%, up from 28.2% a year earlier.

The company said member response to its 2026 price increases matched prior adjustments and its expectations, which it called an indicator that engagement remains healthy. In India, view hours grew 24% from a year earlier, while view hours per member grew low-to-mid single digits, Netflix said.

For the fourth quarter, Netflix expects revenue of $13.4 billion, driven by growth in memberships, pricing and ad revenue. It projects full-year 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion.

Netflix said it will introduce its advertising tier in 15 new countries in 2027. The first group launches in March 2027 and covers nine countries in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, plus Colombia, Peru and New Zealand. In the third quarter, the company extended programmatic access through global connected-TV marketplace deals and added partnerships with MercadoLibre in Latin America and Adform in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Competition for viewer attention is also a factor. YouTube captures about double the portion of American viewing that Netflix does, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited Nielsen. Netflix airs roughly 2.4 minutes of commercials per hour, while Hulu and Disney $DIS+ carry around 8, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited BMO Capital Markets analysts.

The Wall Street Journal also said Netflix plans to report engagement once a year instead of twice.

#5557. Extreme Networks wants the network to run AI, not just be run by it

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

At its recent AI Summit in Amsterdam, Extreme Networks Inc. shared early Agent ONE Coworker results and previewed Exchange zones, which put spare access points and switch compute to work as on-premises artificial intelligence infrastructure. Here’s what it means and what information technology pros should do about it.

Most of the conversation about AI and networking has flowed in one direction. AI comes in, examines the network and helps the network team run it better. That’s useful, but it treats the network as the patient, not as a resource.

At the summit, the company argued that there is a better way. The network should be managed by AI and serve as a place where AI runs, using data that most organizations currently throw away. This would let network teams stop being the people who merely keep the Wi-Fi up for the AI project and become the people who host it.

Extreme made two announcements. The first was a progress report on Extreme Agent ONE Coworker, the ambient AI agent built into Extreme Platform ONE. In its first month, Extreme says, customers saved about 1,000 hours of troubleshooting, 41% of Platform ONE customers used it for daily tasks, and users responded to 98% of critical “nudges,” the proactive alerts the agent raises after running its own pre-investigation. Engagement was roughly 10 times that of Extreme’s first-generation conversational assistant.

The second was a preview of Extreme Exchange zones, planned for the first half of 2027. A zone combines an Extreme Universal Compute Platform or a customer-owned server with spare capacity from Extreme access points and switches already installed at a site. AI applications from the Extreme Exchange marketplace run locally on open-weight models by default, with cloud inference used only when policy allows and logged every time. Agent ONE Operator mode, the autonomous tier, also arrives in the first half of 2027.

The first wave of AI in networking wasn’t a smashing success because it relied on a chatbot built on fragmented data. During his talk, Nabil Bukhari (pictured), Extreme’s chief technology officer and president of AI platforms, called it a design flaw. “Conversational AI requires the user to have the question and the context, and you will be surprised how difficult that is when it comes to technology domains,” he said.

In Extreme’s focus groups, many administrators asked a powerful AI assistant how many devices they had, even though the number was already on the dashboard. Coworker flips that. “We have moved to the world where instead of you prompting AI, AI prompts you,” Bukhari said.

The best evidence came from a customer. Kevin Rocha, chief information officer at Hill College, described a wireless outage in a building housing HR, finance and enrollment. “Agent ONE Coworker told me exactly where to look: One access point needed attention, and several more were due for firmware upgrades. We resolved the issue in about 20 minutes rather than an entire morning,” he said. Platform ONE, he added, “is like having two or three more network engineers on staff.”

That’s the value of AI for networking in most enterprises. It doesn’t replace the network team. It gives a small team the reach of a larger one. Bukhari also admitted that there is more work to be done. He explained that 58% of support cases opened by Agent ONE arrive with all the evidence support needs. “Fifty-eight is pretty good, but 58 is still 58 and not 100.”

Andrew Grill, the opening keynote speaker and author of “Digitally Curious,” discussed the stakes. “When a chatbot gets it wrong, you might have a bad paragraph. If an agent gets it wrong, you have a bad Tuesday,” he said. His test for any deployment: “If your agent does something wrong at 2 in the morning, whose phone rings?”

Extreme’s Operator demo is subject to guardrails. Each of the 268 tools can be configured to auto-authorize, ask first or never use. Four baseline rules apply to everything: do no harm to the network, never expose a credential, never act outside your role and never act in another tenant. Every task has a full audit trace.

An important design criterion is that governance reside within Extreme Exchange, not Platform ONE. “You can’t govern something from within,” Bukhari said. “That is how you get rogue agents.” If the system running the agent also controls its permissions, you don’t have a control plane. You have an honor system.

Networks generate dense, real-time telemetry on location, movement and behavior that far exceeds what operations needs, and cloud platforms drop most of it because moving it is expensive. Bukhari said the valuable uses tend to hit four walls: sovereignty, localization, survivability and economics.

The innovation is where the compute comes from. Higher-end access points have four to eight cores and typically use only one, so organizations already pay for and power idle compute hanging from their ceilings. In one healthcare demo, a fall-detection app that combined camera feeds, Wi-Fi location and paging to find the closest responder ran entirely on access points. A second demo used Seattle Seahawks game data to predict gate congestion and showed that some fans faced a seven- to eight-minute walk to the nearest pro shop.

“This is not a network management use case,” Bukhari said. “These use cases are impossible without that rich, real-time telemetry.” That’s the strategic point. The return goes to operations, facilities and fan experience, giving network leaders something they’ve rarely had: a revenue story.

Zones will ship in 2027, and the demo apps were built in collaboration with design partners. The model needs a real application catalog, so Extreme is pairing it with a free, invitation-only forward-deployed engineering program. Pricing will be consumption-based, measured in “agent actions.” As Grill noted, most organizations haven’t priced the cost of their tasks today, so they’ll struggle to judge value.

As expected, the most valuable insights came from the customer panel. Jonathan Monk, CIO of the Institute of Cancer Research in London, manages roughly 9 petabytes of data, but performance isn’t his primary reason for building sovereign AI. “When we ask people in our organization what’s the biggest thing that holds them back from using AI, it’s that I’m not sure if I’m allowed to,” he said.

Andrew Beynon, chief enterprise architect at Extreme partner ARO, linked that to shadow AI. The goal, he said, is “to make the journey for legitimate adoption of AI easier than the move to illegitimate adoption.” Monk called it building “paved roads.” The industry treats sovereignty as a compliance cost, but these customers see it as an adoption accelerator.

David O’Neill, director of IT operations at Liverpool Football Club, offered a balanced take on AI. “While AI is an answer, it’s not necessarily the answer.” Bukhari highlighted the next challenge: “Adoption is no longer the problem. It’s the optimization of adoption.” After AI-generated product specs ballooned to 200 pages, Extreme capped them at three pages.

Include the network team in the AI plan. If it isn’t involved, decisions about traffic, inference location and data residency will be made without the people who understand them.

Separate governance from execution. Check whether agent permissions, audit logs and the kill switch are outside the system the agent runs in.

Inventory the data your network discards. Identify the location and occupancy telemetry you already generate, and which business units would pay to use them.

Pressure-test the edge-compute math. Ask how workloads are prioritized during RF demand spikes and which model sizes realistically fit on an access point.

Price your tasks first. Without a baseline cost for today’s work, it’s impossible to evaluate consumption-based AI pricing.

Extreme can’t outspend its larger competitors, so it’s betting on speed and focus as a pure-play networking company. The Agent ONE numbers suggest that’s paying off on the operations side.

Exchange zones are the bolder idea. Turning installed access points and switches into a distributed, centrally governed inference fabric is more ambitious than anything I’ve seen from Extreme’s larger rivals. It’s also unproven, and 2027 is a long way off in AI time. As Beynon put it, “today’s knowledge has got an expiry date.”

The direction Extreme is headed is the right one. For 30 years, the network has been the most important infrastructure, yet nobody wanted to talk about it until it broke. AI makes the network the system that connects data, compute and people, and possibly the one that runs the AI, too. Network pros who see that early will have a much bigger role in where their organizations go next.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5556. RideLot Unveils Inventory Intelligence Platform Built to Modernize Powersports Retail

Dealer built technology turns one inventory feed into smarter search, website integration, distribution, marketing and dealer intelligence without replacing the dealership's DMS, CRM or website.

GRAND JUNCTION, Colo., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- RideLot Technologies today announced the launch of its inventory intelligence platform built specifically for powersports and specialty vehicle dealers.

RideLot was created to solve a simple problem that happens every day in dealerships. A dealer can have the right machine in stock, or have the ability to order it for the customer, and still make it difficult for that shopper to find.

RideLot connects to the inventory feed a dealership already sends from its DMS or feed provider.

Built from inside powersports retail, RideLot connects to the inventory feed a dealership already sends from its DMS or feed provider. RideLot normalizes that inventory and turns each unit into a record that can power shopper search, dealer websites, branded storefronts, marketplace distribution, marketing, dealer intelligence and dealer facing tools.

The dealership keeps its existing website, DMS, CRM, phone numbers, lead routing and technology providers.

"Dealers do not need another system asking them to replace everything they already use," said James Wells, Founder and CEO of RideLot Technologies. "The inventory data already exists. RideLot makes that inventory dramatically more useful. We help customers find what the dealership has, help them discover what the dealership can order, help dealers understand demand, help teams market inventory and give the dealership more ways to put that same inventory record to work."

RideLot was co founded by Wells and Nick Citrola around a dealer first philosophy: build technology around the inventory and workflows dealerships already have instead of forcing retailers into another replacement system.

At the center of the platform is RideSpec, RideLot's natural language inventory discovery technology.

Instead of requiring shoppers to know an exact year, make and model, RideSpec lets them search the way they actually talk.

RideSpec interprets what the shopper is asking for, searches dealership inventory and returns relevant machines, including an explanation of why each machine matched.

RideSpec also supports natural language inventory discovery in both English and Spanish.

The same technology can be installed directly into a dealership's current website through RideLot Inventory Finder, giving dealers a significantly different inventory search experience without requiring them to replace their existing website provider.

Search what is in stock and what is available to order

RideLot is designed to help dealers merchandise more than only the units physically sitting on the dealership floor.

Through Available to Order, supported factory orderable models can appear alongside a dealership's current in-stock inventory inside the same RideLot shopping experience.

That means a shopper searching for a specific machine may see:

RideLot clearly distinguishes Available to Order inventory from machines that are physically in stock.

The goal is simple: instead of telling a customer "no results" because the exact machine is not currently sitting on the floor, RideLot can help the shopper understand what the dealership may still be able to sell them.

For multi rooftop dealer groups, RideLot can also connect authorized inventory across locations. A shopper who cannot find the right machine at one store can be connected to relevant inventory at another rooftop.

RideLot Storefront gives dealers a branded inventory shopping experience built from the feed they already send, including RideSpec search, in-stock inventory, Available to Order, categories, brands and multi rooftop inventory.

RideLot Inventory Finder brings RideSpec powered inventory discovery directly into the dealership's existing website.

RideLot SEO Inventory Pages automatically create search readable RideLot inventory pages from live inventory by category, brand and individual machine, giving search engines more inventory specific content to understand.

RideLot Visibility helps dealerships identify important searches, inventory pages that need attention and opportunities where inventory exists but may still be difficult to discover.

RideLot Dealer Intelligence shows dealers what shoppers searched for, which searches returned no matching inventory, which machines received little engagement and which inventory generated customer actions.

RideLot Feed Health identifies missing or incomplete inventory data involving pricing, photos and other merchandising information and shows dealership teams which units need attention.

RideLot Marketing Studio turns live inventory records into dealer ready marketing creative using the machine's actual photos, pricing and inventory information.

RideLot Dealer Transfer allows participating dealers to search other participating dealer inventory from nearby markets to nationwide and request machines another dealer has.

RideLot Marketplace Listings uses the dealership's existing inventory feed to prepare Facebook Marketplace listings for salespeople to review and publish from their own Facebook accounts.

An individual Facebook Marketplace post can be prepared in less than 30 seconds using inventory information already flowing through RideLot instead of requiring the salesperson to rebuild the listing manually.

RideLot then continues monitoring the dealer feed for changes such as sold units and pricing updates.

RideLot Showroom brings the same inventory discovery technology onto the dealership floor through an interactive kiosk experience with RideSpec search and supported bilingual voice interaction.

Dealer tools built around the inventory record

RideLot also provides dealer only monitoring and recordkeeping products built around live inventory.

RideLot MAP Policy Checker evaluates supported eligible inventory against OEM MAP information loaded into the platform and surfaces potential advertised pricing issues for dealer review.

RideLot Recalls reads applicable public CPSC and NHTSA recall notices daily and compares them with live inventory by brand, model and model year. A match is shown as a Possible Recall for the dealership to verify by VIN in its OEM dealer system. RideLot does not determine VIN level recall status.

RideLot Price Record maintains a historical record of advertised prices RideLot records or displays, helping dealerships preserve evidence of what pricing was shown and when it changed.

The inventory record should keep working everywhere the dealership needs it.

Price transparency is getting more attention. RideLot keeps the history.

Vehicle pricing transparency and advertising practices are receiving increased regulatory attention.

In September 2026, Federal Trade Commission staff published automobile industry pricing guidance reiterating that an advertised vehicle price should reflect the actual price a consumer can pay, including dealer required fees other than government required charges.

California's Combating Auto Retail Scams Act, or CARS Act, took effect Oct. 1, 2026 for covered California dealers and covered vehicle transactions. Among other requirements, the law addresses total price disclosures and requires covered dealers to retain certain advertising, pricing and related records for two years.

RideLot Price Record is not legal advice, does not determine whether a dealership is compliant and does not replace a dealership's own legal or regulatory review.

Instead, Price Record solves a straightforward operational problem:

If someone asks what price was advertised months ago, does the dealership still have the record?

Inventory systems generally focus on the current price.

Online advertisements change. Marketplace listings change. Inventory pages disappear when units sell. Employees leave. Screenshots get lost.

Price Record preserves the advertised price history RideLot records or displays so authorized dealership personnel have a durable record to reference later.

"Price Record does not tell a dealership whether it complied with a particular law," Wells said. "It gives the dealer something much more basic that is often missing: a historical record of what RideLot recorded or displayed and when."

Launch offer includes 12 months of Price Record and Marketplace Listings

RideLot Marketplace is available to qualifying dealers beginning at:

During RideLot's Initial Launch offer, qualifying Marketplace and Dealer Suite accounts receive:

12 months of RideLot Price Record included

Dealers can begin preserving advertised price history immediately without adding another software charge during the first year.

12 months of RideLot Marketplace Listings included

Qualifying dealers also receive up to three Marketplace Listings seats during the 12 month launch period.

Salespeople can take an actual unit already in the dealership's inventory and prepare a Facebook Marketplace listing in less than 30 seconds using the photos, pricing and vehicle information already flowing through RideLot.

The salesperson reviews the listing and publishes it through the salesperson's own Facebook account. RideLot continues monitoring the inventory feed afterward for changes such as sold units and pricing updates.

RideLot's current Initial Launch Pricing also includes a $0 setup fee for qualifying dealers.

RideLot subscriptions are billed monthly with no long term subscription requirement, and dealers can cancel according to the terms shown in their RideLot account.

"For a dealer, we think the launch offer makes signing up today a no brainer," Wells said. "You can start with RideLot Marketplace for $0, get 12 months of Price Record, get 12 months of our Facebook Marketplace listing workflow and let the platform prove its value before making a larger commitment."

RideLot was intentionally designed as an integration layer rather than another dealership system of record.

Dealers can continue using their current DMS, CRM, website, website provider, inventory feed provider, phone numbers and existing lead routing.

RideLot connects to the inventory data already moving through that ecosystem and adds capabilities around it.

"We built RideLot from the dealership floor outward," Wells said. "Every product starts with a real dealer question. Can the customer find this machine? What are shoppers asking for? What is missing in our feed? Can another rooftop sell it? Is there inventory we can order? We want the inventory connection to answer more of those questions without asking the dealer to start over."

Built for dealers and a more connected powersports industry

While RideLot was built first around dealership workflows, the company sees a larger opportunity to connect dealers, dealer groups, manufacturers and technology partners around the same inventory data.

The combination of natural language shopper demand, live dealer inventory, multi rooftop availability, factory orderable products, search visibility, pricing records, marketing distribution and dealer intelligence creates opportunities to understand not only what inventory exists, but what customers are actually trying to find.

RideLot is continuing to expand its dealer network and work with industry partners as the platform grows.

Dealers do not need to purchase Dealer Suite or RideLot MAX to begin working with RideLot.

RideLot connects to the inventory feed a dealership already uses and turns that inventory into shopper discovery, dealer branded storefronts, dealer website search, search readable inventory pages, marketplace distribution, marketing tools, dealer intelligence and inventory centered dealer workflows.

RideLot is built for powersports and other specialty vehicle retailers and is designed to integrate alongside the technology dealerships already use rather than requiring them to replace it.

#5555. Northwood Space raised $375 million, reaching a $2 billion valuation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The satellite ground network company plans to add 400 jobs over three years and expand its global antenna network

Northwood Space closed a $375 million Series C equity financing round on Monday, valuing the company at $2 billion, according to Bloomberg. The Torrance, California-based company builds a shared network of ground stations that connect satellites to Earth.

Andreessen Horowitz and DFJ Growth co-led the round, the company said. Alpine Space Ventures, Washington Harbour Partners, Stepstone Activate, In-Q-Tel and others took part. A separate multi-year credit line from HSBC Innovation Banking will help support working capital and the growth of the network.

Northwood said the money will go toward delivering on existing contracts, hiring and building out its ground network for commercial, U.S. government and allied space missions. The company has more than 140 employees and intends to hire 400 more people during the next three years, split between Torrance and Washington, D.C., in roles covering RF engineering, production, software development and site operations.

"This funding lets us scale that network and build the infrastructure the next generation of space missions will depend on," co-founder and CEO Bridgit Mendler said in a statement.

Since its Series B in January, Northwood has deployed six multi-orbit-capable sites on two continents, the company said. It opened a 185,000-square-foot headquarters and factory in Torrance in September. The Series B raised $100 million.

The company sells two antenna products: Portal phased arrays for command and control, and Prism high-throughput dishes for payload data. Northwood produced 29 units across the two lines in the last 12 months, according to Satellite Today, and wants to scale that output to hundreds. Mendler told Satellite Today that the company plans to build a network larger than the biggest existing ground networks, which have hundreds of sites.

Northwood won a $49.8 million U.S. Space Force contract earlier this year to support the Satellite Control Network, according to Satellite Today. Mendler said the contract uses the Portal product line.

Northwood said active satellites grew from about 3,000 in 2020 to more than 14,000 by the end of 2025, while ground infrastructure has not kept pace. The company expects its sites to reach speeds of 100 gigabits per second or more in high-demand regions by the end of 2027. It said it will announce several site and network expansions in the first half of 2027.

#5554. 6 insights from the GSA Women’s Leadership Initiative: AI semiconductor industry trends turn the chip race into a systems race

For decades, the semiconductor industry competed on one thing: the individual chip. One of the biggest AI semiconductor industry trends now under way is the shift toward treating chips as components of much larger systems. Performance, cost and reliability are now determined across the package, the rack and the supply chain, not inside a single die.

That shift moves the hardest problems upstream. Packaging, connectivity, yield, sourcing and verification used to come after design, but now they shape it from the first day. AI is shortening development cycles at the same time as it adds to the complexity engineers have to manage. The next phase will be defined by how well companies coordinate across that whole system.

“I think the AI system is our new chips,” said Letizia Giuliano, vice president of product management and marketing at Qualcomm Technologies Inc. “If we were optimizing everything for the silicon in the past, now these days we’re optimizing everything for the system.”

Giuliano and other industry experts spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and co-host Alison Kosik at the GSA Women’s Leadership Initiative event in Palo Alto, California. The interviews covered AI semiconductor industry trends, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, AI-driven yield learning, physical AI, strategic sourcing and AI-assisted chip design.

Here are six standout insights from the event:

Moving data between chips, memory and racks now limits AI performance more than raw compute, according to Giuliano. At 200 gigabits per second per lane, half of the signal budget goes just to getting out of the package. That is pushing optical interconnect from rack-to-rack links into the rack, the blade and the package itself, with copper and optics in use side by side. Qualcomm has just launched High Bandwidth Compute, a low-power way to attach compute to memory that is tuned for tokens per watt. Building such products at hyperscale volume means product engineering has to join design-for-test, manufacturing and reliability planning early, explained Sophie Wang, senior director of product engineering at Marvell Technology Inc.

The boundary of an AI system is shifting from the chip to the package, emphasized Nisha Ananthakrishnan, senior director of advanced packaging at Intel Corp. Intel uses its EMIB bridge technology to link chiplets and to scale packages from 3x to more than 10x form factors. Outsourced assembly and test providers are becoming system integrators, noted Patricia MacLeod, senior director of corporate communications and industry partnerships at Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. She pointed to ASE’s VIPack platform, which supports technologies ranging from fan-out chip-on-substrate to co-packaged optics. Many of the chips AI depends on, such as power management chips and voltage regulators built at 12 to 28 nanometers, use mature nodes, added Tazrien Kamal, senior director of technology and innovation at GlobalFoundries Inc.

About 70% to 80% of the problems found when scaling up volume manufacturing could have been caught before tapeout, highlighted Preeti Prasher, chief operating officer of Stathera Inc. Using AI to analyze characterization, simulation and inline manufacturing data lets teams start new wafers before a bad lot reaches test. Adaptive testing also cuts test time. Lattice Semiconductor Corp. has released Lattice Prompt, its first AI design assistant, which turns a plain-language request into a field-programmable gate array design and recommends the best part for the form factor and cost, according to Iliana Chen, senior director of program management at Lattice. Demand from robotics and other markets has made volume Lattice’s biggest challenge, Chen noted.

Physical AI is much broader than humanoid robots and covers any autonomous system that senses its surroundings, reasons and acts in the physical world, explained Gina Longoria, VP of external communications at Arm Ltd. The market is in its first inning, and no single company can build the architecture, security and safety standards it needs on its own, she stressed. Firmware is becoming the layer that ties GPUs, CPUs, network cards and Compute Express Link devices into one fleet-scale system, shared Lakshmi Ramagiri, partner for firmware engineering at Microsoft Corp. Security has to move beyond secure boot to continuous trust while a system is running, and the Open Compute Project and DMTF are the standards bodies to watch, Ramagiri added.

Don’t miss the full interview on theCUBE.

Sourcing now goes well beyond negotiating prices and shapes product development, risk and customer experience, emphasized Alisa Wang, AVP of global planning and procurement at Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd. Because AI-driven demand can change within a year, suppliers have to be treated as strategic partners that receive product roadmaps early, she noted. Leading-edge logic capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. is the tightest constraint, followed by packaging, specialty materials and critical equipment. In response, Credo is qualifying second-source suppliers and spreading its manufacturing footprint across more regions. Stathera’s Prasher highlighted dual sourcing for key segments and using supplier feedback during new product introduction to develop lower-cost products together.

AI is moving from a productivity assistant to a built-in part of electronic design automation flows, explained Rimi Dasgupta, chief of staff for product management and markets at Synopsys Inc., and Vidya Neerkundar, director of product management at Siemens Digital Industries Software. Synopsys has seen verification closure on register-transfer-level designs accelerate as much as 50-fold and debug time drop by 40%, according to Dasgupta. Demand for workload-optimized custom silicon has also cut development cycles from 18 months to six to nine months. AI is probabilistic, but chips must be deterministic, so Synopsys pairs AI with multiphysics solvers from its Ansys acquisition and is working with OpenAI Group PBC on a dedicated GPT-Synopsys model. Multi-die design is the next big shift as chips hit reticle limits, Neerkundar noted.

#5553. Belk Kicks Off the Season of Giving While Celebrating 20 Years of Giving Back to Local Communities

Customers can unlock exclusive savings during Charity Sale while supporting local nonprofits Nov. 13-15

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The season of giving starts early at Belk. This November, Belk's annual Fall Charity Sale returns for a weekend-long event that combines shopping with community impact. Taking place Nov. 13-15, the event marks 20 years of helping nonprofit organizations raise funds for programs and services that support families, strengthen neighborhoods and create lasting impact across the Southeast.

Over the last two decades, Charity Sale has become one of Belk's longest-running community initiatives, bringing together customers and nonprofit partners around a simple idea: every purchase can make a difference. By purchasing a $5 Charity Sale ticket and redeeming it at checkout, customers can unlock exclusive discounts on holiday gifts, seasonal essentials and customer-favorite brands, all while supporting causes that matter close to home.

"For the past two decades, Charity Sale has shown what's possible when businesses, customers and nonprofits come together to support causes that matter," said Don Hendricks, CEO of Belk. "What makes this event so special is that its impact extends far beyond our stores. Every ticket purchased helps support organizations that are addressing real needs in their communities. As we head into the season of giving, we're proud to continue this tradition and help our customers make a difference while shopping for family and friends."

Since its launch in 2006, Charity Sale has benefited more than 6,000 nonprofit organizations, helping raise funds to support vital community programs. This season's event includes more than 4,200 nonprofits. Participating organizations span Belk's 16-state footprint, connecting customers with causes close to home. Whether shopping for gifts, seasonal essentials or everyday favorites, customers can feel good knowing their purchases help support organizations making a difference in the places they call home.

Belk welcomes all 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations to participate in Charity Sale. Organizations interested in signing up can contact their local Belk store or visit www.belk.com/CharitySaleResources for more information.

To learn more about Charity Sale, visit www.belk.com/charity.
