#5552. ‘Not a new AI center’: Seattle Children’s launches $10M pediatric innovation institute

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 26, 2026 at 8:01 amOctober 27, 2026 at 7:47 am

Seattle Children’s is announcing today the launch of its Institute for Pediatric Innovation, a $10 million initiative with eight focus areas and a chief innovation officer yet to be named. The hospital is positioning the institute as the “core engine” driving its strategic plan.

CEO Dr. Christopher Longhurst has specific health challenges in mind where he hopes today’s technology could quickly improve care for pediatric patients.

“The question is, with this new generation of tools — not just AI and large language models, but precision health tools, whole genome sequencing, etc. — how can we leverage these tools to solve problems in ways that we have not before?” Longhurst said in an interview with GeekWire.

Seattle Children’s has approximately 600,000 patient visits last year and reported approximately $2.6 billion in expenses.

Longhurst became CEO in January after a decade at UC San Diego Health, where he founded and directed the Joan & Irwin Jacobs Center for Health Innovation. The institute is Seattle Children’s most prominent new organization-wide initiative since he took the job.

The institute “is not a new AI center. This isn’t about the shiny objects or the tools. This is about the outcomes that we can achieve and the impact that we can have,” Longhurst said. “So really, the focus here is impact at scale.”

The organization will concentrate on eight areas:

AI tools. Seattle Children’s plans to develop, test and use new technology tools. One example is a digital care platform specific to pediatric patients where families and providers can manage appointments, medications, results and communications. The hospital is already helping build one with industry partners and Longhurst is eager to include an AI chatbot for caregivers. Other AI work includes a pilot of an automated tool that rapidly generates anonymous copies of medical images for research and a listening tool that drafts clinical notes during appointments.

Industry partnerships. Longhurst said these cut across the other focus areas. The hospital is working with industry on the care platform, for example, and plans to partner on seeking FDA approval for pediatric uses of existing devices.

Innovation unit. The hospital is establishing a facility that offers advanced care and can test new pediatric devices. Longhurst pointed to Ochsner Health’s innovation lab as a model and said he wasn’t aware of a comparable facility focused on children.

Medical device innovation. This focus overlaps with the innovation care unit and aims to serve unmet pediatric needs. Longhurst noted that numerous medical devices designed for adults are being used off-label for children. One piece of the solution is taking data related to these applications and seeking FDA approval for use in kids.

Precision medicine. Seattle Children’s already offers targeted therapies and aims to expand them. A recently published study from the hospital found that genome analysis, usually performed only for critically ill patients, could lead to faster diagnoses for non-ICU patients, particularly children with failure to thrive. “The question for us now is … how do we make a research project into something that we do every day at scale?” Longhurst said.

Biomedical data. Patient monitoring produces vast amounts of electronic data that can be combined with genetic and protein-expression information. The hospital is pursuing technology that recognizes patterns across these sources in real time to guide treatment for critically ill and other patients.

Therapeutics. Research into next-generation cell, gene and protein therapies will expand.

Training for young scientists and clinicians. The hospital’s Invent@SC program provides mentorship and education for early-career researchers and clinicians. The initiative focuses on treatments discovered at Seattle Children’s that can be widely adopted.

Projects from the institute must be approved by a Seattle Children’s AI Review Board, which will assess whether proposed uses of AI are ethical, equitable and responsible. Those involving research will also go to the Institutional Review Board for regulatory compliance.

Seattle Children’s has recruited three external launch advisors to help recruit the CIO and develop the institute’s organizational structure. They are Dr. Matthew Lungren, a Stanford University adjunct professor and former chief scientific officer for health and life sciences at Microsoft; Dr. Kevin Koo, a radiologist whose experience includes leadership at Seattle Children’s and roles at UW Medicine and McKinsey & Company; and Dr. Jessica Mega, a cardiologist and co-founder of Verily, an Alphabet company.

Longhurst said the work will require a cultural shift at the institution, from risk aversion to an openness to change.

The institute’s initial funding comes from a $5 million anonymous gift and $5 million in existing resources. Longhurst acknowledged the amount is limited relative to the scope of the work.

“That’s really just the beginning,” he said. “And what that should signify is a commitment from me as the leader to allocate actual investments in this space.”

#5551. Sony Sonenium Incubation Program Targets PlayStation Games and Anime

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Sony has launched a new Soneium incubation program targeting blockchain-powered entertainment, including PlayStation games, anime, and digital collectibles. The initiative could open new doors for onchain gaming and fan experiences, although Sony has not announced any specific PlayStation crypto integration.

The Sony Onchain Entertainment Incubation Program opened applications on October 29 and will accept submissions through December 2026. It invites startups and creators to develop entertainment products using Soneium, the Sony blockchain network.

1/ Sony Group is launching the Sony Onchain Entertainment Incubation Program: A global program for builders and creators bringing Entertainment and Tokenized IP to life on Soneium.Selected projects will gain access to:💿 Get co-creation opportunities with Sony Group💿… pic.twitter.com/SzMFhKFUE1

Selected projects can receive technical infrastructure, marketing and business development support, community-building opportunities, and potential investment consideration. Sony said the program aims to move projects beyond technical experiments toward entertainment products that deliver tangible value to users.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Sony’s new program covers a wide range of entertainment products, extending beyond traditional blockchain gaming. Its target categories include console, PC and mobile games, anime, manga, music, films, esports, immersive experiences, and creator communities.

The company is also seeking projects that use blockchain to change how audiences interact with entertainment intellectual property. Potential applications include digital collectibles, fan communities, merchandise, and experiences that let users participate more directly in creator-led ecosystems.

Applicants must demonstrate a clear connection between entertainment, intellectual property, and onchain technology. Projects must also support Soneium, although multichain approaches are welcome if the network is properly integrated.

Sony has already built an incubation track record through two earlier initiatives. Soneium Spark selected 32 projects from more than 1,700 applications in 2024, while Soneium For All selected 11 projects from more than 250 applications in 2025.

The new program narrows that ecosystem-building effort toward entertainment experiences. Sony is looking for products that can connect content, communities, and digital assets in ways that encourage sustained user participation.

The announcement follows a fresh Soneium token announcement, and Sony’s wider gaming and blockchain ambitions. PlayStation games are explicitly included in the program’s target categories, and the program invites independent startups and creators to develop entertainment projects compatible with Soneium.

Anime is another notable area of interest, reflecting the overlap between entertainment franchises and highly engaged fan communities. Sony’s program explicitly includes anime and character intellectual property, creating room for developers to explore blockchain-based collectibles and other fan experiences.

Applications will undergo screening and selection from November 2026 through March 2027, with selected startups beginning to receive support on a rolling basis. Sony says participation does not guarantee investment, which remains subject to separate evaluation.

For now, the clearest takeaway is that Sony wants more entertainment businesses built around Soneium.

#5550. 5 changes in the IRS 2027 HSA and HDHP limits, from deposits to deductibles

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The IRS raised 2027 HSA contribution limits to $4,500 for self-only and $9,000 for family coverage. Here are 5 things to know.

Workers in a high-deductible health plan face a choice each year that shapes their finances for the next 12 months. They must decide how much of every paycheck to steer into a health savings account, and they must settle on that amount before the year begins. Rising health care costs have pushed more employees toward these accounts, and many are depositing more money into them. Each dollar set aside now can cover a medical bill that arrives later. The choice hinges on numbers the IRS resets every year. The agency caps what a person may contribute, sets the minimum deductible a plan needs to qualify, and limits how much someone can owe in cost sharing. Neither a household nor an employer can budget with confidence until the new amounts arrive.

Companies waited longer than usual for the 2027 HSA thresholds. In most years, the IRS publishes them in early May. This time the figures landed May 29, close to the end of the month. The delay mattered to anyone who guides staff through these accounts. Open enrollment is the season when many workplaces promote HSAs, and those pitches rely on the new maximums. A benefits team cannot tell someone how much more to save without knowing how far the ceiling moved. The changes take effect Jan. 1, 2027, which leaves the rest of 2026 for individuals and companies to recalculate.

SHRM reported the IRS announcement and set each 2027 value beside its 2026 counterpart. The article covers HSA contribution limits, the minimum deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums that define a high-deductible health plan, and the cap on an excepted-benefit health reimbursement arrangement. The article adds client balances from the HSA provider Lively, the publisher's own data on the share of employers offering the accounts, and findings from the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit, on how employees use HSAs. The five items that follow move from the new contribution rules to the habits of account holders.

Savers with self-only coverage can put up to $4,500 into a health savings account in 2027, a 2.3% increase over the $4,400 ceiling for 2026. The change opens $100 of extra room for single enrollees. Someone who wants to reach the new maximum through even monthly deposits needs $375 a month, and the added $100 accounts for less than $9 of that sum. The bump is real but small, too small to stand out in any one paycheck.

Households with family coverage gain more ground. Their allowance jumps to $9,000 from $8,750, a 2.9% rise worth $250. The family tier collects 2.5 times as many new dollars as the self-only tier, and its growth rate beats the single rate by 0.6 percentage points. Filling a family account in 2027 takes $750 a month, about $21 more than in 2026.

The 2027 family limit equals double the self-only amount to the dollar. In 2026, the family cap sat $50 short of $8,800, twice the $4,400 single-coverage figure. The larger family raise closed that $50 gap in one year.

A high-deductible health plan must carry a deductible of at least $1,750 for self-only coverage in 2027, $50 more than the $1,700 floor that applies in 2026. The amount marks the entry line for HDHP status. A plan whose single-person deductible falls below it will not qualify as an HDHP next year. The rule sets a minimum. Any deductible at or above the line passes this part of the test.

Family plans must clear a $3,500 threshold in 2027, $100 above the $3,400 mark for 2026. The household requirement equals twice the single-person amount in both years. Each tier moved up without disturbing the ratio between them. As a result, the family floor added twice as many dollars as the individual one. A family design that copied the $1,750 self-only deductible would fall $1,750 short of its own floor.

Employers whose plans sit at the 2026 minimums carry the most exposure to the change. A self-only plan with a $1,700 deductible, or a family plan set at $3,400, would fall short of the 2027 requirement. Both would need higher deductibles to keep their HDHP status. Employees in those plans would then face a larger deductible in 2027, even if nothing else about their coverage changes. Any self-only design sitting at least $50 above the old floor, or any family design at least $100 above it, passes with no adjustment.

The gap between the annual deposit ceiling and the minimum deductible widened to $2,750 for self-only coverage and $5,500 for families in 2027, up from $2,700 and $5,350 in 2026. A worker who funds the account to the maximum could pay the entire minimum deductible with money left over. The family cushion grew by $150, three times the $50 gain on the self-only side. Households gain the most new breathing room above the deductible floor next year.

A worker enrolled in a self-only high-deductible health plan faces a cost-sharing ceiling of $8,700 in 2027, $200 above the $8,500 maximum for 2026. The amount marks the most a single enrollee can owe in a plan year. A plan that wants to qualify as an HDHP cannot set its self-only limit any higher. Anyone who reaches the ceiling in both years pays more in 2027 for an identical worst case.

Households on family coverage face a $17,400 cap in 2027, a $400 increase over the 2026 mark of $17,000. The family tier equals twice the self-only cap in both years, and its dollar gain doubles the single-tier gain. A family's worst-case bill moves in lockstep with a single worker's. Neither tier outpaces the other, and households and individuals absorb the same proportional rise.

Deductibles, co-payments, and other charges all count toward these thresholds. Premiums do not. Every dollar an enrollee spends on the deductible chips away at the cap. A household's total health spending for 2027 can surpass $8,700 or $17,400 once premium payments enter the tally. A plan with a modest cost-sharing ceiling can cost more over a year than one with a higher ceiling if its premiums run steep. Enrollees weighing plans need to add a year of premiums on top to see their full annual exposure.

A year of the largest permitted HSA deposits covers about half of a year's cost-sharing bill in either tier. A self-only saver who contributes the full 2027 allowance faces a shortfall in any year that reaches the cap, and so does a family. The cost-sharing caps rose by more dollars than the contribution allowances, twice as much for self-only coverage and $150 more for families. As a result, the uncovered portion of a top-cost year widened from $4,100 to $4,200 for a single worker and from $8,250 to $8,400 for a family. Savers who expect heavy medical bills will need cash or other savings to bridge that remainder, even after filling their accounts to the limit.

An excepted-benefit health reimbursement arrangement can hold up to $2,250 in 2027, a $50 increase over the 2026 cap of $2,200. The self-only minimum deductible climbs by the same $50. Together, the HRA and deductible changes mark the smallest dollar gains in the IRS announcement. Every other figure the agency released grew by $100 or more.

The HRA amount arrives in the package the IRS issues each spring, ahead of the numbers for flexible spending accounts and 401(k) contributions. The early timetable leaves employers and HSA administrators ample room to adjust.

HR and benefits leaders can open the contribution conversation before enrollment season arrives. Many employers use open enrollment to urge workers to raise what they put into an HSA. An earlier push gives employees more months to weigh a larger contribution before the year begins. A team that waits gives up the head start the spring schedule creates. The spring release put the HSA and HRA values in front of employers before the flexible spending account and 401(k) limits came out, giving them an early chance to discuss those two accounts in firm dollar terms.

Most health savings account holders treat the account as a fund for current medical bills, with 67% saying they used their HSA for out-of-pocket expenses from the past year or the near term. Spending on recent or upcoming care dominates how these savers handle their money. Money enters and exits within a short window for this group. The account behaves like a checking account reserved for health expenses.

Retirement planning draws a smaller crowd. Some 35% of participants reported setting money aside in their HSA for health costs in retirement, roughly half the share that spends on near-term bills. Investing claims the thinnest slice, with 28% saying they had put their funds into investments. The remaining 72% did not report taking that step. Their dollars miss whatever growth a long horizon could deliver.

Deposits continue to swell despite those habits. Rising health care costs are steering more employees toward HSAs and prompting them to contribute larger sums. Clients of HSA provider Lively held an average balance of $5,457 in 2025, an 11% gain over the prior year's $4,923. The $534 jump arrived in a single year. About 61% of employers offer an HSA. More than half of firms, in other words, give workers access.

Bigger holdings have not translated into full value for employees. Industry experts want employers that sponsor HSAs to build up their teaching about the accounts and help workers extract more from them. Employers should "proactively educate employees on how HSAs work, from contributions and investments to long-term savings," Uralil said. Two of the areas named in that advice, putting money to work and saving for the long run, match the habits the usage data show a minority practicing.

Climbing account totals paired with low investment rates suggest a widening pool of HSA money sits parked until the next medical bill arrives.

#5549. Hackers steal $6.3B from Binance in biggest-ever crypto heist

Hackers have stolen about $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance, a major cryptocurrency exchange operator.

The heist is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto theft. TRM Labs Inc., a venture-backed blockchain intelligence startup, believes that both cyberattacks were carried out by a North Korean state-backed hacking group tracked as TraderTraitor.

About 40% of the stolen sum comprised stablecoins issued by three major crypto companies: Circle Internet Group Inc., Ripple Labs Inc. and Tether Ltd. They managed to freeze most of the funds before the hackers moved them out of reach. Binance, for its part, has set aside over $6.34 billion to cover users’ losses.

The hackers stole the funds by compromising several of the company’s wallets. One of them powers the infrastructure that Binance uses to process customers’ Ethereum transactions. According to TRM, the hackers breached the wallet late Thursday and sent its entire balance to a wallet they controlled.

TraderTraitor compromised Binance’s wallet by exploiting an Ethereum feature called EIP-7702 that the blockchain’s maintainers released last year. It enables a snippet of code called a smart contract to temporarily control a wallet. EIP-7702 only activates smart contracts if they receive authorization to run from the wallet’s operator. That authorization takes the form of an encrypted message.

The hackers used a malicious smart contract to take over Binance’s Ethereum wallet. It’s currently unclear how they obtained the authorization necessary to run such code.

According to Binance, an internal investigation determined that TraderTraitor had compromised a laptop belonging to one of its DevOps engineers. The company says that it has also “uncovered additional points of breach.”

“Developer and DevOps machines sit close to organizations’ most sensitive systems and hold credentials, tokens and deployment access,” said Kobi Sivilya, chief information security officer of cybersecurity company Checkmarx Ltd. “The question for any organization is how far an attacker could get from a single compromised workstation. Teams should review who has standing access to what systems, whether that access is appropriately limited and whether one machine can reach critical services without a second control.”

TRM determined that TraderTraitor had rehearsed the cyberattack for at least 36 hours before the theft. On Wednesday morning, the hackers deposited a small amount of funds into a malicious crypto wallet. Early Thursday, they tested some of the code that they used in the cyberattack on three different wallets.

According to Binance, the malware contained a “self-destruct mechanism” that deleted the tools the hackers installed on its infrastructure and the activity logs they generated. The mechanism made it more difficult for the company to investigate the attack. Binance did, however, determine that the hackers bypassed the approval workflows it uses to process crypto outflows.

“Organizations that rely on exchanges, custodians or any critical financial counterparty should ask what continuous visibility they have into those relationships,” Rand Davis, chief technology officer at SecurityScorecard, told SiliconANGLE in an email. “They should also ask what their playbook is when a counterparty pauses withdrawals or services. Security leaders can use this moment to map which third parties sit on their critical paths, pressure-test contingency plans, and watch for the phishing and social-engineering follow-on that typically trails a headline event of this scale.”

Binance suspended crypto deposits and withdraws on its exchange after it discovered the breach. The company has since restored deposits, but its withdrawal processing system remains offline. Binance plans to reactivate the feature on Monday.

#5548. Microsoft makes new ‘voluntary exit’ offer to about a quarter of its workforce, including some execs

by Todd Bishop on Oct 26, 2026 at 8:57 amOctober 31, 2026 at 8:48 am

Microsoft is making a new buyout offer to a much broader group of employees, this time including some executives — signaling that it’s not done shrinking its workforce despite thousands of layoffs and retirements this year.

The Voluntary Exit Offer, announced Monday in a memo to employees, is open to about 60,000 people in participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India, the company told GeekWire. That’s about a quarter of its workforce, which numbered 223,000 people at last count.

Microsoft didn’t provide a projection for how many employees will accept, but the company told GeekWire it anticipates a much smaller share than the roughly 30% who took its earlier voluntary retirement offer, which went to longtime employees more likely to take the deal.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” wrote Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s chief people officer, in the memo to employees.

It also gives participating organizations within the company “another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” she added.

Microsoft’s count of 223,000 full-time employees as of June 30 was down from 228,000 a year earlier, according to its annual filings. That latest number came before its July layoffs.

However, Microsoft says the offer isn’t a sign that it needs fewer employees. Instead, a company spokesperson described it as one of several ways it’s adjusting to changing business needs.

The Voluntary Exit Offer includes financial support and career planning resources, according to the memo. It says eligible employees will receive the details by email.

The package is equivalent to Microsoft’s standard severance, according to the company, including base pay based on tenure and level, continued stock vesting, healthcare coverage for a fixed period and career transition services. It doesn’t include the extended healthcare that was a major draw of the retirement program. Employees have until the first week of December to decide.

The new offer does not come with any age or tenure requirement, and performance isn’t a factor, the company said. It goes up to level 70 on Microsoft’s internal scale, which includes general managers and some employees with vice president titles, but not corporate vice presidents.

That’s a big change from the voluntary retirement program that Microsoft offered this spring, which was the first in its history. That program was limited to U.S. employees at the senior director level (level 67) and below whose age plus years at the company reached a minimum threshold. The company described that as a one-time initiative.

Buyouts are still relatively rare among the largest tech companies, which have generally relied on layoffs, stricter performance reviews and return-to-office mandates to thin their ranks.

Like its peers, Microsoft is under pressure from Wall Street to hold down operating expenses as it pours tens of billions of dollars into data centers and AI infrastructure.

Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs in July, about 2% of its global workforce, including about 600 in Washington state, followed by hundreds more across the company in September. The company cut more than 15,000 jobs in 2025.

The company said the new offer is not a replacement for layoffs, which will remain part of the company’s approach depending on business conditions.

When Microsoft offered the retirement program this spring, about 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible U.S. employees took the deal. Coleman told GeekWire in July that the results reduced the size of the layoffs Microsoft announced that month.

At the time, Coleman said Microsoft was studying how to make voluntary exits a more regular part of how it manages its workforce, possibly on an annual or ongoing basis.

Among the other changes this time, Microsoft is leaving it to business leaders to decide whether their groups participate, the company said. The company’s sales organization is not participating, nor are some engineering groups and corporate functions.

“There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee,” Coleman wrote in the memo, explaining that participation by different groups “varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments, and workforce needs.”

She said Microsoft will keep helping employees build new skills and, where it makes sense, move into other jobs inside the company. Microsoft said in July that it had redeployed more than 4,000 employees into new roles over the previous year.

Microsoft reports quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon, which could include projections for the cost of the new buyout offer. The company disclosed a $900 million charge for the retirement program in its April earnings report.

#5546. Suspected cyberattack hit supermarket freezers across Europe in second wave

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Retailers in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Estonia and Ireland reported temperature spikes; no one has claimed responsibility

Ahold Delhaize said an IT incident caused temperatures to climb in refrigeration systems across dozens of supermarkets it runs in Belgium and Luxembourg on Monday, according to The Guardian. Grocers in Sweden, Estonia and Ireland reported similar problems, making this the second suspected cyberattack on European store cooling systems after one in France.

Ahold Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester said the company is investigating the temperature increases, according to The Guardian. Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration firm Sabcobel, said the attack switched the units' evaporators to defrost mode, according to Al Jazeera. Moelans said technicians were called out starting at 1 a.m. to cut the compromised installations off from the grid, according to The Guardian.

A Colruyt Group spokesperson said the refrigeration equipment in five Spar shops was targeted, according to NBC News. Colruyt franchises out the Spar outlets it oversees across Belgium.

In Sweden, Coop said six stores were affected, and ICA said a small number of its outlets had their cooling and freezing equipment knocked offline by an incident, according to The Guardian. Axfood said hackers broke into freezers at a Gothenburg-area hub that handles home-delivery orders, according to Al Jazeera.

John Billow, head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity center, said the agency is handling several incidents tied to cooling equipment in stores, according to Al Jazeera. He said Sweden has many exposed operational technology devices that need updates or patches.

Jann Mutso, CEO of technology supplier Kitman Coldtech, said at least one Estonian grocery chain was hit and that its temperatures had been pushed up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), according to Al Jazeera. Ireland’s SuperValu said a “cyber incident” compromised one particular type of refrigeration unit in 13 of the chain’s 223 stores, according to Al Jazeera.

No one has claimed responsibility for Monday's incidents or the French attack, according to Al Jazeera.

The incidents follow an October attack in France that disabled refrigeration at Intermarché, Coopérative U and Leclerc stores and drove temperatures in refrigerators and freezers up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) through a continuous defrost cycle. French police said hackers took over the cooling equipment of as many as 700 supermarkets, according to The Guardian. The hackers took over control units that came largely from Danfoss, a Danish company.

Ahold Delhaize notified Dutch police last month of a cybersecurity incident, according to The Guardian.

#5545. Former GitHub CEO launches rival platform built for AI coding agents

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Oct 26, 2026 at 10:37 amOctober 26, 2026 at 10:37 am

A startup led by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is introducing its own platform for storing, reviewing and shipping code written by AI agents, competing with the company he used to run.

The startup, Entire, on Monday unveiled what it calls a Git forge — a service for hosting code, reviewing changes and running builds, the core of what GitHub does — designed for teams whose AI agents write code faster than people can review it. The company is pitching it as an alternative to GitHub.

The news comes two days before GitHub’s annual Universe conference in San Francisco. Microsoft acquired GitHub for $7.5 billion in 2018 and has since folded it into its CoreAI division.

The biggest change is Trails, Entire’s replacement for the pull request, the standard way developers propose and review code changes. The pull request “has become an audit log that only the agent reads,” Dohmke wrote in a blog post Monday. Instead of reading through every changed line, developers see a dashboard of scores from AI agents evaluating the code on each update.

According to Entire, multiple AI agents check the quality of each change, so developers can merge code without reading every line. Teams can also require a person’s sign-off, or passing automated tests, before any code goes in, the company said.

The launch comes as GitHub strains under the load from AI agents. The platform has had several significant outages in recent months, including one in August that lasted nearly eight hours. GitHub is moving from its own data centers to Microsoft’s Azure cloud to add capacity. GitHub said developers and agents made 7.38 billion commits, or saved code changes, on the platform in September alone.

Dohmke, who is based in Bellevue, Wash., left GitHub last year after nearly four years as CEO. Entire says it now has 50 employees. The company is fully remote.

Entire isn’t alone in rethinking code hosting for AI agents. AI coding company Cursor launched its own code-hosting service, Origin, in August. And Anthropic recently described building its own source control system as the number of code changes it merged each day grew from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September.

With the latest updates, Entire now lets developers host private code repositories directly on its service in the U.S., Europe, India and Australia, and says its service can handle up to 89 times as many code pushes per second as GitHub, based on its own benchmarks. It’s partnering with Buildkite and Depot on build and test pipelines, giving developers a way to move off GitHub Actions. Public repositories and self-hosting are on the roadmap.

Entire is also adding what it calls Continuous Memory, which lets AI agents search past coding sessions for the context behind earlier changes. The company says one part of it, a map of the codebase, cut token use by up to 71% in its testing.

That goes beyond the startup’s July launch, which mirrored existing GitHub repositories on a faster network rather than replacing them. Developers can still mirror from GitHub, or now move their code to Entire instead.

Microsoft’s venture arm M12 was among the backers of Entire’s $60 million seed round in February. Felicis led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona and Basis Set Ventures, along with individual investors such as Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

“Code review was always a bottleneck,” Dohmke said at a Madrona event last month. “I’ve never worked in a software company where I didn’t wait for somebody else to review my pull request, and you have to ping people in Slack three times. And there was this one guy that had to review everything because he knew what to look for. And now that bottleneck is 10 times bigger.”

#5544. Google X co-founder Sebastian Thrun raises $130M for AI engineering startup Dulo

Dulo Inc., a startup co-founded by prominent artificial intelligence researcher Sebastian Thrun, has raised $130 million in funding.

The Information broke the news of the investment on Thursday. Dulo co-founder Adrian Aoun confirmed the report in a post on X.

Before launching Dulo with Thrun (pictured) earlier this year, Aoun sold an early natural language processing startup called Wavii Inc. to Google LLC for over $30 million. He has also invested in companies such as Pinterest Inc. Thrun, in turn, co-founded Google’s X research lab. He led the X program that later became Waymo and helped establish Google Brain, a precursor to Google DeepMind.

Dulo’s round included contributions from former Google Chief Executive Officer Eric Schmidt and Ram Shriram, one of the search giant’s first investors. They were joined by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, famed venture capitalist John Doerr and more than a half-dozen startup funds. Dulo didn’t disclose its valuation.

The company’s one-page website states that it’s developing foundation models optimized for hardware design tasks. In August, Thrun listed robotics among Dulo’s focus areas. It’s possible the company’s AI is meant to speed up the development of industrial robots and autonomous vehicles.

Thrun joined Google in 2007 after leading the development of Stanley, an early self-driving vehicle that helped kickstart the autonomous driving market. He later founded a flying taxi startup with financial backing from Google co-founder Larry Page.

It’s unclear what hardware design tasks Dulo’s models will automate. One possibility is that the startup hopes to optimize engineering simulations, which hardware teams use to check their product designs for flaws before manufacturing them. Dulo’s website says it’s looking to facilitate “manufacturing at lightspeed.”

Several other engineering-focused AI startups are also working to optimize simulations. One recently funded player, Vinci4D Inc., has built a platform that automates the so-called meshing phase of simulation projects. Meshing is a process through which engineers turn a product’s blueprint into a collection of small, three-dimensional shapes. That arrangement reduces the amount of hardware needed to run simulations.

Other AI startups are working to speed up partially differentiated equations. Simulators rely on such equations to predict the behavior of hardware systems under real-world conditions.

Dulo’s most prominent venture-backed rival is Prometheus Inc., an engineering AI startup co-led by Amazon.com Inc. founder Jeff Bezos. The company raised $12 billion in funding earlier this year from Bezos and a group of financial institutions. Like Dulo, Prometheus is using AI to speed up the development of complex hardware systems such as robots.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The airline's half-year profit fell 15% to €2.15 billion, and a cost review includes a possible temporary pay freeze

Ticket prices across Europe could jump by up to 20% next year once Ryanair’s existing fuel contracts lapse, CEO Michael O’Leary told CNBC on Monday.

"I believe you're going to see airfares rise next year across Europe by 10%, maybe even 20%," O'Leary said, according to CNBC. "There's still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we're all facing next year."

Ryanair reported first-half results on Monday showing after-tax profit fell 15% to €2.15 billion in the six months to Sept. 30, from €2.54 billion a year earlier. Revenue rose 3% to €10.08 billion, and passenger numbers rose 6% to 125.8 million. Average fares fell 4% to €55.70 from €58.

The airline said it expects short-haul fares to climb next year, though not by enough to cover the €2 billion jump in fuel spending it estimates for the fiscal year ending in March 2028, based on current forward prices. It is reviewing its costs, and the options under consideration include staffing flights with fewer crew, possibly holding pay flat for a limited period, renegotiating with airports and leaning more heavily on AI for back-office work.

"Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict, we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027," O'Leary said in a statement.

Ryanair said it has locked in prices for 80% of the fuel it needs through March 2027, at $67 a barrel. For the 12 months after that, Ryanair has now hedged 25% of its fuel at $95 a barrel, up from 15% at an average of $85 at the end of June.

The company said in September that it was trimming its annual passenger goal to 214 million from 216 million, a move meant to limit how much unhedged fuel it must buy this winter. It expects passenger volumes over the November-to-March winter season to hold level with last year.

Ryanair said fares in the current quarter are running above year-earlier levels, after a 2% drop in the quarter that ended in September. Cautious travelers are waiting until shortly before departure to book, so pricing through the remainder of the quarter hinges on how many people reserve seats at the last minute before Christmas, the company said. It said it is too early to offer a profit forecast for the full year, since the outlook remains "highly sensitive to conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine," and also hinges on strikes by European air traffic controllers, macroeconomic shocks and fuel prices.

Chief Financial Officer Neil Sorahan expects demand to stay strong next year, according to RTÉ. “An extra €5 or €10 [on a Ryanair airfare] won’t necessarily dampen people’s willingness to travel,” Sorahan said, according to RTÉ.

Ryanair held €2.6 billion in cash as of Sept. 30 after repaying €1.3 billion in debt, the company said.

Ryanair stock rose 3.7% in Irish trading on Monday and has fallen about 19% this year.

#5541. Stoke Space lines up $150M Pentagon loan for a second launch pad in Florida

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 26, 2026 at 3:13 pmOctober 26, 2026 at 3:14 pm

Kent, Wash.-based Stoke Space has secured a conditional commitment for a $150 million loan from the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital to build a second launch pad at Cape Canaveral for a larger version of its fully reusable rocket.

The loan isn’t final until Stoke meets a list of financial, legal, technical and due-diligence requirements. The announcement Monday comes less than two months after Stoke raised roughly $1 billion in a Series E round, bringing its total funding to about $2.3 billion.

The new pad would serve Stoke’s Nova Block 2 rocket, which is designed to carry up to 15 metric tons to low Earth orbit. That’s five times the capacity of Nova Pathfinder, which Stoke plans to launch for the first time from its existing pad in early 2027. Block 2 is slated to debut in 2029.

The loan would be paired with private capital to pay for the pad, according to the Department of War. Jordan Sebold, senior managing director for investments at the Office of Strategic Capital, said in a statement that adding launch infrastructure would “enhance the overall capacity and resilience of the commercial space industrial base.”

The Office of Strategic Capital was set up in 2022 to draw private investment into technologies seen as critical to national security. The following year, Congress gave it the power to make loans and loan guarantees to companies in those fields. Space launch is one of the technology categories it targets.

“By expanding domestic launch facility capacity, this investment enables launch service providers to ensure our commercial and defense partners have reliable, high-cadence access to space,” David Lorch, the office’s director, said in the news release.

Stoke is already lined up for military launch work. In 2025, the Space Force added the company to a pool of providers that can compete for national security missions under Lane 1 of the program’s third phase. Lane 1 is the tier meant for newer launch companies and less demanding payloads. Stoke can’t bid on those missions until it completes a successful orbital flight.

The company has other federal ties as well. The Defense Innovation Unit awarded Stoke a $4.5 million contract in 2024 to study rapid delivery of cargo to orbit, and possibly back to Earth. In June, Stoke was one of 37 companies NASA chose for unfunded partnerships. Stoke’s project focuses on returning Nova’s upper stage safely through the atmosphere.

Nova is designed so both of its stages can return and fly again. The booster flies itself back for recovery. The upper stage uses a metal heat shield cooled by liquid hydrogen that circulates through channels inside it, to survive the heat of reentry. Only SpaceX, with its much larger Starship, is pursuing the same goal, and it hasn’t fully achieved it yet. Stoke has yet to launch a rocket to orbit.

Stoke was founded in 2019 by two Blue Origin veterans: Andy Lapsa, the CEO, and Tom Feldman, the chief technology officer. The company has about 400 employees. Most work at its 168,000-square-foot factory and headquarters in Kent, and about 50 are at its test site in Moses Lake, which is expanding from 75 to 550 acres. About 50 more work at Cape Canaveral.

GeekWire reached out to Stoke Space for comment and we’ll update this story when we hear back.

#5540. Google, Anthropic and others to support new AI crawling opt-out standard

Google LLC, Microsoft Corp., Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to support an upcoming website crawling standard.

The technology will enable website operators to block artificial intelligence developers from using their content to train their models.

Many websites contain a text file titled “robots.txt” that informs crawlers what content they may access. A publisher can use the file to block scraping across the board or only make specific webpages inaccessible. It’s also possible to include certain other instructions. For example, a company can ask crawlers not to visit its website too often.

Website operators historically used robots.txt files to manage how search engines interact with their properties. Nowadays, the technology also helps regulate the activity of the scrapers with which AI providers collect training data.

A company that wishes to disallow training-related scraping must make multiple edits to its website’s robots.txt file. In particular, it needs to add a separate entry for every single AI provider. If an AI provider uses multiple scrapers to collect data, each scraper requires its own robots.txt entry.

The crawling standard Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI are backing aims to simplify the process. It would allow website operators to block all scrapers that collect training data for generative AI models with a single robots.txt entry. The setting wouldn’t apply to models that “perform exclusively non-generative tasks.”

The structure of robots.txt files follows a standardized format called the Robots Exclusion Protocol. Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI plan to incorporate  their crawling standard into the format. They have already submitted a draft version of their proposal to the Internet Engineering Task Force, the nonprofit that maintains the Robots Exclusion Protocol.

Microsoft stated in a blog post that it will also provide a crawling setting called AI Grounding. It’s designed for situations where an AI model seeks to access a webpage in order to answer a user question rather than to collect training data.

Microsoft’s setting will enable website operators to prevent its services from sending such requests. The feature will also extend to third-party AI tools that use Microsoft technologies to process prompts.

OpenAI plans to offer similar controls. Both the ChatGPT developer and Microsoft intend to add support for the crawling standard in the coming months, while Google will follow suit sometime next year. Meta Platforms Inc. expressed support for the idea behind the technology but hasn’t yet committed to implementing it.

#5538. AI optimism meets data center backlash as protesters disrupt Seattle AI Week kickoff

by Todd Bishop on Oct 26, 2026 at 10:44 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 11:21 am

The Washington Technology Industry Association kicked off the third annual Seattle AI Week on Monday with a reminder that AI affects everyone, from engineers and artists to “someone who learned about ChatGPT today,” as WTIA’s Nick Ellingson put it.

“All of us should be a part of that conversation,” he added.

A few people in the audience took that statement literally.

Members of Troublemakers, a Seattle climate activism group, interrupted the week’s opening panel on AI and economic growth several times before they were led out by security. Outside on Elliott Bay, others floated in kayaks with a banner: “Power for People, Not for Tech.”

“These are not your constituents — we are,” one protester told Beau Perschbacher, Gov. Bob Ferguson’s senior policy advisor, as he addressed the large crowd of tech and startup leaders at Seattle’s AI House. Perschbacher was on a panel with Joe Nguyen of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Mattie Zazueta of OpenAI, the event’s presenting sponsor.

The group’s main message, according to members who spoke with GeekWire: the rush to build data centers and roll out AI is putting the state’s communities, jobs and environment at risk, and Washington should be investing in green jobs and clean energy instead.

The protest comes amid a broader backlash against data centers in Washington state and across the country. The Seattle City Council voted unanimously in June to pause new large data centers in the city for a year, and Washington AI Resistance organized at least 19 protests around the state this month calling for a statewide moratorium.

The event also came the same day Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as it spends tens of billions of dollars on data centers and AI infrastructure.

The backlash contrasts with a push from the business and tech community for Washington state and the Seattle region to do more to stay competitive in the AI era.

“Washington helped build the technology economy of the last generation. We have an extraordinary opportunity to lead the AI economy of the next,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, now CEO of the business group Challenge Seattle, in her opening remarks at the AI Week event.

Gregoire cited efforts to put AI to work on the region’s own problems, including an AI permitting pilot in Everett that she said could cut the median wait for an accessory dwelling unit permit from 252 days to 90. She highlighted the AI-driven protein design work of Nobel laureate David Baker of the University of Washington, with applications in areas including the environment, agriculture and health care.

She also warned that Washington is close to the bottom for its business climate, even though it ranks second in North America for tech talent, as other states court its companies and jobs.

On the panel, Perschbacher said Ferguson’s administration has been focused on data centers since taking office, setting up a work group early last year to study their impact. The group looked for a Washington community that had been harmed by a data center and couldn’t find one, he said.

He added that the state won’t permit data centers to run diesel generators around the clock, and that their water use turned out to be “not out of line with a typical industrial user.”

Electricity is a different story. Data centers “use a really significant amount of electricity,” he said, and with demand also rising from EVs and heat pumps, getting enough power “is a major challenge.”

Perschbacher addressed the protesters directly, saying Washington has some of the strictest environmental laws in the country and that the state’s data center work group reinforced those rules rather than weakening them. Bills on ratepayer protections and transparency for data centers are likely to come back in the next legislative session, he said.

The issue also came up in the event’s second panel, on AI policy. State Sen. Marko Liias, who sponsored a bill this year on high-risk uses of AI, said data centers that want to locate in Washington need to meet “stringent expectations,” including adding clean energy to the grid, recycling water and dropping nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark. Washington’s goal “has never been to be the cheapest or easiest place,” he said.

“When energy becomes scarce, I do think we need to be clear that our communities deserve access to that energy before the data centers do,” Liias said.

Joe Braidwood, founder of AI governance startup Glacis, which works out of AI House, said on the same panel that it was the first event he’d attended there with a public protest. “I think that’s actually kind of promising that people care enough to want to come together and talk and disagree and figure this out,” he said.

Zazueta, OpenAI’s global head of community programs, said in the opening panel that the industry needs to do a better job showing people the benefits of AI. Many people “read about these scary headlines,” she said, but don’t see how the technology applies to their daily lives.

OpenAI runs AI literacy workshops and trains libraries and community groups to lead their own, she said. The company opened an expanded office in Bellevue in March, its largest engineering center outside San Francisco.

Speaking with GeekWire outside the event on Monday afternoon, one of the protesters who had interrupted the panel singled out that remark. She said it dismissed public concerns about AI as the product of bad headlines, and she objected to the idea of using community groups to win people over to the benefits of artificial intelligence.

“They want to infiltrate our communities,” she said.

The opening panel with Zazueta, Perschbacher and Nguyen was titled “The Abundance State: Washington’s Chance to Lead the AI Future.” The protester objected to that framing, saying the panelists’ idea of abundance came down to easing permits for data centers.

It wasn’t the first time the group has protested the tech industry’s energy use. In 2024, it blocked entrances at Amazon’s Seattle headquarters to protest the company’s plans to power data centers in Oregon with natural gas.

Inside the event on Monday, as the interruptions continued, Nguyen, a former state senator who now leads the Seattle chamber, had responded to the protesters directly. “If you want to have your own event, have your own event,” he told them.

After they were led out, Nguyen said he agreed with the protesters, calling their passion “very warranted.” Those concerns are one reason Washington created some of the most stringent energy policies in the country, he said, adding that everyone would be better off if data centers elsewhere were held to the same standards.

“I think we’re very unique in Washington state to be able to actually do this in a way that really is mindful of our values, of the environment, and also pushing for innovation as well,” he said.

At the same time, Nguyen said demand for AI and data centers is market-driven, and it isn’t fair to criticize data centers while using them every day.

“For anybody who’s upset with data centers, I hope that when you email me, don’t email me,” he said. “Print it off and walk it to my office.”

Update, Oct. 27: Protesters interrupted the opening session of WTIA’s Seattle AI Summit six times Tuesday morning, during an on-stage interview of OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji by GeekWire’s Todd Bishop. They objected to AI-related job losses, the climate impact of data centers, OpenAI’s ties to the Trump administration and the leadership of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

#5537. 5 findings on how the president's party fares in midterms since 1934

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Across 22 midterms since 1934, the president's party has lost 28 House seats on average. Here are 5 findings from the data.

A president can win the White House and then watch Congress slip from the party's grip two years later. Midterm elections function as a referendum on whoever occupies the Oval Office, and voters use them to grade a presidency at its halfway mark. The consequences extend beyond the scoreboard. Control of the House and Senate determines whether a legislative agenda advances or stalls. John T. Woolley, whose August 2022 analysis underpins this article, argued that divided government shrinks a president's capacity to pursue ambitious new policy. He also expected an opposition-held chamber to unleash a stream of disruptive congressional investigations into the administration.

Narrow majorities raise the price of even a modest swing. In late August 2022, Democrats held the House by nine seats, with four more vacant, and the Senate split 50-50. A few districts could transfer the gavel to Republicans. History offers one guide to how such a slim edge might hold up, yet it leaves out forces that shape individual campaigns. National fights over abortion and the legal controversies surrounding Trump promised to drive turnout in ways no long-run pattern captures. Local conditions and the strength of candidates in specific races also escape the numbers. Woolley anticipated voter participation climbing above its usual level, a shift that tends to help Democrats.

Woolley, writing for The American Presidency Project on Aug. 30, 2022, examined 22 midterm elections from 1934 through 2018 to gauge what the record implied for that November. His comparison of presidential approval reaches back to 1936, and his economic readings begin in 1946. He tested four variables against the White House party's gains and setbacks in each chamber: approval of the sitting president, the number of seats the party held going in, inflation, and nonfarm jobs growth. Approval showed a moderate positive relationship with seat swings, producing a correlation of 0.61 for the House and 0.45 for the Senate. Exposure mattered too. The count of seats a party had to protect correlated at 0.35 in the House and 0.57 in the Senate. Woolley then built a regression model and ran it both with and without the economic measures. He cautioned that its estimates carry wide margins of error and that the work rests, as many midterm projections do, on aggregated data. The five findings below form a selection from his analysis, which he completed before voters cast their ballots.

Across the 22 midterms held from 1934 through 2018, the party occupying the White House gave up an average of 28 House seats and four Senate seats. Setbacks of this size defined the typical midterm, and the record hands a sitting president few counterexamples to cite. Any White House strategist forecasting a quiet November would have been betting against most of history.

House pickups came in three of those contests, about 14% of the total. In the remaining 19, the president's party failed to enlarge its delegation in the lower chamber. The Senate offered friendlier terrain. The White House party added Senate seats on six occasions, about 27% of midterms and double the House frequency. It still came away without new Senate ground in 16 elections. Even the more forgiving chamber withheld new seats from the incumbent party in most years.

Simultaneous advances in both chambers happened twice across the 84-year span. Two of the three House pickups came in those years. The third arrived in a year when the Senate delegation did not grow. Senate pickups broke the opposite way. Four of the six landed in years when the party could not expand its House ranks. A Senate pickup, then, offered little hint of how the House would go.

Fifteen of the 22 midterms left the president's party with no new seats in either chamber. The other seven brought progress somewhere, and Senate pickups figured in six of them. Four featured Senate pickups alone, two featured growth on both sides of the Capitol, and one featured a House pickup alone. House advances tended to arrive as part of a broader good year for the White House party, while two-thirds of Senate pickups stood by themselves. The pattern suggests that a president hoping to salvage something from a midterm has found it on the Senate side, where new seats can come even in a year the House delegation fails to grow.

Six presidents between 1936 and 2018 headed into a midterm with approval between 40% and 45%, the band Biden occupied in August 2022, and none of their parties added a single House seat. Biden's Democrats entered the 2022 campaign without one historical case of a House pickup at his level of public support.

House damage under these six stretched from 13 seats at the mild end to 63 at the severe end, and the group's mean loss came to 36. A 50-seat gap separated the gentlest outcome from the harshest. Middling popularity foretold the direction of a House result but said little about its scale.

The smallest House setback in this group outstripped the margin Democrats held in August 2022. A president polling in this band could not lean on the most forgiving precedent to protect a thin majority.

The 36-seat figure exceeds the 28-seat norm across all 22 midterms since 1934 by eight seats. Presidents whose standing sat in the low-to-mid 40s paid a measurable premium in the lower chamber over the typical midterm toll. Tepid approval deepened the headwind most White House parties face at midterm time.

Senate results for the same six presidents spanned a nine-seat loss to a two-seat gain. At least one of their parties left the election with a Senate pickup, an outcome none achieved in the House. The upper-chamber average settled at a four-seat loss, matching the standard setback across every midterm in the record. An 11-seat spread separated the best and worst Senate outcomes, a fraction of the distance between House extremes.

Ratings in this band exacted their extra cost in the House alone and left Senate results no worse than an ordinary midterm. An ordinary midterm carried enough force to topple Democrats in a tied Senate, where a loss matching this group's mean would have handed Republicans the chamber.

The party holding the White House went into midterms from 1934 to 2018 guarding an average of 237 House seats and 17 Senate seats, and bigger rosters have brought bigger defeats. Woolley names this exposure as one of two forces that have moved in step with partisan swings across the record, with presidential approval as the other. The logic runs in one direction. A party sitting on a large majority has more districts and states it can surrender, and history bears out heavier surrenders.

Democrats carried a lighter load into 2022. They held 222 House seats and 14 Senate seats, 15 below the historical norm in the House and three below it in the Senate. The Senate gap looks trivial on paper. Scaled against the size of each baseline, though, it cuts deeper. Three seats amount to about 18% of a 17-seat average, while 15 seats come to about 6% of a 237-seat one. By that yardstick, Democrats faced the Senate contests with a much thinner slate than the typical White House party.

The upper chamber shows the tighter bond between exposure and outcome in Woolley's data, and the House link runs looser. The chamber where the pattern has held firmest also proved to be where the Democrats' relative cushion ran widest. Exposure sent its most encouraging signal for Democrats in the Senate.

Exposure covers half of Woolley's two-part picture, and the pair need not point the same way in a given year. A party can defend a modest roster and still absorb heavy losses if voters sour on the president. Democrats' 2022 position eased one source of risk and left the other untouched.

On exposure alone, the 2022 map pointed Democrats toward smaller setbacks than a typical midterm hands the president's party, with the Senate the likelier place for that advantage to surface.

Jobs growth topped 4% year over year in 2022, one of the three strongest readings for any midterm year from 1946 to 2018. Woolley found no relationship between hiring trends and the gains or setbacks of the president's party in either chamber. A booming labor market has offered sitting presidents no reliable cushion at the ballot box across the decades he studied. Democrats in 2022 carried into the campaign an economic asset the historical record valued at nothing.

Inflation showed a faint negative tie to House results across the midterms Woolley examined, and none to Senate outcomes. Years of faster price growth have lined up with House showings a shade worse for the White House party. Senate contests revealed no such pattern. Whatever toll rising prices took would show up in House races and spare the Senate. Woolley judged neither inflation nor jobs growth a strong predictor of seat swings. Even the House connection offers a campaign little forecasting power.

Popular expectations in 2022 ran in opposite directions. Many observers predicted that climbing costs would hurt Biden. Woolley allowed that the strong jobs reports might cancel out that damage. Each camp treated the economy as a lever on the result, one pulling toward Republican pickups and the other toward a softer blow for Democrats.

Woolley opened his discussion of the economy with the question "What about the economy, stupid?" and answered it with a finding he called perhaps surprising. Neither the inflation fear nor the jobs hope finds much backing in past midterms. Approval of the sitting president and the number of seats his party must protect carry the weight in Woolley's account. Midterm voters appear to judge the White House party on something other than paychecks and prices.

Shortfall: Slide 4 runs about 289 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source devotes roughly one short section to the economy (the 2022 jobs reading, the weak inflation link, the zero jobs link, and the competing expectations), and the 8.4% inflation figure could not be verified in the source notes, so it was not used.

John T. Woolley projected in August 2022 that Democrats would cede about 30 House seats and three Senate seats in that fall's midterms. His estimate turned the long-run record into a concrete number for a party clinging to slim control of both chambers.

A drop of that size would have dwarfed the Democrats' single-digit House majority, handing Republicans the gavel with seats to spare. In a tied Senate, a one-seat shift would have tipped control, and Woolley foresaw three. His subtitle delivered the same verdict, warning that history suggested Democrats would surrender both the House and the Senate.

Woolley set a floor beneath which the result would defy his expectations. A Democratic House decline of fewer than 12 seats, he wrote, would catch him off guard. Even this low-end mark exceeded the Democrats' House cushion. By his reckoning, any result that let Democrats keep the House would have counted as an upset.

Woolley's point forecast put the Democratic toll at 29 House seats and three Senate seats. Folding in inflation and jobs growth left those numbers all but unchanged. The rounded 30-seat projection and the 29-seat point estimate differ by one seat, which shows Woolley's headline framing tracked his own calculations. The near match indicates the forecast drew its force from presidential approval and seat exposure, with economic conditions adding little beyond what the historical pattern captured. His 12-seat surprise line sat 17 seats below that central estimate, leaving a wide band of outcomes he would have treated as ordinary.

Every outcome inside that band would have handed the House to Republicans. The heavier turnout Woolley anticipated sat outside his numbers, and any Democratic overperformance would have to come from forces his data could not measure. His forecast spelled out what the past implied and left the rest to campaigns and voters.

#5536. Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

The artificial intelligence buildout is making an enormous bet on what businesses will eventually be willing to pay for intelligence. In our research this summer on forecasting the AI bubble, we argued that a key indicator to watch is productive utilization by enterprise customers.

Specifically, we said at the time, if infrastructure supply catches up before productive monetization materializes, the risk of a bubble popping increases to what we felt were dangerous levels. We forecast that the supply constraints and healthy capital funding appetites at that time could provide conditions for a soft landing. And we pegged 2029 as the highest-risk year.

And that brings us to the next obvious question: What has to happen inside mainstream enterprises for their AI investments to become economically self-funding? Michael Burry’s analysis of Anthropic PBC highlights the scale and interconnectedness of the commitments that Anthropic is making. Apollo’s research by Torsten Slok raises questions about how broadly the financial benefits are showing up today. And the history of the personal computer and internet eras reminds us that productivity gains aren’t always immediate, and that powerful technologies can coexist with what initially seem to be poor investment returns that take time to appear.

We think the path to a soft landing runs through changes in how businesses operate, specifically the work that they do, the people that they need, how they scale and the value that their customers are ultimately going to pay for. Welcome to Breaking Analysis, episode 332: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?

Joining us today is Crawford Del Prete. He’s the former president of IDC and now senior adviser at PSG Equity. For decades, Crawford has had a front-row seat on technology transitions, and he brings current perspectives on how software businesses are adapting to AI, how new AI-native companies are forming, and what the emerging operating model looks like. Crawford, welcome. Good to see you.

Crawford Del Prete: Hey, great to see you, Dave.

Dave Vellante: As of this recording, the Nasdaq is down almost 1,000 points, so it’s getting worse by the minute. It’s not quite at 1,000, it’s only down 937. There are a lot of reasons there. Of course, we had earnings last night from the big hyperscalers which were not well received.

Google’s disappointment in advertising and AWS’ capex spend and negative cash flow were the culprits, but the hyperscalers are cranking in cloud. Anyway, let’s start with what you’re seeing, specifically in the market, but also inside businesses. Where is AI changing economics from your point of view?

Crawford Del Prete: Well, AI is changing economics in so many different areas, right? So we’re starting to see the early signs of productivity gains, but we’re not yet seeing them in the numbers. And what I’m seeing is that companies are starting to automate workflows. They’re starting to use AI in different ways. And those ways are ways that you would expect initially, right? So we saw a big move toward coding. We saw a big move toward customer service. But now we’re starting to get into a lot of the other areas where individual tasks are starting to get automated within organizations.

And as that happens, it becomes very uneven in terms of how we’re starting to see the impact of AI in organizations on an everyday basis. Again, jobs are made up of hundreds, sometimes thousands of tasks. And now we’re starting to automate those tasks, but we haven’t necessarily changed the way work is wired in an organization. So I think that makes for some of the inconsistencies that I think we’ll talk about in a minute in terms of the productivity numbers that we’re seeing.

Dave Vellante: Thank you for that. You and I cut our teeth during the PC era. And of course, we learned Moore’s Law was everything. We learned about the rapidly declining prices. Tech was always deflationary. Now tech is inflationary. Remember, you and I used to follow the disk drive markets, and customers would want to lock in. They’d want to have a forward pricing contract.

Dave Vellante: Historic declines followed a curve according to Moore’s Law. Today you want to lock in current prices because they’re going up. So you’re seeing all kinds of crazy dislocations. The Anthropic S-1 came out this week, and there were definitely some positive numbers in the document. Everybody, of course, talks about the revenue growth. We’ve never seen anything like it before: 14x in the first half of 2026 to $16 billion. But what really stood out to me, Crawford, was the balance sheet. The company says they’ve got $132 billion in liquid assets, so cash and equivalents. And there are only two nonbanks in the U.S. — and this has been reported — that have more cash than Anthropic. That’s, of course, Alphabet and Berkshire.

And remember, they’ve raised about $140 billion. So let that sink in for the audience a bit. It basically has burned $10 billion to get to a $32 billion revenue run rate. But the big question, of course, is around the economic return on that capacity that’s being committed.

Michael Burry, who writes Cassandra Unchained — his work, by the way, is unparalleled. His ideas are often pooh-poohed. He got sort of slammed for the whole GPU lifecycle, and people dismiss him, but his research is deep and unique. And this diagram shows the interconnected financing and commercial relationships around Anthropic. He pulled this all together from the S-1, and you see it’s $537 billion of multiyear compute commitments across all kinds of different arrangements. You’ve got take-or-pay deals, minimum purchase agreements, lease deals, capacity that’s conditioned upon delivery, stuff like that. Of course, this isn’t current debt, but it’s stuff that they’ve committed to.

So Crawford, I’ve got a bunch of questions for you. Just answer them all, or whatever you have best visibility on. First of all, you’ve got capital providers and infrastructure suppliers and model companies. They’re all sort of interconnected. So how much of a concern is that? Are your portfolio companies spending more? Is it because AI is showing better return, or is it because they have FOMO and they’ve gotta remain competitive? Crawford Del Prete: So look, Dave, you and I have been around this industry forever, and we’ve never been at a point where you’ve got an interconnected industry that is built on yesterday’s architecture because a new architecture that came along had to be redefined. So this circular financing is, in my opinion, a way to basically rebuild the stack around the world all at the same time. So I talked to one customer this week that said to me, “I cannot get my hands on enough compute capacity.” And I pushed back and said, “Wait a minute.” “No, no, no, you don’t understand. Other customers are starting to look at token spend. That Opus 4.8 model, not a very bad model. The reality is, it’s all over the map. But I will tell you that I’m not seeing tons of customers saying, “I’ve got to pull back,” because it’s about competitiveness. I’ve got to be competitive, and I’ve got to give my team members the tools to achieve things they never could achieve before with AI.

Dave Vellante: We did slice the workload salami pretty thin at IDC, didn’t we? And to your point about this whole new architecture you’re seeing at Intel today, Intel’s down 30% today.

Dave Vellante: Basically, general-purpose x86 is kind of being absorbed into accelerated computing. I guess PCs are obviously what folks missed. In your quant example, that customer’s monetizing, right? That’s why they want as much compute as possible, right?

Crawford Del Prete: That customer is monetizing all day long and is saying, “Look, I can innovate by giving my users more capacity, and they can do things they never could do before. They can create analysis. They can create deliverables that they never were able to create before.” And so I would say that those kinds of customers exist, and they exist at scale. And I feel like there is not this big dichotomy between customers in terms of who’s willing to spend and who’s not willing to spend. Everybody’s willing to spend. It really just comes down to the amount of resources that they have.

Now, you asked the second question, which is: Are companies spending more because AI is improving their economics, or because they have to do it to remain competitive? And I will tell you that whether it’s a portfolio company or it’s not, there is no software company today that is not investing for AI. They have to. They’ve got to do it to increase their product set to be competitive, because there are many, many competitive factors that never existed before. And these are all things that I’m looking at every single day.

There’s a whole discussion around: Can an adjacent, large, at-scale platform, by using AI, absorb your area, the area you’re innovating in? And then separately, there’s the omnipresent question of — and we can talk about this for a while — can customers vibe code? And can they create a software product as opposed to licensing it or using it? So everybody is investing. And if you’re not investing in AI — there are a few companies in that category, but very, very few — then you’re probably writing your own death sentence.

Dave Vellante: Right. And you, as a capital allocator, aren’t that interested in investing in a company that’s not investing in AI.

Dave Vellante: Okay, so we’re going to try to square this circle, because we see these relationships that Anthropic and others have struck, how they’re funding the buildout. Now, last weekend, Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok put forth his view of how far those benefits, the AI benefits, have spread.
