Then several customers that we talked to wanted to bring AI on-prem for sovereignty and latency, to own their own tech stack, and to have financial controls. But this VP of infrastructure and ops said they needed 80% GPU utilization just to break even. To your point, the neoclouds and the hyperscalers are good at getting high utilization. Most enterprises can’t get there today. So the business case doesn’t pencil out, and they’re paying premiums to cloud companies.

The last example is a German enterprise that said CoreWeave had great technical advantages, but they stayed with Azure because a second cloud would have added operating overhead. Rather than take that on, they went the path of least resistance, stayed with Azure, and tapped their existing relationship and the credits they had. The point is that these concrete customer examples underscore the distance between getting a technology to work and then making money from that deployment.

So, Crawford, are these situations common from what you’re seeing? You pointed out before that technology is not the problem. What’s the way to the future?

Crawford Del Prete: By the way, great research. These are very, very common problems that we continue to see. I think this is where customers are going to be working with cloud providers going forward. They’re going to be working with hyperscalers going forward. People think about it as a binary world where, “Oh, I’m going to have my data on-prem in a data center, and I’m going to have to have very, very high utilization to break even,” to the point you just made. Or, “I’m going to be in the cloud.”

I think what people aren’t thinking about enough is the hybrid permutations that can happen there. For example, what if I get an open-weight or an open-source model from a cloud provider where that utilization can be shared, and I can start to see my utilization go higher going forward? So I think you’re going to see a lot of experimentation. You’re also going to see other compute alternatives start to come onto the market. That’s going to represent incremental capacity, and that’s going to impact pricing as well.

You’re also going to see more efficient AI software going forward. We haven’t talked much about this, but I think we’ll get to it a little bit later. What we’re seeing out of some of the most progressive AI software companies is that they’re not thinking about human interface any longer. They’re thinking about MCP. They’re thinking, “I want to build software for agents to be able to manage.” That brings tremendous efficiency to the overall discussion. That can impact your token costs, get your token costs down and get your utilization better.

I think this gets to that point: I’ve never seen a technology move so fast. Things build on each other in a six-month period, and then you get different solutions that come to bear. So those are real challenges that people are facing today, but they are surmountable. And I’m seeing the trial-and-error happening to be able to get over or around some of those problems.

Dave Vellante: Awesome. Thanks for that. I want to tap your operating experience because you ran a fairly large company at IDC, and now you’re sitting on boards. So let’s explore how software companies redesign the business so the economics can keep pace. We’ve talked about the SaaSpocalypse endlessly. Established software companies have a lot of customers. They have deterministic workflows. They’ve got revenue to protect while they’re introducing these AI extensions into their product. They’re AI-fying it.

Then you’ve got AI-native companies that are building operating models that are modern. They’re agile. They’re designing their architecture and their labor and their pricing around AI from the start. So these create different opportunities and different constraints. Crawford, another sort of multipart question: When you help an established SaaS company become an AI business, how do you think about that? Where do you start? What does an AI-native startup look like?

And the hardest question is, no matter how you price software, you’re going to get it wrong. But if AI reduces the labor that’s required to write code and deliver software or a service, who captures that value? Is the vendor just going to get better margins? Competition comes in. The customer benefits. We talked earlier off-camera about outcome pricing. How do you see all this?

Crawford Del Prete: Let’s unpack it a little bit. It starts at the top, right? When you’re talking about a historically SaaS-based company moving to becoming an AI company, if the ELT and the CEO are not bought into AI, if it’s just, “I’m going to give Copilot to a few people,” it’s over. You’ve got to have buy-in from the very top. It sounds trite. It sounds easy, but it’s super, super important in terms of a transformation.

Probably one of the biggest areas that we see as companies start transforming is that roles are starting to blend. So you used to have a head of product, and then you had product management, and then you had product engineering. We’re seeing those roles all kind of blend together. Product management is probably the area where I’m seeing the biggest redefinition. It’s actually merging with product engineering, and you don’t necessarily need that handoff anymore.

You can start to see massive amounts of scale within how you engineer the product and then how you get that product out to market. You’re seeing technical product managers being able to use AI to kind of blend those roles together. I think that’s probably, in the early days here, one of the biggest changes I’ve seen in companies, whether they be AI-native companies or SaaS companies: Those roles are all kind of getting slammed together.

Obviously, we saw the move to product-led growth under SaaS, and I think we’re seeing that even more so in AI, where you want to give the product a try, you want to be able to download the product, you want to be able to use the product. That’s also a big change. Another really big change is not only in the selling model, but how they think about bringing a product to market.

I’m seeing a lot of these small regional resellers becoming way, way more capable and able to use AI to become more efficient in their selling skills. What I’m also seeing is that a lot of the very large distributors are super interested in bringing on software assets into their marketplaces because they can make higher margins on them. So we’re seeing that the channels to market for AI companies are much more plentiful than we ever saw in the past. I would say those are some of the changes that I’ve seen in the marketplace.

Now, when you start thinking about how you price the product and how you bring that product to market from a pricing standpoint, I think the biggest change associated with AI, whether this is an established company or a company coming out, is that we’re seeing a lot of interest in usage-based pricing. I think the biggest thing for a non-SaaS company who’s bringing in AI, and this is the biggest challenge I see multiple times, is: How do I discretely monetize AI? How can I look and say, “I made these investments in AI, and I’m getting customers to pay more as a function of it”?

Because in so many cases, I see this: You don’t sell AI separately. You sell AI embedded into the core product that you have, and then you get customers to buy in. So what I’m starting to see is, you see it in cross-sell, upsell. You see it in price increases. And then you ultimately start to bring out incremental features that you can charge extra for that are AI-only going forward. You’ve got to start moving away from seat-based. You’ve got to start moving to usage-based, which is what I’m seeing most companies doing.

Now, the problem with the outcome-based stuff — and outcome-based comes up a lot — is that it becomes very episodic. It becomes exactly what you mentioned, which is it’s associated with a project. And when it’s associated with a project, then you don’t get that stickiness. Maybe, if you’re good, you get re-occurring revenue, but you don’t get recurring revenue. You don’t get that subscription revenue, and that’s a problem for these companies. Obviously, for the same reason that they moved to SaaS, they don’t want to move away from that.

Dave Vellante: Right. So, it’s a complicated situation. Pricing always is for software, and it’s early days. But you’re clearly seeing some positivity. In our experience, and you’ve seen this, when we see a new wave, it’s oftentimes the case that the new is not large enough to offset the decline in the old. This time, there may be a difference because you look at what Anthropic’s doing. At the same time, we still want to test whether the monetization for mainstream enterprises happens before the bubble bursts, and that’s kind of what we’re trying to figure out.

I don’t think the bubble is bursting today. We started off down almost 1,000 points on the Nasdaq as we were recording this. We’re coming back a little bit. We’re only down 853 right now. So really a lot of pain. I don’t think this is the bubble-burst moment. In fact, we’re letting a little air out, which I think is a positive thing.

But in this chart, we’re looking at four related factors. One, are customers getting measurable outcomes? And maybe, if those become measurable, we can figure out software pricing a little bit better. Two, is there a product-market fit? In other words, does that product produce repeatable spending after the initial POCs? We’d love to see ARR, not just another project the next year.

Three, can software and model suppliers earn sustainable margins after accounting for their delivery costs? (With) tokens, building intelligence is expensive. And four, does the infrastructure usage produce enough cash to support operations and capital obligations and to fund the next cycle? Customer productivity is necessary to our thesis. But remember, value can flow to customers through lower prices without necessarily supporting the returns of the factory. That’s something that infrastructure investors are looking at to justify the higher valuation. So you’ve got to examine the whole chain.

Crawford, over the next 12 to 18 months — maybe that’s too long of a time frame in this world — what are the key developments that we should be watching that are going to make you more confident that productive customer demand is catching up with the buildout? It’s widely spread. You said it’s not narrow. And what, by the way, would change your mind? What are the metrics and KPIs you look at with your portfolio companies? How do you see it?

Crawford Del Prete: So obviously, you’ve got to be looking at retention, right? You’ve got to be looking at net retention, at gross retention, and seeing how those are moving as they roll out new AI features. What I see is a lot of value in looking at win-loss analysis. Why did a customer leave? Where did a customer go? Did a customer go to a more AI-native factor? Did the customer go to an internal effort where they could create the product themselves? You see that on win-loss.

That’s a super important metric because it gets to what customers are willing to risk that accountability layer on by building it themselves, unless they’re building that accountability layer in. How much the company is able to uniquely monetize AI is also super important, or do you see it in the retention numbers in terms of cross-sell, upsell? The other areas that are really important to me are: Are you attracting more customers with your AI features? And is the product getting better over time because of those customers coming to the platform?

Then, even more importantly, is the product not only getting better, but is each incremental customer getting a better experience? Is the data that’s being created more valuable to that broad set of customers because they’re part of that ecosystem? And of course, that’s all fueled by better decisions associated with AI. The other thing that I’m spending a lot of time looking at is this notion of what is the next action that a company can find and uncover with AI.

So, for example, maybe they’re in the ITSM space. What happened to the ticket? Was it reopened? How long was it until the ticket was closed? Maybe you generated an invoice with a piece of AI software. Well, was that invoice disputed? Was it paid late? Was it written off? What was that next outcome? Maybe you made a recommendation. Did the customer accept it? Did they challenge it? Did they ignore it?

Those kinds of follow-on interactions fuel that two-way customer value, where more customers rejecting a recommendation tell you the recommendation wasn’t very good. So the recommendations get better. Those are all the kinds of things that I’m looking at in order to see the benefits associated with AI.

Dave Vellante: Basically that next best action is really interesting because we’ve been pretty good at what happened and pretty good at why it happened, but we’re not really good at what’s going to happen next and what we should do next, right?

Crawford Del Prete: That’s the possibility AI opens us up to.

Dave Vellante: Well, we continue to believe — we come full circle here — that the path to a durable AI economy goes through the mainstream enterprise operating results. And the good news is, as we talked about today, we have evidence that AI workloads are expanding and new operating models are emerging, as Crawford shared with us. The questions that remain are around how quickly those gains become repeatable customer spending patterns and sustainable cash flows broadly across the industry. And will that happen before a major financing or other dislocation occurs in the market?

What do you in the audience think? Are you making money from AI? Are your individual productivity gains translating into firm-level results that are measurable? If so, you’re likely one of the leaders in your field. And if not, how much time and patient capital do you have before results are proven and AI becomes self-funding? Let us know what you think.

#5535. Ruder Finn Promotes Tejas Totade to Global Chief Technology Officer and Chief Data & AI Officer

NEW YORK, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ruder Finn, one of the world's leading independent communications and integrated marketing agencies, today announced the promotion of Tejas Totade to Global Chief Technology Officer and Chief Data & AI Officer, establishing a global leadership role that brings the agency's technology, data and artificial intelligence capabilities under a shared strategic vision. Tejas has built a strong digital, analytics and engineering team with several dozen specialists in hubs across India, the Philippines, and New York.

The move reflects the growing connection of these disciplines across both Ruder Finn's business and client work. In his expanded role, Totade will widen access to tools and training in every region and build the architecture that supports the agency's AI capabilities end to end. The global mandate formalizes work he has led across markets over the past year, including AI strategy and adoption programs in India and the U.K.

"The greatest opportunity comes when we work together choosing the right technology, grounding it in data, and applying AI to solve a real business problem," said Totade. "This role gives us an opportunity to create that shared vision globally and help our teams and clients translate the enormous potential of AI into measurable value."

"Ruder Finn has always believed that technology should expand what communicators are able to accomplish, and Tejas has been central to building that capability within our agency," said Kathy Bloomgarden, CEO of Ruder Finn. "As technology, data and AI become increasingly interconnected, we're committed to bringing the most cutting edge AI capabilities to clients, under the leadership of Tejas."

Ruder Finn has also appointed Nick Driver as Managing Director, Research and Analytics, reporting to Totade. With 20 years of experience applying insight and analytics to complex challenges, Driver will lead research and analytics in the U.S, working across practices and client teams to advance audience intelligence, AI-driven insights, and measurement. He will also help strengthen the connection between strategy and technology, with a focus on developing more rigorous, practice-specific approaches and demonstrating the business impact of communications.

"What drew me to Ruder Finn is the clarity of the agency's tech-forward vision and the genuine commitment to making it real," said Driver. "The technology, the talent and the ambition are already here. I'm excited to help make research and analytics an even more central part of how we understand audiences, guide strategy and demonstrate impact for clients."

Together, these appointments further build out the leadership and expertise supporting Ruder Finn's integrated approach to technology, data and AI.

Totade has spent more than 16 years at Ruder Finn building the agency's technology, data and AI capabilities. He joined the company as a senior developer and went on to establish rf.TechLab, Ruder Finn's emerging technology incubator, in 2018. Today, he leads an international team spanning engineering, analytics and digital development, co-leads the agency's AI-powered creative studio rf.Studio53, and oversees research and insights capabilities that combine proprietary methodologies with enterprise analytics tools. He has received significant industry recognition, including PRWeek's "40 Under 40", PRovoke Media's Data Professional of the Year award and being named one of the PRNews People of the Year in the Agency Innovators.

Ruder Finn is one of the world's largest independent global communications and integrated marketing agencies, leading the industry in AI strategy and implementation. Founded in 1948, Ruder Finn has defined and redefined PR for over 75 years, shaping communications that move industry-defining brands, companies, and leaders from what's now to what's next. Ruder Finn provides clients with bold strategies based on a global perspective and localized market knowledge that redefine leadership, reimagine the marketplace, and rethink customer experiences. The agency is organized around five core areas of expertiseâHealthcare, Technology, Consumer Brand, Leadership and Workplaceâwith innovative tech incubator RF TechLab providing cutting-edge predictive analytics, AI-powered creative hub RF Studio53 offering breakthrough creative, and specialized teams delivering customer-focused digital engagement. Ruder Finn has offices across four continents including the U.S., Asia, Europe and the Middle East. Wholly owned agencies and offerings within Ruder Finn Group include: Ruder Finn Inc., RF Studio53, RF Engage, Touchdown, Peppercomm, RF Comunicad, Mantis, jacobstahl, Flightpath, Ruder Finn Atteline, Pandan Social, RF Bloom, and Big Sky Communications. #5534. Bitcoin Price Faces $11B Options Expiry After FOMC Uncertainty Clears

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price faces another major test on October 30, when $11 billion in options contracts expire. The FOMC has already delivered its latest interest-rate decision, leaving traders to assess whether Bitcoin can hold its ground as derivatives positioning resets. A relief rally could emerge if the market absorbs the Fed’s message without another selling pressure.

The Federal Reserve held interest rates at 3.75% to 4% on October 28, matching expectations. However, two officials dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike. The decision removed one immediate source of uncertainty, but the Fed’s stance on future policy remains important for risk assets.

Read Chairman Warsh's full opening statement from the #FOMC press conference (PDF):  https://t.co/TPqQ7MKO7m pic.twitter.com/1SUkOfaU0T

Bitcoin now has an opportunity to shift attention back toward market positioning and demand as the approaching option expiry could force another price swing.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Around $11 billion in Bitcoin options are scheduled to expire on Friday, October 30. The contracts represent a substantial concentration of open interest, making the settlement an important event for short-term volatility.

Derivatives data reported ahead of expiry showed more call options than puts. One estimate placed the put-to-call ratio near 0.53, indicating that outstanding call contracts significantly outnumbered puts. Calls generally benefit from higher prices, while puts can provide protection against declines.

This positioning offers a potentially bullish talking point, and options open interest reflects existing contracts. Some calls may be part of hedged strategies, but puts can serve purposes beyond outright bearish bets.

The $78,000 area has also emerged as a key reference point in expiry estimates. Often described as the maximum-pain level, it represents the theoretical settlement price at which aggregate option-holder payouts would be minimized.

But Bitcoin can settle well above or below the $78K price level, depending on market demand, liquidity, and trading activity. For us, the more constructive scenario would be Bitcoin holding support as contracts approach settlement. If dealers adjust their hedges and expiring positions disappear without triggering substantial selling, the market could find room for a directional recovery.

The FOMC decision is behind the market, but its implications extend beyond October. The Fed kept rates unchanged while describing economic activity as strong and inflation as elevated.

The two dissents favoring a rate hike also complicate the bullish interpretation. They signal that policymakers remain concerned about inflation, even as the committee maintains its current target range.

For Bitcoin price, the immediate question is if the markets had already accounted for the expected rate hold. When an anticipated decision arrives without a major surprise, traders can redirect their attention toward positioning, liquidity, and incoming economic data.

This creates room for a relief rally if investors conclude the announcement was less damaging than feared. Conversely, concerns about tighter policy later in the year could continue to weigh on risk appetite.

The next FOMC meeting is scheduled for December 8–9. Until then, inflation reports, employment figures and comments from policymakers could reshape expectations for the next rate decision.

The FOMC has removed one immediate event risk, but monetary-policy uncertainty has not disappeared. The options settlement is the next test, and a stable reaction could help bulls build momentum.

A bullish breakout is possible. Bitcoin price needs confirmation from buyers before traders can confidently treat the expiry as a turning point.

#5533. Who’s getting Anthropic’s compute spending? IPO filing shows where the tech giants really stand

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 6:53 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:58 am

Anthropic’s IPO filing reads like a ledger of who’s getting paid in the AI boom. The Seattle region’s tech giants are on the list, but they aren’t at the top.

The prospectus, filed Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission, details more than $750 billion in computing deals, including firm commitments and estimated future spending, and offers clues about what its founders and biggest investors stand to gain ahead of the company’s planned Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT.

Amazon and Microsoft have invested billions in Anthropic and won high-profile spending commitments from the Claude maker. But both trail Google, chipmaker Broadcom and Elon Musk’s SpaceX in their shares of Anthropic’s planned spending on computing power, the filing shows.

Following the compute money: Google’s chips are the biggest winner. Anthropic has lined up roughly $400 billion in computing capacity, mostly over the next seven years, based on Google-designed AI chips, known as tensor processing units or TPUs.

That total includes $114.5 billion to Google directly through July 2033, $161.2 billion in equipment leases with chipmaker Broadcom, and an estimated $125 billion to $150 billion in additional TPU capacity from 2028 to 2031.

Broadcom’s leases are the largest single arrangement in the filing. The five-year leases provide TPU-based hardware for data centers operated by other companies on Anthropic’s behalf.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is next. Anthropic agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion through 2029 for computing capacity from SpaceX’s AI subsidiary, formerly known as xAI, which runs a rival AI lab.

The filing says payments will reach about $3.1 billion a month once all the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December. The agreements run into 2029, though either side can cancel on 90 days’ notice after early 2027.

Amazon is still a big winner. Anthropic committed in April to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon Web Services over 10 years, through April 2036, and AWS Trainium is one of four chip families that Anthropic uses to train and run its models.

Microsoft’s piece is smaller, which reflects its later start. The company was aligned closely with OpenAI for years before striking its own deal with Anthropic.

Anthropic has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud from November 2026 through May 2033, the filing shows. That’s up from the $30 billion Azure deal announced in November 2025. The deal has been amended twice since, most recently this month.

Claude is built into Microsoft 365, and former Microsoft CFO Chris Liddell joined Anthropic’s board in February.

Two smaller providers have deals in the same range as Microsoft’s. Anthropic agreed to spend up to about $44.6 billion with Nscale, a U.K.-based AI infrastructure company, and about $41.3 billion with GPU cloud provider Lambda, both for capacity powered by Nvidia chips, according to the filing.

Will Anthropic need it all? Most of the commitments can’t be canceled, and the deals with Microsoft, Google and Amazon require Anthropic to pay “regardless of actual usage,” according to the filing.

So far, the demand is there. Anthropic’s revenue hit $11.6 billion in the second quarter, up from $787 million a year earlier, and the company posted its first operating profit, $974 million. It still had a $66.3 billion net loss, mostly from accounting charges tied to its soaring valuation.

The company says it has “consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.”

Its compute commitments assume that demand keeps growing. Anthropic spent less than $2 billion a month on compute and infrastructure in the second quarter. The SpaceX deal alone is expected to cost about $3.1 billion a month at full capacity.

Paper fortunes: Amazon’s biggest payoff is its stake, which it valued at $190.4 billion as of June 30 in its quarterly SEC filing. That includes convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal that Amazon valued at $97.9 billion. The notes would convert into stock, subject to a 12% ownership cap that Amazon can waive.

Amazon is scheduled to report third-quarter results Thursday, its first earnings report since Anthropic’s filing. The Seattle-based company has updated the value of its Anthropic holdings in each of its quarterly filings this year, so a new number could come this week.

Google put $10 billion into Anthropic’s latest funding round and can invest up to $20 billion more under a March financing deal. The filing doesn’t give ownership percentages for Amazon, Google or Microsoft. It says only that the three companies have each made “significant equity investments” in Anthropic.

Anthropic’s seven co-founders hold roughly 230 million to 245 million shares each, worth about $14 billion apiece at the latest private funding price. The company also gave its own Public Benefit Fund about 847 million shares, or 5% of its fully diluted stock as of June 30, worth about $50 billion at that price.

Anthropic could begin formally marketing its IPO to investors as soon as the week of Nov. 9, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. It is aiming to go public the following week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The company expects the offering to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s IPO, according to Bloomberg. SpaceX raised $75 billion in June, the largest IPO on record.

#5532. 10 moments in the history of the NYC marathon, from Central Park to five boroughs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The history of the NYC marathon, from a 1970 loop race in Central Park to a five-borough event, told through 10 moments including founders, champions and two cancellations

In 1970, the New York City Marathon $MPC fit inside a single park. Runners covered loops of the roads in Central Park, in a race organized by the New York Road Runners. The field was small. Only a minority of the runners who started reached the finish. Today the event crosses all five boroughs of New York City. By widely reported figures, it is the world's largest marathon by number of finishers.

The history of the NYC marathon traces how that club race became a citywide event. Gary Muhrcke won the first edition. In 1976, organizers sent the race through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. The expansion was tied to the U.S. bicentennial. The marathon has kept a five-borough format since then, though course details have been adjusted over time. The current course starts on Staten Island near the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. It finishes in Central Park, the same park that held the entire first race.

Fred Lebow, a New York Road Runners official, was a central organizer of that first race. In 1992, after treatment for brain cancer, he ran the course himself alongside Grete Waitz. Waitz, a Norwegian runner, won the women's race nine times. Her first victory, in 1978, set a world best for the marathon.

Events outside the sport have also stopped the race. Hurricane Sandy struck the New York area in 2012. The marathon was canceled shortly before its scheduled date. In 2020, the in-person race was canceled because of the COVID-19 pandemic. The race returned in person in 2021.

The 10 moments below are a selection, not a complete timeline. They begin with the first race and its winner. They move through the founding club, the 1976 expansion and the route. Later slides cover Waitz's run of victories, Lebow's 1992 race and the two cancellations. The final slide looks at the race's present scale. Each slide covers one chapter of New York City Marathon history and can be read on its own.

The first New York City Marathon $MPC, held in 1970, never left Central Park. Runners reached the full marathon distance by repeating laps of the park's internal roads instead of crossing city streets.

The New York Road Runners staged that first race as a club event.

A marathon covers 26.2 miles, or 42.195 kilometers. A closed loop inside a park cannot supply that distance in a single pass. Runners covered it by returning to the same stretches of road more than once.

The starting field was small. Fewer than half of the runners who set out that day completed the distance.

The course sat entirely inside the park, so the start and the finish were both in Central Park. The park lies in Manhattan. The 1970 race never touched Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens or the Bronx.

Central Park still holds the finish line of the modern race. That gives today's event a direct physical link to the 1970 original.

The all-park format ended in 1976, when the marathon expanded beyond the park.

Gary Muhrcke won the first New York City Marathon $MPC in 1970. That result makes him the race's first champion, crowned years before the event grew into the city-spanning marathon it is today.

His win came in a different setting from every later edition. He took the title on a course confined to the park roads of Central Park. No borough line or city street was part of that route.

This sets his name apart in the race's record. Champions from 1976 onward have run a course through all five boroughs. Muhrcke's victory belongs to the earlier period, when the marathon was still a club race held inside one park.

The New York City Marathon $MPC started as a running club's event. The New York Road Runners organized the first race in 1970. Fred Lebow, an official of the club, was one of its central organizers.

Lebow's part in the race came through his club position. He was not an outside promoter brought in to stage it. He was one of the people running the New York Road Runners, and the marathon was the club's own event from its first edition.

The race that Lebow and the club put on in 1970 was modest in scale. It stayed entirely inside Central Park, on loops of the park roads. The field was small. Only a minority of the runners who started went on to finish.

That club-run race in a single park is the origin of the event that carries the New York City Marathon name today.

In 1976, the New York City Marathon $MPC expanded to run through all five boroughs of the city. The expansion was tied to the U.S. bicentennial, the 200th anniversary of American independence in 1776.

Before that year, the marathon had been a Central Park event. The race that began in 1970 kept its runners on the park's own roads, looping the same ground again and again.

The 1976 edition took the race out of the park and onto city streets. For the first time, the route crossed from one borough to the next rather than circling a single park in Manhattan.

The timing connected a local road race to a national anniversary. The bicentennial gave organizers a specific occasion for the change. The expanded route turned the marathon into a citywide event that year.

The five-borough format has stayed in place in every in-person race held since 1976. Organizers have adjusted course details over the years. None of those adjustments has taken the race back to a single borough.

That continuity links the current event to 1976. The modern race still follows the same basic idea: one marathon that passes through all five boroughs of New York City.

The New York City Marathon $MPC starts on Staten Island near the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge and finishes in Central Park in Manhattan. Between those points, the route also passes through Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx.

That puts all five of the city's boroughs on a single course. Few road races in any city link that many separate districts in one continuous route.

The layout makes the marathon a point-to-point race rather than a loop. Runners begin in one borough and finish in another. They do not return to the area where they started.

The two ends of the route sit in very different settings. The start lies beside a bridge on Staten Island, at the city's edge. The finish lies inside a park in Manhattan, near the center of the city.

The route's structure is its defining feature. It is a crossing of New York from one end to the other, with the race ending among the roads of Central Park.

Grete Waitz of Norway won the women's race at the New York City Marathon $MPC nine times. Her first victory came in 1978, and her time that day set a world best for the women's marathon.

A world best is the fastest time recorded anywhere for a distance. Her 1978 result meant the fastest women's marathon on record at that point was run in New York.

That win came two years after the race expanded to all five boroughs in 1976. Waitz set her world best on a course that crossed the city, not on the Central Park loops used in 1970.

The first title opened a long stretch in the women's division. Waitz returned to win the women's race in New York eight more times after 1978.

Fred Lebow, a central organizer of the New York City Marathon $MPC, ran the 1992 race himself after being treated for brain cancer. Grete Waitz of Norway ran the course alongside him.

Lebow came to the marathon as a New York Road Runners club official. He was a central organizer of the first edition in 1970. That race was held entirely on loops of the roads inside Central Park.

The 1992 race put Lebow in a different position. He started as a participant in the event he had helped organize. He did so after his treatment for brain cancer.

Waitz ran with him as a former champion of the women's race. In 1992, she was on the course as Lebow's companion rather than as a contender.

Lebow died in 1994, two years after his run with Waitz.

The 2012 New York City Marathon $MPC was canceled after Hurricane Sandy struck the New York area. Organizers called the race off shortly before its scheduled date.

The storm hit the same region the marathon's course runs through. No 2012 edition of the race was held.

The COVID-19 pandemic canceled the in-person New York City Marathon $MPC in 2020. The race came back as an in-person event in 2021.

The cancellation applied specifically to the in-person race. No runners lined up on Staten Island that year for the standard race-day start.

The 2020 cancellation came eight years after Hurricane Sandy forced the 2012 edition to be called off. The two cancellations had different causes. The first followed a storm that struck the New York area. The second followed a global public health crisis.

The 2021 edition restored the in-person marathon after the pandemic year. It ended the gap in the race's run of in-person editions.

The New York City Marathon $MPC is the largest marathon in the world by number of finishers, based on widely reported figures. The ranking counts the runners who complete the race, not the number who sign up.

A marathon's size can be measured in more than one way. A registration total counts everyone who entered. A starter total counts everyone who began the race. A finisher total counts only the runners who completed the full marathon distance.

Those three numbers can differ. Some entrants never start. Some starters leave the course before the end. A ranking by finishers reflects only the people who covered the whole distance. A comparison between races can therefore depend on which of the three measures it uses.

The finisher total also changes from one edition of the race to the next. The ranking describes the race's position in published comparisons, not a single fixed figure.

#5531. Agent demand can’t be forecast, meaning the database has to be ready for anything

Enterprises building an agentic AI architecture are learning that the database matters as much as the model. AI agents fire off thousands of unplanned queries at once — and expect answers in milliseconds.

PhoenixAI, the trade name of CelerData Inc., raised $80 million this year to develop database technology for AI agents to solve this growing problem. Established players struggle to return answers in real time, according to Ross Armstrong (pictured), senior vice president of global sales of PhoenixAI.

“There was a real gap in the market for real-time analytics, and to be able to not only ask a question but get the response back in real time was something that all the database players that are out there, even the big names in the market, couldn’t do well,” Armstrong said. “If you have customer-facing analytics or agentic AI … you need that response time to be able to meet the SLAs with your customers.”

Armstrong spoke with theCUBE’s Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the database demands of agentic AI, real-time query performance and the need for governance and observability. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents generate queries in real time and may hit several databases at once, according to Armstrong. PhoenixAI’s specific columnar engine handles structured and unstructured data and works out how to answer each query as it arrives.

“I think what the biggest demand is that we don’t know what the demand is going to be from those agents,” Armstrong said. “You could have … thousands and thousands of queries hitting at the exact same time, but you still need that real speedy response.”

PhoenixAI joined Cloudera as a foundational database partner and is now an option in Cloudera’s marketplace. Its self-managed edition, PhoenixAI Anywhere, runs in a customer’s cloud, on-premises or in air-gapped environments. In a market where many early adopters hit governance and observability problems, PhoenixAI plans to address them with AgentBase, a purpose-built context environment that keeps agents away from data they don’t need, Armstrong explained.

“You can design that playground for those agents to be protected and to be governed but also to give them access to the data that you need,” Armstrong said. “It’s not necessary to run agents on a solution like PhoenixAI, but it’s certainly one that helps you put those guardrails in that a lot of organizations are looking for.”

#5530. European supermarket cyberattacks highlight the need for secure remote access to refrigeration systems, says Secomea

A second wave of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems raises urgent questions about how retailers protect critical operational technology while maintaining essential remote services.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Supermarket chains across Europe have reported a new wave of suspected cyberattacks affecting refrigeration systems, just weeks after attackers reportedly manipulated cooling equipment in hundreds of French stores, causing substantial food losses.

The latest incidents, reported in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg, highlight a growing challenge for retailers: the operational technology (OT) responsible for keeping food safe is increasingly connected to external systems and service providers, creating potential security risks when that connectivity is not adequately protected.

Unlike traditional cyberattacks focused on stealing data or disrupting IT services, attacks on operational technology can have immediate physical consequences. Compromised refrigeration systems can mean spoiled food, interrupted operations, significant financial losses, and potential risks to food safety.

"These incidents illustrate why cybersecurity is no longer just about protecting information. When attackers interfere with operational technology, the consequences become physical," says Michael Ferdinandsen, CEO at Secomea, a Danish industrial cybersecurity company specializing in secure remote access.

"For retailers, the question isn't whether they need remote connectivity. They absolutely do. The question is whether they have sufficient control over who can access their equipment, what they can reach, and what they're allowed to do."

The challenge isn't connectivity. It's controlling access

Modern refrigeration systems depend on remote connectivity to operate efficiently. External service providers and maintenance technicians use it to monitor temperatures, respond to alarms, diagnose faults, and maintain equipment across hundreds or thousands of locations.

This connectivity is essential for minimizing response times and preventing equipment failures. But it also introduces potential entry points for attackers, particularly when operational equipment is directly exposed to the internet or remote users are granted broader access than necessary.

For supermarket chains managing multiple locations, refrigeration systems, and external service providers, the challenge becomes even more complex. Different suppliers may use different access methods, making it difficult for IT and security teams to maintain consistent oversight of who can connect to critical infrastructure.

"Many organizations have invested heavily in securing their corporate IT environments, but operational equipment often presents a different challenge," explains Michael Ferdinandsen.

"These systems were designed to operate reliably for years, sometimes decades. They weren't necessarily designed with today's connectivity and cybersecurity requirements in mind. Applying traditional IT remote access approaches without considering those differences can create unnecessary exposure."

Securing access without disrupting operations

Protecting refrigeration systems does not require eliminating remote connectivity. Instead, retailers need an approach that allows external technicians to perform essential maintenance while keeping access to operational equipment controlled and accountable.

Purpose-built OT secure remote access helps address this challenge by controlling connections at the individual asset level, rather than giving users broad access to operational networks.

Secomea's OT-native architecture enables secure connections to operational equipment through Edge Gateways located close to the assets themselves. Centralized access management, granular permissions, and audit logs help organizations govern who can connect, which equipment they can access, and when.

This approach is already being used in the retail refrigeration industry. In Denmark, refrigeration monitoring specialist AK-Centralen uses Secomea technology to support remote monitoring of cooling systems serving more than 1,500 supermarkets. Secure connectivity enables the company to maintain essential monitoring and service operations without requiring direct access to supermarket internal networks.

The example demonstrates that efficient remote maintenance and stronger cybersecurity controls can work together.

Operational resilience depends on visibility and control

The latest incidents raise questions that extend well beyond supermarket refrigeration. From building management and energy systems to production machinery and logistics infrastructure, organizations increasingly rely on connected operational equipment maintained by external specialists.

As these environments become more interconnected, organizations need consistent ways to manage third-party access, restrict permissions to the equipment users actually need, and maintain visibility into remote activities.

Secure remote access is one component of that protection, alongside vulnerability management, network segmentation, system updates, and continuous monitoring.

"Organizations shouldn't have to choose between keeping their operations running and keeping them secure," concludes Michael Ferdinandsen.

"The goal is to enable the remote support that modern operations depend on, while giving IT and security teams the governance and control they need. That's particularly important when the systems involved directly affect physical operations."

While the precise methods behind the latest suspected attacks remain under investigation, the incidents are another reminder that cybersecurity failures in operational environments can quickly become business continuity problems.

Secomea is a Danish industrial cybersecurity company specializing in secure remote access for operational technology (OT). Purpose-built for industrial environments, Secomea helps organizations securely connect to critical equipment while giving IT and security teams centralized governance, granular access control, and visibility into remote access.

By combining secure operational connectivity with enterprise security requirements, Secomea helps organizations strengthen operational resilience, reduce cyber risk, and maintain control over third-party access.

#5529. Nuclear power at sea: Seattle startup targets Norway for ships and floating power plants

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:06 amOctober 27, 2026 at 7:15 am

Emerald Nuclear today announced a $2.1 million award from The Research Council of Norway to support its efforts to bring nuclear energy to the shipping industry and offshore power. The Seattle-based startup is developing high-temperature gas reactors that use an encapsulated fuel designed to resist meltdowns.

“This award will enable Emerald Nuclear to work directly with our marine partners to validate integration of our technology with their state-of-the-art marine power distribution and control systems,” said Wesley Deason, co-founder and CEO.

The funding supports Norway’s Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project, which is being led by Emerald Nuclear’s Norwegian subsidiary.

Shipping accounts for roughly 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions, making it a significant target for lower-carbon energy solutions. Some ferries serving shorter routes are adopting hybrid-electric propulsion. Shipping companies are exploring methanol, ammonia, biofuels and other alternatives to heavy fuel oil, but their climate benefits depend on how those fuels are produced and used.

Nuclear reactors have powered U.S. Navy submarines for more than 70 years. Now, a new wave of companies is working to expand nuclear power’s role in commercial shipping and other marine applications.

The award supports an early development step for Emerald Nuclear, with substantial work remaining before commercial deployment. The company has yet to build its first reactor, and its plans will require additional financing, regulatory approvals and a reliable fuel supply. The startup has previously received an undisclosed amount of funding from angel investors.

Emerald Nuclear has five employees, most of them in Norway, and is targeting two applications: offshore ships that help construct facilities like oil platforms and wind turbines and lay deep-sea cables, and floating power plants for remote communities. Each reactor is designed to produce 5 megawatts (6,705 horsepower), according to the company.

Bringing nuclear to the marine environment poses several significant challenges. They include safety issues, regulations for vessels traveling internationally, management of nuclear fuel and waste, and the way shipping companies frequently buy and sell vessels.

Deason said the company’s approach helps address those concerns:

Emerald Nuclear is designing its technology “to integrate with the unique power needs of the ship, but also to meet the ways that the maritime industry does business,” Deason said.

Other companies pursuing nuclear ship propulsion include Core Power, newcleo and Blykalla. Core Power, Westinghouse, Saltfoss Energy and Prodigy Clean Energy are also developing floating nuclear power stations. Russia’s state-owned Rosatom already has nuclear-powered icebreakers and a floating nuclear power plant in operation.

Prior to launching Emerald Nuclear, Deason, a nuclear engineer, worked for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp. (USNC) developing reactors for space-based applications.

During his tenure at the Seattle company, a professor from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology approached USNC about applications for the maritime sector. USNC declared bankruptcy in October 2024 and the deal wasn’t pursued. But the idea interested Deason and Hallgeir Juliebø, a Norwegian entrepreneur who had been a consultant with USNC. The two co-founded Emerald Nuclear in 2024 and Juliebø serves as chief commercial officer.

Emerald Nuclear has signed a lease for an engineering center in Norway, where it’s designing and building its first prototype, a non-nuclear thermal device that will be used for the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project.

Other partners for the project are VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk, bringing together nuclear technology, ship design and integration, vessel operations and academic research.

The startup will build its first nuclear reactor, named the Gem Microreactor, at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, with 2030 as its goal for completion. Emerald Nuclear will integrate equipment from Peregrine Turbine Technologies in Maine to convert the reactor’s heat into electricity.

The target for the first commercial deployment is 2031, on a Norwegian offshore vessel.

Deason is hoping to open a manufacturing site in the future in Western Washington on Puget Sound with an initial focus on floating nuclear power systems that replace diesel generators. That phase of growth is roughly targeted to the early 2030s.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5528. How hard it is to get into each of the 7 World Marathon Majors

Free daily briefing on global business news.

World Marathon Majors entry ranges from Boston's qualifying times to lotteries in Berlin and Chicago, and this guide orders all seven races by how their entry systems work

A fast qualifying time is the main route into the Boston Marathon $MPC. At most of the others, chance plays the larger role. That split runs through the Abbott $ABT World Marathon Majors, a series of seven races held in Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York City and Sydney. Sydney became the seventh Major in 2025.

World Marathon Majors entry works differently at each race. Boston is the only Major where most general entrants must first run a qualifying time. Its standards vary by age and gender. Meeting the standard does not guarantee a place. The field is capped, and the fastest applicants are accepted first.

London sends most general entrants through a public ballot, and demand far exceeds the places available. Its other routes are Good for Age times, charity places and club places. New York City mixes a lottery with time qualifiers, charity places, tour operators and the New York Road Runners 9+1 program. That program asks runners to complete nine NYRR races and volunteer at one. Berlin and Tokyo rely on lotteries for general entry. Chicago also runs a lottery but adds time-guarantee options for fast runners.

The races are spread across the year. Tokyo runs in March. Boston follows in April on Patriots' Day. Its course runs from Hopkinton to Boston, and the race dates to 1897. Sydney is held in late August, during the Australian winter. Berlin comes in late September on a flat course that has been the site of many men's marathon world records. Chicago is held in October. New York City follows on the first Sunday of November, crossing five boroughs from Staten Island to Central Park.

The order that follows is an editorial ranking. It weighs how each race's entry system works, including how much it depends on running speed and how much on a draw. It does not rest on published acceptance rates or odds. Sydney appears seventh as the newest Major, not because of any measured odds.

Seven slides cover the seven races, one each. The eighth explains the entry routes many of the Majors share — ballots, charity places and tour-operator packages. Those shared routes can give runners another way into a race when a ballot or lottery does not go their way.

The Boston Marathon $MPC is the only World Marathon Major where most general entrants must run a qualifying time before they can apply. Even a qualifying time does not secure a place in the field.

The qualifying standards are not a single number. They vary by age and by gender. Each runner is measured against the target set for their own group. A finishing time that qualifies a runner in one group can fall short in another.

That design ties entry to a runner's own performance. For most applicants, the deciding factor is a finishing time they have already run in a previous marathon. Filling in the application does not create a chance of entry. The time already on record does.

The second hurdle is the field cap. Boston limits how many runners it accepts. When more qualified runners apply than there are places, the race admits the fastest applicants first. A runner who meets the standard for their age and gender can still miss out if enough faster qualifiers fill the field. In practice, applicants are tested twice. They first race the clock to meet the standard, then are compared with every other qualifier who applies.

As a result, the published standard works as a minimum rather than a guarantee. The effective cutoff in a given year depends on how many qualified runners apply and how fast those applicants ran. For a runner close to the line, finishing well inside the standard matters as much as meeting it at all.

Charity places provide a separate route. They sit outside the time-based system. They give runners without a qualifying time another way into the race.

The race dates to 1897. It is held each April on Patriots' Day.

The course runs from Hopkinton to Boston. It is a point-to-point route. Runners start in one place and finish in another.

London Marathon $MPC entry runs mainly through a public ballot, a random draw for general entrants. Demand for ballot places far exceeds the number of places on offer.

The draw does not weigh running ability. A first-time marathoner and a runner with years of racing behind them apply on equal terms. A strong finishing time from another race does not improve anyone's chances in the ballot itself.

Runners who want more control over the outcome have three other routes. Each one comes with a condition attached.

The first is Good for Age entry. It is open to runners who have already completed a marathon within a set time for their age group. This route rewards past performance in a way the ballot does not. It works on a similar principle to the qualifying standards used at the Boston Marathon. In London, though, it runs alongside the ballot rather than serving as the main way in.

A runner preparing for a first marathon has no qualifying time to show. Good for Age is therefore not an option for them.

The second is a club place. These places go to running clubs rather than to individuals. Each club then decides which of its members receive them. Access depends on belonging to a club that holds an allocation. A runner outside the club system cannot use this route.

The third is a charity place. Runners who take this route enter through a charity. They typically commit to raising money for it in return. Charity entry is the only alternative of the three that requires neither a qualifying time nor club membership. A runner of any pace can use it if they make the fundraising commitment.

These routes put London second on this list. Its main open door is a random draw. Every alternative asks for something extra: a fast time, club membership or a fundraising pledge.

The New York City Marathon $MPC has five entry routes: a lottery, time-qualifier entry, charity places, tour-operator places and the New York Road Runners 9+1 program. It sits third in this editorial ranking. The lottery is left to chance, but the other four routes give runners ways around the draw.

The lottery is a random draw. A runner's pace and race history play no part in who is picked.

Time-qualifier entry rewards speed instead. A runner who has already run a fast enough time at an earlier race can apply on that basis rather than rely on the draw. This is an option in New York, not a requirement.

Charity places and tour-operator places add two more paths. A charity place comes through one of the race's charity partners. A tour-operator place is bought as part of a travel package.

The 9+1 program is the route most tied to the city itself. A runner completes nine New York Road Runners races and volunteers at one more. That makes 10 NYRR events in all. Each of those events takes place in person. The program is most practical for runners who can reach NYRR events regularly.

Set beside London, New York's mix differs. Club places are not among New York's routes, while tour operators and the 9+1 program are.

Each route asks for something different. The lottery needs only an application but gives the runner no say in the outcome. The time route needs a fast result from an earlier race. Charity and tour-operator places run through outside organizations rather than through the draw. The 9+1 program asks for time and repeated participation.

The race is held on the first Sunday of November. Its course runs through all five of New York City's boroughs: Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. It starts on Staten Island and finishes in Central Park.

Most runners get into the Tokyo Marathon $MPC through its general entry lottery. Charity places give some runners a separate way in that does not depend on the draw.

The lottery is a random draw. Applicants put their names forward, and the draw decides who receives a place. A fast finishing time from an earlier race does not change the result.

That sets Tokyo apart from the Boston Marathon. There, most general entrants need a qualifying time before they can apply. It also differs from the Chicago Marathon, which pairs its lottery with time-guarantee options for fast runners.

Charity places sit alongside the lottery. A runner who takes one of these places reaches the start line without waiting on the result of the draw.

Applicants from outside Japan usually take one of two paths. They can enter the lottery from abroad, or they can secure a place through an approved tour operator.

The organizer publishes the entry rules for each edition. Overseas applicants can check those rules for the year they plan to run before choosing a path.

The race is held in March. That makes Tokyo the first of the seven Majors on the calendar each year.

Tokyo sits fourth in this order because its general route rests on a draw rather than on speed. Charity places and tour operators are the alternatives to that draw.

Entry to the Berlin Marathon $MPC is by lottery. Runners who are not drawn can still reach the start line through a charity place or a tour-operator place.

The lottery is a random draw. Finishing times play no part in it. A first-time marathoner and an experienced club runner enter on the same terms. A fast result in an earlier race does not improve anyone's chances.

The draw also means a Berlin start cannot be counted on in advance. A runner who applies through the lottery learns only from the result whether that route has worked in a given year.

Charity and tour-operator places sit outside the draw. A charity place links a runner's entry to a charity rather than to the lottery. A tour-operator place comes as part of a travel package. Neither route depends on being picked. For applicants who miss out in the draw, these are the other ways into the race.

The Berlin Marathon is held in late September on a flat course. It has been the site of many men's marathon world records. That reputation for fast times does not extend to the entry process. A runner capable of a fast finish has no better chance in the lottery than anyone else.

Chicago Marathon $MPC entry runs mainly through a lottery. Fast runners have a second option, time-guarantee entry, which lets a qualifying result stand in for the luck of the draw.

For most applicants, the lottery is the starting point. A runner applies and waits for the draw. The result turns on chance, not on how fast that runner has raced before. A runner who is not drawn can still turn to the charity and tour-operator routes covered below.

Time-guarantee entry follows a different logic. A runner who has already posted a fast enough result can apply through this route instead of relying on the draw. Chicago does not ask every entrant to hold a qualifying time. The time standard applies only to runners who choose the guaranteed path.

That gives general entrants in Chicago two separate ways in. Speed is an option there, not a requirement. A slower runner can still get in through the lottery. A faster runner has a route that skips it.

This setup sits between two other models in the series. At Boston, most general entrants must run a qualifying time just to apply. At Berlin, entry is by lottery. Chicago keeps the draw as its main route and adds a time route beside it. New York City also pairs a lottery with a time-based route, time-qualifier entry.

Charity places are another route. A runner takes a place through a partner charity and raises money for that cause. This route does not depend on the draw or on a finishing time.

Tour operators are a further option. They sell race entry as part of a travel package. Like charity places, that route sits outside the lottery.

The Chicago Marathon is held in October. On the series calendar, that puts it after Berlin in late September and before New York City on the first Sunday of November.

The Sydney Marathon $MPC joined the Abbott $ABT World Marathon Majors in 2025 as the series' seventh race. It is the newest Major and the only one held in the Southern Hemisphere.

Before Sydney, every Major took place in Asia, North America or Europe. Tokyo is the only Asian race. Boston, Chicago and New York City are in the U.S. London and Berlin are in Europe. Sydney gave the series its first race in Australia.

The location also puts the race in a different season from the rest of the series. Sydney's late August date falls in the Australian winter. In the cities that host the other six Majors, late August is summer. A runner who prepares at home in the Northern Hemisphere travels from summer weather to a winter race.

Sydney's place in this order reflects its status as the newest Major. It is not a judgment about how easy or hard the race is to enter.

Sydney's current entry system is not described here. Whether general entry runs through a ballot, and whether time-based or charity routes exist, could not be confirmed for this guide. Runners planning to apply should check the race's official entry rules before they do.

Ballots, charity places and tour-operator packages are the entry routes that most of the World Marathon $MPC Majors share. Each asks something different of the runner: luck in a random draw, a fundraising pledge or the purchase of a travel package.

A ballot, which some races call a lottery, is a random draw among everyone who applies during a set window. London runs a public ballot. New York City, Berlin, Chicago and Tokyo use lotteries for general entry.

Finishing times play no part in a general draw. A first-time marathoner and a veteran club runner enter on the same footing. Extra training does nothing to improve a runner's chances of being picked. When applications outnumber places, some applicants miss out regardless of how fast they run.

Charity places are available at Boston, London, New York City, Berlin, Chicago and Tokyo. A charity holds a set of race entries and offers them to runners who agree to raise money for its work. The runner skips the ballot or the qualifying standard. In return, the runner takes on a fundraising commitment set by the charity. Terms differ from race to race and from charity to charity. A charity entrant runs the same course on the same day as everyone else in the field.

Tour-operator places are offered at New York City, Berlin, Chicago and Tokyo. An operator working with the race sells the entry as part of a travel package. The race entry and the trip are bought together rather than separately. This route mainly serves runners traveling from abroad.

Time-based entry is the other main way in. Its form changes from race to race. Boston sets qualifying standards for most general entrants. London offers Good for Age places, New York City accepts time qualifiers and Chicago has time-guarantee entry. Each of these rewards speed rather than luck or fundraising.

Most of the Majors offer more than one of these routes. A runner who is not drawn in a race's lottery can still look for a charity or tour-operator place at the same race.

#5527. Project-by-project security reviews can’t keep pace with enterprise AI agents

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are finding that tokenization and other data protection methods now decide how fast those projects move.

But sensitive data fed into models is hard to pull back — and security reviews built for a slower era are stalling deployments. The challenge is shifting from locking data down to keeping it usable once it is protected. That tension is playing out across Cloudera Inc.’s partner ecosystem, where security is becoming a prerequisite for AI value rather than a final gate, according to Diego Loureda (pictured), vice president of customer success and presales at Protegrity USA Inc.

“Data leaks are still a thing. If you put sensitive data on a model, if you put sensitive data on a vector store or in the memory of an agent that is going to propagate to other agents, good luck removing that sensitive data,” Loureda said. “There’s no way you’re going to be able to do that.”

Loureda spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed data security along with Protegrity being named Cloudera’s Emerging Technology Partner of the Year. (* Disclosure below.)

Traditional encryption can lock data so tightly that analysts and models can no longer use it. Protegrity centers its approach on tokenization, which swaps sensitive values for substitutes instead of relying on a mathematical algorithm, Loureda explained. That design also matters as quantum computing threatens today’s cryptography.

“Our main method of protection, that is tokenization, it’s already quantum ready,” Loureda said. “The reason behind that is because there is no mathematical algorithm behind it. It’s all based on replacement in memory.”

Protection alone doesn’t solve the speed problem, however. In research Protegrity commissioned from Enterprise Management Associates Inc., 83% of leaders reported project delays, Loureda noted.

“The main problem with governance is that companies are approving projects and that will not scale in the age of AI,” Loureda said. “They have to approve patterns.”

The same study found 82% of leaders push agents into production in a diminished state, stripped of the tools and data that would make them useful, he added. Controls such as tokenization let security teams clear the way for those agents instead, according to Loureda.

“Security has always been the business of no, the department of no. That changes now,” he said. “These days security is the team that can enable AI to give you value.”
