#5526. Avago–Broadcom to Skyworks–Qorvo: 10 chip deals worth billions

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These major semiconductor acquisitions, from AMD–Xilinx to Nvidia's abandoned bid for Arm, show how chipmakers have pursued multibillion-dollar deals to reshape the industry

A chip company is rarely bought only for what it sells today. Buyers in the semiconductor industry usually pay for position. That can mean a processor design other firms license or a product category that would take years to build from scratch. It can also mean a foothold in a market such as smartphones, data centers or cars. Programmable chips, wireless components, flash memory, processor blueprints, vision systems for vehicles and analog parts have all changed hands for billions of dollars.

The 10 major semiconductor acquisitions and takeover bids in this list begin in 2015, when Avago Technologies agreed to buy Broadcom $AVGO Corp. They end in 2025, when Skyworks and Qorvo announced plans to combine. In between are two Intel $INTC deals, two separate deals for the chip designer Arm and a merger of two analog chipmakers, Analog Devices $ADI and Maxim Integrated.

Not every deal on the list closed. Qualcomm $QCOM's offer for NXP Semiconductors was terminated in 2018 after it failed to win approval from Chinese regulators. Nvidia $NVDA abandoned its agreement to buy Arm in 2022 after regulatory challenges, including from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and the U.K. competition authority. The Skyworks–Qorvo combination is an announced plan, not a completed deal.

The price attached to a deal also depends on when it is measured. In an all-stock deal, the buyer pays with its own shares. The value therefore rises or falls with the buyer's share price between announcement and closing. AMD $AMD's purchase of Xilinx shows the gap. It was valued at about $35 billion when announced in October 2020. When it closed in February 2022, it was valued at about $49 billion. Each slide below keeps announced and closing figures separate and dates both where the record allows.

This is a selection rather than a ranking. Tallies of chipmaker mergers differ on whether to use announced or closing values. They also differ on whether failed or pending deals count. Software purchases by chip companies, such as Broadcom's deal for VMware, are left out, as are takeover approaches that never became signed agreements. The slides run in chronological order by announcement date. Each one covers what the target made, what the deal was worth and how far it got.

Avago Technologies announced a $37 billion deal to buy Broadcom $AVGO Corp. in May 2015. The purchase closed in February 2016. The combined company took the Broadcom name rather than keeping Avago's.

Broadcom Corp. was founded in 1991 by Henry Samueli and Henry Nicholas. It was based in Irvine, California, and went public in 1998. The company built chips that move data over wireless and wired connections. Its lineup included Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chips for smartphones and laptops, processors for cable and satellite set-top boxes and Ethernet switch chips for data center networks.

Broadcom Corp. was a fabless chip company. It designed its own semiconductors but relied on contract manufacturers such as TSMC $TSM to produce them. That model let it focus spending on chip design rather than on building factories.

Avago had a different history. It began as the semiconductor unit of Agilent Technologies $A, the test and measurement company that Hewlett-Packard spun off in 1999. Private equity firms KKR and Silver Lake bought the chip unit in 2005 and renamed it Avago. The company kept major operations in Singapore and San Jose, California.

Hock Tan became Avago's chief executive in 2006. Under his leadership, the company grew through acquisitions. Its 2014 purchase of LSI Corp. added storage and networking chips. Avago's own products included radio frequency filters for phones, optical components for fiber networks and custom chips built for individual customers.

The Broadcom deal combined those product lines with Broadcom Corp.'s connectivity business. Avago paid with a mix of cash and stock. The merged company, Broadcom Limited, traded under Avago's existing ticker, AVGO. Tan stayed on as chief executive. Samueli joined the combined company as chief technology officer and a board member.

The company kept buying after the merger, including outside the chip business. It moved into enterprise software with purchases of CA Technologies and the enterprise security arm of Symantec. In 2018 it shifted its legal home from Singapore to the U.S. and became Broadcom Inc.

Intel $INTC announced a $16.7 billion purchase of Altera, a maker of programmable chips, in June 2015. The deal closed in December 2015 and gave Intel its own line of field-programmable gate arrays, the chips known as FPGAs.

FPGAs differ from most chips in one basic way. A standard processor or custom chip has its circuitry fixed at the factory. An FPGA can be reconfigured by the customer after it ships. Engineers change what the hardware does by loading a new design onto it.

That flexibility made FPGAs common in telecom gear, networking equipment, industrial controls and defense systems. Chip designers also use them to prototype circuits that will later be manufactured as fixed designs.

Altera, based in San Jose, California, was one of two dominant suppliers in the FPGA market. Its main rival was Xilinx. Altera sold its chips under product family names including Stratix, Arria and Cyclone. Those lines ranged from high-performance parts to lower-cost devices for simpler jobs.

The two companies already had a working relationship before the takeover. Altera had earlier agreed to have some of its most advanced FPGAs manufactured in Intel's factories. That made it one of the few outside customers of Intel's chipmaking operation at the time.

Intel's case for the deal centered on data centers. The company argued that FPGAs could sit alongside its Xeon server processors and speed up specific tasks more efficiently than general-purpose chips alone. Intel also pointed to connected devices and industrial equipment as markets where programmable chips could extend its reach.

After the deal closed, Intel ran the former Altera business as a unit called the Programmable Solutions Group. Altera's product families stayed on the market under their existing names.

The purchase put Intel in direct competition with Xilinx for FPGA customers. It also gave a company built on general-purpose processors a second kind of logic chip to sell. Server customers could now source processors and FPGAs from the same supplier. AMD $AMD's later deal for Xilinx followed a similar pattern. It placed the other leading FPGA maker inside a rival x86 processor company.

Western Digital $WDC agreed in October 2015 to buy SanDisk in a deal valued at about $19 billion. The purchase added a major flash memory maker to a company built on hard disk drives. It closed in May 2016.

The logic of the deal rested on a change in how computers and phones store data. Western Digital had spent decades making hard drives. These record information magnetically on spinning platters, read by a head that moves across the surface. SanDisk made NAND flash, a type of memory that stores data on chips with no moving parts.

A hard drive is a mechanical device, while a flash chip is a semiconductor. Buying SanDisk moved Western Digital into semiconductor manufacturing through flash memory production.

Flash keeps its contents when the power is off. That made it the standard storage for smartphones, digital cameras and thin laptops. Solid-state drives built on flash read and write data faster than hard drives. They also hold up better when a device is dropped or jostled.

Hard drives kept one clear advantage, a lower cost for each unit of storage. That kept them in demand for bulk storage in data centers, where capacity often matters more than speed. With SanDisk, Western Digital could sell spinning disks for capacity-heavy jobs and flash-based drives where speed came first.

SanDisk also brought a familiar consumer name. Its memory cards and USB flash drives were sold widely in retail stores. The company supplied flash storage to device makers and business customers as well. It was based in Milpitas, California, in Silicon Valley.

The deal carried manufacturing ties in Japan. SanDisk produced its flash chips through a long-running joint venture with Toshiba. Western Digital therefore inherited a factory partnership rather than a set of plants it controlled alone.

Memory is a part of the semiconductor business known for sharp swings in prices as supply and demand shift. The acquisition gave Western Digital direct exposure to those cycles. After the deal, the combined company kept the Western Digital name, and SanDisk continued as a brand for flash products.

SoftBank announced in July 2016 that it would buy Arm Holdings for £24.3 billion, or about $32 billion at the time. The deal closed in September 2016. It took the British chip designer private and placed it under the Japanese technology and telecommunications group.

Arm's business model differs from that of most chip companies. It does not manufacture chips. It designs processor architectures and core blueprints, then licenses them to other companies. Those companies build their own chips around the designs and pay Arm licensing fees and royalties.

That model made Arm's designs the standard inside smartphones. Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Samsung and MediaTek have all built mobile processors on the Arm architecture. Arm-based chips also run tablets, embedded devices and networking equipment. More recently they have moved into laptops and data center servers.

Arm is based in Cambridge, England. It began as a joint venture involving Acorn Computers, Apple and VLSI Technology. It later listed its shares on the London Stock Exchange, where it became a member of the FTSE 100 index.

SoftBank's offer came weeks after the U.K. voted in a June 2016 referendum to leave the European Union. The pound fell against other major currencies after the vote. That drop made British assets cheaper for buyers paying in dollars or yen. Masayoshi Son, SoftBank's founder, led the acquisition.

The buyer was not a chipmaker. SoftBank was a holding company with telecom operations in Japan and the U.S. Its U.S. business included the American carrier Sprint, and it also held a large portfolio of technology investments. SoftBank presented the Arm purchase as a way to position itself for the internet of things — the spread of connected sensors, appliances and machines that need low-power processors.

Arm's business depends on neutrality. It licenses the same designs to companies that compete directly with one another. Under SoftBank, Arm continued to operate as a separately run licensing company serving that broad customer base.

The ownership did not stay settled. SoftBank later agreed to sell Arm to Nvidia $NVDA, a deal that fell apart under regulatory pressure. SoftBank then returned Arm to public markets through a listing on Nasdaq $NDAQ in New York. It kept a majority stake after the listing.

Qualcomm $QCOM announced a $44 billion offer for NXP Semiconductors in October 2016. The deal was terminated in July 2018 after it failed to win approval from Chinese regulators, and Qualcomm paid NXP a $2 billion termination fee.

Qualcomm and NXP worked in different parts of the semiconductor business. Qualcomm, based in San Diego, built its business on mobile technology. Its Snapdragon processors and cellular modems are used in many Android smartphones. The company also earns revenue by licensing its wireless patents to device makers.

NXP is headquartered in Eindhoven, in the Netherlands. It began as the semiconductor division of Philips and became an independent company in 2006. Its main markets include automotive chips and the secure chips used in identification and payment cards. It is also a major supplier of near-field communication chips. Near-field communication is the short-range wireless technology behind contactless card and phone payments. NXP expanded its automotive business by merging with Freescale Semiconductor in 2015.

The combination would have taken Qualcomm beyond phones. It would have added a large automotive chip business, along with chips for industrial equipment and connected devices.

Cross-border chip deals of this size need clearance from competition authorities in several jurisdictions. Both companies sold large volumes of chips in China. That brought the deal under review by Chinese regulators. China became the last major approval still outstanding. The review stretched into 2018, a year in which the U.S. and Chinese governments imposed tariffs on each other's goods.

Chinese approval did not come before the agreement's deadline. Qualcomm ended the deal once that deadline passed. The $2 billion payment was a termination fee set out in the merger agreement. A fee of this kind compensates a target company for the cost and disruption of a deal that falls apart. NXP stayed an independent, publicly traded company.

The outcome showed that one national regulator could stop a deal between a U.S. company and a European one, even though neither company was based in that country.

Intel $INTC announced a $15.3 billion purchase of Mobileye in March 2017. Mobileye is a Jerusalem-based company that designs chips and computer vision software for cars.

The bid was Intel's route into automotive driver-assistance systems. Mobileye's core product is the EyeQ family of system-on-chip processors. These chips take the video feed from a camera mounted behind a car's windshield and interpret it in real time. The software identifies lane markings, other vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists and traffic signs.

Automakers use that capability for features drivers encounter every day. Forward collision warnings, automatic emergency braking, lane departure alerts and adaptive cruise control can all rely on camera-based sensing of the kind Mobileye sells. The company often reaches car brands through the large tier-one suppliers that assemble components for them. It does not sell only to automakers directly.

Mobileye was co-founded by Amnon Shashua, a computer science professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and businessman Ziv Aviram. Its engineering approach centered on extracting as much information as possible from a single, inexpensive camera. That set it apart from systems built around costlier sensors such as radar and lidar.

Mobileye was already listed on the New York Stock Exchange when Intel made its bid. The two companies also had an existing working relationship. Before the deal, Intel, Mobileye and BMW had announced a partnership to develop technology for self-driving cars.

For Intel, the bid extended a pattern of buying its way into new chip markets. It came less than two years after Intel announced its purchase of Altera, the programmable chip maker. Intel's business had long depended on processors for personal computers and data-center servers. The company had not built a major position in smartphone chips.

Cars represent a different kind of computing demand. Driver-assistance features need chips that process sensor data instantly. Those chips also have to run reliably for years through heat, cold and vibration. Fully autonomous vehicles would require far more onboard computing, along with high-definition mapping and large-scale data processing in the cloud.

The Mobileye bid differs from a typical chipmaker merger because the target's value is tied to software as much as silicon. Mobileye pairs its own vision algorithms with its own processors. Its customers are automakers and their suppliers, not PC or phone manufacturers. That made the bid a move toward an industry Intel had not previously served at scale.

Analog Devices $ADI agreed in July 2020 to buy Maxim Integrated in an all-stock deal valued at about $21 billion. The merger closed in August 2021. It joined two U.S. makers of analog and mixed-signal chips into a single company.

Analog chips handle the physical world. They take signals such as temperature, pressure, sound, light and electrical current and convert them into data that digital processors can use. They also regulate and distribute power inside electronic devices.

That role sets them apart from the processors that run software and the memory chips that store data. A smartphone, a car or a factory robot can contain many analog parts working alongside a single main processor.

Analog Devices is based in Wilmington, Massachusetts. It built its business on data converters, amplifiers and signal-processing chips. Its parts go into industrial equipment, communications gear, health care devices and cars.

Maxim Integrated was based in San Jose, California. It was known for power-management chips and for parts used in automotive systems, including battery management.

Maxim shareholders received Analog Devices stock rather than cash. The figure of about $21 billion is the deal's value at its announcement.

The transaction took more than a year to complete. Large chip mergers generally need clearance from competition regulators in several countries. That review can stretch the time between signing a deal and closing it.

Analog Devices had grown through acquisitions before. It bought Linear Technology, another analog chipmaker, in a $14.8 billion deal announced in 2016. The Maxim purchase extended that approach with a second large analog acquisition.

After the merger closed, Maxim stopped operating as an independent company. Its product lines became part of the Analog Devices catalog.

The merger also fits a broader pattern in the analog segment. Analog chips often stay in production for many years. Customers in industrial and automotive markets tend to qualify a part once and keep buying it. That makes broad catalogs and long customer relationships central to how analog suppliers compete.

Nvidia $NVDA agreed in September 2020 to buy Arm from SoftBank in a deal valued at roughly $40 billion. The plan was abandoned in February 2022 after regulatory challenges, including from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and the U.K. competition authority.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, does not manufacture chips. It designs processor architectures and core blueprints, then licenses them to other companies that build their own silicon. Arm-based designs power most of the world's smartphones, and companies such as Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM and Samsung all build chips on Arm technology.

Nvidia built its business on graphics processing units, or GPUs. Those chips began as hardware for video game graphics. They later became central to data centers and artificial intelligence workloads. Buying Arm would have put the most widely licensed processor architecture in mobile computing under the same roof as Nvidia's accelerated computing business.

That pairing is what worried regulators and many of Arm's customers. Arm's model depends on licensing its designs to a wide range of chipmakers, including companies that compete directly with Nvidia. The concern was that Nvidia, as Arm's owner, could restrict, delay or raise the price of rivals' access to Arm technology. Qualcomm was among the Arm licensees that publicly objected to the acquisition.

The Federal Trade Commission sued to block the deal. The agency argued that the combined company would have the means and the incentive to undermine rivals that rely on Arm's designs. In Britain, the Competition and Markets Authority reviewed the takeover on competition grounds, and the U.K. government also raised national security questions. The European Commission opened its own in-depth investigation.

Facing those reviews in several jurisdictions, Nvidia and SoftBank ended the agreement. Arm stayed under SoftBank's ownership, and SoftBank later took the company public instead of selling it to another chipmaker. The collapse left Arm operating as an independent supplier to the whole industry, including Nvidia.

AMD $AMD announced an all-stock deal to buy Xilinx in October 2020 at about $35 billion. The acquisition closed on Feb. 14, 2022, when it was valued at about $49 billion.

Xilinx, based in San Jose, California, made field-programmable gate arrays, known as FPGAs. Its co-founder Ross Freeman is credited with inventing the FPGA. A standard processor runs software on circuitry that is fixed at the factory. An FPGA's internal logic can be reconfigured after the chip ships. That lets a customer set up the chip for one specific job. The flexibility made FPGAs common in telecom equipment, aerospace and defense systems, industrial machinery, automotive electronics and data-center networking.

Xilinx sold several product families. Its Virtex, Kintex and Artix lines were FPGAs aimed at different performance levels. Its Zynq chips paired Arm processor cores with programmable logic on a single piece of silicon. Its Versal family added dedicated AI engines alongside the programmable fabric. Its Alveo accelerator cards were designed to slot into data-center servers.

Like AMD, Xilinx was a fabless company. It designed its chips and relied on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to make them.

For AMD, the purchase widened a lineup built around Ryzen PC processors, EPYC server processors and Radeon graphics chips. Xilinx gave the company programmable chips to offer the same data-center customers buying its server CPUs. It also gave AMD a larger position in embedded markets such as industrial, automotive and communications hardware. The deal put AMD in direct competition with Intel $INTC's programmable chip business, which Intel had assembled through its own purchase of Altera.

The closing came after the deal cleared the regulatory reviews it required, including approval from China's market regulator. Xilinx became the core of a new AMD unit, the Adaptive and Embedded Computing Group, led by former Xilinx CEO Victor Peng.

Xilinx technology later moved into AMD's consumer chips. The XDNA neural processing architecture inside AMD's Ryzen AI laptop processors is based on AI engine designs AMD gained through the acquisition.

Skyworks Solutions and Qorvo announced a plan in October 2025 to combine in a deal valued at about $22 billion. Under the plan, two U.S. makers of radio-frequency chips would become one company.

These components let a phone or other wireless device send and receive signals. The category includes power amplifiers, which boost outgoing signals, and filters, which separate the many frequency bands a modern handset uses. Chipmakers often package these parts together into front-end modules. Those modules sit between a device's modem and its antennas.

Radio-frequency hardware grew more complex as phones added support for 4G LTE and then 5G. Each new generation brought additional frequency bands, and each band needs its own filtering and amplification. Both companies built much of their business around supplying those parts for handsets.

Skyworks took its current shape in 2002. That year, Alpha Industries merged with the wireless communications business of Conexant Systems. The company long operated from Woburn, Massachusetts, and later moved its headquarters to Irvine, California. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker SWKS.

Qorvo is itself the product of a merger. RF Micro Devices, based in Greensboro, North Carolina, combined with TriQuint Semiconductor of Hillsboro, Oregon. The merged company began operating under the Qorvo name in 2015 and kept Greensboro as its headquarters. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker QRVO.

The two companies have spent years as direct rivals for the same slots inside smartphones. Apple $AAPL has been a major customer for both. Other suppliers in the radio-frequency market include Broadcom $AVGO, Qualcomm $QCOM and Japan's Murata Manufacturing. Skyworks and Qorvo also sell chips beyond phones, including parts for Wi-Fi equipment, cellular infrastructure and connected devices.

Mergers between publicly traded companies generally need approval from shareholders and regulators before they can close. The figure of about $22 billion reflects the value at announcement.

#5525. Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work

Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.

That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.

Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.

But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.

That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.

This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”

Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.

Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.

Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

#5524. ACTRA Opens Early Bird Access in the U.S., Bringing Personal AI Beyond the Smartphone

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ACTRA, a consumer brand of AIânative startup Stavecho, today unveiled its first product, the ACTRA Mag 4G AI Pendant, as the brand's official website goes live. Alongside the launch, the company has opened an Early Bird program. The first 2,000 ACTRA Mag 4G units are available at the Early Bird price of $199.9, securing first-batch access, exclusive Early Bird benefits and a complimentary wristband. A $19.9 reservation option is also available, allowing customers to lock in Early Bird privileges and receive shipment priority based on order sequence.

ACTRA aims to redefine how people interact with AI and bring it into everyday life. "While most AI interactions today still depend on smartphones, earbuds, smartwatches, or smart glasses, ACTRA adopts a magnetic pendant form factor worn at the chest, on a necklace, or on a wristband. Its lightweight, screen-free design is intended to reduce disruption to existing daily habits, positioning AI as something available whenever it is needed rather than confined to an app on a phone," said Haitian YIN, Founder and CEO of Stavecho.

Building A Personal AI That Stays Present

As the first entry point into Stavecho's personal AI ecosystem, ACTRA is designed around a continuous, always-available assistant rather than a single-purpose device. Four capabilities define the experience.

Natural Interaction in a Lightweight Design

The hardware has been designed to support frequent, low-friction interaction. Weighing approximately 22 grams, ACTRA features three primary interaction methods: Double Tap, Press & Hold, and the voice wake phrase "Hey Stavia."

#5523. Seattle startup Avante raises $30M to bring AI agents to corporate benefits teams

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 27, 2026 at 9:03 amOctober 27, 2026 at 9:29 am

Avante, the maker of an AI platform to help companies manage employee health care and other benefits, has landed a $30 million Series A round.

Frist Cressey Ventures led the round, with participation from Sorenson Capital, Hearst Ventures, Morgan Stanley Next Level Fund and existing investor Fuse. The new funding, announced Tuesday, brings Seattle-based Avante’s total raised to $40 million, following a $10 million seed round led by Fuse in 2024.

Benefits are one of employers’ biggest costs. Avante’s AI agents do work like comparing vendor contracts against actual claims, reviewing plan documents for errors and preparing for renewals. Employees can also use the platform to ask questions about their own coverage.

The startup plans to use the cash to expand internationally and develop more AI agents, building on a beta release of its “Ava Agents” last week.

Avante says it now has more than 70 customers, including Samsung Semiconductor, Real Chemistry, Zscaler and News Corp, and that bookings grew nearly fivefold over the past year. The platform reaches more than 385,000 employees and family members, according to the company.

Avante was founded in 2023 by CEO Rohan D’Souza; Carly Eckert, a physician and epidemiologist who serves as head of innovation and impact; and executive chairman Kabir Shahani, the co-CEO of Amperity.

D’Souza and Eckert previously worked as executives at health care automation company Olive AI, which shut down in 2023. The startup emerged from stealth in early 2024 and launched publicly in April 2025.

“Benefits teams are responsible for one of the largest and most consequential investments their companies make, yet they’re still operating with outdated information, archaic spreadsheets, and technology built for another era,” D’Souza said in a statement.

Avante is pitching its software as employers face rising health care costs. Large employers are projecting a median 9.2% increase for 2027, the company said.

The startup competes with benefits and HR software providers such as Workday, ADP, Deel and Rippling. It has also signed partnerships with benefits advisory firms including Gallagher, OneDigital, Segal Benz, Howden and USI Insurance Services.

Avante ranks No. 156 on the GeekWire 200, our list of top Pacific Northwest tech startups.

#5522. Enterprises bring AI to their data as privacy rules tighten and costs climb

Every enterprise AI strategy eventually comes down to the same question: Should proprietary data travel to the model, or should the model come to the data?

“Rather than saying, ‘Just give us all your data and we’ll in return provide you access to a model that’s then contextualized based on that data,’ we turn things around,” Stoop said. “We say, ‘We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives.'”

Stoop spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can bring AI to their data while maintaining control and managing costs. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s latest move in that direction is a partnership with Mistral AI SAS, which brings Mistral’s models into Cloudera’s data platform. For European customers in particular, the model maker’s local roots matter as much as its technology, Stoop noted.

“Certainly for us in Europe, having a French organization, a local company, that provides these models and provides the complete stack is very attractive for a lot of our customers,” Stoop said. “Mistral was a very easy choice for us to say, ‘Those are the ones that we’re going with.'”

AI is at the top of a maturity curve that starts with sovereign data, sovereign cloud and local operations, according to Stoop. Rules such as the European Union’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and the U.S. CLOUD Act are pushing organizations to prove they have control rather than simply claim it. But control alone won’t move AI out of the pilot phase. For many companies, the bigger obstacle in an enterprise AI strategy is the cost of running models at scale, because generating tokens takes a lot of hardware.

“If you use a public provider for that, the more you use your model, the more you get hit on cost,” Stoop said. “How do I get that high utilization of a good model inside my organization without being exposed to horrific costs? That, I think, is the biggest challenge that organizations are struggling with right now.”

#5521. Foam rollers to sleep masks: 10 post-run recovery tools explained

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Recovery gear for runners ranges from foam rollers to compression boots, and these 10 recovery tools show what each does and what the evidence supports

A hard run applies the stress, but the body does its adapting afterward. Muscles, tendons and the cardiovascular system respond to training in the hours and days that follow a workout. That window is where recovery happens. It is also why many runners treat recovery as part of training rather than time off from it.

That idea underpins a broad market for recovery gear for runners. At one end sit simple, passive items that cost little and fit in a gym bag. A lacrosse ball is a typical example. At the other end are powered devices, such as pneumatic compression boots that inflate around the legs. Between them sit garments, footwear, bath routines and bedroom setups. Each is aimed at a different part of the post-run period. Price, size and setup time vary widely across the category.

The evidence behind these running recovery tools is uneven. Some have a long record of use among athletes and coaches but limited research to back specific claims. Others have been studied more closely, with results that are mixed. A few are mainly about comfort, and this list describes them that way. Each entry says where the research is limited or mixed. It also avoids claims that a tool speeds muscle repair when that has not been established.

The 10 items that follow are a selection, not a ranking. They cover soft tissue work, compression, footwear, water temperature and sleep. Each slide explains what the tool is, how runners use it and what it can reasonably be expected to do. Each slide also stands on its own. Readers can start with whichever tool fits their training.

None of this gear replaces the basics. Easy days, enough rest and adequate food and fluids remain the foundation of any recovery plan. The tools here work around those foundations. Some target specific muscles. Others address the whole body through water temperature or sleep. Choosing among them depends on budget, space, travel habits and how a runner's body responds to training.

A foam roller is a cylinder of dense foam that a runner lies on to press body weight into tired muscles, a practice known as self-myofascial release. Runners mostly use it on the quads, calves and glutes after a run.

It is a low-cost, widely used running recovery tool. A runner places the roller on the floor and rests the target muscle on top. The arms and the opposite leg then move the body slowly back and forth. Shifting weight onto or off those supporting limbs changes how much pressure reaches the muscle. Slow passes are easier to control than fast ones. Many runners pause on a tender spot for a few breaths before moving on.

Each muscle group has a standard position. For the quads, the runner lies face down with the roller under the front of the thighs. For the calves, they sit with the roller under the lower legs and lift the hips to add load. Crossing one leg over the other concentrates the pressure on a single calf. The glutes are usually worked by sitting on the roller and leaning to one side, often with that ankle crossed over the opposite knee.

The outer thigh is a frequent stop because of the iliotibial band. This thick strip of connective tissue runs from the hip to just below the knee. Rolling directly on the band is often uncomfortable. Many runners work the muscles around it instead, including the outer quad and the side of the hip.

Rollers vary in firmness and surface. Smooth, softer foam spreads pressure across a wide area and suits people new to rolling. Firmer models, some built around a hollow plastic core, push deeper into the muscle. Textured rollers have ridges or knobs that focus pressure on smaller points. Short rollers pack easily in a backpack or suitcase. Longer ones make it easier to roll both legs at once.

Research on foam rolling has produced mixed results. It has not been shown to speed the repair of damaged muscle tissue. Its practical appeal lies in cost and convenience. A roller needs no power, and a session takes a few minutes. It can be done on a living room floor right after a run. Rolling directly over bones, joints or a fresh injury is best avoided.

A massage gun is a handheld, battery-powered device that drives rapid, repeated pulses into muscle tissue, a method called percussive therapy. Research on its recovery benefits for runners is still limited and mixed.

Theragun, made by Therabody, and the Hypervolt line from Hyperice are two well-known names in the category. Both companies sell several models in different sizes. Many other brands make similar devices, and most share the same basic design.

Inside the body of the device, a motor pushes a head back and forth in short, fast strokes. Each stroke presses into the muscle and then releases. The user holds the handle and guides the head across the target area.

Most massage guns come with interchangeable attachments. A rounded ball head spreads pressure across large muscles such as the quads and glutes. A flat head also covers broad areas. A narrow cone or bullet head concentrates force on a small spot. A forked head is shaped to sit on either side of a narrow structure.

Most models also offer several speed settings. Lower settings suit sensitive areas or someone new to the device. Higher settings deliver stronger, faster pulses.

Runners usually work on the calves, hamstrings, quads and glutes. A common approach is to glide the head slowly along the length of a muscle. Users generally let the motor supply the force instead of pushing hard into the tissue. Short passes over each muscle group are typical.

Some parts of the body are off-limits. Manufacturers advise against using percussive devices directly on bones, joints or the front of the neck. They also warn against use on injured, swollen or bruised tissue. Anyone with a circulatory condition or a recent injury should check with a doctor before use.

Some runners also use a massage gun briefly before a run as part of a warm-up. That is a separate use from post-run recovery.

Published research on percussive therapy is limited, and many trials are small and short-term. Results on muscle soreness, range of motion and performance are mixed. The devices have not been shown to speed up muscle repair. For many runners, the appeal is that a session can make tight legs feel looser.

Compression socks and calf sleeves are snug, elastic garments that squeeze the lower leg, and many runners wear them during or after hard sessions. Research has not shown that they speed recovery, and the evidence on their benefits is limited and mixed.

Most running compression gear uses graduated compression. The fabric is tightest at the ankle, and the pressure eases toward the knee. The design is meant to encourage blood in the lower leg to move back toward the heart. The same principle underpins medical compression stockings, which doctors prescribe for vein conditions such as chronic venous insufficiency.

Compression pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury, written as mmHg. Packaging usually lists the level or range a product delivers. Sports and medical garments use the same unit, but medical stockings are prescribed to treat specific conditions.

The choice between a sock and a sleeve comes down to coverage. A compression sock wraps the foot, ankle and calf in one piece. A calf sleeve is a tube that runs from just above the ankle to just below the knee. A sleeve lets a runner keep wearing their usual running socks, including a pair they already rely on to prevent blisters.

CEP and 2XU are two widely available brands in this category. CEP is the sports line of medi, a German maker of medical compression garments. 2XU is an Australian brand that sells compression tights, shorts and tops alongside its leg wear.

Fit determines whether a pair works as intended. Brands in this category generally size by calf circumference, and some also use shoe size. A tape measure around the widest part of the calf gives a better match than guessing from a usual clothing size.

Timing varies by runner. Some wear socks or sleeves during long road races or trail runs. Others save them for afterward, such as the drive or flight home from a marathon.

Garments that are too tight can be uncomfortable or leave marks. People with circulation problems, including peripheral artery disease, should check with a doctor before using any compression. Care labels typically call for gentle washing and air drying to protect the elastic fibers.

Normatec boots are inflatable leg sleeves that squeeze in timed waves from the feet toward the hips. They give runners a seated, hands-free form of compression massage after hard sessions. The brand is owned by Hyperice.

Each boot runs from the foot to the upper thigh and contains several separate air chambers. A control unit pumps air into those chambers in sequence, starting at the foot and moving up the leg. The system holds pressure on one section while the next one inflates. It then releases the whole leg and starts the cycle again.

That moving pressure separates Normatec from a compression sock or calf sleeve. A sock applies a fixed squeeze for as long as it is worn. A pneumatic boot changes pressure on a set pattern. The user chooses the intensity and the length of each session.

The mechanism has roots in medicine. Hospitals use intermittent pneumatic compression devices to help prevent deep vein thrombosis in patients who cannot move much. Clinics use similar equipment to manage lymphedema. Sports versions borrow the same principle and apply it to tired legs rather than a medical condition.

A typical session takes place lying down or reclining, with the legs stretched out straight. Runners often use the boots after a long run, a race or a block of hard intervals. Many professional teams, college athletic departments and physical therapy clinics keep a set on hand. Recovery studios in many cities also sell sessions by the visit. That option suits people who do not want to buy the equipment.

The evidence on athletic recovery is limited and mixed. Many users report that their legs feel looser and more comfortable during and after a session. Research has not shown a consistent improvement in how fast muscles repair or how a runner performs in the next workout. The boots are best understood as a comfort tool rather than a proven performance aid.

Hyperice also sells hip and arm attachments for the system. Its Normatec Go model is a smaller wrap that covers only the calves. Therabody's RecoveryAir is one competing pneumatic system. Anyone with a history of blood clots, circulation problems or a recent leg injury should check with a doctor before using pneumatic compression.

Recovery sandals and slides are soft, thick-soled footwear that runners change into after a run. They replace a snug training or racing shoe with something open and cushioned. Oofos and Hoka are two brands that make footwear built for this purpose.

The appeal is comfort. Feet laced into a running shoe for an hour or more can feel tight and tired by the end. An open sandal lets the feet breathe and takes pressure off the toes and the top of the foot. These are comfort products rather than medical devices.

Oofos builds its line around a proprietary foam it calls OOfoam. The material is softer and more compressible than the rubber or firm foam in a typical flip-flop. The brand's range includes the OOriginal, a thong-style sandal with a post between the toes. It also includes the OOahh, a slide with a single wide strap across the top of the foot.

Hoka was founded in France in 2009 and has been owned by Deckers since 2013. The company is known for running shoes with thick, heavily cushioned midsoles. Its Ora Recovery Slide carries that approach into post-run footwear, with a deep foam footbed and an open-toe design. Hoka also sells the Ora line in other styles.

The choice between a slide and a thong sandal comes down to feel. A slide goes on and off with nothing between the toes, which some runners prefer after a hard effort. A thong sandal holds the foot through the toe post and side straps, which gives a more secure feel while walking.

Recovery footwear fits several points in a running routine. Some runners pack a pair in a race-day bag to wear after the finish line. Others keep a pair by the door for the hours after a training run.

Molded foam footwear is also simple to maintain. With no laces and few separate parts, most pairs can be rinsed off after a muddy race-day finish area.

Fit matters when choosing a pair. A slide that is too loose can slip while walking. Soft foam also compresses with use. A pair that has flattened noticeably no longer cushions the way it did when new. Very soft footwear feels different underfoot from a running shoe, and preferences vary from runner to runner. A persistent foot injury calls for an evaluation by a podiatrist or physician rather than a change of footwear.

A lacrosse ball or trigger point ball lets a runner press into one small spot, such as the arch of the foot or a deep hip muscle, with more precision than a wide roller allows. These balls cost little, fit in a pocket and need no power source.

A standard lacrosse ball is made of solid rubber. It is about the size of a tennis ball but much denser, and it barely compresses under body weight. That firmness is why runners reach for it. The pressure lands on a small area instead of spreading across a whole muscle.

Trigger point balls come in a wider range of textures and firmness. Some are smooth. Others have raised nubs or spikes. Some are sold as two balls joined in a peanut shape. The TriggerPoint brand, for example, sells massage balls in more than one size. A tennis ball is a softer option for runners who find a lacrosse ball too intense.

The foot is a frequent target. The plantar fascia is a thick band of connective tissue that runs along the sole from the heel bone toward the toes. Runners roll a ball under the arch while sitting at a desk or standing at a counter. Shifting more or less weight onto that foot adjusts the pressure. Moving slowly from the heel to the ball of the foot covers the full length of the arch.

The glutes are another common use. The piriformis is a small muscle that sits beneath the gluteus maximus and runs from the base of the spine to the top of the thigh bone. A large foam roller has trouble isolating it. A ball placed under one hip while sitting on the floor can settle into the area directly. Pinning the ball between the hip and a wall works the same spot standing up. The wall method also reaches the outer hip.

Evidence on how much self-massage speeds recovery is limited. A ball is not a treatment for injury. Heel pain that lasts for weeks, or pain that sharpens during a run, calls for a doctor or physical therapist rather than harder pressure. Pressing directly on bone, or on a spot that causes numbness or tingling, is also worth avoiding.

The small size makes a ball easy to carry. It survives a packed suitcase and works in a hotel room, an office or a start corral before a race.

A massage stick is a handheld bar with rolling segments that a runner presses into the legs with their arms instead of their body weight. The Stick is one widely used brand. The tool suits runners who want direct control over pressure on the calves and quads.

The build has few parts. A semi-flexible core runs between two handles. A series of spindles or rings rotates along that core as it moves across the skin. Tiger Tail makes a similar tool. Other versions differ in length, stiffness and the texture of the rolling surface. A stiffer stick delivers firmer pressure. A more flexible one bends around the curve of the leg.

The main difference from a floor-based roller is the source of the force. With a stick, the runner pushes down with their hands and can ease off at once if a spot feels too tender. That makes it practical for runners who find it hard to hold themselves up on the floor. It also helps anyone who wants a lighter touch on sore muscles.

Calves are a common target. A runner can sit on a chair or bench and rest one foot flat on the floor. The stick then rolls from just above the ankle toward the back of the knee. Quads work the same way from a seated position. The strokes run from above the kneecap up toward the hip. The hamstrings and the outer thigh can be reached too, though the angle is more awkward.

Slow, even strokes are easier to control than fast rubbing. Pressure belongs on muscle, not bone. The shinbone, the kneecap and the soft hollow behind the knee are areas to avoid.

Portability is part of the appeal. A stick is light, slides into a backpack or carry-on and needs no floor space. Runners can use one in a hotel room, at a desk or while waiting before a race. Shorter travel-length models exist for that use.

As with other rolling tools, research on whether a massage stick improves recovery is limited. Runners mainly use it to ease the feeling of tightness after a run. There is no strong evidence that it speeds muscle repair.

An ice bath means sitting in cold water, usually up to the waist or chest, for a short time after a hard run. Many runners use one to ease sore legs. The evidence on whether it speeds recovery is mixed, and some research suggests it may blunt gains from strength training.

The setup can be simple. Many runners fill a home bathtub with cold tap water and add bags of ice. Others use a galvanized stock tank, the kind sold for watering livestock, or a collapsible inflatable tub that packs flat for storage. More expensive options are dedicated cold plunge units with built-in chillers and filters. These hold the water at a set temperature without fresh ice each time.

The appeal for runners centers on how the legs feel. Long runs, track sessions and races can leave the quads and calves heavy and sore. A cold soak can dull that sensation for a while. Cold water also draws heat out of the body faster than air does. That makes a soak attractive after a run in summer heat.

That cooling effect has a firmer medical role. Cold-water immersion is the standard first-line treatment for exertional heat stroke. Medical teams at many large road races keep tubs of ice water ready at the finish for that reason. This is an emergency treatment for a dangerous condition, not a routine recovery step.

The recovery case is less settled. Research on whether ice baths reduce muscle damage or restore performance faster has produced mixed results. A further caution applies to runners who also lift weights. Some research suggests that regular cold-water immersion right after strength sessions may reduce the muscle and strength gains that training is meant to build. Runners who lift can keep cold soaks away from strength days. Another option is to save them for races and the hardest workouts of a training block.

Safety needs attention with this kind of recovery. Sudden immersion in cold water triggers a cold shock response, with a gasp reflex and rapid breathing. Lowering in gradually is safer than jumping in. People with heart conditions, high blood pressure or Raynaud's phenomenon should talk to a doctor before trying an ice bath. Sessions are typically short. Nobody should soak alone, and anyone who starts shivering hard should get out and warm up.

An Epsom salt bath is a warm soak with magnesium sulfate dissolved in the water. Runners use it to unwind after a long run. The evidence that magnesium passes through the skin in useful amounts is weak. The soak works as a relaxing routine, not as a treatment for sore muscles.

Epsom salt is not table salt. Table salt is sodium chloride. Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, which forms clear crystals. The name comes from Epsom, a town in Surrey, England, where the compound was drawn from a bitter mineral spring centuries ago. Pharmacies and supermarkets sell it in bags and cartons, often with added scents such as lavender or eucalyptus.

The common claim is that soaking lets magnesium enter the body and ease muscle soreness. Human skin is built to keep substances out. Research on absorbing magnesium through it remains limited. No well-established finding shows that an Epsom salt soak speeds muscle repair after a run.

Runners who want more magnesium can get it far more reliably from food. Nuts, seeds, beans, leafy greens and whole grains all supply the mineral.

The warm water itself accounts for most of what a runner can actually feel. Heat widens blood vessels near the skin. A soak also gives tired legs a chance to rest while the water supports them. Some runners use the bath as a signal that the hard part of the day is over. For them, that wind-down routine is the main appeal.

A warm soak works in the opposite direction from cold-water immersion. Its purpose is comfort and relaxation rather than cooling the body down. The two are separate choices, and a runner can pick whichever fits the evening.

Very hot water can add strain after a long run in warm weather, when the body is already working to shed heat. Salt can sting open blisters or chafed skin, both common after long distances. Anyone with a heart condition or broken skin on the feet may want to ask a doctor before making hot baths a habit.

Package directions usually give an amount per bath, and following the label avoids guesswork. Some Epsom salt products are also labeled for oral use as a laxative. That is a separate purpose entirely and has no part in a recovery bath.

Sleep is the recovery tool runners use every night, and a few simple items can help protect it. An eye mask and blackout curtains cut the light that disrupts sleep. A sleep tracker gives a rough nightly record of how long and how restlessly a runner slept.

Much of the body's repair work takes place during sleep. In deep, slow-wave sleep, the pituitary gland releases growth hormone in pulses. That hormone plays a role in rebuilding muscle and other tissue. For a runner stacking hard sessions across a week, short or broken nights leave less time for that process.

Light is the main cue the brain uses to set its internal clock. Evening light suppresses melatonin, the hormone that signals the body to prepare for sleep. A dark room supports that signal instead of working against it.

An eye mask is the simplest and most portable option. Contoured or cup-style masks hold the fabric away from the eyelids. Some sleepers find that more comfortable than a flat strap. Masks also suit runners who travel to races and sleep in hotel rooms with unfamiliar light. They work for a short nap after a long run, too.

Blackout curtains deal with the room itself. They block streetlights, car headlights and the early summer sunrise that can wake a runner before the alarm. Blackout blinds and removable window film do the same job where curtains will not fit.

Sleep trackers fill a different role. Devices such as the Oura Ring, the Whoop strap, Garmin running watches and the Apple $AAPL Watch use motion sensors and optical heart rate readings. From those signals, they estimate when a wearer fell asleep, how often they woke and how the night divided into light, deep and REM sleep.

Those stage breakdowns are estimates. The clinical standard, polysomnography, records brain activity through electrodes in a sleep lab. A wrist or finger sensor cannot do that. Trackers are more useful for spotting trends across weeks than for judging any single night.

Overnight resting heart rate and heart rate variability are the figures many runners watch. Heart rate variability measures how much the time between heartbeats changes from one beat to the next. A resting heart rate that stays above a runner's usual level for several days can accompany accumulated fatigue, illness or poor sleep. That pattern gives a runner a reason to review the training load before the next hard session.

#5520. Seattle’s Kivo Health raises $10M to bring lung disease rehab into patients’ homes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:19 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:52 am

Seattle-based Kivo Health today announced $10 million in funding to help increase access to its services, which target older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Series A round brings the startup’s total funding to more than $16 million.

Kivo ships equipment to patients’ homes and provides a nine-week program of therapist-led, live video sessions focused on exercise, breathing techniques and disease management. The company provides ongoing support following the program and says it uses AI to handle administrative tasks and communicate with patients, supporting its clinicians.

“We’re using the funding to build our AI health coach to blend AI-led care with human-led care,” Dr. Victor Sadauskas, Kivo’s co-founder and CEO, said via email. That pairing, he added, will help patients manage their chronic disease over the long term.

The company has approximately 50 employees, including clinicians.

COPD is an incurable lung disease in which damaged airways and air sacs make breathing difficult and can worsen over time. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, a persistent cough and fatigue. COPD is the third leading cause of death globally and the fifth in the U.S.

However, there are effective treatments to improve the condition, though many patients are not able to easily access care. A study of Medicare beneficiaries with COPD found that only 3.7% received pulmonary rehabilitation in 2012.

Kivo reports that a peer-reviewed study of its program found improvements in participants’ symptoms, physical function and mental health. The company also funded an analysis that estimated its model could reduce annual health care spending by $8,245 per member through fewer hospitalizations, ER visits and time in nursing homes.

Kivo says its program is covered by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Blue Cross, Aetna and Priority Health.

“By thoughtfully combining high quality clinical care with AI, we can now scale proactive, accessible care to every senior, improving symptoms and reducing avoidable costs,” Sadauskas said in a statement.

Sadauskas launched Kivo in 2023 with co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vaughn Koch. Sadauskas previously was an emergency medicine physician for Kaiser Permanente and a senior investment fellow with Life Science Angels. Koch is a serial entrepreneur who sold his startup Movity to Trulia in 2010.

While its current focus is COPD, Kivo aims to expand into other costly chronic conditions affecting older adults.

Allumia Ventures led the round, with participation from Corewell Health Ventures, Y Combinator, Heuristic Capital and MassMutual Ventures.

#5519. European supermarket cyberattacks highlight the need for secure remote access to refrigeration systems, says Secomea

A second wave of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems raises urgent questions about how retailers protect critical operational technology while maintaining essential remote services.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Supermarket chains across Europe have reported a new wave of suspected cyberattacks affecting refrigeration systems, just weeks after attackers reportedly manipulated cooling equipment in hundreds of French stores, causing substantial food losses.

The latest incidents, reported in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg, highlight a growing challenge for retailers: the operational technology (OT) responsible for keeping food safe is increasingly connected to external systems and service providers, creating potential security risks when that connectivity is not adequately protected.

Unlike traditional cyberattacks focused on stealing data or disrupting IT services, attacks on operational technology can have immediate physical consequences. Compromised refrigeration systems can mean spoiled food, interrupted operations, significant financial losses, and potential risks to food safety.

"These incidents illustrate why cybersecurity is no longer just about protecting information. When attackers interfere with operational technology, the consequences become physical," says Michael Ferdinandsen, CEO at Secomea, a Danish industrial cybersecurity company specializing in secure remote access.

"For retailers, the question isn't whether they need remote connectivity. They absolutely do. The question is whether they have sufficient control over who can access their equipment, what they can reach, and what they're allowed to do."

The challenge isn't connectivity. It's controlling access

Modern refrigeration systems depend on remote connectivity to operate efficiently. External service providers and maintenance technicians use it to monitor temperatures, respond to alarms, diagnose faults, and maintain equipment across hundreds or thousands of locations.

This connectivity is essential for minimizing response times and preventing equipment failures. But it also introduces potential entry points for attackers, particularly when operational equipment is directly exposed to the internet or remote users are granted broader access than necessary.

For supermarket chains managing multiple locations, refrigeration systems, and external service providers, the challenge becomes even more complex. Different suppliers may use different access methods, making it difficult for IT and security teams to maintain consistent oversight of who can connect to critical infrastructure.

"Many organizations have invested heavily in securing their corporate IT environments, but operational equipment often presents a different challenge," explains Michael Ferdinandsen.

"These systems were designed to operate reliably for years, sometimes decades. They weren't necessarily designed with today's connectivity and cybersecurity requirements in mind. Applying traditional IT remote access approaches without considering those differences can create unnecessary exposure."

Securing access without disrupting operations

Protecting refrigeration systems does not require eliminating remote connectivity. Instead, retailers need an approach that allows external technicians to perform essential maintenance while keeping access to operational equipment controlled and accountable.

Purpose-built OT secure remote access helps address this challenge by controlling connections at the individual asset level, rather than giving users broad access to operational networks.

Secomea's OT-native architecture enables secure connections to operational equipment through Edge Gateways located close to the assets themselves. Centralized access management, granular permissions, and audit logs help organizations govern who can connect, which equipment they can access, and when.

This approach is already being used in the retail refrigeration industry. In Denmark, refrigeration monitoring specialist AK-Centralen uses Secomea technology to support remote monitoring of cooling systems serving more than 1,500 supermarkets. Secure connectivity enables the company to maintain essential monitoring and service operations without requiring direct access to supermarket internal networks.

The example demonstrates that efficient remote maintenance and stronger cybersecurity controls can work together.

Operational resilience depends on visibility and control

The latest incidents raise questions that extend well beyond supermarket refrigeration. From building management and energy systems to production machinery and logistics infrastructure, organizations increasingly rely on connected operational equipment maintained by external specialists.

As these environments become more interconnected, organizations need consistent ways to manage third-party access, restrict permissions to the equipment users actually need, and maintain visibility into remote activities.

Secure remote access is one component of that protection, alongside vulnerability management, network segmentation, system updates, and continuous monitoring.

"Organizations shouldn't have to choose between keeping their operations running and keeping them secure," concludes Michael Ferdinandsen.

"The goal is to enable the remote support that modern operations depend on, while giving IT and security teams the governance and control they need. That's particularly important when the systems involved directly affect physical operations."

While the precise methods behind the latest suspected attacks remain under investigation, the incidents are another reminder that cybersecurity failures in operational environments can quickly become business continuity problems.

Secomea is a Danish industrial cybersecurity company specializing in secure remote access for operational technology (OT). Purpose-built for industrial environments, Secomea helps organizations securely connect to critical equipment while giving IT and security teams centralized governance, granular access control, and visibility into remote access.

By combining secure operational connectivity with enterprise security requirements, Secomea helps organizations strengthen operational resilience, reduce cyber risk, and maintain control over third-party access.

#5518. With Agentic Studio, LinearB provides the critical context needed to accelerate software delivery

Application development intelligence startup LinearB Inc. said today it’s trying to ease the growing congestion in organization’s software delivery pipelines that has arisen with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence coding tools.

It’s doing so with Agentic Studio, a new offering announced today that’s focused on providing more actionable context for human engineers and autonomous coding agents alike.

The startup says the emergence of generative AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex has led to new headaches for enterprise software development teams. Though writing software code now can be basically effortless, shipping that code into production is still as painful as it has always been, and now they have much more of it to ship.

In its recent Software Engineering Benchmarks report, the company analyzed more than 2.7 million pull requests across 250 organizations and found that those who rely on AI coding tools have almost doubled their merged code changes year-over-year. But the problem is that AI-assisted pull requests are nearly 2.6 times larger, and consequently they’re waiting more than five times longer to be reviewed.

That has led to significant backlogs. And it’s compounded by the fact that AI agent’s proposed code changes are merged just 79% of the time at “elite organizations,” compared with 92% for human-authored code.

LinearB says that human software engineers struggle to clear this backlog because the traditional dashboards they’re forced to work with only provide metrics, rather than the context needed to resolve those pull requests. With Agentic Studio, it’s trying to address this by normalizing the data and insights generated by Git repositories and project tracking tools into a unified context layer. It means that instead of muddling through various charts to try and understand why release velocity has stalled, software engineers can ask questions in plain language to understand the root cause and receive recommendations on how to speed things up.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Ori Keren said context has become the new king, not only for AI tools but also for humans. “We realized we hold a knowledge graph that nobody else has of everything that is happening across the software delivery lifecycle,” he said. “That’s exactly what agents and teams need to deliver high quality software faster, so we rebuilt LinearB around it.”

What’s different about Agentic Studio is that it’s designed to help autonomous coding agents just as much as human software engineers, Keren said. By integrating through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, it feeds historical context such as rework rates, past production incidents and code ownership to AI agents, preventing them from making blind modifications to pull requests.

Early adopters have benefited from dramatically increased productivity with Agentic Studio. A case in point is the cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, which used LinearB’s MCP integration to pinpoint why its code reviews were lagging. It discovered that timezone misalignments were the main culprit rather than pull request sizes, and subsequently reorganized its workflows to cut its review times by more than half within just four months.

“For years, engineering leaders told us the same thing: metrics are useful, but they don’t tell you what to do,” said LinearB’s chief operating officer Dan Lines. “A dashboard says your cycle time is two days, but so what? Now [with Agentic Studio] a leader can ask what to improve in their engineering organization and get a clear answer. When that same context goes to coding agents, the platform is not just reporting, it’s acting.”

To help AI agents operationalize the context it provides, LinearB is developing a bunch of new agent skills. The first one, an “effort skill,” is available in early access now and analyzes the complexity of a pull request and its proposed code changes, its rework history and risk to calibrate dynamically how much computational effort a coding agent needs to expend as it works on it.

Simple, low-risk changes are done faster with minimal tokens. More sensitive, high-priority modifications will be implemented with deeper reasoning and more exhaustive testing to ensure nothing goes wrong.

LinearB said it’s planning to expand its agent skills library in the coming months with additional skills focused on automated code review, merge governance and token cost optimization.

#5517. Bitwise Raises Bitcoin Price Target to $1.6 Million as Institutional Demand Grows

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin could reach $1.6 million by 2036, according to Bitwise latest forecast. The asset manager raised its target from $1.3 million despite Bitcoin’s difficult year. Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan said the updated model points to stronger long-term growth. The new Bitcoin price prediction reflects expanding institutional demand and a larger market for store-of-value assets.

Bitcoin is better positioned today than at any point in its past. We're boosting our 10-year bitcoin target from $1.3m to $1.6m. https://t.co/oQG2kKXbvo

Bitwise published its 2027 Bitcoin Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions on October 28. The report projects a 34.3% compound annual growth rate over the next decade. Last year’s model projected annualized returns of 28.3%.

The revised Bitcoin price prediction comes after Bitcoin fell more than 50% between October 2025 and June 2026. It subsequently recovered from lows below $59,000. Bitwise believes the latest downturn supports its argument that Bitcoin’s market structure is maturing.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitwise builds its Bitcoin price prediction around the market Bitcoin could capture over the next decade. Its model estimates that the global store-of-value market could reach $110 trillion by 2036. That compares with the previous estimate of $91 trillion.

The firm also expects the institutional investment market to expand from $216 trillion to $303 trillion. Its model assumes Bitcoin captures 25% of the store-of-value market. It also assumes institutions allocate between 1% and 5% of their portfolios to Bitcoin.

Those allocations could generate between $1.5 trillion and $7.4 trillion in institutional demand. Bitwise estimates that new Bitcoin issuance will contribute only around $14 billion annually. The growing gap between potential demand and new supply underpins its bullish outlook.

Still bullish, Bitwise bear-case scenario puts Bitcoin at $130,686 by 2036. Its bull case reaches nearly $3.67 million, illustrating the enormous range of possible outcomes.

Institutional adoption is only one part of Bitcoin’s long-term story. The network’s limited supply makes it attractive to investors seeking alternatives to traditional stores of value. However, expanding Bitcoin’s practical uses could also strengthen demand beyond simply holding BTC.

That has created opportunities for projects developing additional functionality around Bitcoin. Layer-2 networks aim to support faster transactions, lower costs, and applications that would otherwise be difficult to run directly on Bitcoin’s base layer.

When your golf swing is Hyper Powered. ⚡️🔥https://t.co/VNG0P4FWNQ pic.twitter.com/FelpOqk99g

Bitcoin Hyper is one project pursuing that direction. Its proposed Layer-2 network combines Bitcoin-focused functionality with Solana Virtual Machine architecture. The goal is to support faster BTC transactions alongside decentralized finance applications and other on-chain activity.

The project has also raised more than $33 million through its token presale. It offers staking rewards of up to 35% APY, while its wallet has entered testnet testing. The team has announced November 26, 2026, as the planned token launch date, so just less than a month to make the most of it.

If Bitcoin reaches Bitwise’s $1.6 million target by 2036, Bitcoin Hyper could ride one of the biggest waves of capital inflows in crypto history. As BTC becomes an increasingly valuable institutional asset, demand for faster transactions, low-cost transfers, and Bitcoin-powered DeFi could accelerate.
