#5516. Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:50 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:02 pm

Update, 10/28: Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations. Read the full story.

Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.

Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance. Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.

In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.

A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.

Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.

The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10%, because investors had privately expected more.

“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees, after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote.

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30, before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September. The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).

Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported, lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.

What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.

Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

#5515. Exclusive: Guardz brings Palo Alto Networks browser protection to MSPs serving small businesses

Cybersecurity startup Guardz Cyber Ltd. today added browser protection from Palo Alto Networks Inc.’s Prisma Browser for Business to its security platform for managed service providers that protect small businesses.

The integration is aimed at phishing attacks that slip between separate security tools. A typical one starts with an email that lures an employee to a counterfeit login page, and the credentials typed there can put connected accounts at risk. “For most small businesses, the browser is now the office,” said Shivam Srivastava, vice president of product at Palo Alto Networks.

Prisma Browser for Business can block the page when the link is clicked. Guardz then matches that browser event to the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity and endpoint telemetry for the same user identity. From there, the provider and Guardz’s 24/7 managed detection and response team can work the whole chain as a single incident.

The browser-side detection comes from Palo Alto Networks. Inline machine-learning models screen pages for phishing, and Advanced URL Filtering helps block malicious sites, including fake sign-in pages and attacks built to steal live session tokens. The company’s WildFire service analyzes suspect files. Uploads and downloads are scanned as they pass through the browser, which also picks out risky extensions.

Guardz Co-founder and Chief Executive Dor Eisner called the browser “the primary gateway to the modern workspace.” Traditional security tools work in silos that leave gaps in visibility and response, he said, and the agents running on Guardz’s platform are meant to let providers investigate threats autonomously anywhere in that workspace.

Setup falls to Guardz, which handles provisioning and default configuration. Kevin Kehoe of early-access provider Datawise Networks Inc. said the rollout through his firm’s remote monitoring and management software was “super smooth.” Within minutes, he said, the browser extension was “on every Chrome and Edge profile.”

For generative artificial intelligence services used in the browser, Guardz’s AI Usage and Control features let technicians set a separate policy for each client. Those policies can restrict copying, pasting and file transfers by website or by category. Guardz has also introduced a report that gives providers a per-client view of AI tool usage.

Palo Alto Networks moved into enterprise browsers with its 2023 acquisition of Israeli startup Talon Cyber Security Ltd. Prisma Browser for Business, its version for small businesses, went on sale in the U.S. in March.

Guardz is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $84 million, including a $56 million Series B round led by ClearSky in June 2025.

#5514. The 20 most venomous snakes in the world, ranked

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Meet 20 deadly snakes, from Australia's inland taipan to Africa's puff adder, and learn where they live and what their venom does.

A farmer clearing brush, a hiker stepping over a fallen log, and a child reaching under a porch all share ground with snakes. Every step into tall grass or leaf litter carries a small gamble. Knowing which species pose a real threat shapes where people put their hands and feet. The same knowledge decides how fast they seek help after a bite. Earth holds more than 3,000 snake species, and few corners of the planet escape them. Antarctica, Iceland, Ireland, and Greenland offer cold refuges where a person faces little risk from the most dangerous kinds. New Zealand joins that short roster, a detail that catches many people off guard. Everywhere else, the identity of the snake under the woodpile carries practical consequences.

Venom turns out to be the exception among snakes. About 15 percent of species, some 450 in all, carry it. About a third of that group, around 150 species, can kill a person or inflict serious injury with a single bite. Roughly one in 20 snake species, then, can do such harm. The other 300 or so venomous species fall short of that mark. Some venoms carry no lethal punch, and some venomous snakes, such as the eastern diamondback rattlesnake, pose less risk than the species profiled here. Venom is not the only route to a fatal encounter. Pythons kill by constricting their prey, with no toxin involved. Sorting the harmless from the lethal starts with learning names, ranges, and what a bite can do to the body.

The entries ahead come from HowStuffWorks, which published "The Most Venomous Snake in the World and 19 Deadly Others" as a guide to 20 dangerous snakes. Sharise Cunningham and Mack Hayden wrote the piece, and the site updated it Oct. 2, 2024. AI technology assisted with that revision, after which an editor at the site fact-checked and edited the text. The authors call their roundup a modest introduction to the subject, not an exhaustive catalog. Their article lays out no scoring system, toxicity measurements, or ranking criteria. This article keeps the original numbering, and readers should not take the order as a measure of venom strength. Each profile covers where a species lives, how it behaves around people, and what its venom does to a victim.

One bite from the inland taipan (Oxyuranus microlepidotus) delivers enough venom to kill as many as 100 people. Scientists regard this Australian species as the world's most venomous snake, and the potency of its venom may make it the deadliest as well. Herpetologists have singled out the inland taipan because its venom showed the highest toxicity in tests against mice, according to ABC News. Its venom also contains hyaluronidase, an enzyme that helps toxins spread through a victim's body and hastens death.

Clay crevices on floodplains in Queensland and South Australia hide the snake, and it seldom crosses paths with people there. Its range stops at a single part of South Australia plus the far west of Queensland. The snake lives and hunts among dry cracks in the clay, across some of the harshest terrain on Earth. Inland taipans come from remote corners of Australia. Isolation shapes the danger this snake poses. A venom of this strength reaches a human bloodstream only on the uncommon occasions when someone enters the floodplains where the snake shelters.

Stephen Mahony, a reptile specialist at the Australian Museum, said the inland taipan does not count as threatened. He pointed to healthy numbers across its habitat and the absence of pressures on the population. The same distance from human activity that protects people appears to leave the snake undisturbed.

A tight S-shaped coil signals an imminent strike. The snake draws its body into that posture an instant before it lunges, which gives anyone who stumbles on one a brief cue to back away. Color offers a weaker clue. Individual inland taipans range from beige and gray to light or dark brown. A person who spots one cannot count on a single shade to identify the species, and the coil carries more meaning than the hue.

Few people ever face the planet's most potent venom, because the snake that carries it thrives in country beyond their usual routes.

The saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus) has earned a name as the snake behind more bite deaths in India than any other species. Its place on this list rests on that human toll. Its venom falls short of the world's most potent, which makes the death count the true measure of its threat.

The saw-scaled viper is the smallest member of India's "big four," a group it shares with Russell's viper, the common krait (Bungarus caeruleus), and the Indian cobra (Naja naja). Its modest frame offers no shield to anyone it bites. The list's authors hold that the viper is thought to cause more bite deaths in India than its three larger companions, framing the claim as a belief and stopping short of a firm count. Even on that hedged footing, a snake this small stands among the country's most feared, a sign that body size reveals little about the danger a snake poses to people.

A distinctive sizzle gives the viper away before it lunges. The snake makes the sound by rubbing its serrated scales together in a sawing motion, and the result differs from a hiss. Anyone who recognizes the grating noise gains a moment to back away before the strike lands. Learning to identify this one sound gives people near the snake a practical safeguard.

Internal bleeding can follow a single bite, and the damage can progress to acute kidney failure. The snake also counts as highly venomous in Sri Lanka. Bites there bring pain and swelling at the wound, abnormal blood clotting, and kidney dysfunction. Reports of thrombotic microangiopathy after its bite remain uncommon.

Kidney damage runs through both descriptions of the bite, marking those organs as a recurring target of this venom. Pain and swelling mark the wound at once, while the bleeding and clotting trouble unfold inside the body, out of a victim's sight. Kidney failure comes last in that sequence, after the bleeding has begun. The visible signs at the wound understate what the venom has set in motion. A bite that looks minor at first can still end in organ failure.

The coastal taipan (Oxyuranus scutellatus) wields venom that differs little from the toxin of its inland cousin. The list judges the coastal species the greater danger, and geography drives that verdict. Its habitat lies within easy reach of people who have no idea a taipan might be close. The inland taipan, by contrast, keeps to places where it meets few people.

Harm to people depends on both potency and proximity, and the coastal taipan supplies both. Its inland relative holds the title of the world's most venomous snake, and the coastal species carries a close match of that toxin into ground that unsuspecting people can enter. A potent venom sealed away in remote country injures few people. The same chemistry on accessible ground threatens far more of them. Matching venoms, then, carry unequal odds of finding a human victim.

A published case report describes one man in northern New South Wales who learned what a taipan bite can do once it lands. Severe neurotoxicity set in, and doctors had to intubate him and put him on a ventilator so he could keep breathing. The venom drained his blood of clotting factors and attacked his muscle tissue. He developed thrombotic microangiopathy with acute kidney injury, and the kidney damage left him needing dialysis.

The man's care team began with brown and tiger snake antivenom, a choice that followed guidelines and matched the snakes that occur in the region. Doctors build their opening treatment around the species they expect to find in a given part of the country. The case traces a single taipan bite through the nerves, blood, muscles, and kidneys of one patient. Damage across four body systems, delivered by a snake that lives close to people, gives weight to the list's view that the coastal taipan poses the greater threat.

A black mamba can move at up to 12 miles per hour (19 km/h), enough to put it among the fastest snakes on land. The species takes its name from the black interior of its mouth. The color that defines it stays hidden until the jaws part. Its territory spans southern and eastern Sub-Saharan Africa, where savannas, hill country, and forests all serve as habitat. A range covering three distinct landscapes means the snake can turn up in open grassland or under a forest canopy. People across a broad stretch of the continent, on plains and in wooded uplands alike, can cross its path.

A warning hiss precedes an attack and gives an intruder a chance to back away. Anyone who ignores the sound faces a barrage of strikes in rapid succession. The snake's pace on the ground pairs with quickness in the attack, letting it close distance and land several bites in a short span. Its behavior follows a sequence, signal first and assault second, which hands much of the outcome to whoever stands within earshot.

Two drops of the mamba's venom can bring on paralysis and cardiac arrest. A dose so small leaves little margin for error. Each extra bite in a series adds to the toxin delivered, and a volley magnifies the danger of so potent a toxin. The hiss marks the clearest moment to avoid harm, before any fang reaches skin.

Clinical research shows that black mamba envenoming targets the nervous system above all. Early symptoms can include unusual skin sensations, trouble speaking or swallowing, and a drooping upper eyelid. Speech, swallowing, and eyelid movement all depend on nerves that command small muscles. Trouble with any of them can signal that the paralysis the venom produces has begun to take hold. A bitten person who notices those changes has a reason to reach medical care without delay.

The banded krait (Bungarus fasciatus) saves its danger for the night, when it leaves cover to hunt, and one bite can shut down the muscles a person needs to breathe. Its venom paralyzes muscle tissue and locks the diaphragm in place. A victim who cannot move that sheet of muscle suffocates. The venom, in other words, strikes at breathing itself, a function no person can pause for long. Kinship with the cobra explains the potency of the toxin.

Size distinguishes the species from most of its relatives. A banded krait can reach 6.9 feet (2.1 meters), a length that puts it among the largest kraits. Black and yellow bands of near-equal width wrap its body. An inverted V on the head gives observers a second mark for identifying the snake. Both marks help in daylight. Once the krait sets out at dusk, a person has little chance to read them.

Shyness shapes how the krait responds to people. A disturbed banded krait tends to hold back its bite. The snake forages after sundown, and its gravest threat falls in those same hours. The animal that restrains itself under provocation becomes a serious hazard to anyone who crosses its path in the dark. The contrast carries a practical lesson. Daytime calm offers no guide to how this snake behaves once light fades, and anyone walking through krait country in those hours meets the creature at its most menacing.

The species occupies a wide swath of Asia, reaching from the mainland out to the islands. Its range covers southern China, the Malay Peninsula, the Indonesian archipelago, and the Indo-Chinese subregion. Across that spread, the peril follows the clock more than the map. A person anywhere in the snake's territory faces the same pattern, a quiet reptile by day and a roaming predator once evening comes.

The king cobra grows up to 18 feet (5.4 meters) long, which makes it the longest venomous snake in the world. Its eyesight matches its size as a weapon. The snake can pick out prey from nearly 330 feet (100 meters) away.

Other snakes form the core of what the king cobra hunts. The species feeds on cold-blooded animals above all, and some individuals settle on one snake species and refuse every other kind. Its menu can include venomous Indian cobras and small members of its own species. A diet of fellow serpents, some of them armed with venom of their own, sets the king cobra apart as a hunter of dangerous prey.

King cobras occupy a broad swath of southern and southeast Asia. Their range opens in northern India, extends to southern China, crosses the Malay Peninsula, and reaches western Indonesia and the Philippines. Within that territory, the snakes gravitate to waterways in dense or thin forest, bamboo groves, nearby farmland, and thick mangrove swamps. Such a spread of settings shows an animal at home in many landscapes.

Long fangs and a striking appearance help earn the king cobra a reputation for aggression. Confronting a predator, it spreads a hood around its head to look bigger. In a full threat display, the snake rears its head, puffs up, and hisses. Nesting females raise the stakes. A mother builds a nest of leaves, lays her eggs, buries them under more leaves, and rests on top until they hatch. Guarding females attack without provocation more often than other king cobras.

The king cobra's venom, loaded with cytotoxins and neurotoxins, makes the hood more bluster than necessity. A single bite can kill a human within 15 minutes and bring down an adult elephant in a few hours. Venom that works this fast leaves a bitten person little time to reach treatment.

The boomslang (Dispholidus typus) carries venom toxic enough to make its victims bleed out, and it keeps to the trees across a core range of Eswatini, Botswana, Namibia, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe. Its playful name masks a serious threat.

Aggression plays little part in the boomslang's temperament. Faced with a predator, the snake inflates its neck to look bigger and more menacing. A threatened boomslang tries to frighten off trouble before it resorts to a bite. Bites from the species are uncommon in South Africa, a pattern that fits a snake so slow to pick a fight.

Stealth and camouflage shape its hunting. The boomslang waits among the branches for a meal to pass, blending into the foliage until the moment it strikes. Its venom kills prey with ease. A snake that shies from confrontation turns into a patient, efficient killer once something edible draws close. The same camouflage that fools the animals it stalks can hide the snake from a person passing beneath.

Blood bears the brunt of the venom's damage. The toxin triggers clotting factors II and X $TWTR, and may trigger factor IX, using up the body's supply, according to PubMed. With those factors spent, blood loses its ability to clot.

South African Vaccine Producers makes a single-species boomslang antivenom that works well for patients who show the venom's blood-related effects, according to PubMed.

Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) causes high mortality among paddy farmers, hiding in the rice fields where they earn their living. India counts the snake among its "big four," and its range stretches into Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka. Its reputation places it among the deadliest true vipers.

The danger here grows out of farm work itself. Farmers must enter the plots to raise their rice, and the viper uses those same plots as cover. Each round of planting and tending brings growers within striking distance of an animal hidden from view. Their income depends on working that ground. Staying clear of the snake would mean giving up the harvest. The pattern repeats across national borders wherever the viper and the paddies overlap.

A bite from this viper reaches the blood, the kidneys, and the nerves. A study of snakebite patients in Sri Lanka documented swelling at the bite site, clotting abnormalities, kidney impairment, and paralysis affecting nerves and muscles. One envenoming can strike several body systems at once. A single patient may need care for clotting trouble, kidney damage, and paralysis during one course of treatment.

Populations of the snake in South India and Sri Lanka produce a distinctive form of nerve and muscle paralysis, one that Russell's vipers in other regions do not trigger. Researchers single out Russell's viper as the Asian snake of greatest medical significance, pointing to the number of envenomings and deaths it causes. Treatment lags in Sri Lanka, where the polyvalent antivenom supplied from India has limited effectiveness against the viper's bites. The venom, in other words, does not act the same everywhere the snake lives. Care built around one population's bite may miss what another population's venom does. A grower bitten in a Sri Lankan paddy confronts a regional venom effect and an antivenom with limited reach at the same moment.

The eastern brown snake (Pseudonaja textilis) kills more people than any other snake in Australia, and it builds that toll without carrying the world's most potent venom. Its record shows that a snake need not hold the strongest toxin to cause the most human deaths. The profile of this species centers on where it lives and what its venom does once a bite lands.

Open spaces suit this snake. Its range sweeps across eastern and central Australia and reaches north into southern New Guinea. The species occupies two landmasses, covering much of the Australian mainland and the southern part of the island to its north.

Four classes of toxins give the venom several routes to harm a victim. The bite can feel painless, and a person who notices little at the moment of contact may underestimate the danger. Paralysis spreads in stages once the toxins take hold, and the venom can trigger bleeding in the brain. A single bite carries enough force to paralyze a human or other prey.

Paralysis and brain bleeding put two separate targets in play, the nerves that move muscles and the blood vessels inside the skull. A victim can lose muscle control while bleeding inside the head, with no sharp pain to raise the alarm.

Clinical researchers have documented a clotting disorder in which the venom strips fibrinogen from the blood. The same work ties envenoming to kidney failure and to a form of anemia in which red blood cells break apart inside small vessels. The damage travels through the bloodstream to the kidneys, far from the wound where it began.

An untreated bite from the eastern tiger snake (Notechis scutatus) can kill a human. The warning hinges on one condition. The danger turns fatal in bites that go without care, which puts medical treatment at the center of any encounter with this species.

Southeast Australia's mountains and grasslands make up the snake's native range. Highland country and open grass country differ in elevation and cover, yet the snake claims both as home ground. A hiker on a ridge and a farmer in a pasture can each cross paths with it. Its reach across two such unlike settings suggests a reptile that copes with more than one kind of terrain.

Protein analysis of tiger snake venom lined up with the harm bite victims suffer. The documented effects include presynaptic neurotoxicity, postsynaptic neurotoxicity, and consumptive coagulopathy. The first two disrupt nerve signals on both sides of the gap where those signals pass between cells. The third drains the blood's supply of clotting factors. One strike can confront a victim with two separate threats, one aimed at the nervous system and one at the blood.

Juvenile and adult tiger snakes carry venoms that differ little in makeup. Electrophoretic studies detected minor differences in protein composition between young and grown snakes, and nothing larger. A small tiger snake offers no distinct chemical profile to set it apart from a large one. The findings address what the venom contains, and they leave open how much a young snake can inject.

The death adder (Acanthophis antarcticus) stands among Australia's most venomous snakes, and its bite can trigger paralysis that leads to respiratory failure and death without prompt treatment. A lightning-fast strike delivers the venom, a cocktail of neurotoxins. Speed matters to a snake that hunts by ambush.

Patience defines its method. Many snakes flee a threat, yet the death adder holds its ground, tucked out of sight in leaf litter. It lies still until prey wanders within reach and lunges. Reporting from Magnetic Island describes a short, thick-bodied snake with brown bands and a triangular head that waits beneath leafy cover. A researcher there said the adder can twitch the tip of its tail so it looks like a grub among fallen leaves, a lure that draws prey closer. The trick lets the adder bring meals to its hiding spot without giving up its cover. An analysis of droppings from the island showed that skinks make up most of the local diet.

Its venom zeroes in on the junction where nerve meets muscle. Researchers believe the toxins act on the muscle side of that connection and produce severe limp paralysis. Fatal cases end when breathing fails.

Delay makes a serious bite harder to reverse. Nerve-related symptoms resist death adder antivenom and anticholinesterase drugs in many cases, and the resistance stiffens in patients who reach care paralyzed. Medicine works best before the toxins finish shutting down muscle control.

Most documented bites stop short of that outcome. A review of confirmed death adder cases in the Australian Snakebite Project found that nerve toxicity dominated and stayed mild in most patients. None of those patients developed venom-induced consumption coagulopathy. A venom capable of killing a person, in other words, leaves the typical confirmed victim with modest symptoms. With no clotting collapse in the picture, a bite's outcome rests on paralysis and on how fast treatment arrives.

The fer-de-lance (Bothrops asper) causes most of the snake bites within its home range. The species also carries a reputation for an aggressive temperament.

Frequency and temper reinforce each other in this snake's profile. Anyone bitten by a snake within its territory has most likely met a fer-de-lance. An aggressive animal leaves people little chance to retreat before it strikes, a trait consistent with its outsized share of local bites.

Destroyed tissue defines the local harm from a bite. The venom's potency lets it wipe out large amounts of flesh around the wound, and the damage can progress to necrosis.

Hemotoxins in the venom interfere with the blood's ability to clot. Researchers who injected mice with Bothrops asper venom, which also goes by the name terciopelo, saw it ravage the animals' capillaries within a short span. Blood escaped through the ruptured vessel walls. The researchers traced the red blood cells' probable exit to gaps in injured lining cells.

A fer-de-lance bite attacks a victim on two fronts, eating away flesh at the wound while weakening the blood's defense against bleeding.

The Gaboon viper grows fangs up to 2 inches (5 centimeters) long, the longest of any snake. Its bite also injects more venom than any other species can deliver. One animal holds both distinctions, pairing record-length fangs with the heaviest toxic payload.

The venom blends hemotoxins that can bring on swelling, intense pain, and tissue damage soon after a strike. A victim of this species absorbs an outsized volume of those blood-targeting compounds from a single bite. The harm surfaces fast, at the wound and in the flesh around it.

Rainforests and savannas across sub-Saharan Africa make up the viper's home ground. Its range spans dense forest and open grassland alike. The snake does not confine itself to one kind of terrain. Anyone moving through either landscape can cross its path.

Temperament cuts against the viper's arsenal. The snake behaves with surprising docility and seldom strikes at people. Camouflage serves as its main defense, and it counts on blending into its surroundings to escape notice. The species with the most formidable fangs and the largest venom yield prefers to stay still and unseen.

The greatest danger falls on the person who steps near a Gaboon viper without spotting it. A snake this placid holds its venom in reserve until contact forces the issue. The disguise that keeps it out of trouble also hides it from anyone about to blunder into it.

The tiger rattlesnake (Crotalus tigris) carries one of the most toxic venoms among rattlesnake species, and neurotoxins dominate its chemistry. The snake itself stays modest in size. Its compact frame gives little hint of the danger it holds, and a person who judges risk by bulk would misread this animal.

Nerve-targeting compounds drive the harm a bite inflicts. A strike can paralyze muscles, and a victim who reaches medical care late faces respiratory failure that can prove fatal. The clock decides the outcome. Swift care separates a survivable encounter from a lethal one.

Temperament holds the toll down. The list's authors credit the snake's shyness and its habit of steering clear of people as the only reasons it does not cause more deaths. The claim cuts two ways. It credits the animal's restraint, and it implies the venom on its own could support a higher toll. A rattlesnake this potent owes the lives it spares to behavior. An encounter that overrides its urge to avoid people strips away the one safeguard the authors name.

The Philippine cobra (Naja philippinensis) spits its venom with deadly accuracy, and without treatment its bite can kill within 30 minutes. The spray lets this snake injure a person it never touches. It also stretches the cobra's reach past the length of its strike. Aim gives that reach its force. A precise spit turns distance into an attack.

Neurotoxins make up most of the venom, and they target the respiratory system. A victim's breathing can fail as those toxins take hold. Thirty minutes leaves little room for travel. The distance between a bite and medical care can decide whether a victim survives. Every minute spent finding a ride or reaching a clinic eats into a margin that starts small.

Sprayed venom brings a separate hazard. This species' venom keeps its potency outside the bloodstream, a trait many cobras lack. The fangs and the spit both threaten anyone nearby. A person who avoids the fangs can still face exposure from a distance. Stepping back offers less protection from this cobra than from a snake that must strike to do harm.

An encounter with this cobra carries two ways to go wrong. A snake that depends on its bite threatens what sits within striking range and nothing more. The Philippine cobra adds everyone in the path of its spray, and its venom loses none of its strength once it leaves the snake's body. Distance, the usual buffer against a snake, counts for less here. Anyone who meets this cobra has to treat the whole space within its spray as the danger zone.

The western brown snake (Pseudonaja nuchalis), also known as the gwardar, can strike a person several times in quick succession. This highly venomous Australian native moves fast. Its speed lets it land one bite after another, and each extra strike gives the snake another chance to deliver venom.

The gwardar's venom falls short of the inland taipan's in potency. Even so, it remains extremely dangerous to anyone bitten. A place below the world's most venomous snake does not make this species safe to approach, and a toxin that ranks as weaker on paper can prove deadly in a real encounter.

The gwardar shares its genus, Pseudonaja, with the eastern brown snake (Pseudonaja textilis), the ninth entry on this list. Two members of one genus among 20 deadly snakes show that Australia's lethal species reach beyond its taipans.

The many-banded krait (Bungarus multicinctus) reaches its peak activity at night, and it often turns up in residential areas.

Nocturnal habits and a presence in settled neighborhoods put this krait close to homes during the hours it moves the most. Ordinary evening routines around a house become the likeliest moments for a person to cross its path. Darkness also strips away the chance to spot the snake before stepping near it.

Shyness defines the krait's temperament. The snake steers clear of confrontations with humans and shows no appetite for a fight. Its reclusive nature offers residents little protection, because the animal keeps appearing where they live during the hours they can least see it. The real hazard lies in accidental meetings after sunset.

The green mamba (Dendroaspis angusticeps) wears a coat that vanishes against the leaves around it, and the match makes the snake hard to spot.

Coastal regions of southern East Africa make up its home range. Its scientific name places it in the genus Dendroaspis with the black mamba (Dendroaspis polylepis), the mamba profiled earlier in this list. The green species keeps to a coastal band, a smaller footprint than its relative's spread across several kinds of terrain. The two snakes share a genus and a continent, but they occupy different parts of the African landscape.

Camouflage defines the hazard this species presents. People struggle to notice an animal that matches the surrounding foliage. A person can wander close to one without any warning. Anyone pushing through leafy coastal growth in this corner of Africa shares ground with a creature whose color keeps it out of view.

The Mojave rattlesnake (Crotalus scutulatus) carries a reputation as the most dangerous rattlesnake in the U.S., and the unusual makeup of its venom explains the label. Its bite delivers both neurotoxins and hemotoxins. Two distinct classes of toxin arrive in a single strike, a pairing that compounds its lethal potential.

The snake's temperament pulls against its chemistry. The species shows little appetite for confrontation, and it tends to shake its distinctive rattle as a warning before it lunges.

The rattle hands anyone who stumbles across this snake a chance to escape harm. A warning buys an intruder time to back away before any contact. Whether people heed the sound decides how much peril they face.

The puff adder (Bitis arietans) causes more snake bite deaths in Africa than any other species on the continent. Its range sprawls across much of Africa. A territory that broad puts the snake within reach of far more people than a species confined to a single region would encounter.

Sluggish habits turn the puff adder into a hidden hazard. The snake has a reputation for slow movement, and unsuspecting people step on it before they notice it lying in their path. Many snakes retreat from a threat. A snake that lies still on a trail gives a passerby little chance to spot it and steer clear.

Repeated strikes raise the stakes of each encounter. The puff adder tends to bite several times in rapid succession, and its venom carries high toxicity. A person who treads on one can absorb several doses before pulling away. Without treatment, a bite can kill.

Africa's grimmest snake bite record grows out of everyday walks across a vast range. Fast medical care separates a survivable bite from a fatal one.

#5513. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 2:15 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

— Lattice Semiconductor, a Hillsboro, Ore.-based company, has added two directors to its board:

#5512. MazeBolt launches native RADAR deployment for Akamai DDoS protection customers

Distributed denial-of-service testing company MazeBolt Technologies Ltd. today launched a native deployment of its RADAR validation platform for customers of Akamai Technologies Inc.

Enterprises using Akamai’s DDoS protection can have continuous testing running within hours without taking services offline. The release targets the configuration gaps that open up as a company adds services, application programming interfaces and regions behind its DDoS protection.

Akamai setups are rarely tested independently against each of those changes, according to MazeBolt, and a gap can stay hidden until an attack reaches a login page or a payment flow. Founder and Chief Executive Matthew Andriani said testing “even a few times a year cannot keep pace” now that artificial intelligence projects keep adding new services and APIs.

Akamai’s own State of the Internet report, published in March, found that Layer 7 DDoS attacks rose 104% over two years, and the company blamed part of that growth on attack tools that use AI to make web applications and APIs easier to hit.

RADAR fires simulated attacks at Akamai-protected services from inside the customer’s own environment. The attack library covers known vectors as well as the AI-orchestrated and AI-generated attacks MazeBolt added with its VectorAI module in June. When RADAR first tests a production environment, about 37% of attack vectors get past the protection already in place, based on MazeBolt’s data from initial deployments.

Each run ends in a report with remediation guidance written for the specific protection vendor, and RADAR repeats the test once a fix is in place. “Deployed protection is not proven protection,” said Eyal Rahimi, vice president of engineering at MazeBolt. Customers also need to be able to prove which gaps they have closed, Rahimi said.

Most financial institutions test far less often. In a MazeBolt survey of 300 of their security leaders last year, 86% said they test their DDoS defenses once a year or less. Akamai reported in May that the median duration of Layers 3 and 4 DDoS attacks on the sector has risen 738% since 2024.

John Grady, chief analyst at Omdia, said misconfigurations and out-of-date rules remain the source of many security incidents. “DDoS is no different,” Grady said. “It is a critical area where security teams must ensure protection is current, because successful attacks impact availability and directly affect the bottom line.”

Native Layer 7 support for Akamai environments is available today to all RADAR customers. Cloudflare Inc., F5 Inc. and Radware Ltd. are among the other mitigation vendors whose products RADAR already tests across scrubbing centers, on-premises equipment and cloud services.
