#5511. Marathon recovery: 15 steps for fueling, sleep, soreness and your return to running

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Knowing how to recover after a marathon starts at the finish line, and these 15 tips cover fueling, sleep, soreness, warning signs and the return to running

A marathon does not end at the finish line. The 26.2 miles (42.195 km) leave a body short on fuel, fluids and salt, with muscle fibers damaged by hours of repeated impact. What a runner does next shapes how quickly normal training can resume. It also shapes how much discomfort comes along the way, from the first hour to the first night and through the weeks that follow.

Recovery is easy to treat as an afterthought. Training plans map out months of long runs, tempo sessions and taper weeks, then stop on race day. The days after the race get far less planning, even though the body is still working hard to repair itself. Soreness often gets worse before it gets better. Sleep can be restless. Appetite may disappear and then return with force. Feet may carry blisters and bruised toenails. For some runners, the end of a long training block also brings an emotional low.

Knowing how to recover after a marathon means handling each of those pieces in order rather than all at once. The early priorities are simple: keep moving gently, replace lost fluids and sodium, and eat carbohydrate and protein. Over the following days, the focus shifts to regular meals, extra sleep and light movement that keeps blood flowing without pounding the legs.

Several popular recovery habits have limits. Massage, foam rolling, ice baths and compression gear are common sights after big races. The evidence behind them is mixed and modest. Any benefit is mostly limited to how sore a runner feels, which makes them optional comfort measures rather than requirements. Over-the-counter painkillers carry their own cautions for runners who finished dehydrated. A short list of symptoms — from chest pain to very dark urine — means a runner should stop managing recovery at home and seek medical care.

The 15 tips below follow that timeline. They start at the finish area and move through fueling, sleep, soreness and the tools runners often reach for. Then they cover medical red flags and the return to running, along with the restlessness that can follow a finished goal. They are a selection of practical steps rather than a rigid protocol. The right pace for coming back varies from one runner to the next. The common thread is patience: the work done in the days after a marathon protects the fitness built over the months before it.

Keep walking after you cross the finish line of a marathon. A slow, steady walk lets heart rate and breathing come down gradually. It also lowers the chance of the dizziness or lightheadedness that can follow an abrupt stop at the end of a long race.

The reason lies in how blood moves during running. With every stride, contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins in the calves and thighs. That squeezing helps push blood back toward the heart, a mechanism often called the muscle pump. Stop dead, and the pumping action stops with it. Blood can pool in the lower legs, less of it returns to the heart, and blood pressure can dip. For some runners, the result is a woozy, faint feeling a few steps past the line.

Large marathons are set up with this in mind. Finishers are typically routed through a long chute rather than left to halt at the timing mat. Runners collect a medal, water, snacks and a thermal blanket while moving forward. Keep walking through that stretch instead of sitting down on the nearest curb.

Pace matters less than continuity. A relaxed stroll is enough. The aim is to keep the legs moving while the heart and lungs shift out of race mode. Walking also gives stiff hips, knees and ankles a gentler transition than going straight from running to sitting.

Body temperature is the other concern in that first hour. A runner produces heat steadily during a race, but that heat production falls quickly once running stops. Sweat-soaked clothing then pulls warmth away from the skin. The chill comes on faster on a cool, windy or wet day. Wrap up in the foil-style blanket handed out at the finish. Change into dry layers from a gear-check bag as soon as practical.

The walk is also a good time to handle small logistics. Head toward the bag check and make your way to the family meeting point without rushing. If you need to stop, lie down with the legs raised rather than standing still for a long stretch.

Organized marathons typically staff medical tents in the finish area. A runner who stays dizzy, cannot walk steadily or feels faint despite moving slowly should go there or flag down a volunteer. Waiting it out alone is the riskier choice.

After a marathon, replace both the fluid and the salt lost in sweat. A sports drink, an oral rehydration solution or water paired with salty food does that job better than large volumes of plain water on their own.

Sweat is not pure water. It carries sodium, along with smaller amounts of potassium and other electrolytes. Over the course of a marathon, a runner can lose a meaningful amount of both. Those losses vary widely from one person to the next. Some runners finish with white, gritty streaks on their shirt, cap or face. That residue is dried salt, and it is a visible sign of heavy sodium loss.

Plain water replaces volume but not sodium. When a runner drinks a lot of it after a race, the sodium left in the blood becomes more diluted. If that sodium level falls too low, the condition is called hyponatremia, meaning low blood sodium. It is a recognized risk in marathons and other endurance events. It can develop on the course or in the hours after the finish. Runners who drank heavily during the race face a higher risk.

Mild hyponatremia can look like ordinary post-race fatigue. Early symptoms can include nausea, headache, bloating and puffy hands or fingers. More severe cases can bring confusion, vomiting, seizures or loss of consciousness. The danger comes from water moving into brain cells, which makes the brain swell. A runner with any of those severe symptoms needs emergency medical care. Drinking more water to wash out the feeling can make the problem worse.

The safer approach is to drink steadily rather than forcefully. Sip according to thirst at the finish and through the rest of the day. Choose fluids that contain electrolytes, such as a sports drink or an oral rehydration solution sold in pharmacies. Salty food adds sodium alongside the fluid. Pretzels, salted crackers, broth and salted potatoes all fit the purpose.

The post-race beer is a tradition at many marathons, but it does not count as rehydration. Alcohol increases urine output, which works against the goal of restoring fluid. Runners who want a drink can have water or an electrolyte drink first and keep alcohol modest.

Urine offers a simple check. Pale yellow urine generally indicates that hydration is returning to normal. A runner who has been drinking but still cannot urinate for many hours after finishing should contact a doctor rather than keep drinking.

A post-marathon snack or meal eaten soon after crossing the finish line should combine carbohydrate and protein. Carbohydrate starts refilling the muscle glycogen the race used up. Protein supplies the amino acids muscles need to begin repairing.

Glycogen is the stored form of carbohydrate that muscles draw on for fuel. Over the full marathon distance, a runner burns through a large share of those reserves. That depletion is part of why many runners slow sharply in the later miles. Runners often call that point hitting the wall. Eating carbohydrate after the finish gives the body the raw material to start rebuilding that store.

Protein does a different job. Hours of racing leave small-scale wear in the working leg muscles. Amino acids, the building blocks of protein, are what the body uses to repair that tissue. Pairing the two nutrients covers both needs in a single sitting.

Practical options are easy to find. Many finish areas hand out bananas, bagels, pretzels and chocolate milk. Chocolate milk is a common runner choice because it contains both carbohydrate and protein. It also goes down easily as a drink. Once home, a turkey or peanut butter sandwich fits the same pattern. So does Greek yogurt with fruit, or a bowl of rice with eggs or chicken.

Appetite is often low at first. Some runners feel queasy or simply uninterested in food for a while after a hard effort. In that case, smoothies or flavored milk can be easier to tolerate than a full plate. Small, frequent bites are another approach until hunger returns.

Familiar foods are the safer choice. A stomach that has just handled hours of running may react badly to rich, greasy or heavily spiced dishes. Simple foods a runner already ate during training tend to sit better.

The celebratory dinner can still happen. A first snack built around carbohydrate and protein does not rule out a bigger meal later in the day. It means the body gets something useful to work with right after the race. The alternative is waiting until evening for its first real fuel.

Recovery nutrition does not end with the first meal after the race. Rebuilding glycogen stores and repairing muscle take days rather than hours. Steady, balanced meals across the following week give the body the raw material it needs.

During a marathon, the legs draw heavily on glycogen. This is the form of carbohydrate stored in muscle and the liver. A single meal cannot restore those reserves. Eating carbohydrate at each meal over several days does that work gradually. Rice, pasta, potatoes, bread, oats and fruit all serve the purpose.

Protein matters over the same stretch of time. Muscle fibers damaged by the race's repeated impact are rebuilt from amino acids. That repair continues well after the finish. Spreading protein across breakfast, lunch and dinner supplies it steadily rather than in one large dose. Eggs, yogurt, fish, chicken, beans, lentils and tofu are common options.

Vegetables and fruit fill a different gap. They provide vitamins and minerals involved in tissue repair. One example is vitamin C, which the body uses to make collagen. Many runners cut back on fiber before race day to avoid stomach trouble. The days after the race are a reasonable time to bring whole grains, legumes and vegetables back into meals.

Appetite after a marathon can be unpredictable. Some runners feel little hunger on race day, then feel unusually hungry in the days that follow. Responding to that hunger with regular, substantial meals is more useful than ignoring it.

The week after a marathon is a poor time to start a strict diet. Cutting calories sharply leaves less energy available for repair. The scale can also mislead. Glycogen is stored alongside water, so body weight often shifts as reserves refill. That change reflects fluid, not fat.

Alcohol calls for moderation in this window. It adds to fluid loss while the body is still rebalancing. It can also disrupt sleep. A celebratory drink is common, but repeated heavy drinking works against recovery.

Planning simple meals in advance helps when tired legs make cooking feel like a chore. Batch-cooked staples, prepared before race week, make it easier to eat well without extra effort.

Delayed onset muscle soreness, often shortened to DOMS, is the stiff, aching tenderness that builds in the legs over the first day or two after a marathon. It is a normal response to the race, and it fades on its own over the following days.

The delay catches many first-time marathoners off guard. A runner can feel tired but mobile at the finish, then wake the next morning with thighs that protest every step.

The cause is microscopic damage to muscle fibers and the connective tissue around them. The body responds with an inflammatory repair process. That response produces the tenderness, swelling and stiffness runners notice.

Lactic acid is not the culprit. Lactate produced during the race clears from the bloodstream long before the soreness arrives.

Two features of a marathon drive the muscle damage. The first is volume. Covering the full marathon distance means many thousands of foot strikes, and each one loads the legs.

The second is downhill running. On a descent, the quadriceps contract while lengthening to brake the body. This type of effort is called an eccentric contraction, and it is especially hard on muscle fibers. Courses with long descents, such as the net-downhill Boston Marathon $MPC, have a reputation for leaving quads sore.

The practical signs are easy to recognize. Walking down stairs is often harder than walking up them. Some runners take steps sideways or backward to spare their quads. Lowering into a chair, getting out of a car and standing up after sitting can all feel stiff.

The affected muscles may be tender to the touch. Range of motion is usually reduced for a time as well.

Strength drops along with comfort. Damaged muscle produces less force until it repairs. Legs can feel heavy and uncoordinated even on a short walk in the days after the race.

Typical DOMS is a broad, dull ache spread across large muscle groups, usually in both legs. It gradually improves rather than getting worse day after day.

The process also leaves a protective adaptation. Muscles that have been through this kind of damage respond to a similar effort later with less soreness. This adaptation is known as the repeated bout effect.

Sleep is one of the most useful recovery tools a marathoner has, and it costs nothing. Much of the body's repair work happens during sleep. That makes the week after a race a good time to protect bedtime and add rest wherever the schedule allows.

During deep sleep, the pituitary gland releases a large share of the day's growth hormone, which supports tissue repair. Leg muscles strained by hours of impact during the race benefit from that repair time. Sleep also supports the immune system. After a long race, that system copes with the physical stress of the event. It also faces everyday exposure to germs at work, at home and on the flight back from a destination race.

The first night after a marathon is often the hardest. Many runners lie awake despite feeling exhausted. Sore legs make it difficult to find a comfortable position. Stress hormones released during the race can keep the body alert for hours afterward. Caffeine from energy gels taken in the late miles may still be active at bedtime. Heavy rehydration can also mean several trips to the bathroom overnight.

A broken first night is normal and does not undo the race. The more useful approach is to treat the following days as a chance to catch up. Going to bed earlier than usual, sleeping in when possible and taking a short afternoon nap can all help make up the shortfall.

The bedroom setup matters too. A cool, dark, quiet room makes it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep. For some runners, an extra pillow placed under or between the legs eases pressure on sore muscles and joints.

A celebratory drink is a common part of finish-line culture, and it has a cost for sleep. Alcohol can make a person feel drowsy at first. Later in the night, though, it disrupts sleep, particularly the REM stage, and leaves rest less restorative.

Runners who crossed time zones for an international marathon such as London, Berlin or Tokyo may also face jet lag on the journey home. Spending time in daylight on the local schedule helps the body clock adjust.

Persistent fatigue is worth watching. Feeling tired for several days after a marathon is expected. Exhaustion that lingers well beyond the first week, even with good sleep, is a reason to talk to a doctor.

In the days after a marathon, gentle movement such as easy walking, light cycling or swimming keeps the body moving and promotes circulation without the repeated pounding of running. The goal is light, low-impact activity, not training.

This approach is often called active recovery. It sits between two extremes: staying completely still and heading straight back out for a run. Leg muscles worn down by the race still need time to repair. Light activity leaves room for that repair while keeping the body in motion.

Walking is the simplest option and needs no equipment. A slow walk around the neighborhood, to a café or through a park counts. Flat routes are easier on the legs than hills. Downhill stretches in particular can aggravate sore quadriceps. If walking feels stiff or awkward at first, a shorter outing is a reasonable place to start.

Cycling takes the body's weight off the legs. A stationary bike at a gym or at home lets a runner pedal against little or no resistance. The pace should allow easy conversation. Turning the pedals moves the knees and hips through a smooth range of motion with no landing impact. An outdoor ride works too, as long as it stays on easy terrain and avoids hard climbs.

Swimming and other pool exercise offer another low-impact choice. Water supports much of the body's weight. The legs can move without bearing the full load of each step. Easy laps, gentle kicking with a float or simply walking in the shallow end all fit. Runners with open blisters may want to wait until those have healed before getting into a shared pool.

Effort level matters more than the activity chosen. Each session should feel comfortable from start to finish, with relaxed breathing and no push for speed or distance. Short sessions are enough. The aim is to finish feeling looser than at the start, not more tired.

Pain is the signal to stop. General soreness that eases as the body warms up is typical after a marathon. Sharp, worsening or localized pain is different. It is a reason to rest and seek medical advice rather than push through.

Active recovery is also optional. Some runners prefer complete rest for the first day or two, and that is a reasonable choice. Easy movement is a tool for comfort and mobility, not a requirement for recovering from the race.

Massage and foam rolling can make sore legs feel better after a marathon, but they work as comfort tools rather than repair tools. Gentle pressure is the safer choice in the first days. Deep, forceful work on badly damaged muscle should wait until the worst soreness has passed.

The main benefit of both methods is in how the legs feel. They may ease the perception of soreness and stiffness. That can make walking, stairs and sleep more comfortable. They do not rebuild damaged muscle fibers any faster. That repair happens on the body's own schedule, driven by rest, food and time.

Many large marathons set up massage areas near the finish line. A short session there should be light. Muscles that have just absorbed hours of repeated impact are already strained. Hard pressure at that point can add discomfort rather than relieve it. Runners who book a massage in the following days should tell the therapist they have just raced a marathon. A light, flushing style of work suits tired legs better than deep tissue at that stage.

A foam roller is a firm cylinder of dense foam. The runner lies on it and uses body weight to apply pressure to the calves, quadriceps, hamstrings and glutes. After a marathon, the safest approach is to roll slowly and keep the pressure moderate. Supporting some body weight with the hands or the other leg reduces the load on a tender muscle.

A few rules make self-massage safer. Stay on the soft, muscular parts of the leg and avoid rolling directly over bones, the kneecap or the back of the knee. Skip any area that is bruised or noticeably swollen. Stop if the pressure causes sharp pain rather than a dull, tolerable ache.

Handheld percussion devices, often called massage guns, call for the same caution. Starting on the lowest setting and keeping the device moving avoids hammering one sore spot for too long.

As soreness fades, firmer pressure becomes more tolerable. Runners can then ease back into their normal rolling or massage routine before resuming regular training.

Ice baths and compression garments are optional after a marathon, not required steps. The evidence for both is mixed and modest. Any benefit shows up mainly as less perceived soreness, not as faster healing of damaged muscle.

An ice bath, more formally called cold water immersion, means sitting in cold water up to the waist or hips for a short period. Some physical therapy clinics and race recovery areas offer tubs. Many runners fill a bathtub at home with cold water and ice. The appeal is straightforward. Cold numbs sore legs, and the relief can feel immediate.

That relief is mostly about how the legs feel. The evidence does not establish that cold water immersion shortens the time muscle fibers need to heal after 26.2 miles. A runner who skips the ice bath is not falling behind on recovery.

Cold water carries its own risks. Sudden immersion can trigger a sharp gasp and a jump in heart rate and blood pressure. Anyone with a heart condition, high blood pressure or a circulation problem such as Raynaud's phenomenon should check with a doctor before trying it. A cool shower is a milder option for runners who want some of the sensation without the shock.

Compression garments include knee-high socks, calf sleeves and full-length tights. Many are graduated. That means they squeeze most tightly at the ankle and less higher up the leg. Runners wear them after a race for the snug, supported feeling they give tired calves. Some also pull them on for a long flight or drive home from a destination race, when hours of sitting still can leave legs stiff.

As with ice baths, the benefit of compression gear is modest and centers on perceived soreness. A garment should feel firm but not painful. One that leaves deep marks, causes numbness or tingling, or changes the color of the feet is too tight and should come off.

Neither tool replaces the basics of marathon recovery. They sit on top of fluids, food, sleep and gentle movement rather than standing in for any of them. A runner who likes how an ice bath or a pair of compression socks feels can keep using them. A runner who finds them uncomfortable, inconvenient or expensive can leave them out without giving up anything essential.

Ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers are not an automatic fix for post-race soreness. These drugs can add strain to kidneys already stressed by hours of running. Runners should check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking them, especially while still dehydrated.

Ibuprofen belongs to a drug class called nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, usually shortened to NSAIDs. Naproxen and aspirin are in the same group. Ibuprofen is sold over the counter in the U.S., the U.K. and many other countries under a range of brand names. That makes it a common reach for sore legs at the finish area or back at the hotel.

The main concern is the kidneys. NSAIDs work by blocking substances called prostaglandins, which play a role in pain and inflammation. Prostaglandins also help maintain blood flow to the kidneys. When that support is reduced, the kidneys can become more vulnerable to injury.

A marathon already puts the body in that vulnerable position. Runners lose fluid through sweat for hours, and many finish with some degree of dehydration. Hard, prolonged exercise also shifts blood flow toward the working muscles. Adding a drug that further limits kidney blood flow on top of those conditions is why caution comes up so often around endurance events.

NSAIDs can also irritate the stomach lining. A runner who has eaten little and whose digestion is unsettled after the race may be more likely to notice that. The same questions apply before the race. Taking these drugs before or during a marathon to head off pain carries the same kidney and stomach concerns as taking them afterward.

None of this means every runner must avoid ibuprofen entirely. It means the decision is worth a short conversation with a professional who knows the runner's health history. People with existing kidney problems, high blood pressure, stomach ulcers or heart conditions have extra reasons to ask first. So does anyone taking regular medications that might interact with an NSAID.

Acetaminophen, known as paracetamol in the U.K., is a different kind of painkiller and does not work the same way. It carries its own dosing limits and cautions, particularly for the liver. A pharmacist can explain which option, if any, suits a particular runner.

A few practical habits apply whatever the choice. Reading the label and staying within the stated dose matters. Some cold and flu remedies contain the same active ingredient as a standalone painkiller. Taking both at once can push the total dose past that limit without the runner realizing it. Pain that does not ease with rest is a reason to see a doctor rather than take more tablets.

Blisters and blackened toenails are common after a marathon, and most heal on their own with basic care. Keep broken skin clean and covered, leave small intact blisters alone and watch for signs of infection.

Blisters form when repeated friction separates the outer layers of skin and fluid fills the gap. Over the course of a marathon, sweat, rain or water poured over the head at aid stations can soften the skin and make rubbing worse. Sock seams, wrinkled fabric and shoes that fit differently as the feet swell add to the problem.

A small blister with its roof intact is usually best left alone. The unbroken skin acts as a natural barrier against bacteria. A soft pad or a blister dressing can take pressure off the spot while it heals.

Large, tense blisters that make walking painful are tempting to pop. Draining one carelessly — with an unclean pin, or by tearing away the loose skin — raises the risk of infection. If a blister has to be drained, clean the area first and use a sterilized needle at the edge. Leave the overlying skin in place as a protective cover, then apply a clean dressing.

A blister that has already torn open should be washed gently with soap and water and covered. Change the dressing whenever it gets wet or dirty. Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus or red streaks running up the foot point to infection and need a doctor's attention. People with diabetes or poor circulation in the feet should have any open wound checked promptly.

Toenails take a different kind of punishment. Each stride can drive the toes into the front of the shoe. Thousands of those impacts over a race can cause bleeding under the nail. The result is a black or purple toenail, known medically as a subungual hematoma.

A dark nail that does not hurt usually needs nothing more than trimming and protection. The nail may loosen and eventually fall off as a new one grows in beneath it. Pulling a loose nail off early can expose the tender nail bed. Taping it down and letting it detach on its own protects that tissue.

Throbbing pain under a nail signals pressure from trapped blood. A doctor or podiatrist can relieve that pressure safely. Trying to do it at home risks infection. Shoes with enough room in the toe box and nails trimmed straight across lower the chance of the same damage at the next race.

Chest pain, fainting, confusion, persistent vomiting, very dark urine, severe or one-sided leg swelling and sharp bone pain after a marathon are signs to seek medical care. They are not part of ordinary post-race soreness. They should not be waited out at home.

Chest pain and fainting are the most urgent. A runner who collapses, feels pressure or tightness in the chest, or is short of breath while resting needs immediate help. At a race, the medical tent near the finish is usually the closest option. Away from the course, call emergency services — 911 in the U.S., 999 in the U.K. and 112 across the European Union.

Confusion, slurred speech or unusual drowsiness after a long race are also red flags. A runner may not notice these changes in themselves. Friends and family who spot them should act rather than wait. Persistent vomiting is a concern for a different reason. It stops a runner from keeping down fluids or food. Without those, the basic tools of recovering at home are gone.

Very dark urine — often described as the color of tea or cola — deserves prompt attention. It is a possible sign of rhabdomyolysis. In this serious condition, damaged muscle breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream. That material can harm the kidneys. Only medical testing can show what is happening. Dark urine combined with severe muscle pain or weakness is a reason to get checked quickly.

Leg swelling is another sign to take seriously, especially when it is severe or affects only one leg. Swelling confined to one calf, or swelling that comes with warmth, redness or pain, should be examined by a doctor without delay.

Sharp pain in one spot on a bone is different from the broad ache of tired muscles. It can signal a stress fracture, a small crack in bone that develops under repeated load. For runners, the shin, the foot and the hip are common sites. Pain that worsens when standing or walking, or that lingers after general soreness fades, is a reason to stop running and have it assessed.

None of these symptoms can be sorted out reliably without a medical exam. When in doubt, a doctor, an urgent care clinic or the race medical team is the place to start.

Start running again after a marathon only once muscle soreness has fully cleared, and begin with short, easy runs instead of picking up the old training plan. No single waiting period fits every runner.

The main reason is variation. Two people can finish the same course and leave it in very different shape. Finishing time, pacing, course profile, weather, training history and age all affect how much strain the legs absorbed. Minor aches carried into the race matter too.

A runner who held back and finished comfortably may feel ready well before one who pushed through cramps in the final miles. A fixed calendar cannot account for those differences. The body's own signals are the better guide.

Everyday movement offers the first test. Walking down a flight of stairs without wincing is one practical sign that the worst soreness has passed. Getting out of a chair without bracing on the armrests is another. So is walking at a normal stride without stiffness. If any of those still hurt, the legs are not ready to run.

The type of discomfort matters as well. General muscle ache spread across the thighs and calves is part of normal recovery. A sharp pain in one spot, a joint that feels unstable or a limp that persists is different. Those are reasons to hold off and get checked, not to test the leg with a run.

The first run back should feel almost too easy. Keep it short, on flat ground and at a conversational pace that allows full sentences. Run by feel and ignore pace data from a watch. Legs can feel recovered before overall energy returns. A sluggish run is a reason to keep the effort low.

How the body responds the next day matters as much as the run itself. Returning soreness, lingering stiffness or heavy legs the following morning signal a need for more rest before another attempt. If the legs feel fine, the next outing can be slightly longer. Rest days still belong between runs at this stage.

Speed work, hill repeats and long runs come later. Intervals and tempo efforts place heavy loads on muscles and tendons that are still repairing, even after the obvious soreness fades. Those sessions fit back in only once several easy runs have passed without setbacks.

Rushing back carries a cost. Hard training on legs that have not recovered raises the chance of an overuse injury. That kind of injury can force a far longer break than the one the runner was trying to avoid.

Feeling flat, restless or low after a marathon is a common experience, and runners widely call it the post-marathon blues. The dip is easier to manage once it is expected and named. It also helps to fill the hours training used to take with routines and people unrelated to race day.

A marathon build typically spans several months. During that stretch, the training plan decides when a runner wakes up, what they eat, how they spend weekends and how they describe their week. Race day is the point that all of that structure leads toward. Once the finish line is crossed, the structure disappears almost overnight.

The contrast can feel sharp. The days before the race are crowded with logistics, nerves and anticipation. The days after can feel empty by comparison, especially for a runner whose legs are still too sore to run. Restlessness and a sense of anticlimax are frequent responses. They can appear whether the race went to plan or not.

A disappointing result can add frustration or second-guessing to the mix. A strong result offers no guarantee against the dip either. Reaching a long-held goal can still be followed by a deflated feeling once the moment has passed.

One practical step is to reflect on the race while it is fresh. Writing down what went well, what went wrong and what the training taught turns a vague feeling into something concrete. Race photos, a finisher's medal and split times can become part of that record rather than reminders of something that is over.

Another step is to give time back to the people and activities that training squeezed out. Long runs often take over weekend mornings for months. Spending those hours on meals with friends, family plans or a neglected hobby can make the gap feel like time gained rather than purpose lost.

Running communities offer a third outlet. Volunteering at a local race or handing out cups at a water station keeps a runner connected to the sport. Joining a club's social events does the same without asking anything of tired legs.

Low mood that deepens, lasts for weeks or interferes with work, sleep or relationships is different from a short post-race dip. In that case, speaking with a doctor or a mental health professional is the appropriate next step.

Pick the next race once soreness has cleared and easy runs feel normal again, not in the hours after crossing the finish line. A goal set at that point rests on a clearer read of current fitness, available time and real interest.

The urge to sign up for another marathon often arrives quickly. Finish-line adrenaline, a near miss on a target time or a friend's plans can push a runner toward a registration page while their legs are still stiff. Waiting until recovery is complete gives a fairer picture of how the body handled the distance.

A practical first step is a review of the race just finished. A training log, a GPS watch file or simple written notes can show where the plan worked and where it broke down. Pacing in the first half, fueling during the race, the longest training runs and any recurring aches are all worth examining. Patterns in those details often say more about the next goal than the finish time alone.

The next target does not have to be another marathon. Some runners turn to shorter events such as a 5K, a 10K or a half marathon. Shorter races leave room for faster workouts and demand less recovery afterward. Others choose a trail race, a triathlon or a block of strength training. Some take a season with no race on the calendar at all.

For runners set on another marathon, entry rules affect timing. The Boston Marathon $MPC requires most entrants to meet a qualifying time based on age and gender. The London Marathon and the New York City Marathon allocate many general entries through a ballot or drawing. Those systems can mean choosing a target race well before training for it begins.

No single fixed gap between marathons suits every runner. Age, training history, how hard the last race was run and any injury picked up along the way all change the picture. A doctor, physical therapist or running coach can help set a realistic schedule. Runners coming back from an injury or planning races close together have the most reason to ask for that input.

Writing the goal down with a date and a reason makes it concrete. A target built around a time, a place, a charity or a group of training partners gives the next training block a clear purpose. It also gives the recovery period a defined end point.

#5509. Google finds ‘LLMjacking’ attackers running up $100K a day in fraudulent cloud charges

A new report out today from Google LLC’s Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that attackers who hijack enterprise access to large language models are running up fraudulent cloud charges of more than $100,000 in a single day.

The report, “The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources,” covers multiple LLMjacking cases Mandiant responded to this year. At some organizations, the cumulative bill reached $1 million before access was revoked.

Cryptojacking, the older way of stealing cloud compute, tends to drain resources gradually. LLMjacking charges can spike in a matter of hours.

Victims in North America, South America and Asia-Pacific included financial services and retail companies, along with technology and transportation businesses. GTIG has tied the intrusions to several financially motivated clusters and sees a growing split between the people who break in and the operators who resell the access.

In most of the investigations, attackers got in with cloud identity credentials that had been stolen or left exposed, including service account keys and GitHub personal access tokens. Others went after LLM endpoints left open to the internet, such as exposed Ollama servers.

A group tracked as UNC6993 broke into a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used that foothold to reach an LLM application programming interface. A fake portal it hosted posed as a sign-up page for a group of LLM users. Visitors were sent to the real LLM service and told to paste back a raw JSON payload containing an active access token. With that token, passwords and multifactor authentication no longer stood in the way.

Another actor scraped LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories and tested each one with a request capped at a single output token. Requests that small slipped under the volume-based alerts in the victims’ security monitoring tools.

Routing software is a target too. In one case a follow-on cluster obtained pre-validated virtual keys from the group that had established access, then exploited a user ID rebind flaw in LiteLLM’s key regeneration endpoint. The bug, CVE-2026-40217, let it turn ordinary virtual keys into master administrator credentials for the victim’s gateway.

Some of the stolen access was burned through directly. UNC6993 tried to generate more API keys and switch on extra services inside victim cloud projects, and the charges quickly passed $100,000. A different actor signed victim accounts up for pay-as-you-go agreements on premium models. To get around rate limits, the actor used what GTIG calls a “burn and rotate” strategy, continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts.

A third went further and planted a containerized backdoor built on the Manus agent framework, which asked an upstream model to reason through instructions and then executed the resulting commands on the compromised host.

Other access ends up for sale through what GTIG calls “LLM Mixers.” These operations run stolen credentials through open-source API gateways and custom relays so usage can be metered and the origin of each request hidden. UNC6993 used tools such as new-api and gcli2api, likely to pool stolen keys, and GTIG believes the group sells access through underground storefronts.

One mixer is Jet Night, a token routing service. An actor that made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours was using stolen third-party keys to power it, and one victim organization was left with nearly $1 million in token costs.

Jet Night sells an unlimited plan claiming frontier model access for about $60 a month. Comparable consumer plans typically cost $100 to $250, and GTIG thinks prices that low only work on stolen keys. Outages advertised on the service’s Telegram channel are likely the result of victims finding the compromise and revoking keys.

GTIG expects attackers increasingly to favor LLMjacking over cryptojacking because the mixers pay out quickly and at high margins. Exposed API tokens and model routing middleware will draw more automated targeting as companies put higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production, the report predicts.

On the defensive side, the report notes that in several of Mandiant’s cases, the victim had never enabled LLM services. Attackers used stolen keys to turn on services such as Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Amazon Bedrock and Google’s Gemini API, and a bill could balloon within minutes from there.

Any unauthorized enablement should be treated as a critical security event, it says. Spending caps, API keys scoped to specific models and environments and log monitoring for the single-token pings used to validate stolen keys are among its other recommendations.

Threat actors want artificial intelligence to give them scale over defenders, according to John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, and they are getting it with agentic tools and tokens stolen from unwitting third parties.

“Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks,” Hultquist said.

The result is color recording even in dimness and clearer cabin audio, providing additional security especially for families, rideshare drivers and urban commuters who want a clearer record of what happens on the road and inside the vehicle.

In Wolfbox's driving tests at 38â41 mph, turning on the K9 Pro's NoiseShieldâ¢ feature reduced background noise in recordings by about 60%. An interior camera can provide valuable evidence, but not everyone in a vehicle wants to be on camera at all times. For example, a rideshare passenger might feel uneasy about being recorded, and a family may want some stretches of a drive to go without interior video.

An included, adjustable circular polarizing filter also helps reduce windshield glare and reflections during daytime recording.

The rear camera can be mounted outside the vehicle, which helps to avoid image degradation or blind spots caused by heavily tinted rear glass or window condensation. The camera is IP69K-rated, which keeps it well protected in dusty and wet conditions.

#5506. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi are the two best-paid soccer players in the world for the fourth season in a row, according to Forbes. The pair have held the top two places in 12 of the last 13 years. The one break came in 2022, when Kylian Mbappé reached No. 1 on the strength of a large signing bonus from his contract extension with Paris Saint-Germain.

Forbes estimates that the 10 highest-paid soccer players in 2026 will earn $942 million this season, compared with $945 million in 2025. Ronaldo and Messi alone account for almost half of that total. Every figure is an estimate of pretax income, counted before agents' fees. Each player's total splits into on-field pay and off-field income such as endorsements and business ventures.

Erling Haaland ranks fourth among soccer's top earners, with an estimated $85 million this season. Forbes splits the Manchester City striker's income into $60 million from his playing contract and $25 million from endorsements and other off-field work.

Haaland, 26, is the only Premier League player in Forbes' 2026 top 10. The other nine play in Spain, Saudi Arabia, the U.S., Germany and Turkey.

His Instagram following roughly doubled to 77 million, according to Forbes. In August, he shaved off his blond hair. The new look went viral again.

Haaland has an endorsement deal with Nike $NKE. In 2026, he added two new partners. One is Revolut, a digital bank based in the U.K. The other is Walovi, a Chinese tea company. Deals like these make up the off-field share of his Forbes estimate.

Vinicius Jr. ranks fifth among the world's highest-paid soccer players, with estimated earnings of $76 million, according to Forbes. The 26-year-old Real Madrid forward makes $48 million on the field and $28 million off it.

The Brazilian signed a six-year contract with Real Madrid in August that runs through 2032. He made his debut for the club's senior team in 2018, at 18. Real Madrid agreed to buy him from Flamengo, his first professional club, in 2017. The fee was widely reported at €45 million. He stayed in Brazil until he turned 18 and was eligible to move.

His scoring has held steady for years. He has scored 20 or more goals across all competitions in each of his last five seasons at Real Madrid. He scored the only goal of the 2022 Champions League final against Liverpool in Paris. He also scored in the 2024 final against Borussia Dortmund at Wembley Stadium.

FIFA named him The Best Men's Player for 2024. That same year, he finished second to Manchester City midfielder Rodri in the Ballon d'Or voting.

At the 2026 World Cup, he scored in all three of Brazil's group matches. Brazil then went out in the Round of 16. The five-time champions have not won the tournament since 2002.

He received a four-game La Liga suspension in October 2026 for pulling an opponent's hair. He has also been the target of repeated racist abuse from crowds in Spain. In 2024, a Spanish court convicted three Valencia fans over racist insults aimed at him at Mestalla stadium in 2023. La Liga described it as the first conviction of its kind in Spanish football.

His off-field income draws on a long list of sponsors. He has 15 active partners, including Fanatics, Hugo Boss and the Chinese smartphone brand Vivo. Forbes calls him the new face of Brazilian soccer as Neymar nears retirement.

Lamine Yamal ranks sixth among soccer's best-paid players, with estimated earnings of $55 million this season at age 19. Forbes puts $35 million of that on the field and $20 million off it.

His total is up from $43 million a year earlier, according to Forbes. He is the youngest player in the 2026 top 10.

The latest estimate covers a year in which Yamal became a World Cup champion. Spain won the 2026 tournament, and he scored one goal along the way.

The victory gave Spain its second World Cup title. Its first came at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Yamal's club season ran in parallel. La Liga named him its top player for 2025-26. He scored 16 goals and added 12 assists as Barcelona won the league. It was the club's second straight La Liga title.

Yamal was born in July 2007 and came through La Masia, Barcelona's youth academy. He made his first-team debut in April 2023, at 15. In May 2025, Barcelona announced a contract extension running through 2031. That summer, he took over the club's No. 10 shirt, the number Messi once wore.

He reached the international stage early. At Euro 2024 in Germany, he scored against France in the semifinals. The goal made him the youngest scorer in the history of the European Championship.

Spain beat England 2-1 in the final in Berlin to win a record fourth European title. Yamal was named the tournament's best young player. He had turned 17 the day before the final.

His individual honors followed. He won the Kopa Trophy, awarded to the best player under 21, at the 2024 Ballon d'Or ceremony. In 2025, he won it again and became its first two-time winner. He also finished second in that year's Ballon d'Or voting, behind Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembélé.

The World Cup gives him two major international titles before his 20th birthday.

Sadio Mané ranks No. 7 among the world's highest-paid soccer players, with estimated earnings of $54 million, according to Forbes. The 34-year-old Senegal forward plays his club soccer for Al Nassr in the Saudi Pro League.

Forbes splits that total into $50 million in on-field pay and $4 million in off-field income. Club pay makes up most of his earnings. Endorsements play only a small part.

Mané and Cristiano Ronaldo led Al Nassr to the Saudi league title last season. It was the club's first league championship in seven years. Both players are now in the final year of their contracts.

Mané built his reputation in Europe at Red Bull Salzburg and Southampton. He then spent six seasons at Liverpool, from 2016 to 2022. He won the Premier League and the Champions League with the club. He also shared the Premier League Golden Boot in 2018-19 with Mohamed Salah and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang. In 2022 he finished second to Karim Benzema in Ballon d'Or voting. He moved to Al Nassr in 2023 after one season at Bayern Munich.

Mané played a central role in the January 2026 Africa Cup of Nations final against Morocco. Morocco was awarded a penalty in stoppage time. Senegal's players walked off the field in protest. Play stopped for about 15 minutes until Mané persuaded his teammates to return.

Morocco missed the kick, and Senegal won 1-0 for its second title. The title was later stripped because of the protest. Senegal is appealing the decision.

Senegal's first Africa Cup title came at the 2021 tournament, which was played in Cameroon in early 2022. Mané scored the deciding penalty in the shootout against Egypt in that final.

Away from the game, Mané has paid for a school and a hospital in Bambali, the village in southern Senegal where he grew up.

Jude Bellingham ranks No. 8 among the world's highest-paid soccer players, with estimated earnings of $45 million, according to Forbes. The 23-year-old Real Madrid midfielder earns $29 million on the field and $16 million off it.

He scored seven goals for England at the 2026 World Cup. Two came in the Round of 16 win over Mexico. He added two more in a 2-1 quarterfinal victory over Norway. England finished the tournament in third place.

His tournament record with England goes back further. At Euro 2024, his stoppage-time overhead kick against Slovakia forced extra time in the Round of 16. England went on to reach the final in Berlin, where it lost 2-1 to Spain.

Bellingham was born in Stourbridge, England, in 2003 and came through the academy at Birmingham City. He made his senior debut for the club at 16. Birmingham retired his No. 22 shirt when he left for Borussia Dortmund in 2020. He won the DFB-Pokal, Germany's main domestic cup, with Dortmund in 2021. His younger brother, Jobe, is also a professional midfielder and signed with Dortmund in 2025.

Real Madrid signed him from Dortmund in 2023. He scored 19 La Liga goals in his first season in Spain, when the club won both La Liga and the Champions League. He also won the Golden Boy award and the Kopa Trophy in 2023. Both honors go to players under 21.

His Real Madrid contract runs through 2029. He is reportedly in talks on an extension that could lift his pay closer to what teammates Kylian Mbappé and Vinicius Jr. earn.

Bellingham's off-field income draws on sportswear, fashion and grooming. He promotes Adidas' Predator cleats, a boot line the company introduced in 1994. He also has partnerships with Louis Vuitton and with Skims, the apparel brand co-founded by Kim Kardashian. He recently invested in Onside, a grooming brand.

Harry Kane ranks No. 9 on Forbes' list of soccer's best-paid players, with estimated earnings of $42 million this season. Forbes splits that into $29 million on the field and $13 million off it, before taxes and agents' fees.

The 33-year-old England striker is back in the top 10 for the first time since 2023. That was also the year he joined Bayern Munich, ending 14 years with Tottenham Hotspur.

Kane was born in July 1993 and came through Tottenham's academy. He passed Jimmy Greaves in February 2023 to become the north London club's all-time leading scorer. He left Tottenham without winning a major trophy there.

His first season in Germany, 2023-24, brought 36 Bundesliga goals and the European Golden Shoe. Only Robert Lewandowski, with 41 in 2020-21, has scored more in a single Bundesliga season. Bayern then won the 2024-25 Bundesliga title. It was the first major team honor of his career.

Kane's current contract with Bayern ends after this season. Rumors say he is close to agreeing an extension through 2029. No new deal has been announced.

Kane is also England's captain and the national team's all-time top scorer. He took that record from Wayne Rooney in March 2023 with a goal against Italy.

He won the Golden Boot at the 2018 World Cup in Russia. This summer he scored four more goals at the tournament, bringing his career World Cup total to 14. He and Jude Bellingham led England to a third-place finish. That was the country's best World Cup result since it won the trophy in 1966.

Off the field, Kane is the primary soccer ambassador for Skechers, the footwear company based in Manhattan Beach, California. His other commercial partners include Crayola, Google $GOOGL Gemini and Oura Ring. Those deals cover art supplies, an artificial intelligence assistant and a wearable health tracker.

Mohamed Salah ranks No. 10 with estimated earnings of $40 million this season, according to Forbes. The 34-year-old Egyptian forward makes $20 million on the field and another $20 million off it.

Salah's Liverpool contract expired before this season. His suitors reportedly ranged from Major League Soccer to the Saudi Pro League, according to Forbes. He signed instead with Trabzonspor, a club in Turkey's Super Lig. Trabzonspor is based in Trabzon, a city on Turkey's Black Sea coast. The club won the Super Lig in 2021-22, its first league title since the 1983-84 season.

The Trabzonspor deal runs for two years. It pays him around $19 million a year, according to Forbes. The contract also guarantees him a 20% royalty on club merchandise tied to him.

The $19 million and $20 million figures measure different things. The first is the yearly value of his new contract. The second is the on-field income Forbes uses for its ranking.

Salah was born in 1992 in Nagrig, a village in Egypt's Gharbia governorate. He played for Basel, Chelsea, Fiorentina and Roma before joining Liverpool in 2017.

At Liverpool, Salah won the Champions League in 2019. He also won Premier League titles in 2019-20 and 2024-25. He took the Premier League Golden Boot four times, in 2017-18, 2018-19, 2021-22 and 2024-25. The Confederation of African Football named him African Player of the Year in 2017 and 2018.

Salah also played for Egypt at the 2026 World Cup. Egypt reached the Round of 16, matching its deepest run at the tournament. It then lost to Argentina after letting a late 2-0 lead slip. Egypt had previously qualified for the World Cup in 1934, 1990 and 2018. Salah scored two goals at the 2018 tournament in Russia.

Off the field, his endorsement partners include Adidas, Pepsi and Vodafone, according to Forbes. Time named him to its list of the 100 most influential people in 2019.

#5504. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

#5503. Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:25 amOctober 28, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.

Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release.

With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.
