#5494. Binance will survive the $6.3 billion hack—but this is the start of a terrifying new era

It’s been more than 72 hours since North Koreans robbed Binance in the biggest hack in crypto history and, by all indications, things will be fine. The company’s executives, who went days without sleep to evict the hackers, have gotten the exchange up and running again—all without imposing a haircut on their customers. That’s the good news. The bad news is that the Binance incident is just part of a scary new wave of hacking that cyber experts are calling Black October—and that could be just a preview of a coming wave of attacks against the broader internet.

Before turning to the bigger picture, it’s worth recounting just what happened at Binance. A simplified version goes like this: The vile North Korean regime, which relies on crime to keep Dear Leader in power, got into a laptop belonging to a Binance engineer and installed so-called sweeping tools that moved crypto from the company’s wallets to ones controlled by the hackers. The operation was sophisticated enough that it not only locked out Binance’s security team, but ripped up log records that provided clues to how the hackers broke in.

Binance’s co-CEO Yi He, who is seven months pregnant, and other execs reacted quickly. They unplugged part of the exchange, halting all withdrawals—but not before the North Koreans stole $6.3 billion. This is a staggering amount, but the Binance team caught a break in the form of a lightning response on the part of longtime rivals Tether, Circle, and Coinbase, which froze around $2.5 billion of stolen USDT and USDC stablecoins. But the rest of the stolen funds—consisting of Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and various off-brand currencies—are gone for good, and will soon be buying more weapons for the DPRK.

All of this went down on Thursday afternoon and evening, New York time. By Saturday, as Halloween went into full swing, Binance had turned on withdrawals again for Bitcoin and other major currencies. Meanwhile, the company has reassured customers their funds are safe and that it will be able to offset the roughly $3.8 billion in net losses. Binance is doing this in part by raiding reserve funds set up to stabilize volatility at its derivatives business. The company will presumably scratch together the rest by tapping into its operating income and, possibly, arranging a short-term loan or two. All’s well that ends well—sort of.

Binance put on a masterclass in crisis management with regular and candid updates, helping reassure customers and the markets that the situation was contained. But there’s still the question of how the hackers could pull off a robbery of this magnitude in the first place. It’s easy to accuse Binance of failing to implement adequate safety protocols but, by all accounts, the North Koreans displayed extraordinary skill and knowledge in order to circumvent the company’s layers of permissions. There’s also the question of AI.

There’s no evidence AI agents directly carried out the attack. But the speed at which it was executed, and subsequent steps to drain the funds to thousands of wallets suggest the North Koreans are, at the least, using AI to hone their tradecraft—in the same way that many of us have used tools like Claude to be more productive at our jobs.

This is the frightening bit: AI is helping hackers get better at every stage of their crimes. That includes making deepfakes of employees in order to get into a company’s system, to writing hyper-polished code capable of stealing as much as possible. Even more sinister, there are reports of criminal syndicates gathering data related to hacks like the one on Binance, and using it to train LLMs that specialize in cybercrime.

It may be tempting to think all of this as a problem that will only afflict crypto. Indeed, some news reports painted the Binance hack as a 2020-style crypto bro escapade, but the broader threat is much greater. The North Koreans and others will almost certainly employ the techniques they honed in the Binance hack to go after traditional Fortune 500 companies.

What’s more, unlike certain industries, crypto companies are typically excellent at security—employing serious people with deep backgrounds in military intelligence and computer science. In the case of Binance, the company has already launched joint investigations into the hack with the Secret Service and the FBI. If the North Koreans can rob Binance, it’s a safe bet they can also find targets among banks, credit unions, government agencies, and nearly anyone who is online. The web is going to become a lot more dangerous.

#5493. The 90-Day Plan to Become AI-Native When You Don’t Have a Transformation Budget

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Becoming AI-native takes one quarter, one revenue process and no new software: Here’s the 90-day plan you can run without a transformation budget.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When I wrote about the difference between using AI and being AI-native, the most frequent response from executives was a polite objection: the distinction is real, but redesigning how work happens is a luxury reserved for companies with transformation budgets.

I spend my working life inside those budgets, and most of what they buy is the expensive undoing of habits that formed when the company was small. A founder has nothing to undo yet, which is why the quarter ahead is worth more than the three-year program a large enterprise will fund.

Here is the plan I would run if I were building a company today with no budget beyond my own calendar. In 90 days, with no new software and no outside help, you can do the three things that separate an AI-native business from one that merely uses AI: Write down how the work actually happens, take ownership of your data, and redesign who decides and what gets measured.

In June, Genpact and HFS Research published a survey of more than 2,000 senior executives, and 85% of them said that accumulated enterprise debt — meaning undocumented processes, unusable data, aging systems and unprepared people — is limiting the value they get from AI. The researchers put the trapped value across the Global 2000 at roughly $18 trillion, found that only 33% of enterprise data is AI-ready and estimated that inefficient or manual processes consume about 40% of a typical employee’s week. More than half of those enterprises have no funded initiative to fix any of it.

Every item on that list is a habit before it is a legacy. Nobody decides to have undocumented processes; they go unwritten while the company grows, and the McKinsey Global Survey published this year found that nearly three-quarters of AI high performers have fundamentally redesigned their workflows, against roughly one-quarter of the rest, while the share of smaller organizations scaling AI agents sat flat at 22%. The gap between the two groups is not spend, and it is not model access. It is redesign, and redesign is cheapest before the habits set.

Choose one process that touches revenue directly, such as quote to cash, customer onboarding or returns, and resist the urge to choose three at once. Sit with the people who run it and have them narrate the real path, including the spreadsheet nobody admits to, the approval stuck in one inbox and the exception handled from memory, because the documented process and the one that actually runs are rarely the same document.

Then mark every step as either production or judgment. Production is the drafting, gathering, comparing and summarizing that a model can increasingly perform; judgment is the deciding, prioritizing and taking of responsibility that a human must own. By day 30, you should hold a one-page map a new hire could follow on their first morning, and if a new hire can follow it, so can a model. A process nobody can describe is a process no model can run and no auditor can defend.

With the map in hand, trace where the information for each step lives, and expect to find it scattered across three tools, several inboxes and one personal drive. For every field that matters — meaning customer, product, price, status and date — name a single owner and agree on a single definition, because enterprises I work with across the Americas, Europe, Australasia and Japan are spending fortunes to rediscover what counts as an active customer, a question you can settle in a single afternoon.

Return to the judgment steps on your map and give each one a name, a definition of what a good outcome looks like and a clear rule for when a human reviews before anything reaches a customer. Then look hard at the approvals that remain, because most approval chains are information poverty in disguise, and once last month’s data is visible to everyone, many of them survive only out of habit.

Finally, retire the metrics that measure the tool and install the ones that measure the business. Baseline the cycle time, cost to serve and customer turnaround of your chosen process on day 61, measure again on day 90, and let the difference, rather than the number of licenses, tell you whether anything changed. In my experience, the first fully redesigned process returns more than the first 10 pilots combined, because a pilot proves that a model works, and a redesign proves that the company does.

Three moves follow. First, run the same quarter on the next process, because the method compounds and the second map takes half the time. Second, only now buy tools, since you can finally specify what a tool must do and measure what it did. Third, make the habit a condition of growth, so every new hire inherits a map, and every new vendor passes the export test before a contract is signed.

In August, I offered a test: If every model disappeared on Monday morning, would your business notice? Here is the companion test once you have run this quarter: If you hired 10 people on Monday morning, would they know by Tuesday how the work happens? The companies spending billions are buying back the quarter you still have, and the only transformation budget it requires is the discipline to spend it.

When I wrote about the difference between using AI and being AI-native, the most frequent response from executives was a polite objection: the distinction is real, but redesigning how work happens is a luxury reserved for companies with transformation budgets.

I spend my working life inside those budgets, and most of what they buy is the expensive undoing of habits that formed when the company was small. A founder has nothing to undo yet, which is why the quarter ahead is worth more than the three-year program a large enterprise will fund.

Here is the plan I would run if I were building a company today with no budget beyond my own calendar. In 90 days, with no new software and no outside help, you can do the three things that separate an AI-native business from one that merely uses AI: Write down how the work actually happens, take ownership of your data, and redesign who decides and what gets measured.

#5492. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

#5490. Wholesale marketplace Faire survived the ‘fog of crazy valuations.’ Now, it’s eyeing an IPO

Phil Wahba here. Faire, the online wholesale market, is eyeing a potential IPO in the next 12 months, after surviving the perils that come from pressure on Bay Area tech darlings to grow, grow, grow.

“It was like the fog of war or the fog of crazy valuations, and the tech industry collectively losing its mind,” co-founder and CEO Max Rhodes tells Fortune. “We got a little addicted to vanity metrics to pump growth.”

Now, Faire has re-engineered itself with a healthier business model for the long haul.

Faire was mostly recently valued at $5.2 billion last November in a $100 million tender offer. That’s less than half its peak valuation of $12.6 billion in May 2022, when its heady rise attracted eager investors. (The company had been valued at $1 billion just 18 months prior.)

The problem Faire ran into, Rhodes recalls, is that the pursuit of fast growth was causing questionable decision-making that could have jeopardized Faire down the road.

The company, whose name means “to do” in French and evokes trade shows, operates as a digital marketplace to connect independent retailers and independent brands. Its platform is similar to Shopify in that it powers smaller businesses’ ecommerce, and democratizes technology once reserved for larger retail players. The brands that list goods on Faire—in categories such as decor, food, beauty, jewelry and apparel—pay a commission on items sold to retailers, which typically have one or two locations, like New York’s Strand bookstore chain or Washington, D.C.’s National Archives Museum. About 500,000 retailers and 100,000 brands now use the site.

Small, independent retailers still largely get their inventory by going to trade shows. Indeed, the idea for Faire, founded in 2017, came from Rhodes’ prior experience selling high-end umbrellas. (He later entered the tech world, including a stint as an early product lead at Square, where he worked on Cash App.) He remembers being deflated after attending a trade show at New York’s Javits Center; he’d paid a $15,000 fee to sell his wares with only $2,000 worth of orders to show for it.

Early on, Faire lined up brands at breakneck speed, which eventually led to retailer churn and high marketing costs to regularly recruit new buyers.

Faire felt like a runaway train. The only way to slow it down to a sustainable speed was to focus on “high-quality supply,” Rhodes said. In 2022, Faire gave many brands the boot and deliberately shrunk the company. It cut jobs and introduced technology aimed at retaining customers long-term.

“Reorder rates for the products retailers are buying have gone way up and that’s leading them to come back,” says Rhodes.

In its most recent quarter, Faire earned $750 million in annualized revenue, up 49% from a year earlier. More crucially for Wall Street, Faire broke even on an EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) basis for the first time.

Faire’s finance chief Jason Lee said he is readying the company for an IPO without committing to a specific timeline. The company’s goal for an IPO and beyond is to maintain the discipline it found in 2022.

“The No. 1 thing on the path to durable success in business is solving problems for customers,” says Rhodes. “Retailers don’t care about how much they’re buying, they care about the quality of what they are buying and whether it actually sells.”

#5489. Corporate boards’ loss of faith in Delaware’s elusive new ‘good faith’ contrivance

Could the corporate flight from Delaware accelerate amidst the controversial Cloudflare Delaware court decision?

Over two-thirds of Fortune 500 firms and 70% of U.S. initial public offerings are incorporated in Delaware given the historic predictability and consistency of its specialized court system; but sadly times are changing. A controversial recent court decision in a widely watched case involving Cloudflare has resparked fresh fears that the unfortunate corporate exodus out of Delaware will only accelerate from here.

Cloudflare’s special committee retained us, based on our four decades of recognized governance expertise, to present our widely published research on when companies with dual-class shares outperform and when companies with dual-class shares underperform as the committee deliberated its dual-class share structure. We shared with the committee what we have published for years in academic outlets and in Fortune, as well as elsewhere. This finding is that well-governed, founder-led companies with dual-class shares have, as a group, outperformed other firms in our studies of the entire universe of major firms with such capital structures. At the same time, we found that dual-class structures should expire in instances where they no longer make sense or are abused. We were not asked to opine on the terms of Cloudflare’s own specific proposed recapitalization design, and we did not.

We take no explicit position on Cloudflare’s proposed reclassification. We have no relationship with Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster, who wrote the opinion, and had no direct dealings with him now or previously. Our glancing role in this matter was just based on a single hour-long presentation before the board. Thus, this piece is not about us. It is about what every Delaware board is now supposed to make of the vague if not vacuous words “good faith.”

With corporate anchoring fees rivaling personal income taxes as Delaware’s primary source of revenue, Delaware’s wise leaders, including its governor and its legislature, saw this exodus coming, and tried to stem its root cause. In March 2025, Delaware passed Senate Bill 21 (SB 21), the most significant rewrite of its corporate code in a generation, to stop the flow of companies out of the state. SB 21 was generally recognized to have been a direct response to a run of activist rulings from the Court of Chancery, which were widely seen as blatant judicial overreach.

In February 2024, the Court of Chancery voided most of a stockholder agreement at Moelis & Co. as an unlawful constraint on the board, calling into question standard governance arrangements across corporate America. Within four months, the Delaware legislature enacted a new provision, Section 122(18), to authorize exactly those agreements; and the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the ruling and vacated the $6 million fee awarded to the plaintiff’s lawyers.

That same month in 2024, the court ruled that TripAdvisor’s decision to move to Nevada would be judged under “entire fairness,” the most hostile standard in corporate law, because leaving Delaware reduced its directors’ exposure to lawsuits. The Supreme Court reversed that too, holding that ordinary business judgment applies and that the choice between Delaware and Nevada belongs to “legislatures, market participants, and directors,” not to the Court of Chancery. Similarly, the Supreme Court reversed a nearly $200 million original judgment against TC Energy in the Columbia Pipeline case.

No less a luminary than revered former Delaware Chancellor William Chandler, who led the Delaware Court of Chancery for 14 years, testified in support of the passage of SB 21 that “Right now, the corporate market is not feeling good about Delaware.” SB 21 followed, drafted with the help of Chancellor Chandler and former Chief Justice Leo Strine, both widely admired objective legal titans.

Now, Laster’s opinion in the new widely watched Cloudflare case represented the first opportunity to apply the new law, SB 21. The case featured a strong-performing company with dual-class shares, which sought a recapitalization and reclassification to retain the company’s founders and maintain voting control, consistent with a superior track record of sustained outperformance with the stock up ~1800% since going public in 2019.

The spirit of SB 21 is simple: if a board routes a possibly ‘conflicted’ deal through a committee of independent directors with real power to reject it, the deal is considered “kosher.” This means no injunctions, no damages, no trial.

Indeed, Laster’s 142-page opinion concedes the legitimacy of SB 21 and its applicability to this case. He held the directors were independent. He held they were not negligent. He wrote that their process showed “all the outward signs of diligent and careful effort.” By his own account, virtually every requirement the legislature wrote was met by the Cloudflare board.

He enjoined the transaction anyway, on a novel basis. SB 21 does require that the committee act “in good faith,” and Laster’s route was to re-define what good faith entails.

The term “good faith” was not a third level of diligence beyond the duty of care and duty of loyalty, but merely presumed to be the spirit of board actions. Before this, good faith had been previously generally assumed, in deference to independent boards, with nary any heightened review threshold, much less any invocation to enjoin a transaction.

Startlingly, Laster largely set aside, in practice, the existing Delaware definition of bad faith, which is grounded in scienter, or the requirement of showing that individuals acted with knowledge and intent of wrongdoing, as well as the requirement that each board member be assessed individually to determine whether a majority intentionally acted in bad faith.

Instead, he pointed in part to the fact that the board understandably used Signal to communicate about sensitive strategic information they presumably did not want competitors obtaining, irrespective of litigation, and to a CEO who was known to have a hot temper, even though the temperament of the entrepreneur is irrelevant to good faith and typical of creative businesses in technology, media, fashion and the like. None of that amounts to anything even remotely resembling scienter, which is knowing or willful misconduct.

The opinion’s strongest argument should be stated plainly, because boards will have to reckon with it. The court did not rest on any one fact, instead pointing to a fact pattern. It pointed to a junior member of the financial advisers team’s contemporaneous notes about building a “narrative” and securing “gets” for the founders despite those notes being discredited subsequently; to one committee member’s unauthorized conversation telling a founder the committee would give him what he wanted; to two non-committee directors inserting themselves into the negotiation after the founder’s threats; to terms that landed where the founder had predicted; and to messages set to auto-delete after litigation had been threatened, from which the court drew inferences.

From those disconnected, misconstrued scraps, the court inferred that the committee was serving the founders rather than bargaining against them. Reasonable readers can weigh that account differently. Our point is narrower: every item in it is evidence about how the committee negotiated, not about what any individual director intended – and the statute’s word is “good faith,” which Delaware law has always defined by intent.

Laster acknowledged that without what he called the defendants’ “credibility problems,” he “could have concluded” the safe harbor applied. In other words, the statute’s protection now turns on whether a trial judge likes the witnesses. And in this case, the trial judge already judged that the defendants have ‘credibility problems’ without hearing live witnesses testify at trial or sizing them up in person, based only on the paper record of a preliminary injunction hearing.

In the appellate process, usually, trial judges are given deference for factual determinations, based upon their direct personal interactions, but how can any trial judge make any credible factual determinations about the witnesses whom they have never met, did not evaluate in person, and based on only a paper record and remote deposition transcripts?

If the Laster opinion is allowed to stand as precedent, the practical meaning of “good faith” for a Delaware board is this: there is no checklist, no process, no roster of advisers and no set of minutes that can secure it in advance. A committee that meets every structural requirement the legislature wrote can still be sent to trial because a single judge, reading advisers’ notes and text messages months after the fact, concludes that its heart was not in it. Boards will have to put up with that, deal by deal and judge by judge, until the Supreme Court or the legislature says otherwise.

Consider one concrete example of what boards are now being asked to anticipate. The opinion faults Cloudflare’s committee for not obtaining a fairness opinion and for not quantifying the value of the benefits the founders would receive — while conceding, in its own footnote, that “Delaware courts have stated that there is no duty to obtain a fairness opinion,” and that Delaware decisions “have shown greater deference to a decision not to secure a fairness opinion, even for purposes of a controller recapitalization.” That concession is not a technicality.

Fairness opinions are strictly instruments of mergers and divestitures, where there is a price to be fair about. They are never obtained for recapitalizations, and no investment bank can credibly opine on the “fairness” of extending founder control against an imaginary alternative that was never on the table — which is why Delaware’s own precedents, from the NRG Yield reclassification onward, have rejected the argument that one is required. A board that reads this opinion learns that it can be faulted for omitting a step the law does not require and which nobody in the market can reasonably perform.

And that is why the Cloudflare decision matters far beyond one company’s share structure, and even beyond dual class shares. Every board in America that is still incorporated in Delaware, especially companies with strong founders and controllers, now has the same question in front of it: if this fair, independent process was not enough, what would be enough to satisfy Delaware judges on what ‘good faith’ entails?

A board that does not know what “good faith” means in practice has no safe harbor at all; it has a lottery ticket with the odds stacked against it. Delaware’s entire value proposition, for a century, was that it was the one jurisdiction where boards could know the rules before they acted, in a predictable and consistent way. That predictability and consistency have now gone up in thin air.

Boards are not sentimental about their legal domicile. The forty-four reincorporation proposals this year, up from seventeen two years ago, represent a natural response to this heightened Delaware risk. Delaware’s legislature understood that in March of 2025, when it passed SB 21 to put a floor under that calculation. Vice Chancellor Laster has now pulled the floor out again for all substantive purposes.

None of this is an indictment of the Delaware Court of Chancery as an institution. In fact, the court’s other distinguished judges have, if anything, been saying the quiet part aloud. For example, highly respected Vice Chancellor Lori Will — who certified the SB 21 constitutional questions to the Supreme Court within weeks in 2025 so that “courts, corporations, litigants, and transaction planners” would have clarity and predictability — published a paper last fall titled Back to Basics: Delaware’s Genius of Simplicity, at the UPenn Law School and forthcoming in the Journal of Corporation Law. Its thesis is that Delaware’s strength lies in “simple, enduring principles,” that “modern pressures invite complexity and the expansion of fiduciary theories [with] clarity put at risk,” and that “preserving stability and judicial restraint is essential to sustaining the predictability that has long defined our law.”

To be fair, this latest ruling is interim, and the Delaware Supreme Court will almost certainly get its turn. Yet this will involve more rounds of litigation. Practically, the unfortunate reality for Delaware is that the damage of each reversal is cumulative, not corrected.

Every company watching the Cloudflare saga play out in Delaware, especially companies with strong founders and controllers, has to wonder whether it is time to reincorporate in Texas or Nevada. The nation’s companies in competitive technology sectors cannot help but note that even if the decision is reversed, such a correction would still mean that Cloudflare will have lost well over a year – in the best case – in implementing its capital structure.

Hundreds of remaining Delaware-based companies are not shrugging this off as “water over the dam” safe to ignore. As historian David McCullough wrote of the tragic inaction ahead of the catastrophic 1889 breach of the Johnstown, Pennsylvania dam, people ignored a growing stream over the structure’s top. The growing over-the-top Chancery Court rulings may well lead to a stream of corporate exits.

Steven Tian is research director of the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute and former quantitative analyst at Rockefeller Capital Management. Cloudflare’s special committee retained Sonnenfeld and Tian to present their research on dual class shares during its deliberations.

#5488. How ‘Ghosts’ Star Asher Grodman Learned to Fly by the Seat of His Pants. (Without Wearing Any Pants.)

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The breakout ‘Ghosts’ star shares his advice on beating imposter syndrome, taking big swings and putting heart at the center of your work.

I’ve interviewed a lot of successful people, but Asher Grodman is the first to become famous mostly without pants. Grodman plays Trevor, the forever-trouserless finance bro on CBS’s hit comedy Ghosts. (Backstory on his wardrobe: On the show, Trevor died while pantsless, hence his spirit is forever pantless in the afterlife.)

On the eve of Ghost’s eagerly awaited Halloween special (look for it on-demand, trust me), I spoke to Grodman over video from his trailer. We talked about the skills, mindset and determination it took for him to break into an industry that is famously impossible to break into. His secret? Don’t be afraid to look silly every now and then.

First question, because I can’t tell on this video call: Are you wearing pants?I am at this moment wearing pants, but I’ve got about two hours left of pantness in my life.

Are there days where you wish the writers wrote your character differently, or do you embrace the pantlessness?There are never days that I wish they wrote it differently, but there are certainly days where you’re just like, pants would be so lovely. When I get to do something else and I get to wear pants, it feels like such a power move. But as a guy who had never done a comedy when we started this thing off, the idea of me not wearing pants was kind of like a safety net because I was like, “Well, if I don’t hit a joke, they’ll just switch up the angle and reveal my thighs, and that should get a chuckle at least.”

Imposter syndrome is a big thing. People face a big moment and think, “I’ve never done this before — I shouldn’t be doing this.” How did you get yourself in the right headspace for comedy?I remember I auditioned and I think it was Joe Port, one of our showrunners, who was like, “Who are you? You’ve never done a comedy.” And do remember saying — I don’t know where this came from — that comedy is just drama but more serious. You’re just committed to being an idiot, to some degree, or whatever the thing asks you to be. The first line Trevor ever says is, “We scooped a copter to beat the traffic out to the Hamptons because that’s how we roll.” It’s just such a specific point of view and a specific guy. I was like, I know who this is, and a lot of my job is going to be to get out of the way of the comedy, because that’s working, and just make sure that there is a heart to this guy. I approached it as an actor. I didn’t approach it with the intention of, I have to make this funny.

So what’s the most Hollywood thing in your fancy trailer? This is going to be really disappointing, because we really haven’t been in these trailers since season two. Our crew here in Montreal built this cast village where we all have our own little rooms, our own little offices with couches in them, and that’s the most Hollywood thing. But in the middle is that long Thanksgiving-style table, and that’s where we sit and work and play and goof off, and we get rowdy.

When guest stars come on the show, they have trailers and stuff that they can go to, but we kind of invite them to sit on those couches with us or sit around the table with us. So they’re kind of part of this gaggle of idiots. Often in this show, to use a sports analogy, the ball gets passed around a lot. We’ve all had the experience of being on other shows and feeling like you’re the guy who was called in to do one play and then they all beat you up on the sideline. So we want it to be a really welcoming place. When I think of my happiest places in the world, that table is one of them.

You’re a big Jaguars fan. How did your “NFL is scripted” viral video series come together, and where did you get the guts to pitch it?I’ve been a Jaguars fan from day one, since I was eight. And I’ve been very vocal about that. Someone from the organization called me as season one of Ghosts was airing and asked, “Is this real?” I told them yes, and that hiring Urban Meyer was the dumbest decision in the history of professional sports. So she was like, “Okay, you’re a real Jaguars fan.” So they brought me into the family. There was this magical season in 2022 where they won the division and went into the playoffs, and there were all these conspiracy theories about the NFL being scripted. So I suggested doing a full mockumentary about the NFL actually being scripted and they were like, “Why don’t you write and direct it?” And I was like, well, I got a really cushy thing going on here as the outsider. I’m sitting with the owner and watching these games on the sideline, and I really don’t want to ruin that, because if you’re going to blame anyone when it fails, you’re going to blame me. But we did it and it was the most joyful creative experience I’ve had in my life. We shot that whole thing in two days. It was like 42 scenes. Trevor Lawrence is a major character in it, and I think we had him for 30 minutes. So Ghosts has taught me to shoot fast.

What advice do you have for creators who haven’t broken through yet, besides “stick to it”?The stick-to-it thing is not wrong. Support yourself, take care of yourself, because it is a little bit about just how many at-bats you get. You can have a hundred auditions and get one. That’s not a reflection of talent. There are so many circumstances outside of your control. I think as much as you can, you want to develop a sense of confidence. And I’m still struggling with this: a sense of confidence without ego. A sense of embracing the unknown and embracing being wrong and being foolish, but also holding on to the confidence and the self-worth to keep trying. To feel comfortable in failure. That’s really important. And show up. For auditions, I get such a thrill walking into a room and meeting a reader who I don’t know and figuring out a way to take this thing that’s written on the page and making it feel like we’re improvising. It is just an electric, thrilling thing. Be in the moment.

I’ve interviewed a lot of successful people, but Asher Grodman is the first to become famous mostly without pants. Grodman plays Trevor, the forever-trouserless finance bro on CBS’s hit comedy Ghosts. (Backstory on his wardrobe: On the show, Trevor died while pantsless, hence his spirit is forever pantless in the afterlife.)

On the eve of Ghost’s eagerly awaited Halloween special (look for it on-demand, trust me), I spoke to Grodman over video from his trailer. We talked about the skills, mindset and determination it took for him to break into an industry that is famously impossible to break into. His secret? Don’t be afraid to look silly every now and then.

#5487. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5486. 10 Thanksgiving food safety mistakes to avoid, from thawing to leftovers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

10 Thanksgiving slipups drawn from USDA guidance, from buying a fresh turkey too early to thawing it on the counter and leaving leftovers out.

Thanksgiving turns an ordinary home kitchen into a short-order restaurant for one high-stakes afternoon. A host juggles a large bird, a single oven, a stack of side dishes, and guests who drift toward the table hours before dinner arrives. Mistakes in that setting give no warning. Harmful bacteria leave no trace the eye, nose, or tongue can catch. A platter that looks and smells perfect can make a guest sick. The stakes reach beyond one bad evening. Foodborne illness strikes the country with 48 million cases, 128,000 hospitalizations, and 3,000 deaths every year. The totals span the full calendar, and they show what unseen germs can do once they reach a plate.

The holiday stacks most of the risky steps of food preparation into a single day. Raw poultry enters the house, thaws, shares space with salads and pies, roasts, and lingers on a buffet while the crowd grazes into the night. Each stage invites its own error. Juices from the raw turkey can drip onto a board reserved for vegetables. A thermometer can stay in the drawer all day. A tray of sliced meat can sit out long after the last guest finishes eating. Federal guidance answers these hazards with four habits: clean, separate, cook, and chill. Each habit guards a different moment, from the first wipe of the counter to the last container headed for the refrigerator. The habits sound simple, yet the pressure of a holiday meal tests every one of them at once.

The Food Safety and Inspection Service's Your Safe Thanksgiving Guide, which the agency last updated on Nov. 25, 2025, walks readers through the feast from the grocery aisle to the last bite. The guide spans buying, handling, thawing, brining, stuffing, cooking, serving, and storing leftovers, and it addresses whole turkeys, turkey parts, and other turkey alternatives. Anyone with questions can call the agency's Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854), which answers Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET except on federal holidays. The hotline's food safety specialists take calls from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Thanksgiving Day. The 10 items below form a selection of the guide's advice and follow the order in which the cooking unfolds.

The guide's advice on buying a turkey points shoppers to three pieces of package wording: "fresh," "Best by," and "Use by." Each term gives a buyer information about the bird before it leaves the store. The first word places the turkey on the fresh side of the fresh-or-frozen choice the guide lays out for holiday shoppers. The other two print a date on the wrapper. A shopper can use that date to match the purchase to the day of the feast.

Fresh poultry packaging should carry a "keep refrigerated" statement as well. The phrase turns the wrapper from a description into a storage instruction. A fresh bird depends on the refrigerator from the moment it reaches the house.

A shopper who reads all four phrases learns both what kind of turkey sits in the cart and where it must wait until roasting day.

Most turkeys on U.S. shelves reach shoppers frozen at 0 degrees F or colder, and that cold start shapes every holiday plan that follows. A buyer who picks one up takes on a scheduling job along with the bird. The Thanksgiving guide tells home cooks to set aside enough time for the turkey to thaw before the meal. The defrost becomes a fixed entry on the calendar, counted backward from the hour the oven needs the bird.

Deep cold keeps the bird safe for as long as it stays frozen, with no time limit on that protection. Freezing slows the movement of molecules, and the microbes on the turkey go dormant. Dormant germs are still alive. Bacteria that sat on the bird before it froze can multiply again the moment thawing begins. The freezer pauses the danger without erasing it, and the defrost restarts the countdown.

Storage location decides whether the bird holds onto its frozen shield until thaw day. The turkey belongs in the freezer until the cook is ready to defrost it. Holding spots such as the back porch, the car trunk, or the basement fall short because nobody can watch the temperature there around the clock. A cool basement can feel like cold storage, yet the guidance treats it as no substitute for a freezer. A bird left in one of those places could slip toward a thaw without anyone noticing, and its bacteria would gain an early lead.

The car trunk warning carries a practical lesson for the drive home from the grocery. A turkey bought days or weeks ahead should travel from the checkout lane to the home freezer without a stopover in the trunk while other errands run.

The open-ended freezer life frees shoppers to buy a frozen turkey on their own schedule. Choosing frozen moves the critical date from the store trip to the freezer door.

The kitchen counter and a sink of hot water both fall outside the guide's list of acceptable ways to thaw a turkey. Three methods earn a place on that list: the refrigerator, cold water, and the microwave. The guide names no fourth option.

The guide pairs no time allowance, wrapping instruction, or follow-up step with either rejected shortcut. It reserves those directions for the three sanctioned routes and marks the counter and hot water as practices to avoid.

A turkey that stays frozen remains safe with no time limit. Freezing slows molecular movement and lulls microbes into dormancy. Defrosting ends that protection. Any bacteria on the bird before it entered the freezer can resume multiplying as soon as the bird starts to soften.

Federal guidance keeps a frozen bird in the freezer until its thaw begins. A back porch, a car trunk, or a basement makes a poor holding spot, since nobody can track the temperature there without pause.

The divide between cold and hot water shows that the temperature of a soak decides whether it qualifies.

Refrigerator thawing takes 24 hours for every four to five pounds of turkey, the longest timeline the guide attaches to any safe method. Per pound, the cold shelf demands between 4.8 and six hours. A host choosing this route commits to a schedule measured in days. The start date belongs on the calendar before anyone preheats the oven.

Patience in cold storage buys flexibility at the other end. A thawed turkey can sit there for one or two days before cooking. A container or dish under the bird catches juices that leak as the turkey softens. The vessel keeps raw drippings off shelves holding other groceries.

Cold water cuts thawing to 30 minutes per pound, a pace between 9.6 and 12 times quicker than the slower method. Speed comes at the price of attention. The turkey stays submerged in its original wrapping, which guards against cross-contamination. The cook swaps in fresh water every 30 minutes until the bird has thawed. Once the ice is gone, the turkey must cook without delay. No grace period applies.

The microwave accommodates a small turkey or a turkey breast, yet most whole birds will not fit inside. Cooks select the defrost setting and follow the manufacturer's recommendations. Some sections can warm and begin cooking during the cycle, which pushes those areas into the Danger Zone. The fix is to cook the turkey the moment defrosting ends. Anyone handling a full-size bird can skip this option and choose between the other two.

Thawing restarts the bacterial clock. Freezing slows molecules until microbes go dormant. A turkey kept frozen stays safe with no time limit, yet any bacteria on it before freezing can resume multiplying once defrosting begins. The refrigerator stands apart as the one approved method that lets a turkey thaw ahead and wait for its turn in the oven.

Rinsing a raw turkey sends bacteria around the kitchen and onto other foods, and the guide names skipping the step as the safest choice. The faucet works against the cook at the first step of handling the bird. Water that runs off the skin can carry germs to nearby counters and to dishes waiting their turn.

A rinse undercuts a second habit, separation. The guide wants raw poultry stored away from cooked foods and from anything that will not get cooked later, and spray from the sink erases that distance.

Soaking the turkey offers no safe substitute. Salt water, vinegar, and lemon juice all fail to kill the bacteria on meat or poultry, whether a cook uses them to wash, rinse, or brine. A dip in salt water or brine comes down to personal taste and serves no food safety purpose. Anyone who soaks the bird must keep the liquid away from other food.

The guide's washing advice targets the kitchen and leaves the bird alone. Its clean principle asks cooks to start with clean hands, utensils, and surfaces and to keep washing them during and after preparation.

Cooks who choose to wash the turkey take on an extra job. The guide directs them to clean and sanitize the sink and the surrounding areas before prep continues. Skipping that cleanup would leave contamination from the rinse on the surfaces where the next ingredient may land.

Heat does the job the tap cannot. The guide's cook instruction calls for a food thermometer and a safe minimum internal temperature, the point where harmful bacteria die before anyone eats. A turkey bound for the oven gains nothing from water that moves germs around without killing them.

A turkey that goes from package to pan without touching water ends up as safe as a rinsed bird once cooked through, and the kitchen around it stays cleaner.

A 20-second scrub with soap and water, before and after touching raw meat or poultry, forms the first barrier between a raw turkey and the rest of the Thanksgiving meal. The guide calls for both scrubs. The earlier scrub lets a cook start prep with clean hands. The second keeps germs from the bird off the bread basket, the gravy ladle, and every other item those same hands reach for next. A host who trims the turkey and plates the rolls without a stop at the sink has skipped half the job.

Raw turkey needs distance from ready-to-eat foods and from anything bound for the table uncooked, a group the guide illustrates with vegetables, fruits, and side dishes. Cooking to a safe internal temperature destroys harmful bacteria. A dish served raw gets no second chance. Juice from the bird that drips onto sliced fruit or a green salad reaches a guest's plate with its germs intact. Keeping raw poultry apart from such dishes stops germs from reaching food that could make people sick.

The separation rule reaches into storage, where the guide asks cooks to keep raw meat and poultry away from cooked foods and from anything that will skip the stove. A raw bird parked on a shelf above a bowl of cut fruit or a finished pie undoes that buffer before anyone picks up a knife.

Utensils and countertops demand the same attention as hands across the entire holiday. The guide's clean habit extends that standard to tools and surfaces, asking cooks to keep washing all three during prep and after it ends. A knife that halves raw turkey and moves on, unwashed, to slice bread carries the bird's bacteria with it. A cutting board or a stretch of counter does the same. A kitchen that handles raw turkey in the morning and tosses salad in the afternoon needs the full routine each time raw poultry touches a new hand, tool, or surface.

A food-grade plastic bag can hold a turkey and its brine, but a household trash bag has no place in the job. Many hosts brine the holiday bird, and the guide flags the step as one with its own safety considerations, the same treatment it gives stuffing. The bag rule separates gear built to touch food from gear built to haul garbage. A trash bag can look like an easy fix for a bird too big for any pot, and the guide closes off that shortcut by name.

Rigid containers give a host three more choices. Another federal poultry page lists food-grade plastic, stainless steel, and glass as suitable vessels for a wet brine. The same page calls for the whole bird to sit beneath the solution, with the container covered and kept in the refrigerator. Those requirements turn brining into a refrigerator task. A host needs shelf space for a covered vessel big enough to hold the entire bird under liquid. The demand can collide with every side dish and dessert waiting for a cold shelf.

Cooks should throw out the used brine once the turkey leaves it. The liquid has bathed raw poultry, and it earns no second life as a gravy base or a fresh soak for another bird. Hosts need to guard against cross-contamination while handling the soak. Every lift, pour, and dump calls for the same care a cook gives the raw turkey itself.

A salt-water soak kills none of the bacteria on raw meat or poultry. Solutions of vinegar or lemon juice fare no better, whether a cook uses them to wash, rinse, or brine. Federal guidance treats brining as a personal preference with no food safety purpose. A cook who skips the brine loses no protection against foodborne illness. Every safeguard in brining comes from the handling, from the food-grade vessel to the cold storage to the discarded liquid.

USDA does not recommend stuffing a whole turkey, and its Thanksgiving guide names two reasons: the practice raises the risk of cross-contamination and adds time to the cook. The agency steers home cooks toward a separate dish for the stuffing, a route it describes as safer and better for even doneness. The guide acknowledges that many people stuff their birds, and it groups stuffing with brining as preparation steps that carry their own safety considerations.

A stuffed turkey carries two temperature targets instead of one. The meat must reach 165 degrees F, and the center of the stuffing must hit the same mark before anyone eats. The guide sets the stuffing's target apart from the bird's. A cook who fills the cavity therefore needs a thermometer reading from the middle of the stuffing as well as from the meat.

Timing sets the second trap. The guide warns against filling a turkey the night before. Bacteria can multiply in stuffing inside a refrigerated bird, and their growth can lead to foodborne illness. Cold storage, the step a host might trust to buy time, offers no protection in this case. A bird filled the evening before the holiday gives those bacteria a full night to work before the oven heats up.

The guide's cooking calculator treats a stuffed turkey as a distinct case. Its roasting option, set for a 325 degrees F oven, asks whether the stuffing will go inside the bird and offers stuffed and unstuffed versions across the same six weight ranges, from a four- to eight-pound breast up to a 20- to 24-pound turkey. The tool lists a stuffed choice for smoking, deep fat frying, grilling, and microwaving as well. Building the stuffing question into every method signals that the agency regards a filled bird as its own planning problem.

Every risk the guide names, from cross-contamination to overnight bacterial growth to a longer stay in the oven, traces back to the cavity, which leaves a separate dish as the one route that sidesteps all three.

Every cooked turkey needs an internal temperature of at least 165 degrees F, no matter which route it takes to the table. USDA holds an oven bird, a deep-fried bird, and a smoked bird to the same floor. Trading the oven for a pot of hot oil or a smoker alters the equipment and the timing. The finish line stays fixed.

Six cooking routes appear in the guide's turkey calculator, and none of them earns a softer target. Beyond a classic roast in a 325 degrees F oven, the tool includes a covered charcoal grill, smoking, deep fat frying, cooking a frozen turkey, and microwaving birds up to 14 pounds. Its roasting choices run from a 4-to-8-pound breast to a 20-to-24-pound whole turkey. A frozen bird sliding into the oven and a small one turning in the microwave answer to the identical 165-degree benchmark.

A food thermometer settles whether the meat has arrived. USDA calls for probing turkey parts as well as whole birds, so a host preparing a lone breast or a few wings needs the instrument in hand. Reaching the safe minimum kills harmful bacteria before anyone takes a bite.

A whole turkey requires three separate temperature checks. The stem goes into the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the wing, and the innermost part of the thigh. Each location covers a different section of the bird.

Bone contact spoils the result. USDA warns that a thermometer resting against bone gives an inaccurate figure. The tip belongs in flesh alone at each of the three positions.

One passing reading proves little about the rest of the bird. A breast at 165 degrees F says nothing about a thigh that has yet to catch up. The turkey meets the guideline once all three sites clear the mark. The coolest of the three sets the moment the host can carve.

Appetizers, side dishes, and turkey all have two hours at room temperature after cooking before they turn into a food safety risk. The clock runs whenever food sits between 40 degrees F and 140 degrees F, a band the guide calls the Danger Zone. Bacteria that cause foodborne illness grow at a rapid clip inside that range. A leisurely meal with second helpings and dessert can carry dishes past the limit before anyone gets up to clear the table.

Hot weather cuts the allowance to a single hour. Food left in surroundings above 90 degrees F needs to reach the refrigerator within that hour, half the standard window. The countdown begins when cooking ends, so whatever leaves the oven first hits its deadline first. A tray of appetizers baked before guests arrive can run out of time on the counter while the turkey still cooks. Dishes held above 140 degrees F escape the rule because they never drop into the Danger Zone.

Portion size governs how fast leftovers chill. Smaller amounts, carved turkey among them, cool faster in covered shallow containers set in the refrigerator or freezer. Cold storage should bring them below 40 degrees F, the guide's ceiling for perishable food. A host who slices meat from the carcass and splits the sides into small covered containers gives every portion the best chance to get cold in time.

Refrigerated leftovers last four days from the first cooking. Turkey roasted on Thanksgiving Thursday reaches the end of that span on Monday. Anyone who expects extras to outlast the stretch should move them to the freezer before the fourth day ends. Reheating closes the cycle, and every leftover should reach 165 degrees F before it returns to a plate. The guide's featured factsheet on leftovers repeats the same pair of habits, cooking food to a safe temperature and storing extras cold without delay. Of all the guide's leftover deadlines, the two-hour mark, which shrinks to one hour above 90 degrees F, arrives first and leaves the least slack. The end of dinner gives a host the least room to postpone the cleanup.

#5484. I’ve Hired Independent Contractors for 20 Years. Here Are 7 Downsides Every Business Owner Should Know

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Independent contractors offer flexibility and specialized expertise, but the savings come with trade-offs.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

After more than two decades of working with independent contractors, I still believe they’re one of the best ways to run a flexible small business. But I’ve also learned that they’re not nearly as cheap, simple or risk-free as many business owners assume.

There are plenty of advantages. I can hire contractors for specific projects without making a long-term employment commitment. I don’t have to provide employee benefits, paid vacation or other traditional employment perks. I can negotiate project rates, define deliverables and avoid worrying about keeping someone busy when the work dries up. Contractors generally manage their own schedules, tools and methods.

It can be a flexible and cost-effective model. But it’s not all rosy.

Here are seven things I’ve learned about working with independent contractors — and what every business owner should consider before building a business around them.

When you hire a contractor instead of an employee, you may save money on payroll taxes, benefits and other employment-related expenses. But contractors have their own business expenses, and those costs have to be covered somehow. That’s why their hourly rates are often higher than what you’d pay an employee doing comparable work.

Their rates can also change as market conditions shift, making long-term costs less predictable.

This may still be a financially sound decision for your company, but I recommend projecting the total cost of hiring a contractor versus an employee for every position you consider. Don’t assume you’re saving money just because you’re not running payroll.

Independent contractors are independent business owners, freelancers and professionals who provide services to other businesses. When you work with them, you need to understand and comply with federal, state and local tax and labor laws.

The distinction between an employee and an independent contractor generally comes down to the nature of the working relationship, including how much control the company exercises over the worker. Factors can include how the work is performed, who provides the tools and equipment, how the worker is paid and whether they operate an independent business.

I generally don’t have the same payroll tax, benefit and wage-and-hour obligations associated with employees — assuming the worker is properly classified as an independent contractor.

I have written agreements with all my contractors. These agreements document the scope of work, payment terms, deliverables and expectations. But a contract alone doesn’t determine someone’s legal classification. Government agencies look at the actual working relationship, not just what the agreement says.

Tax reporting requirements also apply. Depending on the circumstances, you may need to issue Form 1099-NEC to report payments to contractors.

Run these relationships by your accountant and attorney to make sure you’re compliant. Misclassifying an employee as an independent contractor can result in penalties, back taxes and liability for unpaid benefits and wages.

The rules governing independent contractors aren’t necessarily permanent. Federal and state governments have different approaches to worker classification, and regulations can change with new administrations, court decisions and legislative priorities.

Some regulatory changes make it harder for businesses to classify workers as independent contractors, while others give employers more flexibility. These debates often center on worker protections, benefits and the degree of independence a worker actually has.

The takeaway for business owners is simple: Don’t assume today’s rules will remain unchanged. Pay attention to developments in the jurisdictions where you operate, and periodically review your contractor relationships with your legal and accounting advisers.

Because independent contractors are independent, they’re free to follow the money wherever it takes them. They can take on other clients, accept new projects or move on when a better opportunity comes along.

Many of my contractors serve multiple clients, which I actually encourage. It reinforces the independent nature of the relationship and allows them to maintain their own businesses.

But contractors come and go. Some are more entrepreneurial, restless or focused on short-term opportunities than others. That’s why I’ve built relationships with multiple contractors, including some who compete with one another.

This gives me options when someone becomes unavailable, misses a deadline or doesn’t deliver. It also means I’m not dependent on one person to keep an important part of my business running.

Just remember: Finding good people isn’t easy. Building a reliable network of contractors takes time, and you need to invest in those relationships before you need them.

I’ve also learned that hiring an independent contractor who presents themselves as an expert doesn’t guarantee that they actually have the experience or skills you need.

Anyone can hang out a shingle and call themselves an expert. I’ve worked with so-called professionals who were hired to perform specific jobs but misrepresented their experience and capabilities.

When you hire an employee, there’s often a formal vetting process. You review resumes, conduct interviews, check references and involve other people in the decision.

Hiring a capable contractor requires the same level of due diligence. Ask for work samples, speak with previous clients, check references and clearly define expectations before signing an agreement.

Don’t assume someone knows what they’re doing just because they have a website, a business name or an impressive title. You still need to do your homework.

There’s a difference between the relationship a manager has with an employee and the relationship with an outside contractor. Employees generally work within your organization, while contractors maintain their own businesses and client relationships.

My customers understand this, but sometimes I have to explain that the people I’m sending to their projects aren’t my employees. That can raise an eyebrow.

There’s a perception that employees are more dedicated, accountable and easier to manage than outside contractors. Customers may reasonably believe I have less influence over a contractor servicing them than someone on my payroll. They’re not necessarily wrong.

You can’t hide the relationship, and you shouldn’t try to. Customers aren’t necessarily bothered by contractors. They’re bothered by uncertainty over who’s accountable when something goes wrong.

You need to be prepared to explain how you manage quality, communicate expectations and remain responsible for the work being delivered. The customer is hiring your business, and you need to stand behind the results.

Using too many independent contractors can also affect internal relationships and company culture.

Employees may resent the flexibility contractors enjoy or question why certain responsibilities are outsourced instead of handled internally. They may also wonder whether their own contributions are valued if the company regularly turns to outside professionals.

Contractors can become part of a team, but they aren’t employees. How you manage those relationships matters. There are also practical considerations involving confidential information, company data and access to internal systems. Make sure contractors have appropriate agreements and access controls in place to protect your business.

Hiring a contractor for a short-term project is one thing. Relying on contractors for essential, ongoing responsibilities is another. Think carefully about how those decisions affect morale, accountability and the culture you’re trying to build.

I don’t want to discourage business owners from using independent contractors. After more than two decades, I still rely on them, which should tell you something.

But it’s important to understand the trade-offs. Contractors can offer specialized expertise, flexibility and defined deliverables without the long-term commitment of traditional employment. They can also introduce uncertainty around availability, costs, compliance and continuity.

My advice is to use contractors when you need specialized skills, project-based support and flexibility. Hire employees when you need consistency, direct oversight, institutional knowledge and long-term commitment. The right mix can help you build a more flexible and efficient business. Just don’t assume that outsourcing the work means outsourcing the responsibility.

After more than two decades of working with independent contractors, I still believe they’re one of the best ways to run a flexible small business. But I’ve also learned that they’re not nearly as cheap, simple or risk-free as many business owners assume.

There are plenty of advantages. I can hire contractors for specific projects without making a long-term employment commitment. I don’t have to provide employee benefits, paid vacation or other traditional employment perks. I can negotiate project rates, define deliverables and avoid worrying about keeping someone busy when the work dries up. Contractors generally manage their own schedules, tools and methods.

It can be a flexible and cost-effective model. But it’s not all rosy.

#5483. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.
