#5482. The deadliest and biggest blizzards in U.S. history, from 1888 to the Storm of the Century

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A chronological look at all 16 blizzards on one list, from 1888 to 2006, with the snowfall, wind, and death tolls on record.

A winter morning can start calm enough for a walk to school or a drive into town, then turn within a few hours into a wall of blowing snow where a traveler cannot make out the fence post beside the road. The great storms of the past struck with little advance notice. Wind and vanishing sight lines endangered people as much as the depth of the drifts did. A single blizzard can halt travel across a region and leave it digging out for days. Knowing how these storms behaved, and where they hit hardest, explains why a blizzard warning deserves more respect than a forecast of an ordinary snow day.

Visibility sits at the center of the hazard. Falling and blowing snow that cuts the view to less than 500 feet marks one of the thresholds for a blizzard, and the snow does not need to be fresh. In a ground blizzard, wind scoops up settled powder and hurls it back into the air, creating a whiteout beneath a sky that may drop nothing at all. Such events are common across the Plains and the Canadian Prairies. Lead time has grown since the 19th century, and modern long-range forecasts give communities a head start unavailable to residents of that era. The threat persists despite those gains. Heavy snowstorms may be arriving a little less often in some regions, yet they can pack more punch when they form. The atmospheric setup behind the fiercest blizzards on record remains possible.

The chronological record behind this list comes from Farmers' Almanac, whose staff compiled 16 historic blizzards and winter storms from 1888 through 2006 and updated the page on May 7, 2026. The storms covered the Plains, the Upper Midwest, the Great Lakes, the Mid-Atlantic, and the Northeast, and several pushed into Canada. The page records peak local snowfall and deaths wherever a figure exists. The publisher does not rank the storms, explain why it picked these 16, or describe how it gathered the numbers. The slides that follow track the calendar, so each storm's position reflects its date and says nothing about its severity.

A storm swept across the prairies without warning on Jan. 12, 1888, and killed 235 people, most of them children. The young age of so many victims gave the disaster its other name, the Children's Blizzard. A casualty list skewed toward the young shows how little margin the storm left for anyone caught outdoors without cover.

The system pushed south out of Canada and spread over land that now makes up seven states: South Dakota, North Dakota, Nebraska, Minnesota, Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho. Its path stretched from Minnesota west to Idaho. One storm touching that many future states put a vast share of the northern frontier in danger at the same moment.

A crash in temperature drove the catastrophe. In many places, thermometers fell from above freezing to well below zero in a matter of hours. More than six inches of powdery snow arrived with severe winds, and the blowing flakes produced whiteouts over much of the area. Six inches is a modest total for a storm this lethal. The slim accumulation points to the plunging cold and the lost visibility as the chief hazards. The speed of the drop, paired with almost no public notice, accounts for much of the toll.

The chaos of wind, snow, and sudden chill disoriented adults and young people alike, and many could not find any place to shelter. Massive drifts buried roads, houses, and the dead, hampering rescuers. In isolated spots, searchers did not recover some bodies for months.

Grieving families demanded to know why the U.S. Army's Signal Service, the agency then charged with forecasting the country's weather, had issued no alert. The suffering the storm caused pushed the federal government to strengthen and modernize its weather prediction system. A blizzard whose sharpest weapon was surprise helped build the apparatus meant to blunt that surprise.

Violent gusts and deep drifts during the March Blizzard of '88 cut several Northeast cities off from transportation and communication. Temperatures dropped far beneath zero degrees Fahrenheit as the storm raged. Residents boxed in by the drifts endured the cold with no route out and no means of sending word past their own streets.

Isolation paired with severe cold turned a heavy snowfall into a crisis. Halted travel stopped cities from moving people or supplies. Lost communication kept them from reporting conditions or summoning outside aid, and each city faced the blizzard on its own.

New York City absorbed more damage than any other place the storm reached. Its harbor areas took the heaviest blows, and the waterfront became the focal point of the city's losses. The worst harm landed where the city met open water, the ground with the least shelter from the gale.

Two of the 16 storms in this chronology struck in 1888, one on the prairies in January and this one along the Atlantic seaboard in March. The list's compilers trace the severity of both to the same conditions. Temperatures crashed with unusual speed, and the public received little warning. Separated by half a continent and a single winter's weeks, the two storms show that the dangers of that year did not belong to one landscape. Open prairie and a major port city proved equally vulnerable to cold that outran any alert.

Asbury Park, New Jersey, vanished under 24 inches of heavy, wet snow on March 1, 1914, as a storm and its high winds crippled New Jersey and New York. The storm went down as the worst to strike the two states since '88, a mark that had held for 26 years.

New York's barometer sank to a record 28.38 inches during the same storm. The reading gave the 1914 event a second claim to distinction, measured in air pressure instead of snow depth. One state logged the deepest snow. The other logged the record low pressure, and the storm left its imprint on each in a different way.

Downed wires and poles knocked out power and communications across New Jersey. The outages stacked a second crisis on top of the snow, leaving households without electricity and cut off from outside contact. No death toll accompanies the storm's figures.

New Jersey absorbed both the deepest reported snowfall and the only reported loss of power and communication lines, which made the state the place where the 1914 storm inflicted its most visible damage.

The Armistice Day Storm of Nov. 11, 1940, killed 49 people in Minnesota alone, and Minnesota was only one corner of the disaster. Blizzard conditions spread across Minnesota, Wisconsin, Manitoba, and western Ontario as the system swept through the Upper Midwest and the Great Lakes. The storm ignored the international border and pushed whiteouts into two Canadian provinces. Wisconsin, Manitoba, and Ontario carry no death count of their own. The Minnesota figure sets a floor for the toll on land, with no ceiling.

Lake Michigan produced a second catastrophe. Gales churned the lake, wrecked ships, and claimed 59 sailors. The water took 10 more lives than the Minnesota count. Those losses belong to a separate emergency, one that unfolded on open water while snow and wind battered the shore.

Iowa collected 17 inches of snow, the deepest total tied to the storm, despite sitting south of the states and provinces where blizzard conditions raged. The heaviest accumulation fell outside the whiteout zone. The storm's snow reached far beyond the places its wind blinded.

Duluth, Minnesota, registered barometric pressure of 28.66 inches. The reading came from the same state that supplied the only documented deaths on land, so Minnesota holds nearly everything known about the storm's force ashore.

No other storm among the 16 arrived this early in the season. Its losses show that deadly blizzard weather could strike the Upper Midwest and its lakes about a month before the next-earliest storm on the calendar, the Dec. 12, 1960, blizzard.

Note: This slide runs about 240 words, below the 300-word minimum. The source gives the Armistice Day Storm only its date, affected region, the Minnesota death toll, the Lake Michigan sailor deaths, Iowa's snowfall, and the Duluth pressure reading, and no approved supplementary detail covers this storm. Adding more would require padding or invention.

Winds of 85 mph tore through Grand Forks, North Dakota, on March 15, 1941, during a storm the list's compilers describe as the most severe blizzard of the modern era. The system arrived on a Saturday night and battered North Dakota and Minnesota. Parts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba took hits as well, which carried the emergency across the Canadian border.

North Dakota lost 39 people, and Minnesota buried 32 more. Deaths across the storm's full path reached at least 71. North Dakota, home to the strongest recorded wind, accounted for more than half of those fatalities. Minnesota's losses came close behind, and neither state escaped with a glancing blow.

Duluth, Minnesota, clocked 75 mph, about 10 mph short of the Grand Forks peak. Readings this extreme in two states reveal a blizzard that spread its violence across a wide territory. No single city took the full force by itself.

Collegeville, Minnesota, measured 27 inches of snow, and the Twin Cities recorded 16 inches. An 11-inch gap inside one state demonstrates how far a metro total can understate the burden elsewhere. Anyone judging the storm by its big-city numbers would miss its heaviest blow.

The fiercest wind and the deepest snow landed in different states. Grand Forks bore the top wind speed, yet Collegeville, across the line in Minnesota, collected the heaviest total. Minnesota contended with both hazards at punishing strength, absorbing a near-equal gale at Duluth and the storm's biggest snowfall. A death toll tilted toward North Dakota hides how much of the storm's physical force fell on Minnesota.

Newark, New Jersey, absorbed 20.4 inches of snow on Dec. 12, 1960, the deepest city total from a pre-winter blizzard in the Northeast. New York City collected 17 inches during the same storm, and Boston finished with 13. All three cities measured double-digit snow.

Totals thinned along the corridor from Newark toward Boston. Newark ended 3.4 inches ahead of New York City and 7.4 inches ahead of Boston, gathering about 1.5 times the Boston figure. The heaviest load landed on New Jersey, and Massachusetts' capital recorded the lightest of the three big-city counts. New York came close to Newark's mark, while Boston escaped with less than two-thirds of the Newark total.

Nantucket, Massachusetts, complicated that picture. The island logged 15.7 inches, 2.7 inches more than Boston and 1.3 inches short of New York City. Winds there averaged 36 to 51 mph through the storm. Nantucket contended with deep accumulation and sustained wind at once, the pairing that turns a heavy snowfall into a blizzard. Even the low end of that range signals a steady push of air across the island. The island never approached Newark's total, yet it carried the storm's clearest recorded blizzard signature.

The December blizzard opened a punishing season. It struck ahead of the calendar start of winter, the timing behind its pre-winter label. The Kennedy Inaugural Snowstorm in January counts as the second of three major Northeast storms in the winter of 1960-61, which makes this mid-December event the first of the trio. A third followed on Feb. 3-4, 1961. The Northeast endured all three within a span of 54 days. The gap between the December storm and the January storm ran little more than five weeks. Newark's 20.4 inches marked the opening blow of a winter that would bury the region twice more by early February.

The Kennedy Inaugural Snowstorm of Jan. 19-20, 1961, saved its heaviest accumulations for New England, where Connecticut and New Hampshire each measured 25 inches. Massachusetts trailed by a single inch at 24. The system arrived as the second of three major storms to strike the Northeast during the winter of 1960-61, and a third followed in February. Its drifts had little chance to clear before the next round. The February snow came down on leftover piles from the earlier storms. This storm's contribution fed a burden that lingered into the third.

Washington and Baltimore each collected 8 inches, a fraction of New England's depth. New York City measured 10. Connecticut's total outstripped the capital's by 17 inches. The steepest climb came north and east of New York City, where totals jumped another 14 to 15 inches into Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire. The rise from the two Mid-Atlantic cities to New York amounted to 2 inches.

The figures split the storm's footprint into two zones. Along the Mid-Atlantic, totals stayed under 1 foot. Across New England, they reached 2 feet. New York City sat closer to the southern figures than to the northern ones and shared the Mid-Atlantic's modest range. A traveler heading north from the capital would have watched the snow more than triple by the end of the trip.

Inauguration Day gave the storm its name and placed it among famous snowstorms tied to dates on the calendar. Christmas, New Year's, Groundhog Day, Presidents' Day, and Valentine's Day belong to the same group. The publisher reads the clustering as a reflection of when reporters notice storms. By that account, the holidays reveal nothing about when storms reach their peak. The Kennedy name also pins this storm to a single day, even though the snow fell across two. A name borrowed from the calendar steers attention toward the date of the snowfall and away from New England, where the snow climbed highest.

Cortland, New York, collected 40 inches of snow on Feb. 3-4, 1961, the heaviest total anywhere during the third big storm of the 1960-61 winter. The upstate town topped the deepest readings from the season's earlier Kennedy Inaugural Snowstorm by 15 inches. Cortland's figure came close to doubling the largest city total from the December storm that opened the sequence. The winter's final major storm produced the most extreme single-place accumulation of the three.

New York City carried the biggest load among the major metros, with 19 to 24 inches. Boston picked up 14.4 inches, and Washington, D.C., and Baltimore each received 8 to 11 inches. The low end of New York City's range beat the high end in the two southern cities by eight inches. Boston edged past what it measured in December, and Washington and Baltimore matched or exceeded their January totals. The listed totals crested in New York state, from the city up to Cortland, and tapered off toward Baltimore in the south and Boston in the northeast.

New snow settled onto piles still standing from the December and January storms, pushing snow cover across major metropolitan areas near record levels. The February storm gave New York City at least nine more inches than the January storm did. Across all three storms, New York City's totals add up to between 46 and 51 inches. The February storm supplied about 41% to 47% of that winter sum. Street-level depth in the major cities reflected the whole winter's tally, with each storm stacking on the last.

Coastal communities faced damaging winds that ranged from gale strength to hurricane force. Three major storms in less than eight weeks, from Dec. 12 to Feb. 4, left little time for the ground to clear between blows. The 1960-61 sequence shows a winter's danger can build through accumulation as much as through any single storm.

The Groundhog Day Storm of Feb. 2, 1976, drove barometric pressure down to 28.30 inches, lower than many summer hurricanes manage. The system gathered strength off the Delmarva Coast, the shoreline shared by Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia, and then raced northeast. Its reading sat 0.08 inch beneath the record New York barometer from the March 1914 storm and 0.36 inch beneath the Duluth, Minnesota, value logged during the 1940 Armistice Day Storm. No pressure figure elsewhere in this collection dips lower.

Rapid deepening off the Mid-Atlantic coast fueled most of the Northeast blizzards in this collection, a process meteorologists now call bombogenesis. The 1976 system followed that script, intensifying off Delmarva before it swept northeast. Among those coastal storms, none pushed the barometer further down.

Gusts of 100 mph lashed Nova Scotia, the fastest wind the list attaches a number to. The figure beats the 85 mph winds at Grand Forks, North Dakota, during the 1941 blizzard by 15 mph and the 69 mph Buffalo gusts of 1977 by 31 mph. The storm's fiercest measured winds struck in Canada, outside the U.S.

Blizzard conditions gripped the Northeast for a brief window, and temperatures fell 20 to 40 degrees within a few hours.

The list records no snowfall total and no death count for this storm. Its place among these entries rests on barometer readings, wind, and a fast temperature slide, which makes it the clearest case here of a storm remembered for its force instead of its accumulation.

This slide runs about 245 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source gives the Groundhog Day Storm only its Delmarva origin, brief blizzard conditions, a 20- to 40-degree temperature drop, 100 mph gusts in Nova Scotia, and a 28.30-inch pressure reading, with no snowfall or deaths recorded, and no approved web details cover this storm.

Gusts reaching 69 mph drove Buffalo, New York, into whiteouts on Jan. 30, 1977. Visibility collapsed to zero, and the wind chill plunged to minus 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Wind, sight, and cold make up the storm's entire profile, and none of the readings measures snow depth.

Zero visibility marks the extreme end of a whiteout. Snow blowing that thick erased the street ahead and the buildings beside it. Buffalo residents lost their most basic tool for finding their way, their own eyesight. A driver could not judge the edge of a road, and a pedestrian could not pick out a doorway a few steps off.

The wind chill compounded the hazard. A reading of minus 50 captures gusts and cold striking exposed skin together. The same gusts that blinded the city also sharpened the cold. Each threat made the other worse. Anyone stranded outdoors in Buffalo that day faced danger from the air itself, apart from anything piled on the ground.

Buffalo turns up again and again in the record of great American storms, alongside Syracuse and Cleveland. Lake-effect snow hit each of those cities on top of systems that carried considerable force on their own. Lake effect can lift a single location's total far above a storm's average across its whole path.

Buffalo's 1977 entry rests on wind and cold alone, proof that a city famous for lake-effect accumulation can face severe conditions from forces no snow gauge captures.

Reports placed 50 inches or more of snow across a small area of northern Rhode Island after the Blizzard of '78 struck New England on Feb. 6 and 7, 1978. Hurricane-force winds drove the storm, and record-breaking accumulations piled up across parts of the Northeast. Wind and depth together put it among the more intense storms the region faced in the 20th century.

Boston collected 27.1 inches, little more than half the Rhode Island mark. Even this total fell short of the snow the city later took from the Blizzard of 2003, which set Boston's record for a single storm.

The city stayed shut for a full week. Seven days of closure followed a snowfall below what Boston later recorded, so depth alone cannot account for how long the city sat idle. A storm can paralyze a major city for a week without delivering its heaviest snow there or setting a local record.

The Presidents' Day Storm of Feb. 19, 1979, dropped 18.7 inches of snow on the airport serving Washington, D.C., in 18.5 hours. The pace averaged about an inch every hour from start to finish. Any surface cleared at the airport would have gained another inch within an hour. Depth on the ground at the same site reached 23 inches. The 18.5-hour burst supplied about 81% of that depth, which leaves some 4.3 inches outside the window.

Baltimore's airport collected 20 inches, 1.3 inches more than the Washington measurement taken during the storm's main burst. Airports serving two neighboring cities finished within a couple of inches of each other. The match suggests the heaviest snow fell across a broad zone between the two cities and did not concentrate on a single one. Neither Washington nor Baltimore can claim to have taken the worst of the storm alone.

The Middle Atlantic states absorbed the hardest blow, and the storm set snowfall records in many parts of the region. Its footprint stands out in this chronology. The 1914 storm buried Asbury Park, the December 1960 blizzard hit Newark hardest, and the third big snow of 1961 piled its deepest total on Cortland, New York. The Blizzard of '78 reserved its heaviest accumulation for northern Rhode Island.

Washington and Baltimore had shown up on this list before, with smaller amounts. The 1979 totals in both cities outstripped what either 1961 storm delivered there. Southern cities on the Northeast Corridor proved capable of absorbing snowfall on the scale of the heaviest hits farther north.

The Blizzard of '93 killed more than 200 people over March 13-14, 1993, and the National Weather Service judged it "one of the worst storms of the century." The agency reached its verdict at the time, with several years of the 1900s still to run. Its judgment set the 1993 system against nearly a century of predecessors and found few equals.

The system stretched from Cuba to Canada. A track of that length pulled the Caribbean, the U.S. South, and the northern border region into one weather event. The popular nickname for the blizzard, the Storm of the Century, borrows its wording from the weather service's assessment.

Birmingham, Alabama, collected 13 inches of snow, more than a foot in a Deep South city. Syracuse, New York, absorbed 36 inches, nearly triple the Birmingham figure. The two readings bracket the path, with heavy accumulation at its southern end and the deepest piles in New York. A foot-plus snowfall in Birmingham shows how far toward the Gulf states the system carried true winter conditions.

Reports described dozens of tornadoes striking the South as the system advanced. Communities across the region faced snow and twisters from the same event. None of the other 15 storms in this record comes with a tornado report. The Blizzard of '93 stands alone among them as a winter system that hit one region with both a foot of snow and dozens of twisters.

The Blizzard of '96 killed 100 people during a two-day siege of the Northeast on Jan. 7-8, 1996. Snow piled one to two feet deep across the region. The depth appears as a regional range with no single city's total, which points to a storm that spread its harm across many communities at once.

Air travel through the Northeast Corridor halted as major airports there closed for at least two days. The closures matched or outlasted the storm's own two-day run on the calendar. Passengers moving through the corridor's hubs lost flights for the entire span of the blizzard.

The grounded flights cut the region's fastest connection to the rest of the country, which left the snowbound corridor sealed off by air for as long as the storm raged.

The Blizzard of 2003 dropped 28.2 inches on Baltimore, the heaviest snowstorm in the city's records. Boston set its own all-time high in the same event, with 27.5 inches. Only 0.7 inch separated the two figures. One storm broke the standing record in two major cities and gave both near-identical depths.

The storm carries two alternate names, the Presidents' Day Storm of 2003 and Presidents' Day Storm II. It ran from Feb. 14 to Feb. 19, a six-day span that opened on Valentine's Day and stretched across the holiday behind its other titles. The system took shape along the U.S. East Coast and pushed north into Canada. Its track crossed the border after leaving Baltimore and Boston behind.

Every city from Washington, D.C., to Boston lay under 15 to 30 inches. The snow and the cold that came with it brought normal routines across that corridor to a standstill. Baltimore landed 1.8 inches below the range's 30-inch upper limit, and Boston 2.5 inches below it. Even the 15-inch low end of that range would have topped every accumulation either city logged on this list during the 1960s.

Boston's 2003 snow beat its Blizzard of '78 reading by 0.4 inch. Baltimore cleared its biggest earlier snowfall on the list, the airport measurement from the 1979 Presidents' Day Storm, by 8.2 inches. Boston waited 25 years between its two largest storms here, and Baltimore waited 24. Both 2003 totals also exceed the all-time mark New York City set three years later in the Blizzard of 2006.

The same blizzard nudged Boston's best showing on this list up by less than half an inch and lifted Baltimore's by 41%. Boston had absorbed a storm close to that size in 1978. Baltimore had no earlier storm on this list within 8 inches of the 2003 snow.

New York City set its all-time snowfall high in February 2006, when a nor'easter left 26.9 inches on the ground. No storm had buried the city deeper in measurements dating to 1869.

The system took shape on the evening of Feb. 11 and spread heavy snow from Virginia to Maine. Snow kept coming until the early evening of Feb. 12. The Northeast absorbed the bulk of its accumulation in about a day. The storm then moved into Atlantic Canada and wound down there on Feb. 13. Its life cycle spanned three calendar days, from its start in the U.S. to its finish in Canada.

The storm's reach covered the Mid-Atlantic and New England in one sweep. The same coastal belt took the brunt of the 1960, 1961, 1979, 1996, and 2003 storms, a pattern showing how often the corridor's biggest cities endure one system together.

New York's top snowstorm arrived in the 21st century, more than 100 years after the city began keeping track. Earlier storms hit the city hard without approaching the 2006 total. The March Blizzard of 1888 inflicted its worst damage around New York's harbor. The 1914 storm drove the city's barometer to an unprecedented low. Three separate storms then struck New York during the winter of 1960-61.

None of those events matched the 2006 depth in a single blow. The February 1961 storm flirted with a different kind of milestone, dropping fresh snow onto leftover heaps until snow cover in major metro areas neared historic levels. Accumulated cover tracks a whole season's buildup, while a storm total isolates one event's punch. The 2006 nor'easter owns the second distinction.

New York's benchmark survived generations of punishing winters and then gave way to the last storm on this list, a reminder that a city's worst storm need not belong to its distant past.

#5481. A Microsoft exec says AI is killing the career ladder. But its replacement comes with a catch

For the past few months, Microsoft chief economic opportunity officer Aneesh Raman has been predicting the death of the traditional career ladder as AI reshapes the workplace. In its place, he envisions a “climbing wall,” where progress isn’t always upward and workers chart their own paths based on their unique skills, interests, and opportunities.

But if career advancement becomes less predictable, what does that mean for women and other historically marginalized groups, who research suggests benefit from clear criteria for raises and promotions? I put that question to Raman at Aspen Digital’s WIN Summit in late October.

Raman acknowledged that losing the familiar career playbook could initially be intimidating, but argued that it could ultimately give workers more freedom to advance in ways that suit their individual strengths and ambitions. “Over time, you start to climb in ways that are unique to you,” he said.

Part of the answer, Raman said, is “radical transparency”: ensuring workers understand how AI is changing their jobs and what opportunities they have to shape their own careers.

But if AI is helping rewrite the rules of career advancement, there’s reason to question whether women and men will benefit equally. New research from Nicole Smith, a senior researcher at Pew Research Center, found that in more AI-exposed occupations, men’s employment grew 6.3% for each one-point increase in an occupation’s exposure score, while women’s barely changed. Among workers with a high school diploma or less, women’s employment fell.

Smith also pointed to a divide in how men and women are approaching the technology.  Men are much more optimistic about AI than women, she said, and may be more inclined to use it to pursue new opportunities. “We need to change our mindset and to make sure that we open these conversations to women,” she said.

Raman, meanwhile, believes women could have an edge in the AI era. He argues that women over-index on uniquely human skills, such as empathy and judgement that will become increasingly valuable as AI transforms work. He predicts that more women will become CEOs and that women’s representation on corporate boards could climb from roughly a third to half or more.

The question now is whether employers can make career advancement more flexible without making the path to success less equitable.

Kristin StollerEditorial Director, Fortune Live Mediakristin.stoller@fortune.com

This week, author and career coach Jeremy Schifeling answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: I’ve applied to nearly 200 jobs over the past few months and have heard almost nothing back. No interviews, often not even a rejection email—just silence. I’m starting to wonder if AI screening tools are filtering me out before a human ever sees my application.

But another part of me wonders if that’s an excuse, and the real problem is me: my résumé, my experience, or skills that no longer match what employers want. How do I figure out which it is, and what should I change?

A: First, take a breath. Nearly 200 applications and silence isn't a verdict on you—it's a sign the strategy is broken, not the person.

Here's the truth about AI screening: it's rarely a robot rejecting you. Most applicant tracking systems just sort and rank. The real problem is volume. Thanks to AI, everyone's applying everywhere—in my latest survey of 236 job seekers, 81% now use AI to apply, and the people who applied the most got hired the least. When a posting gets 1,000 applicants, recruiters stop reading after the first few dozen good-enough matches.

So how do you figure out which it is? Run a quick test. Pick the five roles you're most qualified for and compare your resume to each posting, line by line. If the posting's top skills aren't in the top third of your resume, that's a fixable resume problem. If they are and you still hear nothing, it's a channel problem.

And the channel fix is the big one: stop sending application No. 201. For every role you really want, find one person at that company—an alum, a former colleague, a friend of a friend—and ask for 15 minutes of advice. A referral moves you from the bottom of the pile to the top of it.

Fewer applications, more humans. That's the whole game now.

#5480. My 5-Part Leadership Playbook for Freeing Up Time and Growing Your Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your business can’t scale if every decision depends on you. These five leadership shifts will help you reclaim your time and build a stronger team.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Throughout my career as a business leader, entrepreneur and executive coach, I’ve learned to focus on the work that matters most — the decisions, challenges and relationships where my experience and judgment make the biggest difference. That means building better systems, developing new skills, strengthening relationships and empowering my team. These investments compound over time, helping my businesses grow without requiring me to weigh in on every decision.

If you want to do the same, here are five practical changes you can make today.

Doing less yourself doesn’t mean working less. Your value isn’t measured by how much you personally execute. Administrative tasks can quickly consume your day without moving your business forward.

I divide my workload into two categories: below-the-line and above-the-line work. Below-the-line tasks include email, scheduling and project tracking. Above-the-line work is where your judgment matters most: setting strategy, making critical decisions, solving problems and building relationships.

AI creates opportunities to move more work below the line. Start by listing what consumes your time, then determine what you can automate, delegate or eliminate. Build a focused ecosystem of AI agents that can research your industry, track competitors, monitor key performance indicators (KPIs) and prepare meeting notes.

This approach helps me protect 90-minute blocks for deep work, giving me more time to focus on challenges that genuinely require my expertise. After spending too many years on below-the-line tasks, my advice is simple: Let AI handle more of the administrative work so you can focus your best skills on what matters most.

The moment you think you know everything may be the moment a competitor passes you by. Maintaining a humble, curious mindset has helped me recognize new opportunities, grow as a leader and strengthen my businesses. Learning doesn’t end with a degree. Keep developing new skills, pursuing relevant credentials and embracing a learner’s mindset throughout your career.

AI is a good place to start. Go beyond basic chatbot prompts and learn how AI agents, automation and interconnected systems can work together to improve your business. One agent might research competitors, another monitor regulatory changes and a third identify potential investors or financing opportunities. AI can also surface emerging industry topics, creating opportunities to contribute thought leadership before a conversation gains momentum.

I recommend programs from Vanderbilt Executive Education and MIT Professional Education. Both offer focused learning opportunities centered on executive strategy without getting lost in the technical details.

Entrepreneurs are often wired to jump in and solve problems immediately. Eventually, that instinct can become counterproductive. You’ve built a team for a reason, and neither you nor your employees need you involved in everything.

I learned this firsthand as an executive at Intel. During a period when I was pushing myself too hard, the pressure spilled over onto my team. Instead of delegating thoughtfully, I sent early-morning emails and created unnecessary work. When team members told me they were stressed, it was a wake-up call. I realized my team needed me to operate at my best and help them do the same.

I started with a simple coaching principle: Stop offering answers and solutions too quickly. When someone brings you a problem, ask them to recommend a solution, too.

If you want your team to think strategically, give them opportunities to contribute to important decisions. Challenge their thinking, encourage them to evaluate trade-offs and let them own the solutions.

You’ll gain a better understanding of their strengths while developing decisive leaders who can exercise sound judgment without relying on you for every answer.

Networking in the digital age can mean little more than accepting an invitation or adding a connection. But a connection is only the beginning. Would that person invest in you or your business? Could you call each other for advice, an introduction or a potential partnership?

The strongest relationships become more valuable over time. Alpine Investors founder Graham Weaver calls these “lifetime relationships.”When Weaver started his company at 28, he struggled to raise funds. Two investors with whom he had built relationships eventually backed him, helping get the business off the ground. He has said the company wouldn’t exist without their belief in him.

Building lasting relationships requires more than accepting another LinkedIn request. Someone you meet today could eventually become a strategic partner, join your board or help you raise capital. One day, you may be the person they turn to.

Prioritize meaningful relationships over simply accumulating social media connections. Invest time in being authentic. Send the card. Check in when you don’t need anything. Pick up the phone when someone calls for advice.

These small gestures build trust over time and create a network of people who will be there when it matters most.

At a certain point in your career, success becomes less about what you accomplish personally and more about the leaders you develop.

Sharing credit is also a performance strategy. It recognizes strong contributions, reinforces positive behaviors and builds a team capable of achieving more without routing every decision through you.

Give talented employees opportunities to take ownership. Include them when recognition is given, let them lead presentations, put them in front of clients and trust them to make important decisions.

Research from Gallup found that 61% of employees who received both feedback and recognition from their manager at least weekly were engaged, compared with 38% of employees who received weekly feedback but less frequent recognition.

When your people deliver results, make sure they receive the credit. Recognizing their contributions reinforces a culture in which people feel valued and motivated to do their best work.

Think of these five shifts as a starting point, not a rigid formula. Put them into practice, pay attention to what works and adjust what doesn’t.

Through experimentation, you’ll develop an approach that fits your leadership style, your business and your team. Keep investing in the systems, skills and relationships that help you operate at your best.

#5479. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5478. Gordon Ritter: who owns the intelligence economy?

The rules governing the AI economy are being written by default.

Back in June, I argued that the AI doomers are incorrectly counting jobs when they should be counting traces. Traces are what people leave behind on every system they touch: corrections, judgment calls, reasoning that closed the deal, workarounds not found in a manual. They are among a company’s most valuable assets. So, who owns them?

No one has decided yet, and that window won’t stay open long. Take the growth of radio in the 1920s. American broadcasters staked out radio frequencies faster than the law could follow. By the time Congress passed the Radio Act of 1927, control had already solidified. The Communications Act of 1934 ratified it.

Radio was a bureaucratic battle about who owned the airwaves. The resource today is human intelligence: how people reason, decide, and create. If we treat it as something to extract rather than cultivate, we drain the source every future breakthrough depends on.

Companies building AI on employees’ work stake a claim about who owns what a system learns. If we don’t shape the rules now, the companies controlling the most powerful models will set the terms, and everyone else will pay rent.

Here is a starting point, a social contract for the intelligence economy with three layers: platform, organization, and individual.

At the platform level: choice. No single model should become the unavoidable infrastructure of intelligence. As foundation model capabilities converge, the durable advantage remains above the model, living in the learning loop an organization builds on top of whichever model it runs.

Providers make switching costly, often binding organizations to the first model they adopted. Access to AI should not require surrendering intelligence as a condition of service.

At the organization level: sovereignty. The learning loops, workflows, and domain expertise organizations build on top of AI belong to organizations.

Human expertise is already being turned into training data for AI: RedCompass Labs trains its Payment Expert Agent with Cognitive Task Analysis (CTA), turning thousands of hours of expert work into datasets that teach AI how specialists’ reason and make decisions.

Employees who use public AI tools at work are teaching an external agent how the organization operates, one of the most valuable things a model can learn. Enterprise contracts often prohibit training on internal data, but protections around behavioral traces and process knowledge are far less settled.

Not every workflow deserves the same protection. Routine operations can stay transparent by default. The outliers are another story: the rep who ignores the script and closes the deal anyway, the engineer’s fix that isn’t in any runbook. That’s the generative part of the loop, and sovereignty claims belong with the judgment that changed the outcome.

At the individual level: appreciation. I mean the word the way an investor does. A person’s judgment should be worth more when they leave a job than when they arrived. Models get smarter by learning from human judgment. Do humans get smarter too? What does each side keep when the relationship ends? This is the least settled layer.

AI can become crutch software, which hands over answers without asking the user to judge accuracy, quality, or offer improvements. In one study, undergraduates who used ChatGPT as a study aid scored significantly lower on a surprise retention test 45 days later than students who stuck with traditional study methods. The tool gave correct answers but removed the recall that makes learning sticky.

But a crutch is a design choice. In a separate study, Harvard researchers tested an AI tutor that withheld answers until students reasoned their way to them. These students achieved more learning gains on tests right after the lessons and spent less time than peers in an active-learning classroom. This study doesn’t establish long-term retention, but it showed how AI can be designed to support learning.

I believe technology should make people better at their work. This is the next layer of our 2017 Coaching Networks thesis. The first generation collects and spreads top performers’ moves to everyone else. The next generation must help people invent new moves, and that requires friction. Without it, workers atrophy as AI ascends.

People should also leave their roles with more than they brought in. A doctor leaves a hospital, and they take their clinical judgment. The hospital keeps patient records and protocols. AI blurs that line by capturing both a person’s output and the approach.

A “cognitive passport” could restore it: a portable, anonymized record of how a person approaches problems, excluding deals, documents, and confidential processes. The company keeps what it learned. The person keeps their judgment. That portability gives people a reason to keep growing and contributing, and companies that support it will recruit against companies that don’t.

Consider an enterprise sales representative moving on from her role. Over four years, her company’s AI watched thousands of her calls and every deal she closed. It learned the company’s pricing and how she handles negotiations, which accounts were in play, and when she brings in senior leaders. It saw how she opens with a question about the buyer’s last quarter instead of leading with the product, how she slows down when a CFO joins, and how she drops the script entirely with technical buyers. It then coaches the rest of the team using her moves.

When she leaves, the calls, records, lead lists, customers, deal details, and pricing stay with the business. So does the coaching model, including everything it learned from her.

Her passport records her patterns and the shape of her work, like when she departs from the script or the moments she overrode the system and was right. Her habit of opening with a question about the buyer’s last quarter is hers. Her company’s 18 percent discount floor is not. The passport is generated by the system that holds the data, cleared by the employer against a confidentiality review, and judged by whoever hires her next, like a portfolio. What doesn’t exist yet is a common format that would make a passport from one company mean something at the next.

The temptation now is to use AI to reduce human work. This is the wrong target. The goal should be to make human thinking more powerful, durable, and portable. People will keep working. The question is whether the intelligence they generate compounds in their favor or flows to a platform they don’t control.

It is early enough that the answer is still a choice. A McKinsey study found that while 89% of organizations are using AI in at least one business function, only 44% started to scale it. That is exactly the window where a genuine-choice principle has the most impact.

To be clear where I sit: Emergence Capital is a venture firm, and we make money when the companies we back become more valuable. But more than twenty years in enterprise software have taught me that technology creates the most value when the people whose thinking feeds it trusts the system.

This framework needs stress-testing from founders, researchers, legal scholars and labor voices, and I expect to be wrong about parts of it.

Humans are the only mutation engine in the age of AI. AI can master any game with fixed rules. Markets keep changing the rules, and people are the first to see the new game. The people whose judgment trains today’s AI systems should be treated as co-authors, not raw material.

#5477. More Isn’t Always Better — How the Constant Push For More Content Makes Everyone’s Branding Identical

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As technology and AI make professional content easier to produce, the real competitive advantage is shifting from production quality to having something genuinely worth saying.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Real estate might produce more marketing per transaction than almost any other professional services industry on earth. Professional photography, drone footage, property films, social reels, brochures, digital advertising, portal listings, email campaigns. A single home sale can generate more content than some companies produce in a quarter. And somehow, most of it sounds exactly the same.

That contradiction is worth sitting with. Because the instinct when marketing isn’t working is almost always to produce more of it. Better cameras. Bigger budgets. More platforms. Higher production value. Real estate has been running that experiment for years, and the result is a market where everything looks increasingly polished and increasingly identical.

Not long ago, professional photography was a genuine differentiator in real estate marketing. Most agents were shooting listings on a phone or hiring whoever was cheapest. The agent who showed up with a real photographer was doing something visibly different. That gap closed fast.

Now AI is closing the remaining gaps even faster. Listing descriptions that once took time to write get generated in seconds. Virtual staging that required a designer now takes minutes. Video editing tools that demanded technical skill are increasingly automated. The production floor for every agent, every brokerage, every proptech startup keeps rising.

Here’s the problem with a rising floor. When everyone’s production quality improves simultaneously, production quality stops differentiating anything. Better cameras didn’t solve real estate marketing. They created better-looking sameness. And AI is about to make mediocre content infinitely easier to produce at scale, which means the volume of indistinguishable marketing is going to increase dramatically before anyone figures out that more isn’t the answer.

This isn’t just a real estate problem. It’s happening across every industry that produces content. Design tools democratized. Video became accessible. Writing assistance arrived. The production barrier dropped everywhere. What used to be scarce, the ability to make something that looked and sounded professional, became abundant. The scarcity moved somewhere else entirely.

Walk through luxury real estate marketing for an hour and a specific vocabulary emerges. Stunning. Exclusive. One-of-a-kind. White-glove. Market leader. Exceptional. Timeless. These words appear so consistently across so many properties, agents and brokerages that they’ve stopped communicating anything. They’re filler. Placeholder language that signals luxury without describing it, claims distinction without demonstrating it and tells the audience essentially nothing about why this particular property or this particular professional is worth paying attention to.

Agent marketing has its own version. Top producer. Local expert. Client first. Results driven. These phrases are so universal that a consumer could copy and paste them between dozens of competing agent websites without anyone noticing. They describe an aspiration, not a reality. They make no claim that a competitor couldn’t make with identical credibility the same afternoon.

Proptech marketing runs the same pattern. Seamless. Transparent. Frictionless. Innovative. Reimagining. Disrupting. The vocabulary of disruption has become so widespread that it now signals nothing about actual disruption. Every company claims to be solving the same friction. Almost none of them tell you what specifically they understand about human behavior that nobody else has figured out yet.

If your story only gets interesting after someone learns the price, you probably don’t have much of a story.

The question most marketers ask is: What should we post? The question that actually matters is: What do we have that’s genuinely worth saying? Those questions produce different answers, and the gap between them is where most marketing fails.

At the property level, stories rarely live in the obvious places. Price is not a story. Square footage is not a story. Photographs of a great kitchen are not a story. Stories live in the things that made a property what it is. An architect who designed a home around how morning light moves through a specific valley at a specific time of year. A restoration that brought back materials the original builder sourced from a place that no longer exists. A working ranch that has passed through the same family for three generations and carries a particular relationship to the land that no newly built property can replicate. These things are specific. Specific is the opposite of forgettable.

At the professional level, the story underneath the obvious claims is almost always more interesting than the claims themselves. Not a top producer, but the agent who noticed a decade ago that a specific type of buyer was quietly moving into a region nobody was paying attention to and spent years learning that market before it became obvious. Not a local expert, but the broker who walked away from a larger firm to focus exclusively on a property type most of her competitors couldn’t competently sell. That kind of specificity is earned. Competitors can claim to be local experts tomorrow. They can’t claim ten years of transactions in a niche they didn’t bother to understand.

At the company level, the story worth telling is almost never about features. It’s about the assumption that turned out to be wrong, the behavior that changed, the customer experience that should have worked differently and didn’t. Why does this company need to exist right now rather than five years ago? What did the founders see that others were explaining away? Those are interesting questions. Feature lists are not.

For most of business history, the ability to produce something polished was itself a competitive advantage. Small companies couldn’t afford it. Individual professionals couldn’t access it. The production barrier kept a lot of people out.

That barrier is gone. Anyone can produce something that looks and sounds professional. The tools exist, the cost has collapsed and AI is accelerating the trend in ways that will make the current volume of mediocre content look modest by comparison.

What hasn’t been automated is having something genuinely worth saying. A perspective that comes from actual experience rather than market research. A story that could only be told by this company, this agent, this property. A claim specific enough that a competitor couldn’t make it without lying.

Real estate doesn’t have a content shortage. It has a story shortage. And the response most of the industry is reaching for, more content, better production, more platforms, more posting, is solving a problem that stopped being the real problem a while ago.

The companies that figure that out will stop asking how to make more marketing and start asking whether they have anything worth marketing in the first place. That’s an uncomfortable question. It’s also the right one.

Real estate might produce more marketing per transaction than almost any other professional services industry on earth. Professional photography, drone footage, property films, social reels, brochures, digital advertising, portal listings, email campaigns. A single home sale can generate more content than some companies produce in a quarter. And somehow, most of it sounds exactly the same.

That contradiction is worth sitting with. Because the instinct when marketing isn’t working is almost always to produce more of it. Better cameras. Bigger budgets. More platforms. Higher production value. Real estate has been running that experiment for years, and the result is a market where everything looks increasingly polished and increasingly identical.

Not long ago, professional photography was a genuine differentiator in real estate marketing. Most agents were shooting listings on a phone or hiring whoever was cheapest. The agent who showed up with a real photographer was doing something visibly different. That gap closed fast.

#5475. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5474. Weil Gotshal’s collapse highlights the risk of building a business around star talent

When Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced plans to wind down last week, the collapse of the 95-year-old law firm stunned the legal industry. Weil had roughly 1,200 lawyers, more than $2 billion in annual revenue, and a roster of major corporate clients. Yet the exit of a handful of powerful partners triggered a wave of resignations that ultimately pushed the firm toward dissolution.At Weil, one of those performers was Michael Aiello, the firm’s highest-paid partner and a leading dealmaker who reportedly earned more than $20 million annually. Aiello oversaw a corporate practice of more than 600 people and maintained a close relationship with longtime leader Barry Wolf. When he left for rival Cravath in September, taking five partners with him, the departures helped unleash a broader wave of defections.Weil’s predicament illustrates the vulnerability of businesses built around individuals whose commercial value gives them extraordinary leverage. Star performers attract clients, generate revenue, and recruit other talented people. But when those relationships and capabilities remain concentrated in a few hands, the company becomes increasingly exposed if they leave.The same risk can exist at investment banks, where a rainmaker controls relationships with major clients; at consulting firms, where senior partners bring in much of the business; and at technology companies, where a founder or influential executive becomes synonymous with the organization’s success. Even within smaller divisions and functions, teams can become overly dependent on a single high performer whose departure leaves a gap in expertise, relationships, or leadership that others aren’t prepared to fill.For leaders at every level, the challenge is capturing the benefits of exceptional talent while ensuring their teams and businesses can withstand losing it. That means expanding client relationships across teams, building a deeper bench of people who can generate business, and distributing knowledge and decision-making authority.For ambitious professionals, the episode raises a related question. How much of one’s career’s value depends on the continued success or the support of one influential leader? The lesson may be to build two kinds of career capital simultaneously: One is the value created within an organization, and the other is the value one can carry elsewhere.

#5473. Staggered Agency Filings Squeeze Stablecoin Issuers as Fed Misses Statutory Rulemaking Target

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The statutory deadline for federal regulators to issue final payment stablecoin implementing rules passed on July 18, 2026, one year after the GENIUS Act’s enactment, with no primary regulator having finalized them.

The Federal Reserve did not publish its core issuer proposal until September 29, leaving the least runway before the Act’s January 18, 2027 outer date.

By waiting until late September to issue its Notices of Proposed Rulemaking, the Fed compressed the remaining timeline for final rule implementation. With no final rules issued in time, the January 18, 2027 date now governs by default.

Under Section 108 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, the law takes effect on the earlier of January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final regulations are published by primary federal payment stablecoin regulators. With public comment windows for late-filing agencies remaining open well into the fourth quarter of 2026, regulators face a tight timeframe to review public feedback, coordinate interagency harmonization, and publish final rules before the statutory outer boundary arrives in 91 days.

As of publication, no primary regulator has issued a final rule across the execution timeline:

Because the Federal Reserve's public comment window under FR Doc. 2026-21104 remains open through November 30, 2026, the central bank cannot legally publish a finalized rule until December 2026 at the earliest.

Under the statutory 120-day transition clause in Section 108, any final rule published after September 20, 2026, fails to trigger an accelerated effective date ahead of January 18, 2027. Consequently, the default January 18 outer limit now serves as the primary target.

However, if the Fed and FDIC require additional weeks in December and January to reconcile public comments against OCC and Treasury frameworks, market participants will face a narrow window between final rule publication and mandatory compliance.

With the Treasury’s main issuance comment period closing today, October 19, attention shifts to the OCC’s imminent final rule release.

If the OCC publishes its final standards this month while the Fed continues accepting comments through late November, national banks and non-bank stablecoin issuers will navigate a staggered compliance environment. Issuers must monitor official Federal Register notices over the next 60 days to determine whether regulators achieve interagency alignment before the statutory deadline arrives.

#5471. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 9:05 am

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications, Luebbe said.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. Luebbe said the site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months, Luebbe said.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5470. Current price of oil as of October 30, 2026

At 8:15 a.m. Eastern Time on October 30, 2026, oil was priced at $118.07 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s an increase of $2.67 compared with yesterday morning and around $53 higher than the price one year ago.

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

Joseph is a staff writer on Fortune's personal finance commerce team. He's covered personal finance since 2016, previously serving as a reporter and editor at sites like Business Insider and The Points Guy. He has also contributed to major outlets such as AP News, CNN, Newsweek, and many more.
