#5469. AI and Emerging Tech Are Changing How People Travel. Here’s How Travel Businesses Can Stay Visible and Valuable

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

See how AI, virtual reality and predictive analytics are changing travel planning, search and advisor value.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Technology has always shaped how we travel. What’s different now is how quickly it’s influencing nearly every stage of the experience.

Artificial intelligence is changing how travelers search for and evaluate their options. Virtual reality is helping people visualize destinations before they arrive. Predictive analytics is helping travel companies anticipate what customers may need before they ask.

As chief information officer of Cruise Planners, I spend a lot of time thinking about what these changes mean for travelers and advisors. The biggest opportunity isn’t removing people from the travel experience. It’s using technology to make them more informed, efficient and valuable.

One of the biggest shifts happening now is the move from traditional search to conversational discovery.

Travelers once searched phrases like “travel agent near me.” Now they can ask, “Who is the best travel advisor near me for a family cruise?” or “Which cruise works best for three generations traveling together?”

AI is being asked not just to find information but to understand intent and identify options that fit.

For travel businesses, that changes what digital visibility means. The question is no longer only, “Do I rank for the right keywords?” It’s also: Does the internet clearly understand who I am, what I specialize in and who I serve?

Before worrying about every new platform, start by making your business clear. Travel advisors should be able to answer three questions: Who are you? What do you specialize in? Who do you serve?

If you specialize in luxury European cruises, your digital presence should reinforce that expertise. If you serve families, groups or travelers in a specific market, that should be clear too.

Your website, Google Business Profile, blog and social media should all tell the same story. One of the first things I tell travel advisors is to maintain a Google Business Profile, but a profile alone isn’t enough. Your website and content should also clearly demonstrate your expertise.

The goal isn’t to create content for machines. It’s to become clearer to people and technology alike.

AI can help travelers compare destinations, organize information and narrow hundreds of possibilities into a manageable list.

But travel isn’t always a simple transaction. A family may be planning a major vacation, or someone may be traveling with an elderly parent who has mobility needs. Those situations require more than information. They require context, judgment and accountability.

That’s why I don’t see the future of AI in travel as a choice between technology and travel advisors. The stronger model is technology plus expertise.

AI can help advisors process information faster and reduce repetitive work, freeing them to spend more time applying judgment where it matters most.

If AI helps travelers understand their options, virtual reality can help them visualize those options.

Think about the difference between reading about a cruise ship cabin and virtually walking through it, or between looking at resort photos and exploring the property before booking.

I don’t think every traveler will plan a vacation through a VR headset. The broader opportunity is immersive visualization. Virtual tours, 3D environments and augmented experiences can help travelers better understand a ship, resort or destination before they buy.

For travel advisors, this becomes another consultation tool. Instead of simply telling clients what an experience looks like, advisors can increasingly help them see it.

Predictive analytics may not get the same attention as generative AI, but its impact could be just as important.

Travel companies generate enormous amounts of data. Predictive analytics can use those patterns to help anticipate what may happen next. For advisors, that could mean recognizing when a client may be ready to plan another vacation or identifying travelers who may be interested in a new itinerary.

Technology can surface the opportunity. The advisor still brings the context.

Travel advisors don’t need to become AI engineers, but they should focus on three things:

Establish a credible digital presence. Maintain an accurate Google Business Profile, and make sure your website clearly explains who you are and what you do.

Define what you want to be known for. Identify your specialties and the customers you most want to serve, then align your website, content and social presence around that.

Stay visible. Regularly publish useful content that demonstrates your expertise and keeps your business active online.

The goal isn’t to publish more content for its own sake. It’s to make your expertise easier to understand and easier to find.

Every major technology shift brings predictions about what will disappear. I think a better question for leaders is: What can this technology help people do better?

AI can process information at scale. Predictive analytics can identify patterns. Immersive technology can help travelers visualize experiences before they arrive.

But travel remains deeply personal. The future of travel technology shouldn’t be about removing the human element. It should be about giving the people who understand travelers better tools to serve them.

Technology has always shaped how we travel. What’s different now is how quickly it’s influencing nearly every stage of the experience.

Artificial intelligence is changing how travelers search for and evaluate their options. Virtual reality is helping people visualize destinations before they arrive. Predictive analytics is helping travel companies anticipate what customers may need before they ask.

As chief information officer of Cruise Planners, I spend a lot of time thinking about what these changes mean for travelers and advisors. The biggest opportunity isn’t removing people from the travel experience. It’s using technology to make them more informed, efficient and valuable.

#5468. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

#5467. Why Playing It Safe Is the Riskiest Marketing Decision You’ll Make

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Best practices are crowded on purpose. The upside sits with whoever moves before they’re proven safe. Here’s how you can be that person.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The safest-looking marketing plan in the room is usually the one most likely to keep you invisible. When you copy the channels, the messaging and the metrics that already work for the category leader, you compete on terms that favor whoever has the bigger budget and the longer head start. That feels like prudence. It is actually the slowest and most expensive way to stay a follower.

Safe feels responsible because failure is easy to defend when you followed the same plan as everyone else. Nobody gets second-guessed for matching the industry norm. That comfort is exactly the problem, because a plan built to avoid blame is not built to win, and the market rewards the brands willing to be wrong in public before they are proven right.

I learned this early. In 2013, I argued that mobile apps needed a strategy of their own rather than a shrunken version of web marketing, back when that sounded like a distraction. The people who moved before the consensus did not have better tools than everyone else. They simply refused to wait for permission and had already taken ownership of the space by the time the cautious crowd arrived.

Best practices earn their name because everyone already uses them. By the time a tactic is safe enough to carry that label, it is crowded and drained of any edge it once held. You can run it flawlessly and still finish exactly where you started, one more voice repeating the same message in the same place as your competitors.

The same trap shows up in how you measure success. Chasing the impressions, followers and engagement numbers every rival reports is the most crowded play in marketing, because those figures are easy to hit and easy to ignore. They make a quarter look healthy while the business underneath them sits still.

That ground is moving faster than the safe playbook admits. A Pew Research Center study of nearly 69,000 searches found that when an AI summary sits atop Google results, users click a traditional link in only 8% of visits, down from 15% when no summary appears. Ranking a page and waiting for the click is losing its footing, and most brands are still optimizing for rules that have already changed.

Bold does not mean reckless. What builds leaders is an asymmetric wager, where the downside is small and survivable, and the upside is owning territory no rival has claimed. You are not gambling the company. You are spending a measured slice of budget and attention on a shift you can already see forming, and planting yourself where it lands before the crowd arrives.

The highest-return version refuses to fight inside a crowded category at all. Instead of scrapping for a sliver of space the leader already defined, you reframe the problem so you become the obvious answer to a question nobody else is asking. Think of the companies that stopped selling a slightly better version of an existing product and instead named a new category they could own outright. They looked risky right up until they looked inevitable.

You can pressure-test the move in a single meeting. Ask what happens if it fails and whether the honest answer is a bruise or a catastrophe. Then ask what happens if it works and whether the payoff is a marginal gain or a foothold nobody can take from you. When failure is survivable and success is defining, hesitation becomes the expensive choice.

The clearest version of this decision sits in front of every marketer right now. AI systems are becoming the layer between your customer and the answer, and the brands that appear inside those answers are the ones deciding today to be there. Waiting until the behavior is undeniable means arriving after the winners are already chosen.

Winning that visibility depends less on budget than on being the clearest and most credible source on the questions you want to own. When an AI system builds an answer, it pulls from information it can trust and quote, so the work is making your expertise easy to find and hard to leave out. That legwork is fundamentals executed better than the competition, aimed at a channel most of your rivals are still ignoring.

In practice, that means publishing direct answers to the questions your customers actually ask, in language a machine can lift without guessing at your meaning. It means keeping your pages clean enough that the facts are easy to extract and quote. It means earning mentions on the outside sources these systems already trust, so when they build an answer, yours is the evidence within reach. That is unglamorous work, and it is exactly why most of your competitors will skip it until the advantage is gone.

Playing it safe shields you from the danger you can see and hands you the one you cannot, the slow erosion of being easy to overlook. The move that feels too bold today is often the only thing that keeps you relevant tomorrow. The real threat was never the leap. It was standing still while the ground moved.

The safest-looking marketing plan in the room is usually the one most likely to keep you invisible. When you copy the channels, the messaging and the metrics that already work for the category leader, you compete on terms that favor whoever has the bigger budget and the longer head start. That feels like prudence. It is actually the slowest and most expensive way to stay a follower.

Safe feels responsible because failure is easy to defend when you followed the same plan as everyone else. Nobody gets second-guessed for matching the industry norm. That comfort is exactly the problem, because a plan built to avoid blame is not built to win, and the market rewards the brands willing to be wrong in public before they are proven right.

I learned this early. In 2013, I argued that mobile apps needed a strategy of their own rather than a shrunken version of web marketing, back when that sounded like a distraction. The people who moved before the consensus did not have better tools than everyone else. They simply refused to wait for permission and had already taken ownership of the space by the time the cautious crowd arrived.

#5466. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

#5465. Cheap AI Output Can Still Be Expensive Work. Here’s How to Tell.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Most owners buy AI for speed and discover the checking cost later. A competent person can verify the output cheaply and still say no.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The first time I watched a machine draft something that looked finished, I almost signed off. The language was clean. The structure made sense. Then I tried to check three claims against the source material and burned more time reconstructing the case than the draft had saved. Speed had moved. The cost had not gone away. It had just changed rooms.

I remember the annoyance more than the draft. The tool had done its job. The review path had not.

Here’s my situation, so you know where I’m coming from. I founded Main & Machine, an AI implementation firm for small and mid-size businesses, and I also sit in the buyer seat when technology lands in a real operating company. (Disclosure for the editor: I have a financial relationship with Main & Machine.) I teach management and entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W.P. Carey School of Business. Across those chairs I keep seeing the same pattern: owners celebrate generation and underbuild verification.

Most shops treat “human in the loop” as a checkbox on a vendor slide. That move fails in practice. The economic value of generated output depends on how cheaply and reliably a competent person can verify it in the real decision. U.S. Census Bureau data from late 2025 through early 2026 put overall business AI use in the 17% to 20% range, with more firms still planning to join them. The next wave will not stall because models got worse. It will stall where checking stays slow, opaque or socially expensive.

I used to treat a second click as proof of judgment. Wrong. A second click can still leave you with one judgment if the reviewer never saw the underlying case on independent terms.

Before you automate a deliverable, write down who will check it, how long that check should take and what happens when the check fails. Generation reduces first-draft cost. Uncertain output creates a checking obligation. When verification is fast and error is reversible, the gain survives. When checking requires scarce expertise, reconstructing evidence or absorbing liability, the apparent speed just moves cost downstream.

The principle fits in one line: Cheap output with expensive verification is still expensive work.

Try the same pricing this week. Pick one workflow you want the machine to touch. Estimate minutes to generate and minutes to verify on a hard case. Skip the polished demo. A restaurant owner might let a tool draft the weekly schedule and still need a manager who can read labor rules and walk the floor. A clinic owner might let a tool summarize intake notes and still need a clinician who can open the raw chart. If the hard-case check cannot fit the day, the automation is not ready.

A reviewer cannot meaningfully check an automated recommendation when the system is also the only account of the underlying case. When evidence, framing and conclusion arrive through one interface, disagreement requires reconstructing information the reviewer never independently saw. Time pressure then makes rubber-stamping rational.

The principle: Review needs an independent path to the facts.

Build that path on purpose. For high-stakes work, keep a sampled set of raw inputs available beside the machine’s summary. Ask the reviewer to name the decisive evidence and the uncertainty before the recommendation appears, then compare reasons. A franchisee can do this on customer-complaint drafts. A contractor can do it on estimate language. A professional-services owner can do it on client memos. Agreement alone proves little. Shared framing can produce shared error. What matters is whether disagreement can change the action and survive in the record.

An override that exists only as a policy or a button is not a reliable safeguard. Automation reduces exposure to normal system dynamics, while the ugly cases compress time and raise uncertainty. People need practice recognizing, deciding and acting without the automated system when the answer feels wrong.

The principle: Practice the no until it is usable.

Run a short drill this month. Take three recent outputs the team almost shipped. Hide the machine’s confidence language. Ask a named owner to reject one of them with a written reason and an alternate next step. Then watch whether the rejection sticks or gets smoothed over because the draft sounded finished. Automation leaves a harder residue: The exceptions that remain are ambiguous, rare and consequential. If your team only ever sees clean demos, they will not keep the skill they need when the residue shows up on a Tuesday afternoon.

Here’s where I’d start this week: Pick one AI-assisted workflow, write the review minutes and the independent evidence route on a single page, and run one override drill with the person who actually owns the outcome. Say it to the team before you expand the tool’s reach.

The draft that looked finished still sits in my mind. The checking cost was the real product. Build that first, and the machine earns its keep.

The first time I watched a machine draft something that looked finished, I almost signed off. The language was clean. The structure made sense. Then I tried to check three claims against the source material and burned more time reconstructing the case than the draft had saved. Speed had moved. The cost had not gone away. It had just changed rooms.

I remember the annoyance more than the draft. The tool had done its job. The review path had not.

Here’s my situation, so you know where I’m coming from. I founded Main & Machine, an AI implementation firm for small and mid-size businesses, and I also sit in the buyer seat when technology lands in a real operating company. (Disclosure for the editor: I have a financial relationship with Main & Machine.) I teach management and entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W.P. Carey School of Business. Across those chairs I keep seeing the same pattern: owners celebrate generation and underbuild verification.

— Two former Amazon executives who helped build Discovery’s direct-to-consumer operation in Bellevue, Wash., are stepping down from their leadership roles following the company’s acquisition by Paramount Skydance. They will remain in advisory roles during the transition.

Avi Saxena joined Discovery in 2019 as chief technology officer of its direct-to-consumer business and led its new Bellevue office. He became CTO of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) following Discovery’s 2022 merger with AT&T’s WarnerMedia business. Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of WBD on Oct. 6, with the combined company taking the name Skydance Corporation.

Before joining Discovery, Saxena was with Amazon for 19 years over two stints, most recently as vice president of technology for Amazon Marketplace. He also held leadership roles at Microsoft and internet infrastructure startups.

Tyler Whitworth is stepping down as executive vice president and chief product officer for WBD’s streaming business. He led teams working on digital products for HBO Max, discovery+, Eurosport, TNT Sports, Food Network and others. Before joining Discovery, he spent more than seven years at Amazon, leading teams developing products and services for customers and third-party sellers.

Dane Glasgow, Skydance’s chief product officer, announced the departures of Whitworth, Saxena and WBD Chief Information Officer Dave Duvall in a memo shared with GeekWire.

“Much of the strength of WBD’s product and technology organizations reflects their leadership and dedication. Please join me in thanking them and wishing them the very best,” Glasgow wrote.

The company has not responded to GeekWire’s inquiries about the future of the Bellevue office.

— Bahadir Onalan is returning to Microsoft as a vice president in its CoreAI organization, focused on responsible AI, after nearly 10 years at Amazon. Onalan first joined Microsoft in 2005 and worked on Azure teams focused on search, analytics, business intelligence and security. He left in 2017 as a principal software group engineering manager to join Amazon, where he worked on machine learning initiatives.

“This second tenure feels like a true homecoming,” Onalan wrote. “Our goal goes beyond shipping a platform or a product; we are here to define the global standards for AI safety.”

— Naria Santa Lucia is leaving Microsoft after seven years, most recently as a general manager with Microsoft Elevate. She previously served as executive director of the Washington State Opportunity Scholarship.

“I’ll carry the lessons I learned from my time at Microsoft as I continue my personal and professional mission to serve people and communities by teaching, advising nonprofits and mission driven organizations, and spreading joy and human connection,” Santa Lucia wrote.

She did not announce a specific next role.

— VertueLab, a Pacific Northwest nonprofit supporting climate tech entrepreneurs, has named Leo Ochoa executive director, promoting him from managing director for Oregon. He succeeds Aina Abiodun, who is transitioning to chair of the organization’s board after more than three years as executive director.

“Leo brings a unique blend of vision, relationships, and entrepreneurship experience,” the organization said, noting his background as a wildland firefighter, startup founder and patent holder for wearable safety gear.

Abiodun’s accomplishments include co-creating the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub, launching the Opalene Climate Challenge and helping lead the Just Future Climate Labs initiative.

— Seattle’s Pulse Space has appointed Leah Sardone as vice president of engineering. The startup is developing laser-based systems to deliver power and enable long-distance communications in low Earth orbit and beyond. In July, the company announced a $40 million U.S. Space Force contract to advance its laser-based space power technology.

Sardone brings more than 23 years of experience in hardware, sensors and embedded systems development. #5463. Arbitrum DAO Votes Thursday on L1 Governance Fail-Safe and Glamsterdam Tuning

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Headline coverage surrounding Arbitrum DAO’s active snapshot voting cycle centers on a high-profile proposal to drive adoption of the Global Dollar Network's USDG stablecoin using 100 million ARB in incentives.

However, four additional temperature check votes close concurrently on Thursday, October 22, 2026.

Chief among these voting initiatives is a constitutional Improvement Proposal (AIP) designed to resolve an existential operational vulnerability: establishing an on-chain fallback mechanism if Arbitrum’s Layer-2 governance machinery stalls or fails completely.

Proposed on the Arbitrum Governance Forum, the L1 Voting Recovery System serves as a constitutional fail-safe for protocol administration.

Under standard operations, Arbitrum DAO executes proposals natively on Layer 2. However, if L2 transaction execution freezes, L2 proposal creation contracts break, or cross-chain message passing experiences systemic disruption, the DAO's governance capacity becomes locked. While the Security Council holds emergency multi-sig powers to intervene during acute protocol crises, it operates as an operational guardian rather than a permanent administrative engine.

The proposed L1 Voting Recovery System constructs a parallel, emergency governance path deployed directly on Ethereum Layer 1. In the event that L2 governance becomes unresponsive or inaccessible, delegates can initiate, vote on, queue, and execute Arbitrum DAO proposals directly on L1 base-layer smart contracts.

By establishing this base-layer fallback, the DAO decouples its long-term administrative survival from L2 sequencer uptime or L2 smart contract execution state. The emergency path preserves the Security Council's authority without forcing the protocol to rely indefinitely on multi-sig intervention during prolonged L2 governance disruptions.

If delegates reject the L1 Voting Recovery System, Arbitrum DAO leaves its governance architecture exposed to single-point-of-failure risks.

Without an operational L1 recovery track, any software defect, state progression freeze, or prolonged outage impacting L2 governance contracts would paralyze the DAO. The community would possess no constitutional or technical mechanism to submit on-chain votes, reconfigure network parameters, or deploy treasury reserves until L2 functionality was manually restored, forcing total dependence on emergency Security Council multi-sig powers.

Alongside the constitutional governance recovery mechanism, three additional temperature checks complete their voting window on Thursday:

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

#5461. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 6:01 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

#5459. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:17 pm

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

#5457. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

Databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and New Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

Aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. The company has raised $25 million to date. TechCrunch has more here.

John Donahoe, the current president and CEO of ServiceNow, is taking over as the CEO and president of Nike in January, replacing Mark Parker who has been since 2006 and lived through numerous controversies over the years. #5456. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

#5455. Jupiter's Q3 Staking Rewards For All Wallets Opens Today, See Who Clears the 50 JUP Bar

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

50 JUP sounds like a threshold almost anyone can meet. It isn't, and today is when many stakers will find that out.

Jupiter's Active Staking Rewards (ASR) for July to September 2026 are now open to every wallet. That means a 50 million JUP pool can be claimed by anyone who qualified. The problem is that "qualified" doesn't mean what most people think. The rule isn't "have 50 JUP staked." It's "average 50 JUP across the whole quarter." Running the numbers this morning and a lot of wallets that look eligible at a glance aren't.

The round started quietly. According to the official Q3 campaign page, the campaign ran from July 1 until earning closed on September 30, and claims opened on October 12. That first week was reserved for Jupiter's own apps. Early access was limited to Jupiter Wallet and the Jupiter Mobile app, and other wallets can claim from 20 October 2026.

So if you stake from Phantom, Solflare, Backpack or a hardware wallet, today is your first real opportunity. Jupiter's documentation explains why the wallet matters. Rewards are linked to the wallet you staked from. If that wallet lives in another app, you either wait for the general opening or import the same recovery phrase into Jupiter Wallet or Jupiter Mobile.

There's no rush to the finish line yet. Reports put the claim deadline at January 12, 2027. Still, I wouldn't leave it to the holidays.

The campaign page states the rules plainly. 50M JUP will be distributed to stakers this period, ASR is calculated on a time-weighted average of your stake, and an average of 50 JUP or more staked during the quarter qualifies.

The words that matter are "time-weighted average." A wallet that held 50 JUP for all 92 days of Q3 averages exactly 50. A wallet that held 500 JUP for only a few days might average less than that. Jupiter designed it this way on purpose. The 7-day unstaking cooldown stops users from staking briefly around distribution periods to collect rewards without sustained participation.

One more detail surprised me, given the program's name. Voting has no effect on ASR, and you do not need to vote to be eligible. The "Active" in Active Staking Rewards now refers to keeping tokens staked, not to governance turnout.

Here's the simple math. It assumes the average is weighted day by day across the 92 days from July 1 to September 30. Jupiter hasn't published its exact snapshot schedule, so treat these figures as close estimates, not guarantees.

The edge cases are where people get caught. Suppose a wallet held 60 JUP from July 1 but started unstaking at the end of August. Its average comes to only about 40 JUP, so it misses. Another wallet held 40 JUP all quarter and added 30 more on September 1. It ends up at roughly 49.8 JUP, just under the line. Adding 31 instead of 30 would have qualified it.

The simplest check is to connect your wallet at Jupiter Rewards. The page will show the amount of ASR you're eligible to claim. If it shows nothing for an older address, the time-weighting is the most likely reason.

Now for the payout. As of mid-October 2026, total staked JUP topped 1.1 billion tokens, roughly 33% of circulating supply, spread across more than 357,000 wallets.

If you divide 50 million JUP by about 1.1 billion staked, you get roughly 4.5% for the quarter. A wallet that just clears the 50 JUP average would receive about 2.3 JUP. An average of 1,000 JUP works out to about 45, and 10,000 to around 455. The quarter's average total stake may have been a bit below the October figure, so actual allocations could come in slightly higher. Your campaign page shows the real number.

Don't expect the tokens to show up as spendable JUP. ASR is paid in JUP and added to your staked balance, which increases your governance power over time.

Three problems come up again and again in Jupiter's support notes:

Squads multisig users have a more manual process. The ASR documentation covers it in detail, including checking that the claim uses the Jupiter Merkle Distributor program, DiS3nNjFVMieMgmiQFm6wgJL7nevk4NrhXKLbtEH1Z2R before you approve anything.

Missing the deadline has real consequences. According to the Jupiter DAO portal, unclaimed ASR goes back to the community treasury once the claim period ends. Jupiter also says that no transfer is made on your behalf after the support deadline.

The bigger picture is a pool that's getting more crowded. Every quarter, 50M JUP goes to eligible stakers, and that figure doesn't change. With staked JUP now above 1.1 billion, each new staker gets a smaller slice of the same pie.

ASR is also the main reward Jupiter is still paying out. The Jupiter DAO voted in February 2026 to postpone Jupuary and send its 700 million JUP back to a community multisig. That leaves this quarterly distribution as the core reason to keep JUP staked.

My advice is to claim this round now and then look ahead. The October to December period is already more than halfway through. The same math applies, and each week you wait raises how much JUP you need to reach a 50 JUP average.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

#5453. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5452. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 3:14 pm

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

#5450. October 25, 2019

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.]

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a new book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

And he was making everybody so much money. And the company was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

#5449. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.
